title: Preface
content:
Preface Every definition of analysis is a sentence about sets and functions. Logic and Proof supplied the grammar of such sentences: the connectives, the quantifiers, and the prose that carries their rules. This volume supplies the nouns, and above all the two that every other one is made of: sets and functions. Around them it builds the natural numbers and induction, the sizes of infinite sets and their arithmetic, relations and orders, and the ways a function is built from others. Who it is for. The reader we have in mind has worked through Logic and Proof, or has its habits from elsewhere: reading a statement with its quantifiers in place, proving a “for every” by taking an arbitrary element, naming a witness before using it. The chapters point back to Logic and Proof where they use one of its rules, so a reader who is unsure of a step can look it up. What it covers. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Chapter What it does ----------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 1 Proofs from definitions: sets and functions. Proofs straight from definitions (direct proof, cases, counterexamples) on even, odd, divides and prime; sets and the working rules that say which sets exist, Russell’s paradox, families of sets, products and relations, functions and their inverses, images and preimages, each section with its method of proof 2 The arithmetic of 
N and 
Z from induction, well-ordering, induction as a craft, definition by recursion, contrapositive and contradiction, infinitely many primes, equinumerous and finite sets and the pigeonhole principle 3 Countable sets, the axiom of choice, diagonal arguments and Cantor’s theorem, the Schröder–Bernstein theorem, infinite sets; cardinal arithmetic: sums, products and powers of sizes, \card{
R} = \card{\powerset{
N}}, 
R^2 and 
N^{
N} as large as 
R (Section 3.6) 4 Relations: properties of relations decided one at a time, equivalence relations and partitions, the integers modulo n, well-definedness, partial orders, maximal and greatest elements, least upper bounds 5 Building functions: restriction, extension and gluing, indicator functions; fibers and the factorization of every function through a quotient; binary operations and their identities and inverses; permutations, iteration, orbits and cycles 6 Zorn’s lemma, stated without proof, and the maximality template: the axiom of choice from Zorn’s lemma, any two sets are comparable in size, every partial order extends to a total order -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The real numbers are used throughout as familiar objects, with their school arithmetic and order, and every use of a school fact is named where it occurs. Analysis on the Real Line turns those facts into consequences of axioms, and Number Systems: From 
N to 
R builds the numbers out of sets. How to read it. Read the chapters in order: each uses the ones before it. Every section has Quick checks with folded answers; answer each one before you unfold it. When a section uses a method of proof for the first time, it sets the method out in a box marked Method, with a template, when to use it and the usual failure; later sections cite the box instead of explaining the method again, and each chapter’s opening page lists its boxes under Named moves. The exercises of a section come in three groups, A to check understanding, B for practice and C to go deeper, and the last section of each chapter adds R items that reach back to earlier chapters. A chapter’s opening page lists what it needs, with links, and the time it takes: about 160 hours for the whole volume on the core track, and about 225 hours for everything.

title: Proofs from Definitions: Sets and Functions
content:
Proofs from Definitions: Sets and Functions Every definition of analysis is a sentence about sets and functions. “The supremum of A is the least element of the set of upper bounds of A.” “A function is continuous if the preimage of every open set is open.” Logic and Proof, Chapters 1 to 8 supplied the grammar of such sentences: the connectives, the quantifiers, and the prose that carries their rules. This chapter supplies the nouns: sets and subsets, unions and intersections of whole families of sets, ordered pairs and products, relations, functions, inverses, images and preimages. It is also where proofs start being about mathematics rather than about logic: each section teaches one method of proof on the material it introduces, starting in Section 1.1 with statements about integers proved straight from their definitions. And it is where the logic of the first eight chapters becomes visible inside mathematics. Inclusion is a “for every” around an “implies”, a union is an “or”, the union of a family is a “there exists”, and a function is a “for every there exists exactly one”. The laws of sets are the laws of logic, read through membership, and the chapter uses this from its second section to its last. Two surprises drive the chapter. The first is that the naive rule “any property defines a set” is contradictory (Russell’s paradox), so we must say which sets exist, and every set in this book is cut out of a set already given. The second is the chapter’s motivating problem. For f(x) = x^2, is f(A \cap B) = f(A) \cap f(B)? Is f^{-1}(C \cap D) = f^{-1}(C) \cap f^{-1}(D)? Why is the second always true and the first not? The answer is a single quantifier: membership in an image hides a “there exists”, and membership in a preimage hides nothing. Preimages therefore respect every set operation, and images only unions. This asymmetry is why analysis defines continuity by preimages. What you need. Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–8. From Logic and Proof, Chapters 1 and 2: the rules for the connectives and the derived laws used as rules, above all distributivity (@fd1:prp-distributivity), De Morgan’s laws (@fd1:prp-de-morgan), an iff as two implications (@fd1:prp-iff-two-implications), the contrapositive (@fd1:prp-contrapositive), vacuous implication (@fd1:prp-vacuous-implication), and derived rules (@fd1:def-derived-rule). From Logic and Proof, Chapter 4: induction (@fd1:ax-induction), the standard equivalences (@fd1:prp-standard-equivalences) and completeness (@fd1:thm-completeness). From Logic and Proof, Chapters 5 and 6: the rules for “for every” and “there exists”, bounded quantifiers (@fd1:def-bounded-quantifier) and their rules (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-rules), the rules for equality (@fd1:def-rules-equality), unique existence (@fd1:def-unique-existence, @fd1:prp-unique-existence-use), and the laws for negating quantifiers. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 8: plain-prose proofs, the convention on which steps may be silent, and the catalogue of what is not allowed (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue). The number sets 
N, 
Z, 
Q, 
R are used as familiar sets, with their school arithmetic and order. Time. About 40 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 55 hours for everything. Roadmap - Proofs from definitions. Even, odd, divides and prime; a direct proof unwinds a definition and rewinds another; proofs by cases and without loss of generality; refuting a claim by one counterexample; a puzzle about lattice points that the book finishes in Chapter 2. - Sets, subsets and Russell’s paradox. What a set is allowed to be, equality by elements, the subset relation and the element-chasing proofs that establish it, equality by two inclusions, describing sets by a property cut out of an ambient set, the empty set, and why no set contains every set. - Unions, intersections, complements and families. The set operations as the connectives read through membership, laws of sets proved by a chain of equivalences, the algebra of sets as propositional logic, power sets, unions and intersections of arbitrary families, and De Morgan’s laws for families, including the empty one. - Ordered pairs, products and relations. An object that remembers order, proofs of existence and uniqueness, the product A 	imes B and how it interacts with the set operations, and relations as sets of pairs. - Functions, composition, injections and surjections. A function as a graph with a declared target, when two functions are equal, composition, and the two questions of injectivity and surjectivity, each with its method of proof (the second solved backwards and proved forwards), with the squaring map as three different functions. - Left, right and two-sided inverses. Proofs that construct an object and then verify it: a left inverse exists exactly for injective maps (on a nonempty domain), a right inverse forces surjectivity, bijections are the maps with a two-sided inverse, and the question whether every surjection has a right inverse, which needs a new principle. - Images and preimages. What a function does to sets, why preimages respect every operation and images only unions, where injectivity and surjectivity repair the failures, how to hunt for a counterexample, and sets of numbers such as -A and A + B as images. Named moves The first ten are method boxes; each section that introduces one cites it from then on. - Direct proof from a definition (@exm-method-direct-proof). Unwind the hypothesis into its definition, naming each witness; say what the goal demands; close the gap by computation; write it forwards. (Section 1.1) - Proof by cases (@exm-method-cases). Split on a disjunction you already have, such as even or odd, and reach the same goal in every case; “without loss of generality” when the cases are symmetric. (Section 1.1) - Disproof by counterexample, proof by example (@exm-method-counterexample). One instance refutes a “for every”; one witness proves a “there exists”. (Section 1.1) - Element-chasing (@exm-method-element-chasing). To prove A \subseteq B: “let x \in A”, unwind the definition of A, and rewind into the definition of B. (Section 1.2) - Two inclusions (@exm-method-double-inclusion). To prove A = B: prove A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A. (Section 1.2) - A chain of equivalences (@exm-method-chain-of-iff). For L = R: x \in L \iff \dots \iff x \in R, each step a definition or a named law of logic. (Section 1.3) - Existence and uniqueness (@exm-method-uniqueness). Produce one object, then show that any two are equal. (Section 1.4) - Proving injectivity (@exm-method-injectivity). From f(x_1) = f(x_2), derive x_1 = x_2. (Section 1.5) - Proving surjectivity (@exm-method-surjectivity). Solve f(x) = y backwards on scrap paper; prove forwards: “let y \in Y; put x \coloneqq \dots”, and check. (Section 1.5) - Construct and verify (@exm-method-construct-and-verify). Find where the object’s values are forced and where they are free, define it, check it is the kind of object claimed, then verify the property. (Section 1.6) - Unwind the image. “y \in f(A)” means “there is a \in A with f(a) = y”: name the witness before using it. A preimage has no witness to name. (Section 1.7) - Refute with a small witness. The method of @exm-method-counterexample for statements about sets and functions: a two- or three-element set, the map x \mapsto x^2, the empty set. Threads - The lattice points. Section 1.1 asks why, among any five points with integer coordinates, two have a midpoint with integer coordinates, and states the principle the answer needs without using it. Section 2.5 proves the pigeonhole principle and comes back to the five points. - The five strings. Section 1.5 plants a game: given five strings of five symbols 0 or 1, write one not on the list. Section 3.3 comes back to it with the diagonal argument. - Russell to Cantor. Russell’s theorem in Section 1.2 is the first contradiction about sets: a set built to disagree with each candidate on the candidate itself. Cantor’s theorem in Section 3.3 is the same shape of argument, as a theorem rather than a paradox. - Same size. The bijections of Section 1.6 are how the book says that two sets have the same size; Section 2.5 makes this a definition, and Section 4.2 meets it again as an example of an equivalence-like relation. Summary Statements about integers were proved from the definitions of even, odd and divides: divisibility is transitive (@prp-divides-transitive), and every integer is even or odd and not both (@thm-even-or-odd), the first proof by cases of the volume. Sets are equal when they have the same elements (@def-set-equality), inclusion is proved by element-chasing, and no set contains every set (@thm-russell). The laws of sets are the laws of propositional logic (@thm-set-algebra), and De Morgan’s laws hold for families of any size (@thm-de-morgan-families). A function has a left inverse exactly when it is injective, on a nonempty domain (@thm-left-inverse-iff-injective); a right inverse forces surjectivity (@prp-right-inverse-surjective); the bijections are exactly the maps with a two-sided inverse (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse). Preimages respect every set operation (@thm-preimage-operations), images respect unions (@thm-image-union), and injectivity repairs intersections (@thm-image-intersection). What is open: does every surjection have a right inverse? Nothing proved so far builds one without a rule, and Chapter 3 adds the principle that does. Before that, Chapter 2 turns to the natural numbers, induction and finite sets, and finishes the lattice-point puzzle. Terms - bijective: injective and surjective (@def-bijective). - Cartesian product: A 	imes B, the set of pairs (a, b) with a \in A, b \in B (@def-cartesian-product). - complement of A in X: X \setminus A, for A \subseteq X (@def-set-operations). - composite: g \circ f, “g after f” (@def-composition). - difference: A \setminus B, the elements of A not in B (@def-set-operations). - disjoint: A \cap B = \emptyset (@def-set-operations). - divides: a \mid b if b = ka for some k \in 
Z (@def-divides). - empty set: a set with no elements (@def-empty-set). - equality of sets: the same elements (@def-set-equality). - even, odd: n = 2k, n = 2k + 1, for some k \in 
Z (@def-parity). - function: a graph with exactly one value at each input, and a declared codomain (@def-function). - image: f(A), the values of f at points of A (@def-image). - indexed family: a set A_i for each i \in I (@def-indexed-family). - injective: different inputs, different outputs (@def-injective). - intersection: A \cap B; of a family,  igcap_{i \in I} A_i (@def-set-operations, @def-family-union-intersection). - inverse, two-sided: a left and a right inverse at once, written f^{-1} (@def-inverse-function). - left inverse, right inverse: g \circ f = \id_X; f \circ g = \id_Y (@def-left-right-inverse). - ordered pair: (a, b) = (c, d) exactly when a = c and b = d (@def-ordered-pair). - power set: the set of all subsets (@def-power-set). - preimage: f^{-1}(B), the inputs whose values lie in B (@def-preimage). - prime: an integer p \ge 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p (@def-prime). - relation: a subset of A 	imes B (@def-relation). - specification: \{ x \in A : P(x) \}, a set cut out of a given set (@def-set-builder). - subset: A \subseteq B, every element of A is in B (@def-subset). - surjective: every element of the codomain is a value (@def-surjective). - union: A \cup B; of a family,  igcup_{i \in I} A_i (@def-set-operations, @def-family-union-intersection).

title: 1.1 Proofs from Definitions
content:
Proofs from Definitions Logic and Proof taught the rules of proof and how to write them as prose. From here on the statements are about mathematical objects, and every word in them that matters has a definition. A proof begins by writing the hypotheses out by their definitions, writes out what the conclusion demands, and closes the gap between them. This section practices that on the integers, where the definitions are one line long and every claim can be tested by hand. It teaches five moves: direct proof, proof by cases, without loss of generality, disproof by counterexample, and proof of existence by an example. A puzzle about lattice points A lattice point is a point (a, b) of the plane whose coordinates a and b are both integers, as in school geometry: the corners of the squares on squared paper. The midpoint of (a, b) and (c, d) is \Bigl(  rac{a + c}{2},  rac{b + d}{2} \Bigr), and it may or may not be a lattice point. The points (0, 0) and (2, 4) have midpoint (1, 2), a lattice point; the points (0, 0) and (1, 4) have midpoint (	frac12, 2), which is not. That raises two questions. - (Q1) Among any five lattice points, must there be two whose midpoint is a lattice point? - (Q2) Among any four lattice points, must there be two whose midpoint is a lattice point? Before reading on, place a few sets of points on squared paper and compute their midpoints. Both answers come from two words this section defines, even and odd. Question (Q2) is settled in this section. Question (Q1) needs, besides parity, a principle about finite collections that sounds too obvious to need proof; we will state it but not yet prove it. Definitions first The first two words are the ones the puzzle needs. [Even and Odd] An integer n is even if n = 2k for some k \in 
Z, and odd if n = 2k + 1 for some k \in 
Z. Logic and Proof used these words informally, and wrote “n is even” as \exists k\, (n = 2k) in its derivations (for instance @fd1:exm-sum-of-evens); from now on they mean exactly this, a “there exists”. Evenness is divisibility by 2, so the next word generalizes it. One might define “a divides b” as “b/a is an integer”. That works for 3 and 12, but it says nothing when a = 0, since 0/0 and 5/0 are undefined; yet 0 = 0 \cdot 0 suggests that 0 should divide 0. The definition avoids division altogether and asks for a multiplier. [Divisibility] Let a, b \in 
Z. We say that a divides b, written a \mid b, if there exists k \in 
Z with b = ka. Then a is a divisor of b, and b is a multiple of a. Decide, from the definitions alone: (a) Is 0 even? (b) Does -4 divide 6? Does 0 divide 5? (c) Is -7 odd? (d) Does 12 divide 3? (a) Yes: 0 = 2 \cdot 0, with k = 0 \in 
Z. (b) No. If 6 = k \cdot (-4) with k \in 
Z, then k \le -2 gives -4k \ge 8 and k \ge -1 gives -4k \le 4, so -4k 
e 6 in either case. And no: k \cdot 0 = 0 
e 5 for every k. (c) Yes: -7 = 2 \cdot (-4) + 1, with k = -4 \in 
Z. (d) No. If 3 = 12k with k \in 
Z, then k \ge 1 gives 12k \ge 12 and k \le 0 gives 12k \le 0. So 3 \mid 12, with k = 4, and -3 \mid 12, with k = -4. Every integer a divides 0, with k = 0; this is the degenerate case, and it shows that “a \mid b” is a statement, not the number b/a: 0 \mid 0 is true, while 0/0 is not defined. Also 1 \mid b and b \mid b for every integer b, and “n is even” is “2 \mid n”. We write a 
mid b when a does not divide b. The last definition singles out the integers with as few divisors as possible. [Prime Number] An integer p is prime if p \ge 2 and the only positive divisors of p are 1 and p. A prime factor of an integer n is a prime p with p \mid n. So 2, 3, 5 and 7 are prime (for 7: a positive divisor of 7 is at most 7, and none of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 divides it); 9 = 3 \cdot 3 and 15 = 3 \cdot 5 are not, and neither is 1, which fails the clause p \ge 2. Direct proof The first claim to prove from these definitions is that divisibility passes along a chain. [Divisibility Is Transitive] For all integers a, b, c, if a \mid b and b \mid c, then a \mid c. [Scratch work] Unwind every defined word. The hypotheses a \mid b and b \mid c are two “there exists” statements, so each hands us a multiplier. Give them different names, k and l: nothing says the two multipliers agree, and one name for both is the error (N4) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, met in @fd1:exm-sum-of-evens. The goal a \mid c is also a “there exists”: we must produce an integer m with c = ma. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ----------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------- a \mid b, b \mid c a \mid c b = ka, c = lb, with k, l \in 
Z c = ma for some m \in 
Z: find m b = ka, c = lb c = l(ka) = (lk)a: try m = lk, and check that lk \in 
Z ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The last row closes the gap. The proof writes this forwards: the witness m is named, then checked. Let a, b, c \in 
Z with a \mid b and b \mid c. By @def-divides there are k, l \in 
Z with b = ka and c = lb. Then c = l(ka) = (lk)a, and lk \in 
Z, as a product of integers. So a \mid c, with witness lk, by @def-divides. The proof used only the definition of divisibility and integer arithmetic, and it read the definition in both directions: once to unwind the hypotheses, once to rewind the conclusion. [Method: direct proof from a definition] Template. To prove “if P, then Q”: (1) assume P and write it out by its definition, giving each witness a new name; (2) write out what Q demands, for example which object must be produced; (3) close the gap by computation, on scrap paper if need be; (4) write the proof forwards: assume, unwind, compute, and rewind into the definition of Q, naming the witness and checking that it is of the required kind. When to use it. The hypotheses and the conclusion are defined notions, and the gap between them is computation. The usual failure. Stopping at the computation, as in “c = (lk)a, done”, without checking that lk \in 
Z, which is the clause the definition demands. Also one name for two witnesses (N4), and using what is to be proved (N9). [Divisors of a combination] Let a, b, c \in 
Z with a \mid b and a \mid c. Show that a \mid bx + cy for all x, y \in 
Z. By the method of @exm-method-direct-proof: unwind both hypotheses with two names, then look for a multiplier of a in bx + cy. Let x, y \in 
Z. By @def-divides there are k, l \in 
Z with b = ka and c = la. Then bx + cy = kax + lay = (kx + ly)a, and kx + ly \in 
Z, since sums and products of integers are integers. So a \mid bx + cy, with witness kx + ly. Three special cases are used constantly. With x = y = 1, a \mid b + c; with x = 1 and y = -1, a \mid b - c; with y = 0, a \mid bx. With a = 2 and x = y = 1, the first case is “even plus even is even”, the claim derived in @fd1:exm-sum-of-evens. The proof of @prp-divides-transitive named two witnesses, k and l. Find integers a, b, c with a \mid b and b \mid c for which one name could not serve for both. Take a = 1, b = 2, c = 6. Then b = 2a and c = 3b, and no single k has both 2 = k \cdot 1 and 6 = k \cdot 2: the first forces k = 2, the second k = 3. Writing one name would claim that the two multipliers are equal, which is (N4). Proof by cases Some claims depend on what kind of integer we have. The first such fact is the one behind every parity argument. [Every Integer Is Even or Odd] Every integer is even or odd, and no integer is both. [Scratch work] Start on 
N, where induction is available (@fd1:ax-induction), with P(n): “n is even or n is odd”. The base P(0) is 0 = 2 \cdot 0. The step needs P(n + 1) from P(n). But P(n) is an “or”, and knowing that n is even or odd does not tell us which. So split into the two cases, as ulename{\vee E} does (@fd1:def-rules-disjunction). Each case is a new given, and each must reach the same goal. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ----------------------------------- ----------------------------------- P(n): n even or n odd n + 1 even or n + 1 odd Case 1: n = 2k n + 1 = 2k + 1: odd Case 2: n = 2k + 1 n + 1 = 2(k + 1): even ----------------------------------------------------------------------- The negative integers come next, by cases again: for n < 0, -n \in 
N is already known to be even or odd, and the sign can be moved inside. Finally “not both” is a negation: assume n = 2a and n = 2b + 1, and aim for a contradiction (ulename{
eg I}). The two equations give 2(a - b) = 1, and no integer doubles to 1. Every natural number is even or odd. We argue by induction on n. For n = 0, 0 = 2 \cdot 0 is even. Let n \in 
N be even or odd. Case 1: n = 2k with k \in 
Z. Then n + 1 = 2k + 1 is odd. Case 2: n = 2k + 1 with k \in 
Z. Then n + 1 = 2(k + 1), with k + 1 \in 
Z, is even. In either case n + 1 is even or odd. By @fd1:ax-induction, every n \in 
N is even or odd. Every integer is even or odd. Let n \in 
Z. If n \ge 0, then n \in 
N, and we are done. If n < 0, then -n \in 
N is even or odd. If -n = 2k, then n = 2(-k) is even. If -n = 2k + 1, then n = -2k - 1 = 2(-k - 1) + 1 is odd. No integer is both. Suppose n = 2a and n = 2b + 1 with a, b \in 
Z. Then 2(a - b) = 1, with c \coloneqq a - b \in 
Z. If c \ge 1, then 2c \ge 2; if c \le 0, then 2c \le 0. Either way 2c 
e 1, a contradiction. So no integer is both even and odd (ulename{
eg I}). A fact Logic and Proof took from school is now proved from the definitions. The proof has four case splits, each into cases that together cover everything. [Method: proof by cases] Template. Find a disjunction you already have, such as “n is even or n is odd” (@thm-even-or-odd), “x \ge 0 or x < 0”, or excluded middle (@fd1:prp-excluded-middle). Write one paragraph per case, labeled Case 1., Case 2.. In each, add the case to the givens, unwind it, and reach the same goal. When to use it. The definitions or the algebra behave differently on different kinds of input, so the givens give no grip until you know which kind you have. The usual failure. Cases that do not cover every possibility (N8), or a case forgotten (N7). Before splitting, say why the cases are exhaustive. [A proof by cases] Show that n^3 + 5n is even for every integer n. A general n gives no grip, but 2k and 2k + 1 can be expanded, and by @thm-even-or-odd these two cases cover 
Z. So use @exm-method-cases, and in each case pull out a factor 2. Let n \in 
Z. By @thm-even-or-odd, n is even or odd. Case 1: n = 2k with k \in 
Z. Then n^3 + 5n = 8k^3 + 10k = 2(4k^3 + 5k). Case 2: n = 2k + 1 with k \in 
Z. Then n^3 = 8k^3 + 12k^2 + 6k + 1 and 5n = 10k + 5, so n^3 + 5n = 8k^3 + 12k^2 + 16k + 6 = 2(4k^3 + 6k^2 + 8k + 3). In each case the bracket is an integer, so n^3 + 5n is even by @def-parity. Why does the proof of @exm-cubes-plus-five-n need no third case? By @thm-even-or-odd every integer is even or odd, so the two cases already cover every n \in 
Z. Without loss of generality When two cases are mirror images, a proof writes one and says that the other is “the same with the roles exchanged”. Logic and Proof, Section 8.2 read the phrase “without loss of generality” as a ulename{\vee E} whose second box is the first with the letters swapped, and it is licensed only when the statement and the hypotheses are unchanged by the swap (@fd1:exm-rhetoric-induction (b)). [The parity of a sum] Let m, n \in 
Z. (a) If m and n have the same parity (both even or both odd), then m + n is even. (b) If they have opposite parity (one even and the other odd), then m + n is odd. (a) Case 1: both even. Then 2 \mid m + n by @exm-divides-combination with a = 2, x = y = 1. Case 2: both odd, say m = 2k + 1 and n = 2l + 1 with k, l \in 
Z. Then m + n = 2(k + l + 1), with k + l + 1 \in 
Z. In both cases m + n is even. (b) The statement is symmetric in m and n: m + n = n + m, and “opposite parity” does not change when the two are exchanged. So, without loss of generality, m is even and n is odd, say m = 2k and n = 2l + 1 with k, l \in 
Z. Then m + n = 2(k + l) + 1 is odd. The case m odd and n even is the same with m and n exchanged. Check the symmetry first. “Without loss of generality m \le n” is legitimate for a claim about m + n, and not for a claim about m - 2n: exchanging m and n changes that claim. Before writing the phrase, exchange the letters in the statement and in the hypotheses, and check that nothing changes. Counterexamples and examples A universal claim, “for every x, if P(x) then Q(x)”, is refuted by one x with P(x) true and Q(x) false. That is the negation laws at work (@fd1:prp-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication): 
eg  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) is equivalent to \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge 
eg Q(x)), and an existential is proved by one example (ulename{\exists I}). [A pattern that breaks] Is 2p + 1 prime for every prime p? For p = 2, 3, 5 we get 5, 7, 11, all prime. At p = 7 the pattern breaks: 7 is prime, and 2 \cdot 7 + 1 = 15 = 3 \cdot 5 has the positive divisor 3 
otin \{1, 15\}, so 15 is not prime (@def-prime). The claim is false, and p = 7 is a counterexample. The three successes proved nothing, since verifying instances never gives a “for all” (N1); one failure settles the question. A counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis. The choice p = 4 makes 2p + 1 = 9, which is not prime; but 4 is not prime either, so p = 4 says nothing about the claim. A counterexample to “if P(x), then Q(x)” needs P(x) true and Q(x) false, and both are checked on the page. [Two divisors, one product] Prove or disprove: for all integers a, b, c, if a \mid c and b \mid c, then ab \mid c. [Scratch work] Try small a and b. For a = 2, b = 3, the c with 2 \mid c and 3 \mid c are 0, \pm 6, \pm 12, \dots, and 6 divides each of them: no counterexample there. The pair a = 2, b = 5 resists too. What made those work? The two divisors had nothing in common, so c had to contain both separately. Try a and b sharing a factor, as small as possible: a = b = 2, and then c = 2. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal --------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------ (none: we are looking for an example) integers a, b, c with a \mid c, b \mid c, ab 
mid c a = b = 2, c = 2 2 \mid 2 (twice), and 4 
mid 2 2 = 1 \cdot 2 4 
mid 2: no k \in 
Z with 2 = 4k ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- False. Take a = b = c = 2. Then 2 = 1 \cdot 2, so a \mid c and b \mid c. But ab = 4, and 4 
mid 2: if 2 = 4k with k \in 
Z, then k \ge 1 gives 4k \ge 4 and k \le 0 gives 4k \le 0, so 4k 
e 2. The search failed while a and b had no common factor greater than 1, and that is no accident: for coprime a and b the statement is true, a fact Number Systems, Chapter 3 proves. [Method: disproof by counterexample, proof by example] Template. To refute “for every x, if P(x) then Q(x)”: name one x, check P(x), and check that Q(x) fails. To prove “there is an x with P(x)”: name one x and check P(x). When to use it. The claim survives a few tries, yet you doubt it; or the statement is existential. Search small and extreme cases first: 0, 1, negative numbers, the smallest sets. The usual failure. A “counterexample” that does not satisfy the hypothesis; refuting a different claim from the one stated; and the mirror error, concluding “for every” from examples (N1). One example refutes a universal claim, and no number of examples proves one. An existence claim, proved by one example: there is an integer n > 1 with n \mid 2^n + 1, namely n = 3, since 2^3 + 1 = 9 = 3 \cdot 3. Is p = 2 a counterexample to the claim of @exm-refute-2p-plus-1? Is p = 11? No and no. For p = 2, 2p + 1 = 5 is prime; for p = 11, 2p + 1 = 23 is prime. In each case the conclusion holds. Back to the lattice points (Q2) is false. Take the four corners of a unit square, (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1). Their six midpoints are (0, 	frac12), \quad (	frac12, 0), \quad (	frac12, 	frac12), \quad (	frac12, 	frac12), \quad (	frac12, 1), \quad (1, 	frac12), and none is a lattice point. A counterexample to a universal claim is also an existence proof by example: there are four lattice points no two of which have a lattice point as midpoint. The parity pattern of a lattice point (a, b) is the pair of words (parity of a, parity of b): even–even, even–odd, odd–even or odd–odd. By @thm-even-or-odd every integer is even or odd and not both, so every lattice point has exactly one of the four patterns. The four corners above have one pattern each, and that is why they fail. [Same pattern, lattice midpoint] Show that if two lattice points have the same parity pattern, then their midpoint is a lattice point. Let (a, b) and (c, d) have the same parity pattern. Then a and c have the same parity, so a + c is even by @exm-parity-of-sums (a): a + c = 2s with s \in 
Z, and (a + c)/2 = s \in 
Z. Likewise b and d have the same parity, so (b + d)/2 \in 
Z. Hence the midpoint is a lattice point. Which pattern does (-3, 8) have? Find a second point with the same pattern, and their midpoint. Odd–even: -3 = 2 \cdot (-2) + 1 and 8 = 2 \cdot 4. For example (1, 0), with midpoint (-1, 4). (Q1), almost. Among five lattice points, each point has one of only four patterns, so two of the points must share a pattern, and then @exm-lattice-midpoint finishes. The step “five objects in four boxes put two in one box” is the pigeonhole principle. It is stated here, not proved, and so the answer to (Q1) is “yes, once the principle is proved”. The four corners show that five cannot be lowered to four. [Looking ahead] Section 2.5 proves the pigeonhole principle, from a precise definition of “finite”, and comes back to these five points. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write out “6 \mid n” and “n is odd” by their definitions, each as a “there exists”. 2. True or false, with reasons: -1 is odd; 7 \mid 0; 0 \mid 7; 1 is prime. 3. What must a counterexample to “every multiple of 4 is a multiple of 8” satisfy? Give one. 4. In the proof of @thm-even-or-odd, name the four case splits and say why each is exhaustive. (a) 6 \mid n: there exists k \in 
Z with n = 6k (@def-divides). n is odd: there exists k \in 
Z with n = 2k + 1 (@def-parity). (b) True: -1 = 2 \cdot (-1) + 1. True: 0 = 0 \cdot 7. False: k \cdot 0 = 0 
e 7 for every k \in 
Z. False: 1 < 2, so 1 fails the clause p \ge 2 of @def-prime. (c) It must be a multiple of 4 that is not a multiple of 8. For example 4 = 1 \cdot 4; and 4 = 8k has no integer solution, since k \ge 1 gives 8k \ge 8 and k \le 0 gives 8k \le 0. (d) First, even or odd in the induction step: this is the induction hypothesis itself, a disjunction already derived. Second, n \ge 0 or n < 0: every integer is one or the other, by the order of 
Z. Third, -n even or -n odd, for n < 0: the first half of the proof, applied to -n \in 
N. Fourth, c \ge 1 or c \le 0: no integer lies strictly between 0 and 1. B. Practice [B1: Direct proofs] Prove, for all integers a, b, c, d: 1. if a \mid b, then a^2 \mid b^2; 2. if a \mid b and c \mid d, then ac \mid bd. (a) Let a \mid b. By @def-divides, b = ka with k \in 
Z. Then b^2 = k^2 a^2, and k^2 \in 
Z, so a^2 \mid b^2. (b) Let a \mid b and c \mid d. By @def-divides, b = ka and d = lc with k, l \in 
Z, two different names since nothing says the multipliers agree. Then bd = (ka)(lc) = (kl)(ac), and kl \in 
Z, so ac \mid bd. [B2: Two cases] Prove that for every integer n, either 4 \mid n^2 or 4 \mid n^2 - 1. Let n \in 
Z. By @thm-even-or-odd, n is even or odd. Case 1: n = 2k with k \in 
Z. Then n^2 = 4k^2, so 4 \mid n^2. Case 2: n = 2k + 1 with k \in 
Z. Then n^2 - 1 = 4k^2 + 4k = 4(k^2 + k), with k^2 + k \in 
Z, so 4 \mid n^2 - 1. In either case one of the two divisibilities holds. [B3: Name the move, then complete it] Here is the frame of a proof that if m, n \in 
Z have opposite parity, then m^2 + n^2 is odd. The statement is unchanged when m and n are exchanged, so we may assume … \vdots … Hence m^2 + n^2 is odd. Name the move, then complete it. The move is without loss of generality: the statement and the hypothesis are symmetric in m and n, so we may assume that m is even and n is odd, say m = 2k and n = 2l + 1 with k, l \in 
Z. Then m^2 + n^2 = 4k^2 + 4l^2 + 4l + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2l^2 + 2l) + 1, with 2k^2 + 2l^2 + 2l \in 
Z. Hence m^2 + n^2 is odd. The case m odd and n even is the same with m and n exchanged. [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement and refute each false one with a counterexample. 1. For all integers a, b, c: if a \mid b + c and a \mid b, then a \mid c. 2. For all integers a, b, c: if a \mid b + c, then a \mid b or a \mid c. 3. For every integer n, n^4 + n^2 + 1 is odd. 4. The sum of any three odd integers is even. 5. There is an integer n > 5 with n \mid n + 6. 6. For all integers m, n: if mn is even, then m and n are both even. (a) True. Let a \mid b + c and a \mid b: b + c = ka and b = la with k, l \in 
Z. Then c = (b + c) - b = (k - l)a, with k - l \in 
Z, so a \mid c. (b) False. Take a = 2, b = c = 1. Then b + c = 2 = 1 \cdot 2, so a \mid b + c. But 2 
mid 1: 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 is odd, hence not even (@thm-even-or-odd), and the same holds for c = 1. (c) True. By @thm-even-or-odd, n is even or odd. Case 1: n = 2k. Then n^4 + n^2 + 1 = 16k^4 + 4k^2 + 1 = 2(8k^4 + 2k^2) + 1. Case 2: n = 2k + 1. Then n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2j + 1 with j \coloneqq 2k^2 + 2k \in 
Z, so n^4 + n^2 = n^2(n^2 + 1) = (2j + 1)(2j + 2) = 2(2j + 1)(j + 1), and n^4 + n^2 + 1 = 2(2j + 1)(j + 1) + 1. In both cases the bracket (8k^4 + 2k^2, respectively (2j + 1)(j + 1)) is an integer, so n^4 + n^2 + 1 is odd by @def-parity. (d) False. Take 1, 1, 1: their sum 3 = 2 \cdot 1 + 1 is odd, hence not even (@thm-even-or-odd). (e) True. Take n = 6: n + 6 = 12 = 2 \cdot 6, so 6 \mid 12. (f) False. Take m = 2, n = 1. Then mn = 2 = 2 \cdot 1 is even, but n = 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 is odd, hence not even (@thm-even-or-odd). C. Going deeper [C1: Three cases] 1. By the method of @thm-even-or-odd, show that every integer has the form 3k, 3k + 1 or 3k + 2 for some k \in 
Z, and that no integer has two of these forms. 2. Deduce that for every integer n, n^2 has the form 3k (exactly when 3 \mid n) or the form 3k + 1. 3. Prove that for all integers a, b: if 3 \mid a^2 + b^2, then 3 \mid a and 3 \mid b. [Hint 1] For (c), use (b) on a and on b, and look at the cases. [Hint 2] First line: “Suppose 3 \mid a^2 + b^2, and suppose 3 
mid a.” (a) Every natural number has one of the forms, by induction on n. For n = 0, 0 = 3 \cdot 0. In the step, n = 3k gives n + 1 = 3k + 1; n = 3k + 1 gives n + 1 = 3k + 2; n = 3k + 2 gives n + 1 = 3(k + 1). So every n \in 
N has one of the forms (@fd1:ax-induction). Every integer. For n < 0, write -n \in 
N in one of the forms; then -3k = 3(-k), -(3k + 1) = 3(-k - 1) + 2 and -(3k + 2) = 3(-k - 1) + 1. No two forms. Suppose 3a + r = 3b + s with a, b \in 
Z and 0 \le r < s \le 2. Then 3(a - b) = s - r \in \{1, 2\}. With c \coloneqq a - b \in 
Z, c \ge 1 gives 3c \ge 3 and c \le 0 gives 3c \le 0, so 3c 
otin \{1, 2\}, a contradiction (ulename{
eg I}). (b) By (a), n has one of the three forms. If n = 3k, then n^2 = 3(3k^2). If n = 3k + 1, then n^2 = 9k^2 + 6k + 1 = 3(3k^2 + 2k) + 1. If n = 3k + 2, then n^2 = 9k^2 + 12k + 4 = 3(3k^2 + 4k + 1) + 1. So n^2 has the form 3k in the first case and 3k + 1 in the other two. Since no integer has two forms, n^2 has the form 3k exactly in the first case, that is, exactly when 3 \mid n. (c) Suppose 3 \mid a^2 + b^2, and suppose 3 
mid a. By (b), a^2 = 3j + 1 with j \in 
Z. Case 1: 3 \mid b. Then b^2 = 3l by (b), and a^2 + b^2 = 3(j + l) + 1. Case 2: 3 
mid b. Then b^2 = 3l + 1 by (b), and a^2 + b^2 = 3(j + l) + 2. In both cases a^2 + b^2 has a form other than 3k; but 3 \mid a^2 + b^2 says it has the form 3k, against the “no two forms” half of (a). This contradiction refutes 3 
mid a, so 3 \mid a (by ulename{RAA}, or by excluded middle on 3 \mid a, with the case 3 
mid a closed by ulename{ ot E}). The statement and the hypothesis are unchanged when a and b are exchanged, so the same argument gives 3 \mid b. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) existence on 
N by induction, with the three step cases. - 1: (a) the negative integers. - 1: (a) uniqueness of the form, by the bound on 3c. - 1: (b) the three cases computed. - 1: (b) “exactly when” derived from uniqueness, not only from the computation. - 2: (c) the case split complete (cases on b under 3 
mid a, or all four cases on a and b), each giving the right form. - 1: (c) the contradiction named as one with the uniqueness in (a). - 1: (c) both conclusions 3 \mid a and 3 \mid b obtained (by licensed symmetry, or by the full case split). Fatal errors (0 for the step): treating 3 
mid a as “a = 3k + 1” only, forgetting 3k + 2 (N7); concluding 3 \mid a from 3 \mid a^2 without (b). [C2: Find the error] Claim: if n \in 
Z and n^2 is odd, then n is odd. “Proof”: Let n be odd, n = 2k + 1. Then n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1 is odd. 1. Is the conclusion true? 2. Does the argument prove it? Name the failing line. 3. Give a counterexample to the illegal step itself. 4. Write a correct proof. The conclusion is true: it is one half of @fd1:thm-odd-iff-square-odd. The argument does not prove it. Its first line assumes the conclusion, “n is odd”, and its last line reaches the hypothesis, so it proves the converse, “if n is odd, then n^2 is odd”: entry (N5) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. The ulename{{	o}I} box must open with “n^2 is odd”. The step “from Q 	o P, conclude P 	o Q” is illegal, and one instance shows it: “if n > 0, then n^2 > 0” is true, but the converse “if n^2 > 0, then n > 0” is false at n = -1. A correct proof, by cases on n (@thm-even-or-odd). Let n \in 
Z with n^2 odd. Case 1: n = 2k. Then n^2 = 2(2k^2) is even, hence not odd (@thm-even-or-odd), against the hypothesis; so this case cannot occur (ulename{ ot E}). Case 2: n = 2k + 1. Then n is odd, as claimed. So n is odd. Marking scheme. (6 points) - 1: (a) the conclusion is true, with the citation. - 2: (b) the error named as proving the converse (N5), pointing at the first line. - 1: (c) a false instance of the pattern “Q 	o P, hence P 	o Q”. - 2: (d) a correct proof, using @thm-even-or-odd (cases on the parity of n with the even case shown impossible, or the contrapositive). Fatal errors (0 for the step): calling the conclusion false; “fixing” the proof by assuming n odd again. [C3: Lattice points in space] A lattice point of space is a point (a, b, c) with a, b, c \in 
Z. 1. Give eight lattice points of space no two of which have a lattice point as midpoint. 2. Show that two lattice points of space with the same three parities have a lattice point as midpoint. 3. Which principle, stated in this section and not yet proved, would show that among any nine lattice points of space two have a lattice point as midpoint? (a) The eight points whose coordinates all lie in \{0, 1\}. Two different such points differ in some coordinate, where one has 0 and the other 1; the sum there is 1, and 1/2 
otin 
Z, so the midpoint is not a lattice point. (b) As in @exm-lattice-midpoint, coordinate by coordinate: in each coordinate the two entries have the same parity, so their sum is even by @exm-parity-of-sums (a), and half of it is an integer. (c) The pigeonhole principle. Each coordinate is even or odd, so there are 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 2^3 = 8 parity patterns; nine points in eight patterns put two points in one pattern, and (b) finishes.

title: 1.2 Sets, Subsets and Russell's Paradox
content:
Sets, Subsets and Russell’s Paradox Section 1.1 proved statements about integers straight from their definitions. Analysis needs the same for collections, and it talks about collections all the time: the set of upper bounds of a set of numbers, the set of points where a function is positive, the set of all formulas. This section says what a set is allowed to be, what it means for one set to lie inside another, and how sets are described. One new notion carries the weight, the subset; the rest is the vocabulary it needs. We begin with the simplest possible idea of a set, and we will see it fail. A naive idea, and what goes wrong with it In everyday speech a collection is given by a property. “The students in this room”, “the even numbers”, “the prime numbers below 100”: in each case we say what an object must satisfy, and the collection is everything that satisfies it. The naive rule is: For every property, there is a set whose elements are exactly the objects having that property. It sounds harmless, and for the properties of everyday mathematics it gives the right answer. But a property may talk about sets themselves, and then the rule can be turned against itself. A set may be an element of another set: the set \{ 
N, 
Z \} has two elements, and each of them is a set. So it makes sense to ask of a set x whether x \in x, and the property “x 
otin x” is a property like any other. Most sets we know have it: the set of even numbers is not an even number, so it is not an element of itself. Apply the naive rule to this property. It promises a set R = 	ext{the set of all } x 	ext{ with } x 
otin x . Now ask whether R \in R. By the way R was made, an object belongs to R exactly when it is not an element of itself; applied to the object R, this says R \in R exactly when R 
otin R. A statement that is equivalent to its own negation leads to a contradiction by the rules of Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 alone; lines 4–11 of the derivation after Russell’s theorem, at the end of this section, carry out exactly this argument, with an extra conjunct carried along. So the naive rule is contradictory: it cannot be part of mathematics. This is Russell’s paradox. We hold it until the end of the section, where it becomes a theorem, Russell’s theorem, about the sets that do exist. First we set out what does work. Sets and membership We do not define “set” or “element”. They are the primitive notions of this chapter, in the way that “statement” was primitive in Logic and Proof, Chapter 1: we say how they are used, not what they are made of. A set is a collection of objects, its elements, and we write x \in A for “x is an element of A”, or “x belongs to A”, or “x lies in A”. Its negation is written x 
otin A. The objects may be numbers, or sets, or (later in this chapter) pairs and functions. In the language of Logic and Proof, Chapter 5, “\in” is a two-place predicate: x \in A is a statement about the two objects x and A, true or false like x < y. So everything Logic and Proof, Chapter 5 says about predicates, quantifiers, and their rules applies to it unchanged. A statement such as “every element of A is positive” is  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x > 0), which the bounded notation of @fd1:def-bounded-quantifier shortens to  orall x \in A\ (x > 0). Two conventions fix what kind of objects we deal with. First, the number sets 
N, 
Z, 
Q, and 
R are given: we use them as familiar sets, with their school arithmetic and order, as Logic and Proof and Section 1.1 did. (Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 turns the facts we use about 
R into consequences of axioms.) Second, numbers are not sets: a number has no elements, and no number is equal to a set. So 1 
e \{1\}, and z \in 5 is false for every z. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 1, 2 and 5 explain how numbers can be built out of sets; nothing in this volume depends on how that is done. The single most important fact about sets is that a set is determined by its elements. It has no other features: no order in which the elements come, no count of how often each is listed, no color. Two sets with the same elements are the same set. [Equality of Sets] Sets A and B are equal, A = B, if and only if they have the same elements:  orall x\, (x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B). In words: every element of A is an element of B, and every element of B is an element of A. This principle is called extensionality: a set is fixed by its extension, the things it contains, and not by the words used to describe it. The sign = here is not new: it is the equality of @fd1:def-rules-equality, “names of the same object”. The direction from A = B to the same elements is ulename{{=}E}, with \varphi the formula x \in z and z the variable replaced (and symmetry, @fd1:prp-equality-symmetric-transitive, for the way back from B to A). The converse direction is the principle just stated, that a set has no features beyond its elements; it is what lets an equation proved from “same elements” be used with ulename{{=}E} like any other. The principle is an “if and only if”, so it is used in both directions: to prove A = B, prove the  orall statement; from A = B, conclude x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B for any x we like. Sets with finitely many elements can be written by listing their elements between braces: \{1, 2, 3\} is the set whose elements are 1, 2, and 3, and nothing else. Extensionality has two immediate consequences for such lists. - Repetition does not matter. \{1, 1, 2\} = \{1, 2\}. An object x belongs to the left side exactly when x = 1 or x = 1 or x = 2, and to the right side exactly when x = 1 or x = 2; the two conditions are equivalent, since “x = 1 or x = 1” says no more than “x = 1”. - Order does not matter. \{1, 2\} = \{2, 1\}. Here the two conditions are “x = 1 or x = 2” and “x = 2 or x = 1”, which are equivalent because \vee commutes (@fd1:exm-disjunction-first-derivations). Order and repetition are exactly what a list has and a set does not. When order matters we will need a different object, the ordered pair of Section 1.4. A set with one element, \{a\}, is a singleton. A singleton and its element are different things: \{1\} is a set, and 1 is a number, so 1 
e \{1\} by our convention. For sets the difference is just as real. The set \{
N\} has exactly one element, namely 
N, while 
N has infinitely many; so they differ, by extensionality, as 2 \in 
N and 2 
otin \{
N\}. Are the sets \{1, 2, 2, 3\}, \{3, 2, 1\}, and \{1, \{2\}, 3\} equal? The first two are equal: each has exactly the elements 1, 2, 3, and repetition and order do not count. The third is different: its elements are 1, \{2\}, and 3. The number 2 lies in the first set, but not in the third, since 2 
e 1, 2 
e 3, and 2 
e \{2\} (a number is not a set). So by @def-set-equality the third set differs from the other two. Subsets Most statements about sets in analysis are not equalities but inclusions: every Cauchy sequence converges, every continuous function on [a, b] is bounded, every upper bound of a set is at least its supremum. Each has the shape “everything of this kind is also of that kind”. Before a definition, look at one such statement in the language of sets. The multiples of 6 and the multiples of 3 form sets S = \{ \dots, -12, -6, 0, 6, 12, \dots \}, \qquad T = \{ \dots, -6, -3, 0, 3, 6, \dots \}, and every element of S is an element of T, because 6k = 3 \cdot (2k). The sets are not equal (3 \in T but 3 
otin S), yet one sits inside the other. This relation between sets deserves a name. A set is a subset of another if everything in the first is also in the second. [Subset] Let A and B be sets. A is a subset of B, written A \subseteq B, if every element of A is an element of B:  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x \in B). We also say that A is contained in B, or that B contains A. If A \subseteq B and A 
e B, then A is a proper subset of B, written A \subsetneq B. In words, clause by clause. The quantifier  orall x ranges over every object whatsoever, not over the elements of A only; the implication x \in A 	o x \in B restricts attention to the elements of A, and says nothing about objects outside A. With the bounded notation of @fd1:def-bounded-quantifier, the same condition is  orall x \in A\ (x \in B): “for every x in A, x is in B”. The symbol \subseteq allows equality, as \le does for numbers; the symbol \subsetneq excludes it, as < does. This book never writes \subset, which some books use for \subseteq and others for \subsetneq. The definition is a  orall around an 	o, and its rules are the rules of those two symbols. To prove A \subseteq B, we prove the  orall statement: by the rule ulename{ orall I} of Logic and Proof, Chapter 5 we open a box for an arbitrary x (in prose, “let x be arbitrary”), and inside it we prove x \in A 	o x \in B by ulename{{	o}I} (@fd1:def-rules-implication): assume x \in A and reach x \in B. The two openings are always written together, as “let x \in A”. To use A \subseteq B, we apply ulename{ orall E} (Logic and Proof, Chapter 5) at the element we care about, and then ulename{{	o}E}: from A \subseteq B and a \in A, conclude a \in B. This gives the first named move about sets. We call this move element-chasing: [Method: element-chasing] Template. Begin “Let x \in A.” Unwind the definition of A to see what is known about x. Rewind the definition of B to see what must be shown, and reach it. End “Hence x \in B; since x was arbitrary, A \subseteq B.” When to use it. The goal is an inclusion A \subseteq B, or any statement of the shape  orall x\, (x \in A 	o \dots). The usual failure. Checking some elements of A and stopping, entry (N1) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue (the second warning below shows it). Starting from x \in B instead, which proves the converse inclusion, entry (N5). Choosing a particular x, such as x = 0, where an arbitrary one is needed. Write the first and the last sentence of an element-chasing proof that \{ n \in 
Z : 4 \mid n \} \subseteq \{ n \in 
Z : 2 \mid n \}. Then fill in the middle. First: “Let n \in 
Z with 4 \mid n.” Last: “Since n was arbitrary, the inclusion holds.” Middle: by @def-divides, n = 4k for some k \in 
Z. Then n = 2(2k) with 2k \in 
Z, so 2 \mid n. (Or cite @prp-divides-transitive with 2 \mid 4.) Here is the move three times: two ordinary inclusions, then the degenerate one. In each, the first sentence is the pair of openings, ulename{ orall I} and ulename{{	o}I}, and the rest reaches x \in B. [Three inclusions] 1. Show that [1, 2] \subseteq [0, 3]. 2. Let S be the set of integer multiples of 6 and T the set of integer multiples of 3, as above. Show that S \subseteq T. By @def-divides, S consists of the integers x with 6 \mid x, and T of those with 3 \mid x. 3. Let A be any set. Show that A \subseteq A. (a) Let x \in [1, 2]. Then 1 \le x \le 2, by the meaning of the interval. Hence 0 \le 1 \le x and x \le 2 \le 3, so 0 \le x \le 3, that is, x \in [0, 3]. Since x was arbitrary, [1, 2] \subseteq [0, 3]. (b) Let x \in S, that is, let x be an integer with 6 \mid x.
