N starts at 0. The witness -1 lies in the first set and not in the second (-1 
otin 
N). [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement, by two inclusions where it is an equality, and refute each false one with a concrete counterexample. 1. \{ n \in 
Z : n = 2k + 1 	ext{ for some } k \in 
Z \} = \{ n \in 
Z : n = 2k - 1 	ext{ for some } k \in 
Z \}. 2. \{ n \in 
Z : 2 \mid n 	ext{ and } 4 \mid n \} = \{ n \in 
Z : 8 \mid n \}. 3. \{ x \in 
R : x^3 = x \} = \{-1, 0, 1\}. 4. For all sets A, B, C: if A \subseteq B and B 
ot\subseteq C, then A 
ot\subseteq C. 5. For all sets A, B, C: if A \subseteq B, B \subseteq C and C \subseteq A, then A = C. (a) True. (\subseteq) Let n = 2k + 1 with k \in 
Z. Then n = 2(k + 1) - 1, and k + 1 \in 
Z, so n lies in the right set. (\supseteq) Let n = 2k - 1 with k \in 
Z. Then n = 2(k - 1) + 1, and k - 1 \in 
Z, so n lies in the left set. Each direction re-indexes the witness; both sets are the odd integers. (b) False. The integer 4 lies in the left set, since 4 = 2 \cdot 2 and 4 = 4 \cdot 1. It does not lie in the right set: 4 = 8k has no integer solution k, because k \ge 1 gives 8k \ge 8 and k \le 0 gives 8k \le 0. (The left set is the set of multiples of 4.) (c) True. For real x, x^3 - x = x(x - 1)(x + 1). (\subseteq) If x^3 = x, this product is 0, so one factor is 0, and x \in \{0, 1, -1\}. (\supseteq) 0^3 = 0, 1^3 = 1 and (-1)^3 = -1. (d) False. Take A = C = \emptyset and B = \{1\}. Then A \subseteq B, and B 
ot\subseteq C with the witness 1; but A \subseteq C, since \emptyset \subseteq \emptyset. (e) True. From A \subseteq B and B \subseteq C, @prp-subset-transitive gives A \subseteq C. Together with the hypothesis C \subseteq A, @prp-subset-antisymmetric gives A = C. C. Going deeper [C1: Every set has something outside it] Let A be a set, and let R_A = \{ x \in A : x 
otin x \} as in @thm-russell. 1. Let A^{+} be the set whose elements are the elements of A together with the object R_A (it exists by (W2) and (W3)). Show that A \subsetneq A^{+}. 2. Deduce from @thm-russell that no set A has the property “every subset of A is an element of A”. [Hint 1] In (a), a proper inclusion needs two things: the inclusion, and a witness in the larger set that is not in the smaller one. The theorem supplies the witness. In (b), look for a subset of A that the theorem says is not an element of A. [Hint 2] For (b): suppose, for ulename{
eg I}, that every subset of A is an element of A. First show that R_A \subseteq A. (a) First, A \subseteq A^{+}: an element of A is an element of A^{+} by the description of A^{+}. Second, A^{+} 
e A: the object R_A lies in A^{+}, and R_A 
otin A by @thm-russell. So R_A is a witness, and A \subsetneq A^{+}. (b) Suppose, for ulename{
eg I}, that A is a set such that every subset of A is an element of A. The set R_A is a subset of A: if y \in R_A, then y \in A (and y 
otin y) by @def-set-builder. So by the assumption, R_A \in A, which contradicts @thm-russell. Hence no set has the property. Part (a) says that no set is “as large as possible”: there is always a set with one more element. Part (b) rules out a set containing all of its own subsets; for instance, no set A has as its elements exactly the subsets of A. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) proves the inclusion A \subseteq A^{+} from the description of A^{+}. - 3: (a) names R_A as the witness to A^{+} 
e A, citing @thm-russell for R_A 
otin A. - 3: (b) proves R_A \subseteq A by element-chasing through @def-set-builder. - 2: (b) combines the assumption with R_A \subseteq A to get R_A \in A, and cites the theorem for the contradiction. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using “the set of all sets” or any set-builder without an ambient set; taking A^{+} 
e A as obvious “because an element was added” (if R_A were already in A, nothing would have been added). [C2: Antisymmetry for sets of sets] Can there be sets A and B, whose elements are themselves sets, such that A \subseteq B, B \subseteq A, and A 
e B? Explain why the answer does not depend on what the elements of A and B are. No. By @prp-subset-antisymmetric, A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A give A = B, for all sets A and B. The answer does not depend on the elements, because nothing in the proof of @prp-subset-antisymmetric looks at them. The proof works with the statements x \in A and x \in B for an arbitrary object x, and uses only @def-subset, @def-set-equality, and the propositional law @fd1:prp-iff-two-implications applied to those two statements. Whether x is a number, a set, or a set of sets never enters. For example, with A = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\} and B = \{\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset\}, the two inclusions hold and indeed A = B. The point of the question is a habit: an element-chasing proof treats its element as a black box, and so it proves the statement for sets of anything at all.

title: 1.3 Unions, Intersections, Complements and Families
content:
Unions, Intersections, Complements and Families Section 1.2 said what sets are, when two of them are equal, and when one lies inside another. It gave us ways to describe a single set, by listing or by a property cut out of an ambient set. This section makes new sets from old ones. Each connective of Logic and Proof, Chapter 1 gives a set operation: “or” gives the union, “and” gives the intersection, “and not” gives the difference. That observation is the thesis of the chapter: the laws of sets are the laws of logic, read through membership. We state it, prove the standard laws of set algebra from it, and then take the step analysis needs constantly, from two sets to a whole family of them, where “or” becomes “there exists” and “and” becomes “for all”. Union, intersection and difference Here is the standard example of a new set. Let A be the set of integers divisible by 2 and B the set of integers divisible by 3. Three natural questions about an integer x are: is it divisible by 2 or by 3? by 2 and by 3? by 2 and not by 3? Each question collects integers into a set, and each set is built from A and B by one connective applied to the statements x \in A and x \in B. The pattern does not depend on divisibility at all, so we name the three constructions once, for any sets. The union collects what lies in either set, the intersection what lies in both, the difference what lies in the first and not the second. [Union, Intersection, Difference] Let A and B be sets. 1. The union A \cup B is the set whose elements are exactly the objects lying in A or in B: x \in A \cup B \iff (x \in A \vee x \in B). 2. The intersection A \cap B is the set \{ x \in A : x \in B \}: so x \in A \cap B \iff (x \in A \wedge x \in B). 3. The difference A \setminus B is the set \{ x \in A : x 
otin B \}: so x \in A \setminus B \iff (x \in A \wedge x 
otin B). Sets A and B are disjoint if A \cap B = \emptyset. If A \subseteq X, the difference X \setminus A is called the complement of A in X. In words, clause by clause. The union exists by the working rule (W3) of Section 1.2; it is not cut out of an ambient set, since its elements come from two sets at once. The intersection and the difference are cut out of an ambient set, namely A, so they exist by specification (W1), and the description \{ x \in A : \dots \} names its ambient set as Section 1.2 requires. The “or” of the union is inclusive, as \vee always is: an object in both sets is in the union. “Disjoint” means “no common element”. The complement is always written X \setminus A, with the ambient set X named. Many books write A^c and leave X to the reader, and a reader who guesses X wrongly gets a different set: the complement of [0, 1] in [0, 2] is (1, 2], and in 
R it is (-\infty, 0) \cup (1, \infty). There is no “complement of A” on its own: by Russell’s theorem (@thm-russell) there is no set of everything outside A (such a set, joined with A, would contain every set). So this book never writes A^c. Examples, simplest first, each checked against the membership conditions. - Finite sets. For A = \{1, 2, 3\} and B = \{2, 4\}: A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}, A \cap B = \{2\}, A \setminus B = \{1, 3\}, B \setminus A = \{4\}. For instance 3 \in A \setminus B because 3 \in A and 3 
otin B; and 4 
otin A \setminus B because 4 
otin A. - Intervals. For A = [0, 2] and B = [1, 3]: A \cup B = [0, 3], A \cap B = [1, 2], A \setminus B = [0, 1). The last one shows how an endpoint behaves: 1 \in B, so 1 
otin A \setminus B, while every x with 0 \le x < 1 lies in A and not in B. - Divisibility. With A and B the multiples of 2 and of 3 in 
Z, as in the opening, A \cap B is the set of multiples of 6 (this uses the school fact that an integer divisible by 2 and by 3 is divisible by 6), and 
Z \setminus A is the set of odd integers, the complement of A in 
Z. - Degenerate cases. For every set A: A \cup \emptyset = A, A \cap \emptyset = \emptyset, A \setminus \emptyset = A, and A \setminus A = \emptyset. Each is one line: for example, x \in A \setminus A would mean x \in A and x 
otin A, which is impossible, so A \setminus A has no element. They matter because \emptyset behaves for \cup as 0 does for +, and for \cap as 0 does for 	imes. Three inclusions hold for all sets and are used without comment from now on: A \cap B \subseteq A \subseteq A \cup B, \qquad A \setminus B \subseteq A . Each is one element-chase that drops or adds a disjunct or a conjunct: if x \in A \cap B, then x \in A (ulename{\wedge E}); if x \in A, then x \in A \cup B (ulename{\vee I}); if x \in A \setminus B, then x \in A (ulename{\wedge E}). A nonexample by minimal change: the “difference” of two sets is not “everything in one but not in both”. The set \{ x \in A \cup B : 	ext{not both } x \in A 	ext{ and } x \in B \} is a different set: for A = \{1, 2, 3\} and B = \{2, 4\} it is \{1, 3, 4\}, while A \setminus B = \{1, 3\}. The element 4 is in the first and not in A \setminus B, because the difference keeps only elements of A. The difference is not symmetric. In general A \setminus B 
e B \setminus A. With A = \{1\} and B = \{2\}, A \setminus B = \{1\} and B \setminus A = \{2\}, and the witness 1 lies in the first and not the second. In fact A \setminus B and B \setminus A are always disjoint, since an element of both would lie in A and not in A; they are equal only when both are empty, that is, when A = B. Let X = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}, A = \{1, 2, 3\}, and B = \{2, 4, 6\}. Compute A \cup B, A \cap B, X \setminus (A \cup B), and (X \setminus A) \cap (X \setminus B). A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 6\} and A \cap B = \{2\}. Then X \setminus (A \cup B) = \{5\}. Also X \setminus A = \{4, 5, 6\} and X \setminus B = \{1, 3, 5\}, whose intersection is \{5\}. The last two answers agree. This is the two-set case of De Morgan’s law for sets, which is proved for arbitrary families later in this section. Laws of sets are laws of logic Unwinding the three definitions turns every question about \cup, \cap, and \setminus into a question about \vee, \wedge, and 
eg. Here is the dictionary, with the notions of Section 1.2 included. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- On sets Unwound through membership Logic ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------- ------------------------------- x \in A \cup B x \in A \vee x \in B \vee x \in A \cap B x \in A \wedge x \in B \wedge x \in A \setminus B x \in A \wedge 
eg(x \in B) \wedge and 
eg A = \emptyset  orall x\, 
eg(x \in A) 
eg under  orall A \subseteq B  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x \in B) 	o under  orall A = B  orall x\, (x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B) \leftrightarrow under  orall ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The dictionary makes an idea precise. Fix an object x and write p, q, r for the statements x \in A, x \in B, x \in C. Then membership of x in any set built from A, B, C by \cup, \cap, \setminus is a propositional formula in p, q, r: for instance, x \in A \cap (B \cup C) \iff p \wedge (q \vee r) . Two such sets are equal if their membership formulas can each be derived from the other, for then x lies in one exactly when it lies in the other, and x was arbitrary. So a law of propositional logic, with letters replaced by membership statements, is a law of sets. That is the thesis of this chapter. The laws of sets are the laws of logic, read through membership. Here are the laws used most. [Algebra of Sets] For all sets A, B, and C: 1. (commutativity) A \cup B = B \cup A and A \cap B = B \cap A; 2. (associativity) (A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C) and (A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C); 3. (distributivity) A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C) and A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C); 4. (differences) A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C) and A \setminus (B \cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C). Each law is a propositional equivalence under  orall x. Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 gives a uniform license for all of them at once: an equivalence that holds in every row of a truth table is derivable in both directions, by completeness, and a derived sequent may be used with its letters replaced by any statements. So one argument covers every law, and the table after the proof names, for each law, the equivalence it comes from. Two of the laws are written out as element-chases in the fold after the proof, and the chain-of-equivalences method below is how a reader proves a new law by hand. The uniform argument. Fix one of the eight equations, L = R, and let \varphi and \psi be the propositional formulas in the atoms p, q, r that describe membership in L and in R, as in the dictionary: for the first distributive law, \varphi = p \wedge (q \vee r) and \psi = (p \wedge q) \vee (p \wedge r). For (a)–(c), the semantic equivalence \varphi \equiv \psi is a clause of @fd1:prp-standard-equivalences, with p, q, r in the places of \varphi, \psi, \chi: (f) for (a), (h) for (b), (g) for (c). For (d), it is checked by the truth table displayed below. By @fd1:def-semantic-equivalence, \varphi \models \psi and \psi \models \varphi, so by @fd1:thm-completeness (as in the step TAUT, @fd1:def-rule-taut), \varphi \vdash \psi and \psi \vdash \varphi. Now let x be arbitrary. Each of these two sequents may be pasted in, like a derived rule (@fd1:def-derived-rule), with p, q, r replaced by the statements x \in A, x \in B, x \in C; with @def-set-operations, the first gives x \in L 	o x \in R and the second x \in R 	o x \in L. Hence x \in L \leftrightarrow x \in R, and since x was arbitrary, L = R by @def-set-equality. The truth table for (d), with the atoms in the book’s order (T before F, the last atom alternating fastest):  egin{array}{ccc|cccc} p & q & r & p \wedge 
eg(q \vee r) & (p \wedge 
eg q) \wedge (p \wedge 
eg r) & p \wedge 
eg(q \wedge r) & (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (p \wedge 
eg r) \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \end{array} The fourth and fifth columns agree in every row, and so do the sixth and seventh. This proves all eight laws. Here are two of the laws as element-chases. The first distributive law, in full. (\subseteq) Let x \in A \cap (B \cup C). Then x \in A and x \in B \cup C, that is, x \in A and (x \in B or x \in C). By @fd1:prp-distributivity, with P, Q, R replaced by x \in A, x \in B, x \in C, we get (x \in A and x \in B) or (x \in A and x \in C); that is, x \in A \cap B or x \in A \cap C, so x \in (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C). (\supseteq) The same chain read backwards, using the second sequent of @fd1:prp-distributivity. By @prp-subset-antisymmetric the two sets are equal. The second difference law, in full. (\subseteq) Let x \in A \setminus (B \cap C). Then x \in A and 
eg(x \in B \wedge x \in C). By @fd1:prp-de-morgan (d), x 
otin B or x 
otin C [ulename{RAA}, inside (d)]. So x \in A and (x 
otin B or x 
otin C), and by @fd1:prp-distributivity, (x \in A and x 
otin B) or (x \in A and x 
otin C); that is, x \in (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C). (\supseteq) Let x \in (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C). By the second sequent of @fd1:prp-distributivity, x \in A and (x 
otin B or x 
otin C). By @fd1:prp-de-morgan (c), 
eg(x \in B \wedge x \in C), so x 
otin B \cap C, and x \in A \setminus (B \cap C). By @prp-subset-antisymmetric the two sets are equal. Each law is a propositional equivalence, and the table records where each comes from: the clause of @fd1:prp-standard-equivalences, and the derivations of Logic and Proof, Chapters 1 and 2, where they exist, that prove one or both directions directly. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Law Clause of @fd1:prp-standard-equivalences Derived in Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–2 --------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------ --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- A \cap B = B \cap A (f) @fd1:prp-and-commutes (either direction, letters exchanged) A \cup B = B \cup A (f) @fd1:exm-disjunction-first-derivations (likewise) (A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C) (h) @fd1:prp-and-associative (left to right) (A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C) (h) @fd1:exm-disjunction-regroup (right to left) A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C) (g) @fd1:prp-distributivity (both directions) A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C) (g) none in the text (both directions are exercises in Logic and Proof, Chapters 1 and 2) A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C) (b), then regrouping of \wedge @fd1:prp-de-morgan (a), (b) A \setminus (B \cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C) (b), then (g) @fd1:prp-de-morgan (c), (d); @fd1:prp-distributivity -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The two difference laws look alike, but their element-chases are not alike. The first needs De Morgan’s laws (a) and (b), which Logic and Proof, Section 2.5 derives without ulename{RAA}, followed by regrouping the conjunction x \in A \wedge (x 
otin B \wedge x 
otin C) into (x \in A \wedge x 
otin B) \wedge (x \in A \wedge x 
otin C), which takes only ulename{\wedge E} and ulename{\wedge I}. The second needs De Morgan (d) in its (\subseteq) direction, and (d) is the one of the four De Morgan laws that Logic and Proof, Section 2.5 derives with ulename{RAA}; its (\supseteq) direction uses (c), derived without it. Knowing that x is not in both B and C does not by itself tell us which of the two it misses; De Morgan (d) supplies the answer “one of them”, and it is the classical rule that supplies it. [Method: a chain of equivalences] Template. For L = R: let x be arbitrary, and write x \in L \iff \dots \iff x \in R, one step per line. Each step either unwinds a definition (@def-set-operations) or applies a propositional equivalence to membership statements, with its name on the line; a step may act on a part of the line (@fd1:prp-replacement). Since \dashv\vdash is used like = (@fd1:prp-provable-equivalence-basics (b)), the chain gives x \in L \dashv\vdash x \in R, so x \in L \leftrightarrow x \in R by (a), and @def-set-equality finishes. When to use it. Identities built from \cup, \cap, \setminus and families, where every step is reversible. The usual failure. A step that holds in one direction only, written as \iff: for example x \in A \implies x \in A \cup B. When a chain will not close, look for a small witness instead (@exm-method-counterexample); a truth table in the statements x \in A, x \in B, x \in C finds one, each row saying which of A, B, C a witness should lie in. [A law by a chain] Show that (A \setminus B) \setminus C = A \setminus (B \cup C) for all sets A, B, C. [Scratch work] Work from both ends. Unwind the left side as far as the definitions go, then the right side, and see what is left between them. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------- x arbitrary x \in (A \setminus B) \setminus C \iff x \in A \setminus (B \cup C) left unwound: x \in A \wedge x 
otin B \wedge x 
otin C right unwound: x \in A \wedge 
eg(x \in B \vee x \in C) gap: x 
otin B \wedge x 
otin C \iff 
eg(x \in B \vee x \in C) closed by De Morgan (a), (b) (@fd1:prp-de-morgan) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The gap is a propositional law with x \in B and x \in C in the places of P and Q, so the chain will close. Let x be arbitrary. Then  egin{aligned} &x \in (A \setminus B) \setminus C \ &\quad\iff (x \in A \wedge x 
otin B) \wedge x 
otin C && 	ext{[definition of } \setminus 	ext{, twice]} \ &\quad\iff x \in A \wedge (x 
otin B \wedge x 
otin C) && 	ext{[regrouping } \wedge 	ext{]} \ &\quad\iff x \in A \wedge 
eg(x \in B \vee x \in C) && 	ext{[De Morgan (a), (b)]} \ &\quad\iff x \in A \wedge x 
otin B \cup C && 	ext{[definition of } \cup 	ext{]} \ &\quad\iff x \in A \setminus (B \cup C) && 	ext{[definition of } \setminus 	ext{]} \end{aligned} The definitions are those of @def-set-operations, the regrouping is @fd1:prp-and-associative from left to right and takes only ulename{\wedge E} and ulename{\wedge I} from right to left, and De Morgan (a), (b) are @fd1:prp-de-morgan, with x \in B, x \in C for P, Q, applied to the second conjunct (@fd1:prp-replacement), as is the definition of \cup. By @def-set-equality the two sets are equal. No step needs ulename{RAA}. Which step of the chain fails if B \cup C is replaced by B \cap C? Show with a small witness that (A \setminus B) \setminus C = A \setminus (B \cap C) can fail. The De Morgan step. De Morgan’s laws give 
eg(q \wedge r) \iff 
eg q \vee 
eg r, not 
eg q \wedge 
eg r. Take A = \{1, 2\}, B = \{1\}, C = \{2\}: then B \cap C = \emptyset, so the right side is \{1, 2\}, while the left side is \{2\} \setminus \{2\} = \emptyset. The laws let us calculate with sets as with numbers, but more symmetrically: each of \cup and \cap distributes over the other, whereas 	imes distributes over + and not conversely. They also let us drop brackets: by associativity, A \cup B \cup C and A \cap B \cap C are unambiguous. Which propositional equivalence proves A \cap (A \cup B) = A? Is it one of the clauses of @fd1:prp-standard-equivalences? Membership in the left side is p \wedge (p \vee q), and in the right side p. The equivalence p \wedge (p \vee q) \equiv p holds in all four rows: if p is true, both sides are true; if p is false, both are false. It is not one of the clauses of @fd1:prp-standard-equivalences, so the uniform argument applies with a two-atom truth table instead of a clause. (Directly: (\subseteq) is ulename{\wedge E}; (\supseteq) is ulename{\vee I} followed by ulename{\wedge I}.) This is one of the absorption laws. Power sets The operations so far build sets whose elements are elements of the old sets. The next construction collects sets as elements. Many questions of analysis quantify over subsets: “every non-empty set of reals that is bounded above has a supremum” is a statement about all subsets of 
R. So the subsets of a set deserve to be collected into one set. [Power Set] Let X be a set. The power set of X is the set \powerset{X} whose elements are exactly the subsets of X: S \in \powerset{X} \iff S \subseteq X . The set exists by the working rule (W4) of Section 1.2. Its elements are sets, and “S \in \powerset{X}” is just another way of writing “S \subseteq X”. Two elements are always present: \emptyset \in \powerset{X}, because the empty set is a subset of every set, and X \in \powerset{X}, because X \subseteq X. [Small power sets] Compute \powerset{\emptyset}, \powerset{\{\emptyset\}}, and \powerset{\{1, 2\}}. \powerset{\emptyset} = \{\emptyset\}. The only subset of \emptyset is \emptyset itself: if S \subseteq \emptyset, then an element of S would be an element of \emptyset, so S has no elements, and S = \emptyset by @prp-empty-set-unique. And \emptyset \subseteq \emptyset. So \powerset{\emptyset} has exactly one element, \emptyset. It is not empty: the empty set has one subset. \powerset{\{\emptyset\}} = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}. Let S \subseteq \{\emptyset\}. Either \emptyset \in S or \emptyset

Let X be a set, and consider some starting elements of X and some steps, each of which turns elements of X into an element of X. De Morgan’s laws for families The laws of set algebra have versions for families, and the most used are De Morgan’s laws: the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements, and the complement of an intersection is the union of the complements. The false ones (b) and (d) are the minimal changes of (c) and (e): (b) forgets that the elements of A \cap B are removed, and (d) forgets that C is removed from A too. C. Going deeper [C1: Power sets and operations] Let A and B be sets. 1. Decide whether \powerset{A \setminus B} = \powerset{A} \setminus \powerset{B} can hold. Then prove that every non-empty element of \powerset{A \setminus B} lies in \powerset{A} \setminus \powerset{B}. 2. [Hint 1] In (a), test the empty set against both sides. In (b), one inclusion always holds; for the other, ask which subset of A \cup B could fail to be a subset of A and of B. otin \powerset{A} \setminus \powerset{B}. The empty set is a witness for every A and B. Now let S \in \powerset{A \setminus B} be non-empty, and choose s \in S. Since S \subseteq A \setminus B \subseteq A, we have S \in \powerset{A}. Since s \in A \setminus B, s 
otin B; so s is an element of S outside B, and S

otin \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B}. One inclusion always holds. If S \in \powerset{A}, then S \subseteq A \subseteq A \cup B (@prp-subset-transitive), so S \in \powerset{A \cup B}; likewise for S \in \powerset{B}. So \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B} \subseteq \powerset{A \cup B}. (\Leftarrow) Suppose A \subseteq B. Then A \cup B = B (if x \in A \cup B, then x \in A \subseteq B or x \in B; and B \subseteq A \cup B). Let S \in \powerset{A \cup B}. Then S \subseteq B, so S \in \powerset{B} \subseteq \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B}. With the inclusion above, equality holds. The case B \subseteq A is the same with A and B exchanged. (\Rightarrow) We prove the contrapositive. Suppose that neither A \subseteq B nor B \subseteq A. By the negation of \subseteq (@exr-sets-and-subsets-a1 (a) records it), there is a \in A with a 
otin B, and there is b \in B with b 
otin A; choose such a and b. Let S \coloneqq \{a, b\}. Then S \subseteq A \cup B, so S \in \powerset{A \cup B}. But S 
ot\subseteq A, because b \in S and b 
otin A; and S 
ot\subseteq B, because a \in S and a 
otin B. So S 
otin \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B}, and the two sets differ. Two steps here are classical: turning “A 
ot\subseteq B” into a witness uses the classical directions of quantifier negation and of the law for negated implications (Logic and Proof, Chapter 6; see @exr-sets-and-subsets-a1 (a)), and concluding the implication from its contrapositive is @fd1:prp-contrapositive-converse. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) the empty set as the witness that the equality never holds, with both memberships checked. - 2: (a) a non-empty S \subseteq A \setminus B is shown to lie in \powerset{A} and, via an element outside B, not in \powerset{B}. - 1: (b) a counterexample with the offending subset named. - 2: (b) the inclusion \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B} \subseteq \powerset{A \cup B} and the direction (\Leftarrow). - 3: (b) (\Rightarrow): witnesses a \in A \setminus B and b \in B \setminus A named, and \{a, b\} shown to lie in \powerset{A \cup B} and in neither \powerset{A} nor \powerset{B}. A direct proof also earns the 3: assume equality and A 
ot\subseteq B, fix a \in A \setminus B (1 point); for arbitrary b \in B, \{a, b\} \in \powerset{A \cup B} = \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B}, and \{a, b\}

otin B, so \{a, b\} \subseteq A and b \in A, giving B \subseteq A (2 points). Both routes also end with a classical step: excluded middle on A \subseteq B in the direct route, the contrapositive in the book’s. Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (a), testing only non-empty subsets and concluding equality; in (b) (\Rightarrow), in the contrapositive route, using one witness a for both failures, or a set such as \{a\} that lies in \powerset{A}. [C2: Find the error] Here is a “proof” that (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C) \subseteq A \cup (B \cap C) for all sets A, B, C. (1) Let x \in (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C). (2) Then x \in A \cup B and x \in A \cup C. (3) We consider two cases, according to x \in A \cup B. (4) Case x \in A. Then x \in A \cup (B \cap C). (5) Case x \in B. Since x \in A \cup C, x \in C. (6) So x \in B \cap C, and hence x \in A \cup (B \cap C). (7) In both cases x \in A \cup (B \cap C), which proves the inclusion. 1. Is the conclusion true? 2. Which line fails, which rule does it break, and which entry of the catalogue of Logic and Proof, Chapter 8 does it commit? 3. Give a counterexample to the illegal step itself: sets and an element for which the line’s premise holds and its conclusion fails. 4. Repair the proof. (a) Yes. It is the (\supseteq) half of the second distributive law of @thm-set-algebra (c). (b) Line (5). From x \in A \cup C, that is, x \in A or x \in C, it concludes x \in C, dropping the case x \in A. A disjunction is used by ulename{\vee E}, which needs both cases; the line uses only one. This is a missing case, entry (N7) of the catalogue of Logic and Proof, Chapter 8. (c) Take A = \{1\}, B = \{1\}, C = \emptyset, and x = 1. Then x \in B (the case of line (5)) and x \in A \cup C (the premise of the line), but x 
otin C. The step is illegal although the conclusion of the whole proof is true: here x \in A, so x \in A \cup (B \cap C) by the other case. (d) Replace lines (5)–(6) by: Case x \in B. Since x \in A \cup C, there are two sub-cases. If x \in A, then x \in A \cup (B \cap C). If x \in C, then x \in B \cap C, so x \in A \cup (B \cap C). In both sub-cases x \in A \cup (B \cap C). title: 1.4 Ordered Pairs, Products and Relations
content:
Ordered Pairs, Products and Relations Sections 1.2 and 1.3 built sets and combined them: a set is fixed by its elements, and \cup, \cap, \setminus are \vee, \wedge, \wedge
eg read through membership. None of this can yet say “the point (1, 2) of the plane”, “3 is less than 5”, or “y is the square of x”. Each of these is about two objects in a given order, and a set forgets order. This section adds one new kind of object, the ordered pair (with its longer versions, the n-tuples), and then uses it twice: to build the product A 	imes B of two sets, and to say what a relation between two sets is. The next section needs exactly this much: a function will be given by a relation of a special kind, its graph, together with a declared target set. Order matters: ordered pairs A set remembers which objects are its elements and nothing else. By extensionality (@def-set-equality), \{1, 2\} = \{2, 1\}, since both sets have the elements 1 and 2; and \{1, 1\} = \{1\}, since both have the element 1 and nothing else. For a set that is exactly right. For a point of the plane it is exactly wrong. The point (1, 2) lies one unit to the right of the vertical axis and two units above the horizontal one; the point (2, 1) lies elsewhere. And the point (1, 1) on the diagonal is a perfectly good point, with the same number in both places. So we need an object built from two objects a and b that remembers which came first, and that still has two places when a = b. What we need to know about such an object is one fact: when two of them are equal. An ordered pair is equal to another exactly when they agree in the first place and in the second place. [Ordered pair] For any objects a and b there is an object (a, b), the ordered pair of a and b; we call a its first coordinate and b its second coordinate. Ordered pairs have the characteristic property: for all a, b, c, d, (a, b) = (c, d) \iff a = c 	ext{ and } b = d . In words: to decide whether two pairs are equal, compare first coordinates with first coordinates and second with second; nothing else matters, and both comparisons must succeed. The direction (\Leftarrow) is nothing new: equal inputs give equal pairs, as for any construction (ulename{=E}, @fd1:def-rules-equality). The direction (\Rightarrow) is the content. It says that from the pair we can read off its coordinates, each in its place. We do not say here what the object (a, b) is. Besides the characteristic property, we use one working convention: pairs and n-tuples are a different kind of object from numbers, just as sets are (Section 1.2), so a pair is not a number; and tuples of different lengths are different kinds of object, so a triple is not a pair. Nothing else about pairs is used in this chapter. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 1 shows that a pair with this property can be built from sets alone, so that nothing new has to be assumed. Until then, the existence of pairs with this property is taken as given, alongside the working rules (W1)–(W6) of Section 1.2. A convention about parentheses. The symbol (a, b) now has two meanings. For real numbers a < b it is also the open interval \{ x \in 
R : a < x < b \}. The book keeps both, and context decides, as it does in every analysis text. In “(0, 1) contains 	frac{1}{2}” it is an interval. In “the point (0, 1) lies on the unit circle” it is a pair. Where both readings are near each other, the text says which is meant. This convention is stated once, here. [Solving an equation between pairs] Find all real numbers x and y with (x + y, x - y) = (3, 1). Then decide whether (1, 2) = (2, 1) and whether (1, 1) = (1, 1). Uniqueness. By the characteristic property, (x + y, x - y) = (3, 1) holds if and only if x + y = 3 \quad 	ext{and} \quad x - y = 1 . Adding the two equations gives 2x = 4, so x = 2; subtracting them gives 2y = 2, so y = 1. Existence. Conversely, x = 2 and y = 1 give (x + y, x - y) = (3, 1). So there is exactly one solution, x = 2, y = 1. The pairs (1, 2) and (2, 1) are not equal. If they were, the characteristic property would give 1 = 2 for the first coordinates. So (1, 2) 
e (2, 1), by ulename{
eg I}. The same test on (1, 1) and (1, 1) passes in both places, so they are equal; and (1, 1) has two places, although both hold the same number. The first part is typical. One equation between pairs is two equations between coordinates, and this is how pairs are used: an equation of pairs is split by the characteristic property, and the coordinates are compared one at a time. The solution also has a shape worth naming. “Exactly one solution” was two claims, proved separately: any solution must be (2, 1), and (2, 1) is a solution. Claims of this kind come with every “the” in a definition, so the shape gets a box. [Method: existence and uniqueness] Template. “There is exactly one x with P(x)” is two claims (@fd1:def-unique-existence, @fd1:prp-unique-existence-use). For existence, name a candidate x_0 and check P(x_0), or obtain one from a given “there exists”. For uniqueness, take x and x' with P(x) and P(x'), two names about which nothing else is assumed, and prove x = x'; or show that every x with P(x) equals x_0. When to use it. Whenever a definition says “the”: the coordinates of a pair, the value f(x), the empty set (@prp-empty-set-unique), an inverse. The usual failure. Proving only one half: a uniqueness proof with no candidate, or a candidate never shown to be the only one. Also checking P(x_0) twice and calling it uniqueness, and naming “the” object before either half is proved (entry (N14) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue). Is there exactly one real x with (x^2, x^3) = (4, -8)? Is there exactly one with (x^2, x) = (4, 3)? Yes for the first: x^3 = -8 forces x = -2 (uniqueness), and (-2)^2 = 4 (existence). No for the second: x = 3 is forced, but 3^2 = 9 
e 4, so there is no such x at all. Uniqueness held and existence failed. Nonexample by minimal change. Replace the parentheses by braces. The set \{1, 2\} has the same two numbers as the pair (1, 2), but the characteristic property fails for sets: \{1, 2\} = \{2, 1\}, and yet 1 
e 2. What survives is membership: 1 and 2 are both in \{1, 2\}. What is lost is order, the one thing the pair was made to keep. Why this definition. Only (\Rightarrow) carries content. Without it, the pair could forget its coordinates, as \{1, 2\} forgets which number came first. The direction (\Leftarrow) could be dropped from the definition without loss: ulename{=E} already gives it for (a, b), as for any construction. It is stated so that the property reads as a single test for equality of pairs. Longer lists. The same idea gives ordered triples (a, b, c), and more generally ordered n-tuples (x_1, \dots, x_n) for n \in 
N, n \ge 2. Like pairs, n-tuples are taken as given, and the n-tuples with all coordinates in a set form a set, by the working rule (W5) of Section 1.2. Two n-tuples are equal if and only if they agree in every place: (x_1, \dots, x_n) = (y_1, \dots, y_n) means x_k = y_k for every k \in \{1, \dots, n\}. A triple is a new kind of object, not a pair whose first coordinate is a pair (by the convention stated after @def-ordered-pair). The pairs ((1, 2), 3) and (1, (2, 3)) carry the same three numbers in the same order, and it is tempting to call both “the triple (1, 2, 3)”; that is an identification made by convention, and exercise A1 asks whether the two pairs are equal. For which real numbers t is (t^2, t) = (1, -1)? For which is \{t^2, t\} = \{1, -1\}? The pair equation holds if and only if t^2 = 1 and t = -1, so exactly for t = -1. The set equation holds for t = -1 too, since \{1, -1\} = \{1, -1\}. It holds for no other t: the element -1 of the right side must be t^2 or t, and t^2 \ge 0, so t = -1. Here the sets agree exactly where the pairs do, but that is luck. The pair equation (t, 1) = (1, t) holds only for t = 1, while the set equation \{t, 1\} = \{1, t\} holds for every t. Cartesian products With pairs in hand, the plane is the set of all pairs of real numbers. More generally, from any two sets we can collect all pairs whose first coordinate comes from the first set and whose second comes from the second. Taking such a collection is the working rule (W5) of Section 1.2: it is a set. [Cartesian product] Let A and B be sets. Their Cartesian product is the set A 	imes B \coloneqq \{ (a, b) : a \in A, \ b \in B \} of all ordered pairs with first coordinate in A and second coordinate in B. Written out, an object p is an element of A 	imes B if and only if \exists a \in A \ \exists b \in B \ \ p = (a, b) . For a set X we write X^2 \coloneqq X 	imes X, and, for n \in 
N with n \ge 2, X^n is the set of all n-tuples (x_1, \dots, x_n) with every x_k \in X. In words: an element of A 	imes B is a pair, and there exist coordinates, one in A and one in B, from which it is made. The membership condition hides two existential quantifiers, so using it means naming the coordinates, by ulename{\exists E} (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-rules), and then matching them against any other naming by the characteristic property of pairs. That two-step move is the basic move for products; (\ast) below packages it. For a pair the condition simplifies, and we use the simpler form constantly: (x, y) \in A 	imes B \iff x \in A 	ext{ and } y \in B . 	ag{$\ast$} Here is why. If x \in A and y \in B, then x and y themselves are coordinates of the required kind, and (x, y) \in A 	imes B by ulename{\exists I}. Conversely, let (x, y) \in A 	imes B. Then there are a \in A and b \in B with (x, y) = (a, b) [ulename{\exists E}], and the characteristic property (@def-ordered-pair) gives x = a and y = b. So x \in A and y \in B. The characteristic property is used exactly once, in the direction (\Rightarrow); without it, (x, y) might equal (a, b) with the coordinates swapped or lost, and nothing could be concluded. We write (\ast) for this equivalence in the rest of the section. It is the reason a product is easy to work with: membership of a pair in a product is checked one coordinate at a time. The membership condition says that an element of A 	imes B is made from some pair of coordinates. Can it be made from two different ones? The method of @exm-method-uniqueness answers this, and the answer is what lets us speak of “the first coordinate” of an element of a product. [The coordinates of an element of a product] Let p \in A 	imes B. Show that there is exactly one a and exactly one b such that a \in A, b \in B and p = (a, b). [Scratch work] Existence should come straight from the definition, since membership in A 	imes B is an existence statement. For uniqueness, take two namings of p and ask what connects them. Only p itself does, so the two pairs are equal, and an equation between pairs is exactly what @def-ordered-pair splits. As givens and goal: -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- p \in A 	imes B some a \in A, b \in B with p = (a, b); any two such agree p = (a, b), a \in A, b \in B (ulename{\exists E} twice, @def-cartesian-product) existence: done p = (a, b) and p = (a', b') a = a', b = b': the gap is (a, b) = (a', b') (ulename{=E}), then @def-ordered-pair -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The last row is the gap. Once (a, b) = (a', b') is written down, the characteristic property closes it in one step. Existence. By @def-cartesian-product there are a \in A and b \in B with p = (a, b). Uniqueness. If also p = (a', b') with a' \in A, b' \in B, then (a, b) = p = (a', b'), so a = a' and b = b' by the characteristic property (@def-ordered-pair). This licenses “the first coordinate of p”, and so the assignment p \mapsto its first coordinate, which the next section will call a function. Which half of the solution used @def-cartesian-product, and which used @def-ordered-pair? Existence used @def-cartesian-product: membership in the product hands over the coordinates. Uniqueness used @def-ordered-pair: the characteristic property matches two namings of the same pair. Set-builders with a pair pattern. We write \{ (x, y) \in A 	imes B : P(x, y) \} for \{ p \in A 	imes B : 	ext{there are } x, y 	ext{ with } p = (x, y) 	ext{ and } P(x, y) \}, a set-builder in the sense of @def-set-builder. By (\ast) and the characteristic property, (x, y) belongs to it if and only if x \in A, y \in B and P(x, y). The notation \{ (a, b) : a \in A, \ b \in B \} in @def-cartesian-product is different: it names no ambient set, so it is not a set-builder. It is notation for the set that (W5) provides, and the displayed membership condition is its definition. [Products, small and large] (a) Let a, b, c be three different objects, none of them a number. List \{1, 2\} 	imes \{a, b, c\} and \{a, b, c\} 	imes \{1, 2\}. (b) Describe 
R^2 and [0, 1] 	imes [0, 1] as sets of points of the plane. (c) What is \{1, 2\} 	imes \emptyset? (a) Each of the 2 first coordinates is paired with each of the 3 second coordinates: \{1, 2\} 	imes \{a, b, c\} = \{ (1, a), (1, b), (1, c), (2, a), (2, b), (2, c) \}, six pairs, all different by the characteristic property, since 1 
e 2 and a, b, c are different. Swapping the factors gives the six pairs (a, 1), (a, 2), (b, 1), (b, 2), (c, 1), (c, 2). No pair of the first list is in the second: every pair in the first list has a number as its first coordinate, and every pair in the second list has one of a, b, c there, none of which is a number; so by the characteristic property no pair of one list equals a pair of the other. (b) 
R^2 = 
R 	imes 
R is the set of all pairs (x, y) of real numbers: the plane, with x the horizontal and y the vertical coordinate. By (\ast), (x, y) \in [0, 1] 	imes [0, 1] if and only if 0 \le x \le 1 and 0 \le y \le 1: the closed unit square, with its four sides. (c) It is empty. An element p would be (a, b) with b \in \emptyset, and \emptyset has no elements. So \{1, 2\} 	imes \emptyset has no elements, and a set with no elements is \emptyset (@prp-empty-set-unique). Part (c) is the degenerate case, and it matters: a product is empty as soon as one factor is. The general statement is part of the next proposition. List \{0, 1\} 	imes \{0, 1, 2\}. Is (1, 1) \in \{1\} 	imes \emptyset? \{0, 1\} 	imes \{0, 1, 2\} = \{ (0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 0), (1, 1), (1, 2) \}, six pairs. And (1, 1) 
otin \{1\} 	imes \emptyset: by (\ast) it would need 1 \in \emptyset. In fact \{1\} 	imes \emptyset has no elements at all, as in part (c) of the example. The product is not commutative: A 	imes B and B 	imes A are in general different sets. For A = \{1\} and B = \{2\}, A 	imes B = \{(1, 2)\} and B 	imes A = \{(2, 1)\}, and (1, 2) 
e (2, 1) by @exm-pair-equations. The two products have “the same size”, but they do not have the same elements. (They are equal when A = B, and when one of the sets is empty. Exercise C2 finds exactly when even the inclusion A 	imes B \subseteq B 	imes A holds.) Products and the set operations Section 1.3 showed that \cup, \cap, and \setminus obey the laws of \vee, \wedge, and \wedge 
eg. The product interacts with them just as simply, one factor at a time. We use these laws for regions of the plane (exercise B1) and for functions out of the empty set (Section 1.5), so we state them all. Relations “Is less than”, “divides”, “is the square of”, “lies on the unit circle with”: each of these connects an object of one set with an object of another, or of the same set. Each can be described by a rule, a formula, or a sentence. But two different descriptions can pick out exactly the same connections: “x < y” and “y - x > 0” are different sentences about real numbers, and they hold for exactly the same pairs (x, y). In mathematics we want these to count as the same relation. The way to make them the same is to forget the description and keep what it picks out: the set of pairs (x, y) for which it holds. Two descriptions that pick out the same pairs then give the same set, by extensionality. A relation is the set of pairs it relates. [Relation] Let A and B be sets. A relation from A to B is a subset R \subseteq A 	imes B. For a \in A and b \in B we write a \mathrel{R} b, read “a is R-related to b”, to mean (a, b) \in R. A relation on A is a relation from A to A, that is, a subset of A^2. The domain of R is the set of first coordinates that occur, \{ a \in A : \exists b \in B \ \ a \mathrel{R} b \}, and its range is the set of second coordinates that occur, \{ b \in B : \exists a \in A \ \ a \mathrel{R} b \}. Turning every pair of R around gives a relation from B to A, the inverse relation R^{-1} \coloneqq \{ (b, a) \in B 	imes A : (a, b) \in R \} . In words: a relation is a set, namely a set of pairs whose coordinates come from the two given sets. The notation a \mathrel{R} b is only a way of writing “(a, b) \in R” that reads like “a < b”. The domain collects the elements of A that are related to at least one element of B; the range collects those of B that something is related to. The inverse relation turns each pair around: b \mathrel{R^{-1}} a exactly when a \mathrel{R} b. Two relations are equal exactly when they relate the same pairs, since relations are sets (@def-set-equality). So the relation “x < y” on

A relation could be defined as a rule, a sentence, or a formula. Each of those raises the question of when two rules are “the same”, and that question has no good answer: “x < y” and “y - x > 0” are different sentences. The definition as a set answers it by extensionality. The price is small: a relation may be any set of pairs whatever, such as \{ (1, 3), (2, 2) \} on \{1, 2, 3\}, and the definition never asks for a rule that produces it. That is a gain, not a loss: in analysis we meet relations and functions that no formula describes. With B = \emptyset there is no b_0, and indeed then A 	imes B \subseteq B 	imes A holds for every A, including A 
e B: the inclusion \{1\} 	imes \emptyset \subseteq \emptyset 	imes \{1\} is \emptyset \subseteq \emptyset. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (\Leftarrow): all three cases, including that an empty factor makes A 	imes B empty and hence a subset of anything. - 2: (\Rightarrow): splits off the empty cases and, in the remaining case, names witnesses a_0 \in A and b_0 \in B. - 2: A \subseteq B, through a pair (a, b_0) with an arbitrary a \in A. - 2: B \subseteq A, through a pair (a_0, b) with an arbitrary b \in B. - 2: uses the characteristic property (directly or through (\ast)) to read the coordinates off a pair of B 	imes A, and concludes A = B by two inclusions. Fatal errors (0 for the step): testing inclusion on particular elements only (entry (N1) of Logic and Proof, Chapter 8’s catalogue); using b_0 without having shown that B has an element; concluding A = B from A 	imes B = B 	imes A “by canceling” without an element argument. A proof of (\Rightarrow) by contraposition (assume A 
e B and both nonempty, and exhibit a pair of A 	imes B outside B 	imes A) earns full marks if it finds the pair: 2 points for the witnesses and 4 for the pair and the check that it is outside B 	imes A, in place of the two inclusions.

title: 1.5 Functions, Composition, Injections and Surjections
content:
Functions, Composition, Injections and Surjections Section 1.4 made “the pairs a description picks out” into a set: a relation from A to B is a subset of A 	imes B. Among its examples, the graph of squaring relates each real number to exactly one number, and the unit circle relates 0 to two numbers and 2 to none. This section gives the first kind its name, function, and builds the rest on it: we restrict functions, use them to make families, sequences and the set Y^X precise, compose them, and ask the two questions that the rest of the chapter turns on: does a function send different inputs to different outputs, and does it reach every point of its target? What is a function? Everyone has used functions since school, and the everyday definition is “a rule that assigns to each input one output”. Look at the word “rule”. The rules x \mapsto x^2 and x \mapsto (x + 1)^2 - 2x - 1 are different: one squares, the other adds, squares, subtracts, and subtracts again. Yet on every real number they give the same answer, and nobody would call them different functions. Other functions have no rule at all that one could write down. A table of measured temperatures, one per day, assigns to each day one number, and no formula produces it. So the rule is not what matters. What matters is which output goes with which input: the set of input–output pairs. That set is a relation, and Section 1.4 said exactly when two relations are the same, namely when they contain the same pairs. So we forget the rule and keep the pairs. One more piece of data is needed, the set in which the outputs are declared to lie; the reason is given after the definition. A function is its graph, with a declared target. [Function] Let X and Y be sets. A function from X to Y, written f \colon X 	o Y, is given by a relation G \subseteq X 	imes Y, the graph of f, such that 	ext{for every } x \in X 	ext{ there is exactly one } y \in Y 	ext{ with } (x, y) \in G , together with the set Y, the codomain of f. Formally, f is the pair (G, Y). The set X is the domain of f. For x \in X, the unique y with (x, y) \in G is written f(x), the value of f at x. We write (x, y) \in f for (x, y) \in G, and x \mapsto f(x) for the whole function when its domain and codomain are clear. In symbols, the condition on the graph is  orall x \in X \ \ \exists! \, y \in Y \ \ (x, y) \in G , where, as with the bounded quantifiers of @fd1:def-bounded-quantifier, \exists! \, y \in Y \ \psi abbreviates \exists! \, y \, (y \in Y \wedge \psi). The whole definition is the quantifier pattern  orall \exists!. By @fd1:def-unique-existence, “\exists! \, y” is an existence claim and a uniqueness claim, and by @fd1:prp-unique-existence-use the uniqueness claim may be stated without reference to the witness; so the condition on the graph is two clauses: - (Fn1) (existence) for every x \in X there is at least one y \in Y with (x, y) \in G: every input has an output; - (Fn2) (uniqueness) for every x \in X and all y, y' \in Y, if (x, y) \in G and (x, y') \in G, then y = y': no input has two outputs. In words: the graph is a set of input–output pairs, with inputs from X and outputs from Y; (Fn1) says no input is left without an output, and (Fn2) says no input is given two. The codomain Y is where outputs are allowed to lie. It need not consist of outputs: x \mapsto x^2 can be declared as a function from 
R to 
R, although no output is negative. The set of outputs that actually occur is the range of f, \{ y \in Y : \exists x \in X \ \ f(x) = y \} , which Section 1.7 will call the image of X and write f(X). The domain needs no slot of its own in the pair (G, Y): by (Fn1) every x \in X occurs as a first coordinate in G, and since G \subseteq X 	imes Y, nothing else does. So the graph determines the domain. The notation f(x) is well defined. Writing “the y with (x, y) \in f” is legitimate only if there is one, and only one. Clause (Fn1) supplies one, and clause (Fn2) says that any two are equal; together they license the article “the”. This gives the equivalence that every argument with functions uses: (x, y) \in f \iff y = f(x) \qquad (x \in X, \ y \in Y). 	ag{$\ast\ast$} For (\Leftarrow): (x, f(x)) \in f by the choice of f(x), and if y = f(x) then (x, y) \in f by substituting equals (ulename{=E}, @fd1:def-rules-equality). For (\Rightarrow): both (x, y) and (x, f(x)) lie in f, so y = f(x) by (Fn2). Two consequences follow at once. Equal inputs give equal outputs: if x_1 = x_2, then f(x_1) = f(x_2). And every value lies in the codomain: f(x) \in Y for every x \in X. Functions given by formulas. Most functions in this book are introduced by a formula: “let f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = x^2”. This means the function whose graph is \{ (x, y) \in 
R^2 : y = x^2 \}. Clause (Fn2) holds for any such graph: if y = x^2 and y' = x^2, then y = y'. So for a formula only (Fn1) needs checking, and it says: for each x in the domain, the formula makes sense and its value lies in the codomain. For x^2 on 
R both are clear. For “f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = 1/x” the formula makes no sense at x = 0, and (Fn1) fails there; for “f \colon 
R 	o [0, \infty), f(x) = x^2” the value must be checked to lie in [0, \infty), which it does, since squares are nonnegative. A function whose domain is a product A 	imes B is a function of two variables. Its inputs are pairs, and we write f(a, b) rather than f((a, b)). Addition (m, n) \mapsto m + n from 
N 	imes 
N to 
N is an example. [First functions] Check (Fn1) and (Fn2), and find the range, for each of the following. (a) f \colon \{1, 2, 3\} 	o \{a, b\} with graph \{ (1, a), (2, b), (3, a) \}. (b) The identity function \id_X \colon X 	o X, \id_X(x) = x, for a set X. (c) A constant function X 	o Y, x \mapsto c, for a fixed c \in Y. (d) The indicator function \ind_A \colon X 	o \{0, 1\} of a subset A \subseteq X: \ind_A(x) =  egin{cases} 1 & 	ext{if } x \in A, \ 0 & 	ext{if } x \in X \setminus A. \end{cases} (a) The graph is a subset of \{1, 2, 3\} 	imes \{a, b\}. Each of 1, 2, 3 occurs as a first coordinate (Fn1), and each occurs exactly once, so no input has two outputs (Fn2). So f is a function, with f(1) = a, f(2) = b, f(3) = a. Its range is \{a, b\}, the whole codomain. A function on a small finite set is often given this way, by listing its values; no formula is needed. (b) The graph is the diagonal \{ (x, x) : x \in X \}. For each x, the pair (x, x) is in it (Fn1); and if (x, y) is in it, then (x, y) = (z, z) for some z \in X, and the characteristic property (@def-ordered-pair) gives x = z = y (Fn2). The range is X. (c) The graph is X 	imes \{c\}. For each x \in X, (x, c) is in it (Fn1); if (x, y) is in it, then y \in \{c\} by the membership test (\ast) for pairs in a product (@def-cartesian-product), so y = c (Fn2). If X has an element, the range is \{c\}. If X = \emptyset, the range is \emptyset. (d) The graph is  igl(A 	imes \{1\} igr) \cup  igl((X \setminus A) 	imes \{0\} igr). For (Fn1), let x \in X. By excluded middle (@fd1:prp-excluded-middle), x \in A or x 
otin A; in the first case (x, 1) is in the graph, in the second x \in X \setminus A and (x, 0) is. For (Fn2), the two cases cannot both hold, so x never receives both 0 and 1, and each case gives only one pair with first coordinate x. The range is \{0, 1\} if A has an element and X \setminus A has an element; it is \{0\} if A = \emptyset and X has an element, \{1\} if A = X and X has an element, and \emptyset if X = \emptyset. This is the first function of the chapter whose existence clause needs excluded middle: the definition by cases is a function only because every x falls into one of the cases. The next example collects relations that fail to be functions. Each failure is one clause, and it pays to say which. [Relations that are not functions] (a) Is the unit circle S = \{ (x, y) \in 
R^2 : x^2 + y^2 = 1 \} the graph of a function 
R 	o 
R? (b) “Send a fraction p/q to its numerator p.” Is this a function from 
Q to 
Z? As a relation it is N \coloneqq \{ (r, p) \in 
Q 	imes 
Z : \exists q \in 
Z_{>0} \ \ r = p/q \} . (a) No, and both clauses fail, at different points. Clause (Fn2) fails at x = 0: both (0, 1) and (0, -1) lie in S, and 1 
e -1. Clause (Fn1) fails at x = 2: a pair (2, y) \in S would need y^2 = 1 - 4 = -3, and no real square is negative. Restricting the inputs to [-1, 1] repairs (Fn1) but not (Fn2); keeping only the upper half, y \ge 0, repairs (Fn2) as well, and gives the function [-1, 1] 	o 
R, x \mapsto \sqrt{1 - x^2}. (b) No. Clause (Fn1) holds: every rational number is p/q for some p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0}. But (Fn2) fails, because a rational number has many ways of being written as a fraction. Since 	frac{1}{2} = 	frac{2}{4}, both (	frac12, 1) and (	frac12, 2) lie in N, and 1 
e 2. The “rule” gives an output that depends on how the input is written, not on the input. A function may not do that, since its value is attached to the input itself. This is why definitions of the form “write x as …, then send it to …” must be checked for well-definedness, a check that returns in Chapter 4 for functions defined on classes. Here the repair is to fix the way of writing: let q_0 be the least q \in 
Z_{>0} with rq \in 
Z (such q exist, by the first sentence, so there is a least one by well-ordering, proved in Chapter 2; a least element is unique), and send r to r q_0. This is a function. Why this definition. Each clause has a job, and dropping one lets in the failures of @exm-not-a-function. Without (Fn1), a “function” could be undefined at some inputs, like 1/x at 0; then f(x) would not name anything, and statements “for every x \in X” about f(x) would lose their meaning. Without (Fn2), f(x) would not name one thing, and f(	frac12) in part (b) would be both 1 and 2. The graph replaces the rule because two rules can describe one function, and sets are compared by their elements. Why is the codomain part of the data? A relation is a set, so if a function were only its graph, two functions with the same graph would be equal (@def-set-equality), whatever target was declared. The graph of x \mapsto x^2 as a function [0, \infty) 	o 
R is the same set as its graph as a function [0, \infty) 	o [0, \infty). But these should be different functions, because the second reaches every point of its target and the first does not: this is the property called surjectivity below, and an example later in this section shows it changing with the codomain. Recording the codomain in the pair (G, Y) keeps the two apart. Many books take the same convention, some without saying so. A formula is not yet a function. “The function 1/x” names no function until a domain and a codomain are given, and the domain must be chosen so that (Fn1) holds: x \mapsto 1/x is a function 
R \setminus \{0\} 	o 
R, and there is no function 
R 	o 
R given by this formula. Likewise \sqrt{x} makes sense on [0, \infty) and not on 
R. When you meet “let f(x) = \dots”, ask first where x lives and where f(x) is meant to lie. Which of these relations on \{1, 2, 3\} are graphs of functions \{1, 2, 3\} 	o \{1, 2, 3\}: \{ (1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 2) \}, \{ (1, 1), (2, 2) \}, \{ (1, 3), (2, 1), (3, 2), (2, 3) \}? For each that is not, name the clause that fails. The first is a function: the constant function with value 2. The second fails (Fn1) at 3, which has no output. The third fails (Fn2) at 2, which has the two outputs 1 and 3. When are two functions equal? A function is a pair (G, Y), so two functions are equal when their graphs are equal and their codomains are equal. In practice we compare functions by their values, and the next result says that this is the same test. [Equality of Functions] Let f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon X' 	o Y' be functions. Then f = g if and only if X = X', Y = Y', and f(x) = g(x) for every x \in X. Write f = (G, Y) and g = (G', Y'). The characteristic property of pairs splits f = g into “same graph” and “same codomain”. Two graphs are equal when they have the same elements, and by (\ast\ast) an element of a graph is a pair (x, f(x)); so “same graph” is “same inputs, same outputs”. Write f = (G, Y) and g = (G', Y'), as in @def-function. (\Rightarrow) Suppose f = g. By the characteristic property of pairs (@def-ordered-pair), G = G' and Y = Y'. The domain is determined by the graph, as the set of first coordinates of its elements, so X = X'. Let x \in X. By (\ast\ast), (x, f(x)) \in G = G', so (x, f(x)) \in g, and (\ast\ast) for g gives f(x) = g(x). (\Leftarrow) Suppose X = X', Y = Y', and f(x) = g(x) for every x \in X. We show G \subseteq G'. Let p \in G. Since G \subseteq X 	imes Y, p = (x, y) with x \in X and y \in Y. By (\ast\ast), y = f(x), so y = g(x) by the hypothesis, and then p = (x, y) \in G' by (\ast\ast) for g. The same argument with f and g exchanged gives G' \subseteq G, so G = G' by @prp-subset-antisymmetric. Since also Y = Y', the characteristic property gives (G, Y) = (G', Y'), that is, f = g. So to show two functions equal, check three things: the same domain, the same codomain, and the same value at an arbitrary point. To show them different, one witness suffices: a point where the values differ, or a difference in domain or codomain. [Equal and unequal functions] Decide which of these functions are equal. (a) f, g \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = (x + 1)^2 - 2x - 1 and g(x) = x^2. (b) h, k \colon 
R 	o 
R, h(x) = \abs{x} and k(x) = \sqrt{x^2}. (c) s_1 \colon [0, \infty) 	o 
R and s_2 \colon [0, \infty) 	o [0, \infty), both given by x \mapsto x^2. (a) Equal. The domains are both 
R and the codomains both 
R. For every real x, (x + 1)^2 - 2x - 1 = x^2 + 2x + 1 - 2x - 1 = x^2. By @prp-function-equality, f = g: two rules, one function. (b) Equal. Same domain and codomain, and for every real x, \sqrt{x^2} = \abs{x}: the number \abs{x} is nonnegative and its square is x^2, and \sqrt{x^2} is by definition the nonnegative number with square x^2, which is unique by @fd1:thm-squares-order. (c) Not equal. They have the same domain, the same values, and even the same graph; but their codomains 
R and [0, \infty) are different sets (-1 is in one and not the other), so by @prp-function-equality s_1 
e s_2. Restriction. A function can be cut down to a smaller domain. For f \colon X 	o Y and A \subseteq X, the restriction of f to A is the function f|_A \colon A 	o Y, \qquad f|_A(a) \coloneqq f(a) , whose graph is G \cap (A 	imes Y): the pairs of f whose input lies in A. The squaring function 
R 	o 
R restricted to [0, \infty) is s_1 of part (c). The bar in f|_A is one of the uses of a vertical bar that the book’s colon-for-set-builder convention keeps free. Families, sequences, and the set of all functions Section 1.3 used families of sets (A_i)_{i \in I} and described them informally, as “a set A_i for each index i \in I”. We can now say exactly what a family is, once its members are known to lie in some set. A family of subsets of X indexed by I is a function I 	o \powerset{X}, i \mapsto A_i, with the power set \powerset{X} as the codomain the definition asks for. More generally, if S is a set whose elements are sets, a family of members of S indexed by I is a function I 	o S. A codomain must be named, because there is no set of all sets (@thm-russell). The value of a family at i is written A_i rather than A(i), and the family is written (A_i)_{i \in I}, in parentheses because it is indexed. A family is not the same thing as its set of values \{ A_i : i \in I \}: the family (A_i)_{i \in \{1, 2\}} with A_1 = A_2 = \{0\} has two indices and one value. In the same way, a sequence of real numbers (a_n)_{n \ge 1} is a function 
Z_{>0} 	o 
R, n \mapsto a_n, with the value at n written a_n. The sequence (1/n) is the function n \mapsto 1/n, and its set of values is \{ 1/n : n \ge 1 \}. Sequences are the main object of Analysis on the Real Line. Finally, all functions from X to Y form a set, written Y^X \coloneqq \{ f \in \powerset{X 	imes Y} 	imes \{Y\} : f 	ext{ is a function from } X 	ext{ to } Y \} . It is a set by the working rules of Section 1.2: every function X 	o Y is a pair (G, Y) with G \in \powerset{X 	imes Y}, so Y^X is the subset of \powerset{X 	imes Y} 	imes \{Y\} cut out by the condition of @def-function, and this product is a set by (W2), (W4), and (W5), so Y^X is a set by specification (W1). The letters are in this order because, for finite sets, Y^X has m^n elements when Y has m and X has n, as the next example suggests; counting is the business of Section 2.5. The set \{0, 1\}^{
N} of all sequences of zeros and ones, indexed from 0, plays a leading role in Chapter 3. [All functions between two small sets] List the elements of \{0, 1\}^{\{1, 2\}}, and say which are indicator functions of subsets of \{1, 2\}. A function f \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{0, 1\} is determined by its two values f(1) and f(2) (@prp-function-equality), and each may be 0 or 1. So there are four: f(1) f(2) graph indicator of ------ ------ ---------------------- -------------- 0 0 \{ (1, 0), (2, 0) \} \emptyset 0 1 \{ (1, 0), (2, 1) \} \{2\} 1 0 \{ (1, 1), (2, 0) \} \{1\} 1 1 \{ (1, 1), (2, 1) \} \{1, 2\} Every one of them is an indicator function: f = \ind_A for A = \{ x \in \{1, 2\} : f(x) = 1 \}. The four subsets of \{1, 2\} and the four functions correspond one to one. The correspondence at the end of the example, between subsets of X and functions X 	o \{0, 1\}, holds for every set X: send f to \{ x \in X : f(x) = 1 \} and A to \ind_A. So counting the subsets of a finite set and counting the functions from it to \{0, 1\} are one problem, which Section 2.5 solves. A game with five strings. A string of five symbols 0 or 1, such as 01101, is a function \{1, \dots, 5\} 	o \{0, 1\}: its value at k is its k-th symbol. One player lists five strings, say 00000, 11111, 01010, 10101, 00111; the other must write a string not on the list. Searching all 32 always works, but is there a rule that builds a missing string from any list of five in five steps? Try one. Chapter 3 comes back to this game. Which string is the indicator function of \{1, 4\} \subseteq \{1, \dots, 5\}? What is the value at 2 of the string 01100? The indicator of \{1, 4\} has value 1 at 1 and 4 and value 0 elsewhere, so it is the string 10010. The value of 01100 at 2 is its second symbol, 1. The empty set gives the degenerate cases, and they are worth settling now, since they are the test cases of many later statements. [Functions and the Empty Set] (a) For every set Y there is exactly one function from \emptyset to Y: the pair (\emptyset, Y), called the empty function. (b) If X is nonempty (it has an element), there is no function from X to \emptyset. (a) Existence. The empty relation satisfies \emptyset \subseteq \emptyset 	imes Y, since \emptyset is a subset of every set (Section 1.2). The condition of @def-function reads “for every x, if x \in \emptyset, then there is exactly one y \in Y with (x, y) \in \emptyset”. For each x the hypothesis x \in \emptyset is false, so the implication holds (@fd1:prp-vacuous-implication). So (\emptyset, Y) is a function from \emptyset to Y. Uniqueness. Let (G, Y) be any function from \emptyset to Y. Its graph satisfies G \subseteq \emptyset 	imes Y = \emptyset, by the mirror-image \emptyset law of @prp-product-set-laws. So an element of G would be an element of \emptyset; G has no elements, and G = \emptyset by @prp-empty-set-unique. Hence (G, Y) = (\emptyset, Y). (b) Let x_0 \in X, and suppose f \colon X 	o \emptyset were a function. By (Fn1) there would be y \in \emptyset with (x_0, y) \in f; but \emptyset has no elements. So there is no such function [ulename{
eg I}]. In the notation Y^X: the set Y^{\emptyset} has exactly one element for every Y, including Y = \emptyset; and \emptyset^X = \emptyset whenever X is nonempty. The empty function \emptyset 	o Y returns in Section 1.6 as the witness that a hypothesis there cannot be dropped. Composition Two functions can be applied one after the other when the outputs of the first are inputs of the second. Temperature in degrees Celsius, as a function of the day, followed by the conversion to degrees Fahrenheit, gives temperature in Fahrenheit as a function of the day. Composition Let f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon Y 	o Z be functions, the codomain of f being the domain of g. Their composite is the function g \circ f \colon X 	o Z, \qquad (g \circ f)(x) \coloneqq g(f(x)) , read “g after f”. This is a function by the remark on formulas: for x \in X, the value f(x) lies in Y, the domain of g, so g(f(x)) makes sense, and it lies in Z. Its graph is \{ (x, z) \in X 	imes Z : z = g(f(x)) \}. The order of the letters is the order of the formula g(f(x)), which is the reverse of the order in which the functions act: f acts first. [The order of composition matters] Let f, g \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x. Compute g \circ f and f \circ g, and decide whether they are equal. By @def-composition, (g \circ f)(x) = g(x + 1) = 2x + 2 and (f \circ g)(x) = f(2x) = 2x + 1. At x = 0 the values are 2 and 1, so by @prp-function-equality g \circ f 
e f \circ g. In words: “add one, then double” is not “double, then add one”. (In fact the two composites differ at every x, since 2x + 2 
e 2x + 1; one point already suffices.) Composition can also fail to be defined in one order only. For f \colon \{1, 2\} 	o 
R and g \colon 
R 	o 
R, the composite g \circ f \colon \{1, 2\} 	o 
R is defined, and f \circ g is not: g’s outputs are real numbers, and f accepts only 1 and 2. Composition is not commutative, but it is associative, and the identity functions do nothing. [Composition Is Associative] Let f \colon X 	o Y, g \colon Y 	o Z, and h \colon Z 	o W be functions. Then h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f , and f \circ \id_X = f = \id_Y \circ f. Both sides of the first equation are functions from X to W, by @def-composition. For x \in X, applying @def-composition twice on each side gives  igl(h \circ (g \circ f) igr)(x) = h igl((g \circ f)(x) igr) = h(g(f(x))) = (h \circ g)(f(x)) =  igl((h \circ g) \circ f igr)(x) . So the two functions agree at every point, and they are equal by @prp-function-equality. Likewise f \circ \id_X and \id_Y \circ f are functions from X to Y with values f(\id_X(x)) = f(x) and \id_Y(f(x)) = f(x), so both equal f. Because of associativity, we write h \circ g \circ f without brackets: every way of bracketing gives the same function, x \mapsto h(g(f(x))). For f, g \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = x^2 and g(x) = x - 3, compute (g \circ f)(2) and (f \circ g)(2). (g \circ f)(2) = g(4) = 1 and (f \circ g)(2) = f(-1) = 1. The values agree at this point, but the functions are different: at x = 0, (g \circ f)(0) = -3 and (f \circ g)(0) = 9. Agreement at one point proves nothing about equality; disagreement at one point proves inequality. Injective, surjective, bijective Two questions can be asked of any function f \colon X 	o Y, and much of mathematics turns on them. First: can we recover the input from the output, or can two different inputs give the same output? Second: is every point of the codomain an output? The first question is about how f treats X; the second is about how it covers Y. Injective functions An injective function never sends two different inputs to the same output. [Injective] A function f \colon X 	o Y is injective (an injection, or one-to-one) if, for all x_1, x_2 \in X, f(x_1) = f(x_2) implies x_1 = x_2. In symbols:  orall x_1 \in X \ \  orall x_2 \in X \ \  igl( f(x_1) = f(x_2) 	o x_1 = x_2  igr) . In words: if two inputs give the same output, they were the same input. By @fd1:prp-contrapositive, the definition gives the contrapositive form  orall x_1 \in X \ \  orall x_2 \in X \ \  igl( x_1
