Z. The pair (-k, k) lies in 
Z 	imes 
Z, and 2(-k) + 3k = k. (The scrap-paper search: 3 - 2 = 1, so multiply that solution of 2m + 3n = 1 by k.) (d) False. The witness is 1. For all integers m and n, 2m + 4n = 2(m + 2n) is even, and 1 is odd; no integer is both (@thm-even-or-odd). So 2m + 4n 
e 1. (e) True. First, the formula is a function into [-4, \infty): x^2 + 4x = (x + 2)^2 - 4 \ge -4. Injective: let x_1, x_2 \ge -2 with x_1^2 + 4x_1 = x_2^2 + 4x_2. Then (x_1 + 2)^2 = (x_2 + 2)^2, and both bases are \ge 0, so x_1 + 2 = x_2 + 2 by @fd1:thm-squares-order (used twice, as in @exm-square-three-ways (b)), and x_1 = x_2. Surjective: let y \ge -4 and put x \coloneqq -2 + \sqrt{y + 4}, defined since y + 4 \ge 0. Then x \ge -2, and x^2 + 4x = (x + 2)^2 - 4 = (y + 4) - 4 = y. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: composites] Let f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon Y 	o Z be functions. 1. Prove that if g \circ f is injective, then f is injective. 2. Give an example in which g \circ f is injective and g is not injective, and check both claims. (a) Suppose g \circ f is injective. Let x_1, x_2 \in X with f(x_1) = f(x_2); we must show x_1 = x_2. Applying g to both sides gives g(f(x_1)) = g(f(x_2)), because a function gives equal outputs at equal inputs. By @def-composition, this says (g \circ f)(x_1) = (g \circ f)(x_2). Since g \circ f is injective, x_1 = x_2. So f is injective. (b) Let X = \{1\}, Y = \{1, 2\}, Z = \{1\}; let f(1) = 1, and let g \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{1\} be the constant function g(1) = g(2) = 1. Then g \circ f \colon \{1\} 	o \{1\} is injective, because its domain has only one element: if x_1, x_2 \in \{1\}, then x_1 = 1 = x_2. And g is not injective: g(1) = g(2) with 1 
e 2. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: fixes arbitrary x_1, x_2 \in X with f(x_1) = f(x_2) and states the goal x_1 = x_2. - 2: applies g to both sides, with the reason that a function gives equal outputs at equal inputs. - 3: rewrites the result as an equation of values of g \circ f and invokes the injectivity of g \circ f. - 3: an example with explicit sets and functions, and both claims checked: g \circ f injective, and two different points with the same value under g. Fatal errors (0 for the step): assuming g is injective; starting from x_1 = x_2 and deriving f(x_1) = f(x_2) (the converse, entry (N5) of Logic and Proof, Chapter 8’s catalogue); an example in which g \circ f is not defined because the codomain of f is not the domain of g. A proof by contrapositive (from x_1 
e x_2, g \circ f injective gives g(f(x_1)) 
e g(f(x_2)), hence f(x_1) 
e f(x_2), since equal values of f would give equal values of g) earns full marks: 2 points for fixing x_1 
e x_2 and the goal, 3 for the use of the injectivity of g \circ f, and 2 for the step from g(f(x_1)) 
e g(f(x_2)) to f(x_1) 
e f(x_2). [C2: When the composite is a bijection] Let f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon Y 	o Z be functions. 1. Deduce from @exr-functions-c1 and @exr-functions-b2 that if g \circ f is bijective, then f is injective and g is surjective. 2. Give an example in which g \circ f is bijective and neither f nor g is bijective. (a) Suppose g \circ f is bijective. Then g \circ f is injective, so f is injective by part (a) of @exr-functions-c1. And g \circ f is surjective, so g is surjective by the proof put in order in @exr-functions-b2. (b) Take the functions of @exr-functions-c1 (b): f \colon \{1\} 	o \{1, 2\}, f(1) = 1, and g \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{1\}, g(1) = g(2) = 1. Then g \circ f \colon \{1\} 	o \{1\} sends 1 to 1, so g \circ f = \id_{\{1\}} by @prp-function-equality, which is bijective. But f is not surjective, since 2 is not an output; and g is not injective, since g(1) = g(2). So neither is bijective. Part (a) is sharp: it gives exactly the half of each property that survives, and this example shows that the other halves can fail together.

title: 1.6 Left, Right and Two-Sided Inverses
content:
Left, Right and Two-Sided Inverses Section 1.5 sorted functions by two questions. Does f ever send two different inputs to the same output? Does f reach every point of its codomain? The answers were the words injective and surjective (@def-injective, @def-surjective). This section asks a question that sounds different: can the work of f be undone? It turns out that it asks the same two questions again, one for each side of f. Undoing f after it has acted forces f to be injective, and when X is non-empty injectivity is also enough. Undoing it before, so that f finishes the job, forces f to be surjective. The one new idea in the section is an inverse on one side; an inverse on both sides, written f^{-1}, is simply a map that is both. Throughout, f \colon X 	o Y is a function in the sense of @def-function, and composites are formed as in @def-composition: g \circ f is defined when the codomain of f is the domain of g, and (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)). Undoing a function Start with a function we can compute in our heads. Let d \colon 
N 	o 
N be the doubling map, d(n) = 2n. Suppose someone applies d to a secret number and tells us the result, say 14. We recover the secret by halving: it was 7. Halving undoes doubling. But halving is not quite a function from 
N to 
N: 7 has no half in 
N. If we want a function h \colon 
N 	o 
N that undoes d, we must give h a value at every odd number as well. Those values do not matter for the undoing, because d never produces an odd number. Any choice will do. So one answer is h(m) \coloneqq  egin{cases} m/2 & 	ext{if } m 	ext{ is even}, \ 1 & 	ext{if } m 	ext{ is odd}, \end{cases} and another is h'(m) \coloneqq m/2 for even m and h'(m) \coloneqq m for odd m. Both are functions 
N 	o 
N: every m \in 
N is even or odd and not both (@thm-even-or-odd), and an even m is 2k for exactly one k \in 
N, which is m/2. Both undo d: for every n \in 
N, the number 2n is even, so h(d(n)) = h(2n) =  rac{2n}{2} = n, and the same computation holds for h'. In the language of composition, h \circ d = \id_{
N} and h' \circ d = \id_{
N}. Now try to undo in the other order. Is there a function k \colon 
N 	o 
N with d \circ k = \id_{
N}, so that d undoes k? Such a k would give d(k(1)) = 1, that is 2k(1) = 1, and 1 is odd, not twice a natural number. So there is no such k. The obstacle is visible: 1 is not in the range of d, so no input to d, however chosen, comes out as 1. Two things happened here, and they are the whole section in miniature. Undoing d afterwards was possible, in more than one way, and the reason is that d loses no information: different inputs give different outputs. Undoing it beforehand was impossible, and the reason is that d misses a point of its codomain. The two sides behave differently, so they get two names. Left and right inverses A left inverse undoes f after it acts; a right inverse is undone by f. Left and Right Inverses Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function, and let g \colon Y 	o X be a function in the opposite direction. 1. g is a left inverse of f if g \circ f = \id_X, that is, g(f(x)) = x for every x \in X. 2. g is a right inverse of f if f \circ g = \id_Y, that is, f(g(y)) = y for every y \in Y. In words: a left inverse is written on the left of f in the composite, and the composite g \circ f does nothing to points of X. A right inverse is written on the right, and f \circ g does nothing to points of Y. The two phrasings in each clause say the same thing. Two functions X 	o X are equal exactly when they agree at every point (@prp-function-equality), and g \circ f and \id_X have the same domain and codomain X; so g \circ f = \id_X means (g \circ f)(x) = \id_X(x) for every x \in X, which is g(f(x)) = x. The phrase “g is a left inverse of f” and the phrase “f is a right inverse of g” say the same thing: both say g \circ f = \id_X. Which word applies depends on which function we are talking about. Check the definition against the doubling map. With d(n) = 2n on 
N, the functions h and h' above are left inverses of d: the composite h \circ d sends every n back to n. And d has no right inverse, because clause (b) fails at the single point y = 1. For a right inverse the “for every y \in Y” is the demanding part: one bad y is enough to rule it out. [Left inverses on small sets] Let X = \{1, 2\}, Y = \{1, 2, 3\}, and e \colon X 	o Y, e(1) = 1, e(2) = 2: the inclusion of X into Y. 1. Show that g \colon Y 	o X with g(1) = 1, g(2) = 2, g(3) = 2 is a left inverse of e, and that e is a right inverse of g. 2. Is g a right inverse of e? 3. Let c \colon X 	o Y be constant, c(1) = c(2) = 3. Does c have a left inverse? (a) Clause (a) of @def-left-right-inverse asks for g(e(x)) = x at each of the two points of X: g(e(1)) = g(1) = 1 and g(e(2)) = g(2) = 2. So g \circ e = \id_X, and g is a left inverse of e. Read with the roles exchanged, the same equation g \circ e = \id_X is clause (b) for g \colon Y 	o X and e \colon X 	o Y: e is a right inverse of g. (b) No. Clause (b) would need e(g(y)) = y for every y \in Y, and at y = 3 we get e(g(3)) = e(2) = 2 
e 3. The equation e \circ g = \id_Y fails at one point, which is enough. (c) No. A left inverse g would need g(c(1)) = 1 and g(c(2)) = 2, that is g(3) = 1 and g(3) = 2. A function has one value at 3, and 1 
e 2. The information “which input was it” is gone once both inputs land on 3, and nothing applied afterwards can bring it back. Part (c) is the degenerate case of the example, and it is the one to remember. A left inverse must recover x from f(x), so it cannot exist when two inputs share an output. Part (b) shows the other side: g undoes e, but e does not undo g, because e never produces 3. A left inverse need not be a right inverse. For the doubling map d(n) = 2n on 
N and its left inverse h above, h(d(n)) = n for every n, but d(h(1)) = d(1) = 2 
e 1. The equation h \circ d = \id_{
N} says nothing about d \circ h: composition is not commutative (Section 1.5), and here the two composites are different functions. Let s \colon 
N 	o 
N be the successor map, s(n) = n + 1. Does s have a left inverse? Does it have a right inverse? It has a left inverse, for instance p(m) \coloneqq m - 1 for m \ge 1 and p(0) \coloneqq 0. This is a function 
N 	o 
N, since m - 1 \in 
N when m \ge 1, and p(s(n)) = p(n + 1) = n because n + 1 \ge 1. It has no right inverse: a right inverse k \colon 
N 	o 
N of s would need s(k(0)) = 0, that is k(0) + 1 = 0, which no k(0) \in 
N satisfies. The number 0 is not reached by s. A left inverse exists exactly for injective functions The examples point to a pattern. The doubling map, the inclusion e, and the successor map are injective, and each has a left inverse. The constant map c is not injective, and it has none. Here is the pattern as a theorem. Its hypothesis X 
e \emptyset looks like a technicality; after the proof we will see that it is not. We need the range of f from Section 1.5, and from now on we write it as f(X): f(X) = \{ y \in Y : f(x) = y 	ext{ for some } x \in X \}. Section 1.7 extends this notation to the image of any subset of X. [Left Inverses and Injectivity] Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function. 1. If f has a left inverse, then f is injective. 2. If X 
e \emptyset and f is injective, then f has a left inverse. Consequently, if X 
e \emptyset, then f has a left inverse if and only if f is injective. Part (a) carries no hypothesis on X, on purpose: the last theorem of this section uses it for every X, the empty set included. The hypothesis X 
e \emptyset sits in (b) only, where it is used. As in @prp-empty-function (b), “X 
e \emptyset” is read as “X is non-empty: it has an element”, and the proof uses it in that form. (From an element, X 
e \emptyset follows at once, since the empty set has none (@def-empty-set). The passage back, from “X is not the empty set” to “X has an element”, is the classical law “not all fail, so one holds” of Logic and Proof, Chapter 6; reading the hypothesis as “has an element” avoids it.) [Scratch work] For (a), start from the goal. Injectivity asks: from f(x_1) = f(x_2), get x_1 = x_2. A left inverse g turns each f(x) back into x, so apply g to both sides. For (b), build g point by point, the way halving was extended to the odd numbers. ① A point y of the range has a preimage, and injectivity says it has only one; let g(y) be that one. ② A point outside the range has no preimage; send it to a fixed point x_0 \in X. This is where X 
e \emptyset is needed. ③ Check that ① and ② together define a function, and that g(f(x)) = x. ① and ② are the two cases of a proof by cases on y \in f(X) (@exm-method-cases). Laid out as givens and goal, the plan for (b) reads: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal --------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------- f injective, x_0 \in X g \colon Y 	o X with g(f(x)) = x for all x \in X Case y \in f(X): y = f(x), with x unique by injectivity g(y) \coloneqq that x Case y 
otin f(X): nothing is forced g(y) \coloneqq x_0 g defined on all of Y check (Fn1), (Fn2); then g(f(x)) = x ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The last row is the gap: a recipe for g(y) is not yet a function, and the proof must show that the recipe gives every y exactly one value before it may use g at all. Before reading on: where is X 
e \emptyset used, and what would go wrong at that line if X were empty? (a) Let g \colon Y 	o X be a left inverse of f. Let x_1, x_2 \in X with f(x_1) = f(x_2). Since g is a function, equal inputs give equal outputs, so g(f(x_1)) = g(f(x_2)). By @def-left-right-inverse (a), g(f(x)) = x for every x \in X, so x_1 = g(f(x_1)) = g(f(x_2)) = x_2 . Since x_1 and x_2 were arbitrary, f is injective by @def-injective. (b) Suppose X 
e \emptyset and f is injective. Since X has an element, fix one and call it x_0 [ulename{\exists E}]. Let G be the subset of Y 	imes X given by specification (@def-set-builder): G \coloneqq \{\, (y, x) \in Y 	imes X :  igl(y \in f(X) 	ext{ and } f(x) = y igr) 	ext{ or }  igl(y 
otin f(X) 	ext{ and } x = x_0 igr) \,\}. We show that for every y \in Y there is exactly one x \in X with (y, x) \in G, by checking the two clauses (Fn1) (existence) and (Fn2) (uniqueness) into which Section 1.5 splits the condition of @def-function (@fd1:prp-unique-existence-use). Then G, with codomain X, is a function g \colon Y 	o X. Let y \in Y. Existence (Fn1). By excluded middle (@fd1:prp-excluded-middle), y \in f(X) or y 
otin f(X). Case 1: y \in f(X). Then f(x_1) = y for some x_1 \in X; name it x_1 [ulename{\exists E}]. The pair (y, x_1) satisfies the first alternative, so (y, x_1) \in G. Case 2: y 
otin f(X). Then (y, x_0) satisfies the second alternative, so (y, x_0) \in G. In either case some x \in X has (y, x) \in G. Uniqueness (Fn2). Let x, x' \in X with (y, x) \in G and (y, x') \in G. Each pair satisfies one of the two alternatives. If both satisfy the first, then f(x) = y = f(x'), so x = x' because f is injective. If both satisfy the second, then x = x_0 = x'. If one satisfies the first and the other the second, then y \in f(X) and y 
otin f(X), a contradiction, so this case cannot occur. Hence x = x'. So g \colon Y 	o X is a function, and g(y) = x means (y, x) \in G. It remains to show g \circ f = \id_X. Let x \in X. Then f(x) \in f(X), with x as the witness [ulename{\exists I}], and f(x) = f(x), so the pair (f(x), x) satisfies the first alternative: (f(x), x) \in G, that is, g(f(x)) = x. The functions g \circ f and \id_X have domain and codomain X and agree at every point, so they are equal by @prp-function-equality. Hence g is a left inverse of f. The last sentence of the theorem combines (a) and (b). This proves the theorem. Look at where each hypothesis did its work. Injectivity was used once, in the uniqueness step: it is what makes “the preimage of y” a single point. The hypothesis X 
e \emptyset was used once, in the first line of (b), to have a point x_0 for the second alternative. The case split on y \in f(X) used excluded middle, a classical step: the proof does not tell us, for a given y, which case we are in. Neither hypothesis of (b) can be dropped. - Without injectivity. The constant map c of @exm-left-inverses-small-sets (c) sends 1 and 2 to 3, and it has no left inverse. In the proof, the uniqueness step breaks: (3, 1) and (3, 2) both lie in G, so G is not a function. - Without X 
e \emptyset. The empty function \emptyset 	o \{1\} is injective: the condition “for all x_1, x_2 \in \emptyset …” holds vacuously. A left inverse would be a function \{1\} 	o \emptyset, and there is none, since the point 1 would need a value in the empty set (@prp-empty-function). In the proof, the first line fails: there is no x_0 to fix, and the point 1, which lies outside the range, has nowhere to go. The proof of (b) builds an object and then checks it. The same pattern serves for many existence claims: build the object explicitly, then check it. [Method: construct and verify] Template. To prove that an object with property P exists: on scrap paper, find where its values are forced and where they are free; define it explicitly, by cases if need be; check that it is the kind of object claimed (for a function, (Fn1) and (Fn2), with values in the codomain); then verify P. For an “if and only if”, two directions: one uses the object, the other builds it. When to use it. Existence of an inverse, a function or a set with stated properties. The usual failure. Verifying P for an object never shown to exist or to be well defined, (N14) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue; and a definition that depends on how an input is written (@exm-not-a-function (b)). Construct a left inverse of u \colon 
N 	o 
N, u(n) = 2n + 1, verify it, and say where its values are free. Let g(m) \coloneqq (m - 1)/2 for odd m and g(m) \coloneqq 0 for even m. This is a function 
N 	o 
N: every m \in 
N is even or odd and not both (@thm-even-or-odd), so exactly one clause applies, and for odd m \ge 1 the value (m - 1)/2 lies in 
N. For every n \in 
N, the number u(n) = 2n + 1 is odd, so g(u(n)) = (2n + 1 - 1)/2 = n. The values at even m are free: no even number is of the form u(n), so the equation g(u(n)) = n never looks at them. The proof of (b) describes g explicitly in terms of f and x_0, so on a small example the construction can be run by hand. [Running the construction] Let f \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{a, b, c\} be given by f(1) = a and f(2) = c, where a, b, c are three different objects. Run the proof of @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (b) with x_0 = 1, then with x_0 = 2. How many left inverses does f have? First the hypotheses: \{1, 2\} 
e \emptyset, and f is injective because its two inputs have the different outputs a and c. The range is f(\{1, 2\}) = \{a, c\}. With x_0 = 1: the points a and c of the range go back to their unique preimages, g(a) = 1 and g(c) = 2. The point b lies outside the range, so g(b) = x_0 = 1. Check: g(f(1)) = g(a) = 1 and g(f(2)) = g(c) = 2, so g \circ f = \id_{\{1, 2\}}. With x_0 = 2: g'(a) = 1, g'(c) = 2 as before, and g'(b) = 2. The same check shows g' \circ f = \id_{\{1, 2\}}. These are all the left inverses. Any left inverse k must satisfy k(a) = k(f(1)) = 1 and k(c) = k(f(2)) = 2, so its values on the range are forced. Its value at b is free, and there are two points of \{1, 2\} to choose from. So f has exactly 2 left inverses, and the construction with x_0 = 1 and with x_0 = 2 produces both. The example shows that a left inverse is not unique in general. The values on the range are forced by the equation g(f(x)) = x; the values off the range are free, and they may go to any point of X. (They are free but not always varied: if X has only one point, there is only one place to send them.) A right inverse forces surjectivity The doubling map has no right inverse because it misses 1. The same obstacle works for every function. [Right Inverses Give Surjectivity] Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function. If f has a right inverse, then f is surjective. Let g \colon Y 	o X be a right inverse of f, and let y \in Y. By @def-left-right-inverse (b), f(g(y)) = y. So x \coloneqq g(y) is an element of X with f(x) = y [ulename{\exists I}]. Since y was arbitrary, f is surjective by @def-surjective. The proof names its witness, as in @exm-method-surjectivity, with the right inverse supplying x \coloneqq g(y): the right inverse is a rule that hands us, for each y, a preimage g(y). No hypothesis on X or Y is needed. If Y = \emptyset, then f is surjective vacuously; and X = \emptyset as well, since there is no function from a non-empty set to \emptyset (@prp-empty-function). Right inverses are not unique either. Here is a small surjection with several. [All right inverses of a small surjection] Let q \colon \{1, 2, 3, 4\} 	o \{0, 1\} send each number to 0 if it is even and to 1 if it is odd: q(1) = 1, q(2) = 0, q(3) = 1, q(4) = 0. Find all right inverses of q. A right inverse is a function k \colon \{0, 1\} 	o \{1, 2, 3, 4\} with q(k(0)) = 0 and q(k(1)) = 1. The first condition says that k(0) is a preimage of 0, so k(0) \in \{2, 4\}. The second says k(1) \in \{1, 3\}. The two choices are independent, and each combination gives a function \{0, 1\} 	o \{1, 2, 3, 4\} satisfying both conditions. So q has exactly 4 right inverses: (k(0), k(1)) = (2, 1), \quad (2, 3), \quad (4, 1), \quad (4, 3). Each one picks one preimage of each point of the codomain. By @prp-right-inverse-surjective, the fact that one exists shows again that q is surjective. Does every surjection have a right inverse? @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective went both ways: for X 
e \emptyset, a left inverse exists exactly when f is injective. Does @prp-right-inverse-surjective go both ways too? Suppose f \colon X 	o Y is surjective. Must f have a right inverse? Read what a right inverse must do. For every y \in Y, g(y) must be a preimage of y: an x with f(x) = y. Surjectivity promises that each y has at least one preimage. It does not say which, and there may be many. So the right inverse must choose one preimage for every y, all at once, and assemble the choices into one set of pairs. Now look at what our rules can do. - One y. For a single y, the statement “there is x \in X with f(x) = y” lets us name a preimage by \existsE (Logic and Proof, Section 5.6). That is one choice, made inside one proof. - Finitely many y. For a particular finite Y = \{y_1, \dots, y_n\}, with n a fixed number, we can apply \existsE n times, once for each point, and write down the n pairs. (To get this for every finite Y at once, with n arbitrary, one inducts on n, @fd1:ax-induction.) @exm-right-inverses-finite picked one preimage per point in the same spirit, by listing the preimage sets and choosing from them. - Infinitely many y. A proof is a finite object. It cannot contain one \existsE for each of infinitely many points, and no rule of Logic and Proof, Chapter 5 makes infinitely many choices in one step. Sometimes the difficulty does not arise, because a rule picks the preimage. The squaring map from 
R onto [0, \infty) is surjective, and each y \ge 0 has the preimages \sqrt y and -\sqrt y. The rule “take the non-negative one” defines g(y) \coloneqq \sqrt y, and g is a right inverse: (\sqrt y)^2 = y. Likewise the projection 
N 	imes 
N 	o 
N, (m, n) \mapsto m, is surjective, and m \mapsto (m, 1) is a right inverse. In each case the specification of @def-set-builder writes g down, because the rule names one preimage for each y. For a surjection with no such rule, nothing proved so far produces a right inverse. The missing ingredient is a new principle of set formation, which says that a choice of one element from each set of a family can be made. Chapter 3 states it and proves, with it, that every surjection has a right inverse. Until then, we use only the implication proved above: a right inverse gives surjectivity. Two-sided inverses The two halves meet in a single fact about composition: when a function has an inverse on each side, the two inverses coincide. [Left and Right Inverses Agree] Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function. If g \colon Y 	o X is a left inverse of f and h \colon Y 	o X is a right inverse of f, then g = h. As in the uniqueness half of @exm-method-uniqueness, two names, shown equal by computing g \circ f \circ h two ways; consequently a two-sided inverse is unique. By @prp-composition-associative (associativity and the identity laws), g = g \circ \id_Y = g \circ (f \circ h) = (g \circ f) \circ h = \id_X \circ h = h , where the first and last equalities are the identity laws, the second uses that h is a right inverse, the third is associativity, and the fourth uses that g is a left inverse. This proves the proposition. The chain is worth reading twice. The composite g \circ f \circ h can be simplified from either end: the left pair g \circ f collapses to \id_X, the right pair f \circ h collapses to \id_Y. Associativity says both simplifications are of the same function. [Inverse Function] Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function. A function g \colon Y 	o X is a two-sided inverse, or an inverse, of f if it is both a left inverse and a right inverse of f: g \circ f = \id_X \quad	ext{and}\quad f \circ g = \id_Y . A function with an inverse is invertible. Its inverse is unique: if g and g' are both inverses of f, then g is a left inverse and g' a right inverse, so g = g' by @prp-inverse-unique. We call it the inverse of f and write it f^{-1} \colon Y 	o X. In words: f^{-1} undoes f on both sides. It sends f(x) back to x, and f sends f^{-1}(y) back to y. The article “the” was earned by @prp-inverse-unique; without it, f^{-1} could name several functions, as “a left inverse” does. The definition is symmetric in f and f^{-1}. The two equations that say f^{-1} is an inverse of f also say that f is an inverse of f^{-1}. So f^{-1} is invertible, and by uniqueness its inverse is f: (f^{-1})^{-1} = f . This is the pattern for every identity about inverses: to show that some function is the inverse of f, check the two equations of @def-inverse-function, and uniqueness does the rest. [Inverses found and checked] Show that each function is invertible by finding its inverse and checking both composites. 1. a \colon 
R 	o 
R, a(x) = 3x - 2. 2. r \colon (0, \infty) 	o (0, \infty), r(x) = 1/x. 3. s \colon 
R 	o 
R, s(x) = x\abs{x}, that is, s(x) = x^2 for x \ge 0 and s(x) = -x^2 for x < 0. Idea. Solve y = f(x) for x to find a candidate, then check both equations of @def-inverse-function. The solving is scratch work; the two checks are the proof. (a) Solving y = 3x - 2 gives x = (y + 2)/3. Let b(y) \coloneqq (y + 2)/3, a function 
R 	o 
R. For every x \in 
R, b(a(x)) = (3x - 2 + 2)/3 = x, and for every y \in 
R, a(b(y)) = 3 \cdot (y + 2)/3 - 2 = y. So b = a^{-1}. (b) For x > 0, 1/x > 0, so r does map (0, \infty) to (0, \infty). Here r(r(x)) = 1/(1/x) = x for every x > 0. This one equation is both checks at once, with r in the roles of f and g. So r^{-1} = r: the function is its own inverse. (c) Solve by cases on the sign of y, since s(x) has the sign of x. For y \ge 0 the candidate is \sqrt y; for y < 0 it is -\sqrt{-y}. Let t(y) \coloneqq  egin{cases} \sqrt{y} & 	ext{if } y \ge 0, \ -\sqrt{-y} & 	ext{if } y < 0. \end{cases} First check, t(s(x)) = x, by cases on x. If x \ge 0, then s(x) = x^2 \ge 0, so t(s(x)) = \sqrt{x^2} = x, the non-negative square root of x^2 being x. If x < 0, then s(x) = -x^2 < 0, so t(s(x)) = -\sqrt{x^2} = -(-x) = x, since the non-negative square root of x^2 is -x. Second check, s(t(y)) = y, by cases on y. If y \ge 0, then t(y) = \sqrt y \ge 0, so s(t(y)) = (\sqrt y)^2 = y. If y < 0, then t(y) = -\sqrt{-y} < 0, so s(t(y)) = -(\sqrt{-y})^2 = -(-y) = y. Both checks hold, so t = s^{-1}. Notice that each check needs its own case split: the first splits on the sign of the input x, the second on the sign of y. Give the inverse of f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = 2x^3 - 5, and verify both composites. Solving y = 2x^3 - 5 gives x^3 = (y + 5)/2. Let g(y) \coloneqq \sqrt[3]{(y + 5)/2}, with the real cube root, which exists and is unique for every real number (a school fact). Then f(g(y)) = 2 \cdot (y + 5)/2 - 5 = y for every y \in 
R, and g(f(x)) = \sqrt[3]{(2x^3 - 5 + 5)/2} = \sqrt[3]{x^3} = x for every x \in 
R. So g = f^{-1}. Now the theorem that connects inverses with the words of Section 1.5. [Bijections Are the Invertible Functions] A function f \colon X 	o Y is bijective if and only if it has a two-sided inverse. (\Leftarrow) is already proved in two halves: an inverse is a left inverse, which gives injectivity by @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (a), and a right inverse, which gives surjectivity by @prp-right-inverse-surjective. Neither half asks anything of X. (\Rightarrow) looks like the open question of the last subsection, since we must pick a preimage of every y. But for a bijection there is nothing to pick. Surjectivity gives each y a preimage and injectivity says there is only one. So the set of pairs (y, x) with f(x) = y already has the  orall\exists! property of @def-function. The proof is @exm-method-construct-and-verify with every value forced: define g by this set of pairs, check that it is a function, then verify the two equations. (\Leftarrow) Let g be a two-sided inverse of f. Then g is a left inverse of f, so f is injective by @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (a); and g is a right inverse, so f is surjective by @prp-right-inverse-surjective. Hence f is bijective by @def-bijective. (\Rightarrow) Let f be bijective, and let G \coloneqq \{ (y, x) \in Y 	imes X : f(x) = y \}, a subset of Y 	imes X by specification (@def-set-builder). Let y \in Y. Since f is surjective, there is x \in X with f(x) = y, so some x has (y, x) \in G. If (y, x) \in G and (y, x') \in G, then f(x) = y = f(x'), so x = x' since f is injective. So G satisfies (Fn1) and (Fn2) (@fd1:prp-unique-existence-use): for every y \in Y there is exactly one x \in X with (y, x) \in G, and G with codomain X is a function g \colon Y 	o X (@def-function). By construction, g(y) = x holds exactly when f(x) = y. Now let y \in Y. Then g(y) = x for the x with (y, x) \in G, so f(g(y)) = y. And let x \in X. The pair (f(x), x) lies in G, since f(x) = f(x); so g(f(x)) = x. By @prp-function-equality, f \circ g = \id_Y and g \circ f = \id_X. So g is a two-sided inverse of f. This proves the theorem. Why does the inverse of a bijection need no fixed point x_0 and no case split? Every y \in Y has exactly one preimage: at least one because f is surjective, at most one because it is injective. So g(y) is forced at every point of Y. There is no point outside the range to send to an x_0, and no second case to split off. Compare the two constructions of this section. The left inverse of @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (b) needed a fixed point x_0 and a case split by excluded middle, because some y have no preimage. The inverse of a bijection needs neither. Every y has exactly one preimage, so the definition “g(y) is the preimage of y” names one element for each y without any choosing. This is why no new principle is needed here, while the open question about surjections needs one. The difference between the two is exactly the difference between “exactly one” and “at least one”. A bijection f \colon X 	o Y pairs each element of X with exactly one element of Y, and its inverse pairs them back. Section 2.5 takes the existence of such a pairing as the definition of “X and Y have the same size”. The theorem also covers the degenerate case. A function f \colon \emptyset 	o Y is surjective only if Y = \emptyset, since a point of Y would need a preimage in \emptyset. The empty function \emptyset 	o \emptyset is bijective, and it is its own inverse: both composites are the empty function \emptyset 	o \emptyset, which is \id_\emptyset. The proof of (\Leftarrow) runs at X = \emptyset without change, because it cites only part (a) of @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective, which has no hypothesis on X. The notation f^{-1} is reserved, as a function, for a bijection f. For a function that is not bijective, “f^{-1} \colon Y 	o X” names nothing. Section 1.7 uses the symbol in a second way, f^{-1}(B) for a set B, which makes sense for every function; it shows that for a bijection the two readings give the same set. Do not write f^{-1} for a left inverse. The doubling map d has the two different left inverses h and h' of the first subsection, so “d^{-1}” would not say which one is meant. And neither is an inverse: d(h(1)) = 2 
e 1. The notation is earned by @prp-inverse-unique, which needs an inverse on both sides. Does x \mapsto x^3 from 
R to 
R have a two-sided inverse? Does x \mapsto x^2 from [0, \infty) to 
R? The first does: y \mapsto \sqrt[3]{y}, the real cube root, which exists and is unique for every real y (a school fact). Indeed \sqrt[3]{x^3} = x and (\sqrt[3]{y})^3 = y. The second does not. It is injective (@exm-square-three-ways (b)), but it is not surjective, since -1 has no preimage; by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse it has no two-sided inverse. (It has left inverses, by @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective, for instance y \mapsto \sqrt y for y \ge 0 and y \mapsto 0 for y < 0.) What the section proved For a function f \colon X 	o Y, the section proved four facts and left one question open. - A left inverse makes f injective (@thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (a)). - If X 
e \emptyset, an injective f has a left inverse (@thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (b)). The empty function \emptyset 	o \{1\} shows that the hypothesis is needed. - A right inverse makes f surjective (@prp-right-inverse-surjective). - A two-sided inverse exists exactly when f is bijective (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse), and it is unique (@prp-inverse-unique). - Open: a surjective f has a right inverse. Chapter 3 proves it, with the new principle. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These parts are about @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective and its proof. 1. At which line of the proof of (b) is X 
e \emptyset used, and for what? 2. The proof shows that the set G is a function by proving two things about the case split into y \in f(X) and y 
otin f(X). What are they, and which step of the proof uses each? 3. Run the construction on f \colon \{1, 2, 3\} 	o \{1, 2, 3, 4\}, f(k) = k + 1, with x_0 = 3. Write out the left inverse g and check g \circ f = \id_{\{1, 2, 3\}}. 4. Give the idea of the proof of (b) in two sentences. 5. Let f \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{1\} be the only function between these sets. Which step of the proof of (b) fails for f, and why? (a) In the first line of (b): “fix one and call it x_0”. The point x_0 is the value g(y) for every y outside the range f(X); without it, the second alternative in the definition of G would have nothing to send such y to. (b) The two cases exhaust every y: by excluded middle, y \in f(X) or y 
otin f(X); this is used in the existence step. And they do not overlap: a y cannot satisfy both, since y \in f(X) and y 
otin f(X) contradict each other; this is used in the uniqueness step, to rule out a pair from each alternative. (Uniqueness inside the first case uses injectivity; inside the second, it is automatic.) (c) The hypotheses hold: \{1, 2, 3\} 
e \emptyset, and f is injective, since k + 1 = k' + 1 gives k = k'. The range is f(\{1, 2, 3\}) = \{2, 3, 4\}. On the range, g returns the unique preimage: g(2) = 1, g(3) = 2, g(4) = 3. The point 1 is outside the range, so g(1) = x_0 = 3. Check: g(f(1)) = g(2) = 1, g(f(2)) = g(3) = 2, g(f(3)) = g(4) = 3. So g \circ f = \id_{\{1, 2, 3\}}. (d) A point of the range has exactly one preimage, by injectivity, and g sends it there; a point outside the range is sent to a fixed point x_0 of the non-empty domain. Then g(f(x)) is the unique preimage of f(x), which is x. (e) The uniqueness step fails. The point y = 1 lies in the range and has the two preimages 1 and 2, so (1, 1) and (1, 2) both lie in G, and G is not a function. The step “f(x) = y = f(x'), so x = x'” needs injectivity, which this f lacks. (By part (a) of the theorem, f has no left inverse at all.) B. Practice [B1: Counting one-sided inverses] 1. Find all left inverses of f \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{1, 2, 3\}, f(k) = k. 2. Find all right inverses of g \colon \{1, 2, 3\} 	o \{1, 2\}, g(1) = g(2) = 1, g(3) = 2. (a) A left inverse h \colon \{1, 2, 3\} 	o \{1, 2\} must satisfy h(f(1)) = 1 and h(f(2)) = 2, that is h(1) = 1 and h(2) = 2. The point 3 is outside the range \{1, 2\}, so h(3) is free: 1 or 2. Each choice satisfies both equations. So there are exactly 2 left inverses: h(3) = 1 and h(3) = 2, with h(1) = 1, h(2) = 2 in both. (b) A right inverse k \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{1, 2, 3\} must satisfy g(k(1)) = 1 and g(k(2)) = 2. The preimages of 1 under g are 1 and 2, so k(1) \in \{1, 2\}; the only preimage of 2 is 3, so k(2) = 3. So there are exactly 2 right inverses: k(1) = 1 or k(1) = 2, with k(2) = 3 in both. [B2: The inverse of a composite] Let f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon Y 	o Z be bijections. Prove that g \circ f is invertible and that (g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}. Hint: check the two equations of @def-inverse-function for the candidate f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}. The candidate f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} \colon Z 	o X is defined, since g^{-1} \colon Z 	o Y and f^{-1} \colon Y 	o X exist by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. We check the two equations of @def-inverse-function, using @prp-composition-associative to regroup and for its identity laws k \circ \id = k = \id \circ k:  egin{aligned} (f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}) \circ (g \circ f) &= f^{-1} \circ (g^{-1} \circ g) \circ f = f^{-1} \circ \id_Y \circ f = f^{-1} \circ f = \id_X , \ (g \circ f) \circ (f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}) &= g \circ (f \circ f^{-1}) \circ g^{-1} = g \circ \id_Y \circ g^{-1} = g \circ g^{-1} = \id_Z . \end{aligned} So f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} is a two-sided inverse of g \circ f. By the uniqueness of inverses (@prp-inverse-unique, as in @def-inverse-function), it is the inverse: (g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}. Notice the order: to undo “first f, then g”, undo g first. [B3: A bijection between an interval and the line] Let h \colon (-1, 1) 	o 
R, h(x) = x/(1 - \abs{x}), and k \colon 
R 	o (-1, 1), k(y) = y/(1 + \abs{y}). Show that h and k are well defined (each denominator is non-zero, and k takes values in (-1, 1)), and that k is the inverse of h, by checking both composites by cases on the sign. Hence h is a bijection. Well defined. For x \in (-1, 1), \abs{x} < 1, so 1 - \abs{x} > 0. For y \in 
R, 1 + \abs{y} \ge 1 > 0, and \abs{k(y)} = \abs{y}/(1 + \abs{y}) < 1 because \abs{y} < 1 + \abs{y}; so k(y) \in (-1, 1). First check, k(h(x)) = x for x \in (-1, 1). If 0 \le x < 1, then h(x) = x/(1 - x) \ge 0, so k(h(x)) =  rac{x/(1 - x)}{1 + x/(1 - x)} =  rac{x/(1 - x)}{1/(1 - x)} = x . If -1 < x < 0, then \abs{x} = -x and h(x) = x/(1 + x) < 0, so \abs{h(x)} = -x/(1 + x) and k(h(x)) =  rac{x/(1 + x)}{1 - x/(1 + x)} =  rac{x/(1 + x)}{1/(1 + x)} = x . Second check, h(k(y)) = y for y \in 
R. If y \ge 0, then k(y) = y/(1 + y) \in [0, 1), so h(k(y)) =  rac{y/(1 + y)}{1 - y/(1 + y)} =  rac{y/(1 + y)}{1/(1 + y)} = y . If y < 0, then k(y) = y/(1 - y) \in (-1, 0), so \abs{k(y)} = -y/(1 - y) and h(k(y)) =  rac{y/(1 - y)}{1 + y/(1 - y)} =  rac{y/(1 - y)}{1/(1 - y)} = y . Both composites are identities, so k = h^{-1}, and h is a bijection by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement and refute each false one with a counterexample. 1. The function f \colon 
Z 	o 
Z, f(n) = n + 3, has a two-sided inverse. 2. The function f \colon 
N 	o 
N, f(n) = n + 3, has a right inverse. 3. The function f \colon 
N 	o 
N, f(n) = n + 3, has a left inverse. 4. For functions f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon Y 	o X, if g \circ f = \id_X and f \circ g 
e \id_Y, then f is not surjective. 5. Every function \{1, 2\} 	o \{1, 2, 3\} has a left inverse. (a) True. Let g \colon 
Z 	o 
Z, g(n) \coloneqq n - 3. For every n \in 
Z, g(f(n)) = (n + 3) - 3 = n and f(g(n)) = (n - 3) + 3 = n, so both composites are \id_{
Z} and g is a two-sided inverse (@def-inverse-function). (b) False. Every value is n + 3 \ge 3, so 0 is not a value and f is not surjective. By @prp-right-inverse-surjective, f has no right inverse. (c) True. Let g(m) \coloneqq m - 3 for m \ge 3 and g(m) \coloneqq 0 for m < 3. This is a function 
N 	o 
N: each m \in 
N falls under exactly one clause, and m - 3 \in 
N when m \ge 3. For every n \in 
N, f(n) = n + 3 \ge 3, so g(f(n)) = (n + 3) - 3 = n. The values at 0, 1, 2 are free; any choice in 
N works. (d) True. Suppose g \circ f = \id_X and f \circ g 
e \id_Y, and suppose, for a contradiction, that f is surjective. By @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (a), f is injective, since g is a left inverse; so f is bijective, and it has a two-sided inverse h by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. Then h is a right inverse of f and g a left inverse, so g = h by @prp-inverse-unique, and f \circ g = f \circ h = \id_Y, against the hypothesis. So f is not surjective. (e) False. The constant map c \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{1, 2, 3\} with value 1 has c(1) = c(2) and 1 
e 2, so it is not injective, and by @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (a) it has no left inverse. C. Going deeper [C1: One composite equal to the identity] Let f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon Y 	o X be functions with g \circ f = \id_X. 1. Prove that f is injective and g is surjective. 2. Show by an example that neither f nor g need be bijective. 3. Prove that if, in addition, f is surjective, then g = f^{-1}. [Hint 1] Read the equation g \circ f = \id_X twice: once as a statement about f, once as a statement about g. [Hint 2] For g: let x \in X; you need a point of Y that g sends to x. (a) The equation says that g is a left inverse of f, so f is injective by @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (a). The same equation says that f is a right inverse of g, so g is surjective by @prp-right-inverse-surjective. (Directly: for x \in X, the point f(x) \in Y satisfies g(f(x)) = x.) (b) Let f \colon \{1\} 	o \{1, 2\}, f(1) = 1, and g \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{1\}, g(1) = g(2) = 1. Then g(f(1)) = 1, so g \circ f = \id_{\{1\}}. But f is not surjective (2 has no preimage) and g is not injective (g(1) = g(2) with 1 
e 2), so neither is bijective. (c) If f is also surjective, it is bijective by (a), so f^{-1} exists by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, and it is in particular a right inverse of f. Also g is a left inverse of f. By @prp-inverse-unique, g = f^{-1}. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: f injective, from the left-inverse equation (citing @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (a) or arguing directly from f(x_1) = f(x_2)). - 2: g surjective, either by citing @prp-right-inverse-surjective (f is a right inverse of g) or directly, naming the witness f(x) for a given x \in X. - 3: an example with explicit sets and both failures checked (a point missed by f, two points identified by g). - 3: (c) obtains a right inverse of f (from bijectivity) and applies uniqueness of one-sided inverses, or checks f \circ g = \id_Y directly (for y = f(x), f(g(y)) = f(g(f(x))) = f(x) = y, using surjectivity to write y = f(x)). Fatal errors (0 for the step): assuming f \circ g = \id_Y in (a) or (c) without proof; in (c), writing f^{-1} before showing f bijective. [C2: When is a left inverse unique?] Let f \colon X 	o Y be injective, with X 
e \emptyset. 1. Prove that if f is surjective, or X has exactly one element, then f has exactly one left inverse. 2. Prove that if some y_1 \in Y is not in f(X), and X has two different elements x_0 
e x_1, then f has at least two different left inverses. 3. Let f \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{1, 2, 3, 4\}, f(k) = 2k. List all left inverses of f, and explain in one sentence why there are 2^2 = 4 of them. [Hint 1] For (a), a left inverse exists by @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (b); only “at most one” needs proof. For (b), run the construction of that proof twice. [Hint 2] For (a), let g and g' be left inverses of f. If f is surjective, write a given y \in Y as y = f(x) and compare g(y) with g'(y). (a) A left inverse exists by @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (b). For “at most one”, let g and g' be left inverses of f. Case 1: f is surjective. Then f is bijective (@def-bijective), so it has the inverse f^{-1} (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse), which is in particular a right inverse of f. By @prp-inverse-unique, g = f^{-1} and g' = f^{-1}, so g = g'. Case 2: X has exactly one element x_0. For every y \in Y, both g(y) and g'(y) are elements of X, so g(y) = x_0 = g'(y); hence g = g' by @prp-function-equality. In either case any two left inverses are equal, so f has exactly one. (b) Run the proof of @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (b) once with the fixed point x_0 and once with x_1; call the resulting left inverses g_0 and g_1. The point y_1 is outside the range, so the second alternative in the definition of G applies to it: g_0(y_1) = x_0 and g_1(y_1) = x_1. Since x_0 
e x_1, the functions g_0 and g_1 differ at y_1, so g_0 
e g_1. (c) The range is \{2, 4\}. A left inverse g \colon \{1, 2, 3, 4\} 	o \{1, 2\} must satisfy g(f(1)) = 1 and g(f(2)) = 2, that is g(2) = 1 and g(4) = 2. The values g(1) and g(3) are free, each in \{1, 2\}, and every choice gives a left inverse. The four are (g(1), g(2), g(3), g(4)) = (1, 1, 1, 2),\ (1, 1, 2, 2),\ (2, 1, 1, 2),\ (2, 1, 2, 2). The values on the range are forced, and each of the two points 1, 3 outside the range may go to either of the two points of the domain, independently: 2 \cdot 2 = 4 choices. This is the situation of (b): f is not surjective and its domain has two elements. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: (a) existence of a left inverse, citing @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (b). - 2: (a) surjective case: an inverse exists, and uniqueness of one-sided inverses (@prp-inverse-unique) forces every left inverse to equal it (or a direct argument: for y = f(x), g(y) = x = g'(y)). - 2: (a) one-element case: any two functions into a one-element set agree at every point, so they are equal. - 3: (b) two left inverses that take the values x_0 and x_1 at y_1 (by the construction or defined directly), each checked to be a left inverse, and shown to differ at y_1. - 2: (c) the forced values g(2) = 1, g(4) = 2, the four left inverses, and the count 2 \cdot 2. Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (a), writing f^{-1} before showing f bijective; in (b), concluding g_0 
e g_1 without exhibiting a point where they differ.

title: 1.7 Images and Preimages
content:
Images and Preimages A function f \colon X 	o Y sends points to points. Much of analysis asks what it does to sets of points. Where does f send an interval? Which inputs land in a given set of outputs? The first question is answered by the image f(A), the second by the preimage f^{-1}(B), and the two are the subject of this section. They look like mirror images of each other, and they are not: preimages respect every set operation of Section 1.3, while images respect only unions. The reason is one quantifier, and by the end of the section we will be able to point at it. Throughout, f \colon X 	o Y is a function (@def-function), and the unions and intersections of families are those of @def-family-union-intersection. An intersection of a family of subsets of Y is taken inside Y; of subsets of X, inside X. A question about squares Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = x^2, and take the two intervals A = [-1, 0] and B = [0, 1]. Squaring A gives every number from 0 to 1, and so does squaring B. Fatal errors (0 for the step): fixing one i and concluding for all i (entry (N1) of Logic and Proof, Chapter 8’s catalogue); stating the example’s two sides without checking an element that lies in one and not the other. R. Review [R1] Here is a derivation of “if A \subseteq B, then \powerset{A} \subseteq \powerset{B}”. The steps “by def.” unwind or rewind @def-subset and @def-power-set. Write the proof as plain prose, the way a mathematician would. Then say which sentence of your proof carries each of the five boxes. Proof. Suppose A \subseteq B. Let S \in \powerset{A}, so S \subseteq A. Let x \in S. Then x \in A, since S \subseteq A, and so x \in B, since A \subseteq B. Hence S \subseteq B, that is, S \in \powerset{B}. This proves \powerset{A} \subseteq \powerset{B}. The boxes. “Suppose A \subseteq B” opens the ulename{{	o}I} box \lines{1}{17}; its closing line 18 is the silent frame of the whole proof. “Let S \in \powerset{A}” opens two boxes at once: the ulename{ orall I} box for S_0 and the ulename{{	o}I} box \lines{3}{14} inside it. “Let x \in S” likewise opens the ulename{ orall I} box for x_0 and the ulename{{	o}I} box \lines{6}{10}. “Hence S \subseteq B” closes the two inner boxes (lines 11 and 12) and rewinds the definition (line 13). “This proves \powerset{A} \subseteq \powerset{B}” closes the S boxes (lines 15, 16) and rewinds (line 17). This is the passage from level 0 to level 3 of Logic and Proof, Section 8.3: each “let” carries a ulename{ orall I} box together with the ulename{{	o}I} box of a subset statement, the ulename{ orall E} and ulename{{	o}E} lines 7–10 become the two “since” clauses, the unwinding lines 2 and 5 go silent, line 4 becomes a “so” and line 14 a “that is”, and the rewinding lines 13 and 17 are the two conclusions the prose states. If the two sides can differ, turn a row where they differ into a counterexample. Write P, Q, R for the statements x \in A, x \in B, x \in C. Take the first row: put the point 1 in exactly the sets whose statement is true, all three, so A = B = C = \{1\}. Then B \setminus C = \emptyset, so A \setminus (B \setminus C) = \{1\}; and A \setminus B = \emptyset, so (A \setminus B) \setminus C = \emptyset. The two sides differ, so the identity is false. (The third row gives A = C = \{1\}, B = \emptyset, with the same two answers.) Why a table suffices: each side’s membership condition is a formula in P, Q, R, and a row with the two columns different gives sets directly, which are then checked by computing both sides, as above. The truth tables of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 add one more thing: by @fd1:cor-refuting-row, the first row shows that the sequent P \wedge

title: Induction, Contradiction, and Finite Sets
content:
Induction, Contradiction, and Finite Sets Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 took one fact about the natural numbers on trust: induction. Everything else we have used about them came from school: that 7 - 3 is a natural number, that none lies strictly between 3 and 4, and that every non-empty set of them has a least member. This chapter derives all of these from induction, extends them to the integers, and proves that the least-member property, well-ordering, is induction in another form. It then turns induction from a principle into a craft: which form fits a claim, where to start, when to argue by contrapositive, by contradiction or from a smallest counterexample, when to prove more than was asked, and how a flawed induction fails at exactly one step. It also proves that a starting value and a rule for the next value really do define a sequence, which is what makes \sum, \prod, n! and powers definitions rather than abbreviations. The first motivating problem comes from Logic and Proof, Chapter 2, which reduced a fraction by halving numerator and denominator for as long as both were even: what stops the halving from going on for ever? It proves that there are infinitely many primes, and that \sqrt[3]{2} is irrational. The second half of the chapter is about size. Section 1.1 left a puzzle waiting for a principle: five objects in four boxes put two in one box. What does “finite” mean, so that this can be proved? The answer is a pairing: two sets have the same size when a bijection joins them, a set is finite when it pairs with \{1, \dots, n\}, and the pigeonhole principle becomes a theorem, with the facts about counting that the earlier chapters took on trust. The proofs of these facts are where proof by contradiction works at full scale. What you need. Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–8, and Sets and Functions, Chapter 1. From Logic and Proof, Chapters 1 and 2: the ulename{{	o}I} box (@fd1:def-rules-implication), proof by contradiction (@fd1:def-rule-raa), De Morgan’s laws (@fd1:prp-de-morgan), the contrapositive and the converse (@fd1:prp-contrapositive-converse), odd squares (@fd1:thm-odd-iff-square-odd), the irrationality of \sqrt 2 (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational), whose fact (L) this chapter proves, and @fd1:thm-square-even-implies-even, whose parity fact Section 1.1 proved and Section 2.2 derives again. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 4: the principle of induction (@fd1:ax-induction) and strong induction (@fd1:thm-strong-induction), with the worked examples that introduced them (@fd1:exm-sum-consecutive-products, @fd1:exm-power-inequality, @fd1:exm-threes-and-fives), the cure of proving more (@fd1:exm-strengthen-the-claim), and structural recursion and induction (@fd1:thm-structural-recursion, @fd1:thm-structural-induction), which appear here as pointers back and in one review exercise, with truth values (@fd1:def-truth-value) and the set \{\wedge, \vee, 	o\} that cannot express negation (@fd1:thm-adequate-connectives). From Logic and Proof, Chapters 5 and 6: the rules for “for every” and “there exists” (@fd1:def-rules-universal, @fd1:def-rules-existential, @fd1:prp-exists-forall-swap), the rules for equality (@fd1:def-rules-equality, @fd1:prp-equality-symmetric-transitive), bounded quantifiers (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-rules), and negating quantifiers and implications (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication). From Logic and Proof, Chapter 7: the counter-model exercises (@fd1:exr-models-c1, @fd1:exr-models-c2). From Logic and Proof, Chapter 8: how an induction is written in prose (@fd1:exm-rhetoric-induction), the three faces of “by contradiction” (Section 8.1; @fd1:exm-rhetoric-contradiction, the costume examples @fd1:exm-costume-direct and @fd1:exm-costume-contrapositive, Euclid’s list argument @fd1:exr-connective-rhetoric-c1), existence without a witness (Section 8.7, @fd1:thm-irrational-power-rational), and the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue). From Chapter 1: the method boxes for direct proof, cases, counterexamples, double inclusion, injectivity and surjectivity (@exm-method-direct-proof, @exm-method-cases, @exm-method-counterexample, @exm-method-double-inclusion, @exm-method-injectivity, @exm-method-surjectivity); even, odd, divides and prime (@def-parity, @def-divides, @def-prime, @thm-even-or-odd, @exm-parity-of-sums, @prp-divides-transitive, @exm-divides-combination, @exm-lattice-midpoint); Russell’s paradox (@thm-russell) and equality of sets by two inclusions (@prp-subset-antisymmetric); sets cut out by a property (@def-set-builder), power sets (@def-power-set), unions of families (@def-family-union-intersection); ordered pairs and products (@def-ordered-pair, @def-cartesian-product); relations and functions, equality of functions, the empty function (@def-relation, @def-function, @prp-function-equality, @prp-empty-function); injections, surjections, composites and inverses (@def-injective, @def-surjective, @exm-injective-surjective-first, @def-composition, @def-inverse-function, @thm-composition-injective-surjective, @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective); images and preimages (@def-image, @def-preimage). The arithmetic and order of 
R are school facts, as in the earlier chapters; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 states them as axioms. Time. About 30 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 40 hours for everything. Roadmap - The natural numbers and well-ordering. From induction alone, the arithmetic of 
N and 
Z, the proof that every non-empty set of natural numbers has a least element, and the theorem that induction and well-ordering are equivalent, with a witness for each hypothesis it needs, and the least element as a tool of proof. - Induction, strong induction and divisibility. Induction from any integer, finding the inductive hypothesis inside the step and choosing the base, the division algorithm, lowest terms and prime factors, and a gallery of broken inductions, each located at one step. - Definition by recursion. The theorem that a starting value and a rule define exactly one sequence, its variants from another base and with two previous values, sums, products and powers defined by it, and inductions that follow a definition’s clauses or prove more than was asked. - Contrapositive and contradiction in practice. Choosing among a direct proof, the contrapositive and a contradiction; infinitely many primes; an irrational cube root by lowest terms; the smallest counterexample as a method; existence without a witness. - Equinumerous sets and finite sets. “The same size” defined by a bijection, finite sets and their number of elements, the pigeonhole principle, which settles the five lattice points of Section 1.1, and the uniqueness of that number, subsets, disjoint unions and the 2^n subsets of an n-element set, and the theorem that no finite set is equinumerous with a proper subset, which Hilbert’s hotel turns into a proof that 
N is infinite. Named moves The first five are method boxes; each section that introduces one cites it from then on. - The least element (@exm-method-least-element). Name a set whose least element would help, show it is a non-empty set of natural numbers, take its least element, and use leastness: an element below it is a contradiction, or leastness says what it must be. (Section 2.1) - Finding P(n) inside P(n + 1) (@exm-method-induction-step). Write P(n + 1) out, split off the part that is P(n), apply the induction hypothesis to it, close the rest by computation, and choose the base as the first n from which this works. (Section 2.2) - Choosing direct, contrapositive or contradiction (@exm-method-choosing-the-form). Unwind P, Q and their negations: go direct when P gives something to compute with, prove the contrapositive when 
eg Q is the richer hypothesis, and assume the positive statement when the claim is a negation. (Section 2.4) - Smallest counterexample (@exm-method-smallest-counterexample). Suppose the claim fails; well-ordering gives a least failure m; below m the claim holds, and from that produce a failure smaller than m, or the claim at m itself. (Section 2.4) - Pigeonhole (@exm-method-pigeonhole). Choose pigeons and fewer holes, define “the hole of a pigeon”, conclude that two pigeons share a hole, and translate “same hole” back into the property you want. (Section 2.5) - Prove more (strengthen the hypothesis). When the inductive step will not go through, ask what the induction hypothesis would need to say, and prove that stronger statement instead. - Recursion, then induction. Define an object by a recursion, and prove facts about it by an induction that follows the same clauses: the base case uses the starting value, and the step uses the rule. Threads - The halving. Section 2.1 opens its subsection on well-ordering with the halving question of Logic and Proof, Chapter 2, and answers it with the first use of the least element (@exm-no-infinite-descent). Section 2.2 writes the argument out as the existence of lowest terms (@lem-lowest-terms), and Section 2.4 uses lowest terms to prove that \sqrt[3]{2} is irrational (@prp-cube-root-two-irrational). - The lattice points. Section 1.1 asks why, among any five points with integer coordinates, two have a midpoint with integer coordinates, and leaves the principle it needs unproved. Section 2.5 opens on the puzzle, proves the pigeonhole principle (@thm-pigeonhole) under the heading “Back to the pigeons”, and finishes the five points (@exm-five-lattice-points). - Same size. The bijections of Section 1.6 are how the book says that two sets have the same size; Section 2.5 makes this a definition (@def-equinumerous), and Section 4.2 meets it again as an example of an equivalence-like relation. - Infinitely many primes. Section 2.4 proves that above every natural number there is a prime (@thm-primes-infinite), before “infinite” has a definition; Section 2.5 defines infinite sets, and a Quick check there concludes that the set of primes is one. Summary Induction and well-ordering are one principle (@thm-induction-iff-well-ordering). Every integer can be divided by a positive integer with a unique quotient and remainder (@thm-division-algorithm). Every integer at least 2 has a prime factor (@thm-prime-factor), and there are infinitely many primes (@thm-primes-infinite). A starting value and a rule define exactly one sequence (@thm-recursion), which makes sums, products and powers definitions. The number \sqrt[3]{2} is irrational (@prp-cube-root-two-irrational), by lowest terms and a smallest counterexample. For m > n there is no injection from \{1, \dots, m\} to \{1, \dots, n\} (@thm-pigeonhole), so a finite set has exactly one number of elements (@cor-finite-size-unique), and no finite set is equinumerous with a proper subset of itself (@thm-finite-no-proper-copy). What is open: are 
Q and 
R the same size as 
N? Chapter 3. Terms - equinumerous: there is a bijection between the two sets (@def-equinumerous). - factorial: n! = \prod_{k=1}^{n} k, with 0! = 1 (@def-sum-product). - finite, has n elements: equinumerous with \{1, \dots, n\} for some n \in 
N (@def-finite). - greatest element: an element m \in S with s \le m for every s \in S (Section 2.1, before @thm-well-ordering). - infinite: not finite (@def-infinite). - least element: an element m \in S with m \le s for every s \in S (Section 2.1, before @thm-well-ordering). - maximum, minimum: the greatest and the least element of a set (Section 2.3, before @prp-finite-max). - power: u^0 = 1, u^{n+1} = u^n u (@def-power). - prime factor: a prime that divides the integer (@def-prime, Section 1.1); every integer \ge 2 has one (@thm-prime-factor). - quotient, remainder: the q and r of a = qn + r, 0 \le r < n (@thm-division-algorithm). - smallest counterexample: the least integer at which a claim fails, given by well-ordering (@exm-method-smallest-counterexample). - sum, product: \sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k and \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k, defined by recursion, empty sum 0, empty product 1 (@def-sum-product).

title: 2.1 The Natural Numbers and Well-Ordering
content:
The Natural Numbers and Well-Ordering Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 took one fact about the natural numbers on trust: the principle of induction (@fd1:ax-induction), which says that a property holding at 0 and passing from each n to n + 1 holds for every n \in 
N. From it, Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 proved strong induction (@fd1:thm-strong-induction), whose step may use the property at every smaller number. Everything else we have said about 
N was school knowledge: that 7 - 3 is a natural number, that none lies strictly between 3 and 4, that every non-empty set of natural numbers has a least member. This section derives those facts from induction, extends them to the integers, and then proves that the least-member property, well-ordering, is induction in another form. What we assume about the natural numbers The principle of induction is usually used with a property written as a sentence. It has an equivalent form about sets, which is the one Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 uses. Let S \subseteq 
N contain 0, and suppose n + 1 \in S whenever n \in S. Apply @fd1:ax-induction to the property “n \in S”: its base case is 0 \in S, and its step is the closure of S. So every n \in 
N lies in S, that is, 
N \subseteq S, and with S \subseteq 
N this gives S = 
N (@prp-subset-antisymmetric). In words: the only subset of 
N that contains 0 and is closed under n \mapsto n + 1 is 
N itself. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 states this as “
N is contained in every inductive set”, where an inductive set contains 0, as here. Here is everything the section assumes about 
N. The natural numbers form a subset 
N \subseteq 
R of the familiar real numbers such that - (( )0) 0 \in 
N; - (
NS) for every n \in 
N, also n + 1 \in 
N; and @fd1:ax-induction holds. The arithmetic and the order of the real numbers (the laws of +, -, \cdot and \le, trichotomy, multiplying an inequality by a positive number) are school facts in this volume and in Logic and Proof; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 states them as axioms of an ordered field. These three items are a description of 
N, not new axioms: Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 already used all of them. The rule for this section. From here to the end of the section, a fact about 
N is used only if it is (( )0), (
NS), @fd1:ax-induction, a statement proved earlier in the section, or @fd1:thm-strong-induction once the paragraph after @lem-naturals-arithmetic has shown that its Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 proof rests only on these. The real-number arithmetic is used freely. In particular “n \ge 0” for a natural number n, which looks too obvious to mention, is not available until it is proved below, in @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a). The integers and the rationals are then defined from 
N, as subsets of 
R:  egin{aligned} 
Z &\coloneqq 
N \cup \{ -n : n \in 
N \} , \ 
Z_{>0} &\coloneqq \{ n \in 
N : n 
e 0 \} , \ 
Q &\coloneqq \{ m/n : m \in 
Z, \ n \in 
Z_{>0} \} . \end{aligned} In words: an integer is a natural number or the negative of one; a positive integer is a natural number other than 0; a rational number is a quotient of an integer by a positive integer. These are word for word the definitions of Analysis on the Real Line, Section 1.5, so the two chapters speak of the same sets. Examples: -3 \in 
Z because 3 \in 
N; 0 lies in 
Z twice over, as 0 \in 
N and as -0, which a union does not mind; -	frac12 = (-1)/2 \in 
Q. The definitions do not yet tell us that 	frac12 
otin 
Z, or that 
Z_{>0} is the set of natural numbers \ge 1. Both need the lemma below. Two pieces of notation will save words later. For n \in 
N, \{1, \dots, n\} \coloneqq \{ k \in 
N : 1 \le k \le n \} , \qquad \{0, \dots, n\} \coloneqq \{ k \in 
N : k \le n \} . So \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset, since no k has 1 \le k \le 0. We do not write [n] for these sets: square brackets will mean an equivalence class in Section 4.2. The arithmetic of the natural numbers The facts below are the ones Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 used without proof. Each of (a)–(d) is one ordinary induction, and the only work is to choose the property to induct on; (e) follows from (a) and (d). [Arithmetic of the Natural Numbers] For all m, n \in 
N: 1. n \ge 0; and if n 
e 0, then n \ge 1; 2. m + n \in 
N and mn \in 
N; 3. if n 
e 0 (equivalently, by (a), n \ge 1), then n - 1 \in 
N; 4. if m \le n, then n - m \in 
N; 5. there is no k \in 
N with n < k < n + 1; equivalently, if m < n, then m + 1 \le n. In words: (a) says that 0 is the smallest natural number and that nothing in 
N lies between 0 and 1. (b) says 
N is closed under sums and products, (c) that every natural number except 0 has a predecessor in 
N, and (d) that a difference “larger minus smaller” stays in 
N. (e) says the natural numbers come one unit apart, with no gaps to hide in. Each induction needs a property that is true at 0 and survives the step, and the statement as written does not always qualify. “If n 
e 0, then n \ge 1” says nothing useful at 0, so for (a) we induct on the disjunction “n = 0 or n \ge 1”. For (b) we fix one of the two numbers and induct on the other. For (d) we induct on m. The step from m to m + 1 uses the hypothesis only at the same n, with the weaker bound m \le n, and then subtracts 1 using (c). So n could be fixed first, as m is in (b); the proof below puts “for every n” inside the property instead, which is harmless. (a) Let P(n) be “n = 0 or n \ge 1”. Base case: P(0) holds by its first disjunct. Step: let n \in 
N with P(n). If n = 0, then n + 1 = 1 \ge 1; if n \ge 1, then n + 1 \ge 2 \ge 1. In both cases n + 1 \ge 1, so P(n + 1) holds by its second disjunct. By @fd1:ax-induction, every n \in 
N satisfies n = 0 or n \ge 1. In both cases n \ge 0; and if n 
e 0, the first disjunct is excluded, so n \ge 1. (b) Fix m \in 
N. Sums: let P(n) be “m + n \in 
N”. Then P(0) holds, since m + 0 = m \in 
N. If m + n \in 
N, then m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1 \in 
N by (
NS). By @fd1:ax-induction, m + n \in 
N for every n \in 
N; as m was arbitrary, this holds for all m, n \in 
N. Products: let Q(n) be “mn \in 
N”. Then m \cdot 0 = 0 \in 
N by (( )0). If mn \in 
N, then m(n + 1) = mn + m, a sum of the two natural numbers mn and m, so it lies in 
N by the half just proved. By @fd1:ax-induction, mn \in 
N for every n. (c) Let P(n) be “n = 0 or n - 1 \in 
N”. P(0) holds by its first disjunct. Let n \in 
N; then (n + 1) - 1 = n \in 
N, so P(n + 1) holds by its second disjunct. By @fd1:ax-induction, P(n) holds for every n \in 
N, and for n 
e 0 its second disjunct is the claim. (d) Let P(m) be “for every n \in 
N, if m \le n, then n - m \in 
N”. Base case: n - 0 = n \in 
N. Step: let m \in 
N with P(m), and let n \in 
N with m + 1 \le n. Then m < m + 1 \le n, so n - m \in 
N by P(m). Moreover n - m \ge 1 > 0, so n - m 
e 0, and (c) gives (n - m) - 1 \in 
N. Since (n - m) - 1 = n - (m + 1), this is P(m + 1). By @fd1:ax-induction, P(m) holds for every m \in 
N. (e) Let m < n. By (d), n - m \in 
N, and n - m > 0, so n - m 
e 0 and (a) gives n - m \ge 1, that is, m + 1 \le n. Now suppose k \in 
N with n < k < n + 1. Applying what we just proved to n < k gives n + 1 \le k, which contradicts k < n + 1. So no such k exists. This proves the lemma. Read the proof of (c) again. Its inductive step never mentions P(n). [An induction that ignores its hypothesis] Logic and Proof, Chapter 4, after its first worked induction (@fd1:exm-sum-consecutive-products), said: “A proof by induction that never uses its induction hypothesis is either not an induction or is hiding a gap.” The proof of @lem-naturals-arithmetic (c) never uses its induction hypothesis. Is it an induction, and is it hiding a gap? It is an induction, and it hides no gap. Its base case P(0) is proved, and its step “P(n) \Rightarrow P(n + 1)” is a valid implication for every n \in 
N: the conclusion P(n + 1) is proved outright, so the implication holds whatever P(n) says. Then @fd1:ax-induction delivers P(n) for every n. The hypothesis n \in 
N of the step is used, through (n + 1) - 1 = n \in 
N; only P(n) is not. Nor can a case analysis replace the axiom here. A direct proof would have to say which numbers lie in 
N, and the only thing that says so is induction: the step shows that every number of the form n + 1 with n \in 
N has the property, and it is @fd1:ax-induction that tells us every natural number other than 0 is of this form. Logic and Proof, Chapter 4’s sentence is a rule of thumb, and a good one: an unused hypothesis is a reason to check the proof line by line. Here the check passes. The exception is a step whose conclusion is reached without the hypothesis, and the axiom is still what carries the property from 0 to every n. Well-ordering A fraction with even numerator and denominator can be halved, and halved again, and Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 claimed that this cannot go on for ever (the fact (L) in the proof of @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational). The reason is that the absolute values of the denominators form a strictly decreasing list of positive integers, and such a list must stop. The precise form of “must stop” is a statement about least elements. A least element of a set S \subseteq 
R is an element m \in S such that m \le s for every s \in S. Not every set has one: (0, 1] has none, since for every x \in (0, 1] the number x/2 lies in the set and is smaller. The empty set has none either, as a least element must be an element. Reversing the inequality, a greatest element of S is an element m \in S with s \le m for every s \in S; this is the maximum of Logic and Proof, Section 5.8.
