e 0 and 	frac12 - 1 = -	frac12 
otin X; (e), since 0 < 	frac12 < 1 with 	frac12 \in X. Each clause had to be decided by its own witness. The proofs of (a)–(d) were inductions over 
N, and X does not have the induction property (
N \subseteq X contains 0 and is closed), so none of those proofs carries over; some conclusions survive anyway. (c) fails because the predecessor property fails at 	frac12. (e) fails through the second clause of (a), not through (d), which still holds. The set 
Z \cup \{ k + 	frac12 : k \in 
Z \} has the predecessor property and still has 	frac12 between 0 and 1, so the predecessor property alone (with 0 and closure) does not give (e); together with the least-element property it does: the set then has the induction property by @thm-induction-iff-well-ordering, and, as in the proof of its (\Rightarrow) half, it equals 
N. B. Practice [B1] Use only @lem-naturals-arithmetic and the arithmetic of 
R. 1. Prove that if m, n \in 
N and mn = 1, then m = n = 1. 2. Prove that n^2 \ge n for every n \in 
N. (a) Since 0 \cdot n = 0 
e 1, we have m 
e 0, and likewise n 
e 0. By the second clause of @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a), m \ge 1 and n \ge 1. Suppose m > 1. Multiplying by n > 0 gives mn > n \ge 1, which contradicts mn = 1. So m = 1, and then n = mn = 1. (b) Let n \in 
N. By @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a), n = 0 or n \ge 1. If n = 0, then n^2 = 0 = n. If n \ge 1, multiplying n \ge 1 by n > 0 gives n^2 \ge n. In both cases n^2 \ge n. [B2: Putting a proof in order] The lines below, (i)–(ix), include the seven lines of a proof of (\Leftarrow) in @thm-induction-iff-well-ordering, shuffled, and two lines that do not belong. Here X has 0 \in X, closure and the predecessor property, and the least-element property. Write the seven lines in an order that makes a correct proof, and say why each of the other two lines fails. 1. So m - 1 \in X, by the predecessor property. 2. Let m be the least element of S. 3. Then X \setminus S is non-empty, so it has a least element m. 4. Hence m = (m - 1) + 1 \in S, a contradiction; so S = X. 5. Let S \subseteq X contain 0 and be closed under n \mapsto n + 1. 6. m - 1 < m, so m - 1 
otin X \setminus S, that is, m - 1 \in S. 7. Since m is least and m - 1 < m, m - 1 \in X \setminus S. 8. Suppose S 
e X. 9. m 
e 0, since 0 \in S. The order is (v), (viii), (iii), (ix), (i), (vi), (iv). It is the only admissible one. (v) introduces S, (viii) is the supposition the rest contradicts, and (iii) introduces m from it. (ix) must sit between (iii) and (i): it needs the m of (iii), and (i) applies the predecessor property, which needs m 
e 0. (vi) uses the m - 1 \in X of (i): only an element of X can be sorted into S or X \setminus S. (iv) uses (vi) and closure. Line (ii) takes the least element of the wrong set. The set whose least element locates a failure is X \setminus S: its least element is the first number of X missing from S. A least element of S says nothing about where S and X differ; in the case X = 
N it is 0, which lies in S by (v) and is no failure at all. Line (vii) reads leastness backwards: “m is least in X \setminus S” says that nothing below m lies in X \setminus S, so a smaller number of X is in S, not outside it. [B3] Prove the second half of @cor-well-ordering-integers directly from @thm-well-ordering, without using the first half: if S \subseteq 
Z is non-empty and b \in 
Z is an upper bound of S, then S has a greatest element. Hint: shift by s \mapsto b - s. Let T \coloneqq \{ b - s : s \in S \}. For s \in S, b - s is an integer by @prp-integers-closed (a), and b - s \ge 0 because s \le b; so b - s \in 
N by @prp-integers-closed (b). Thus T is a non-empty subset of 
N, and by @thm-well-ordering it has a least element, of the form b - s_0 with s_0 \in S. For every s \in S, b - s_0 \le b - s, so s \le s_0. Hence s_0 is a greatest element of S. [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement, by the method of @exm-method-least-element where it applies, and refute each false one with a concrete counterexample. 1. Every non-empty set of integers has a least element. 2. Every non-empty set of negative rational numbers has a greatest element. 3. Every non-empty set of even natural numbers has a least element. 4. Every non-empty subset of \{ 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} has a greatest element. 5. Every non-empty subset of \{ 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} has a least element. 6. If S \subseteq 
Z is non-empty and s \ge -	frac{13}{3} for every s \in S, then S has a least element. (a) False. Take 
Z itself. For every n \in 
Z, also n - 1 \in 
Z by @prp-integers-closed (a), and n - 1 < n, so no element is least. (b) False. Take \{ -1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \}, a non-empty set of negative rationals. For each -1/n in it, -1/(n + 1) is in it too, and -1/n < -1/(n + 1), so no element is greatest. (c) True. Such a set is a non-empty subset of 
N, so @thm-well-ordering gives it a least element. (d) True. Let T be a non-empty subset, and let N \coloneqq \{ n \in 
Z_{>0} : 1/n \in T \}. Then N \subseteq 
Z_{>0} \subseteq 
N, and N is non-empty: T has an element, which is 1/n for some n \in 
Z_{>0}, and that n lies in N. So N has a least element n_0 (@thm-well-ordering). Then 1/n_0 \in T, and for every 1/n \in T we have n \in N, so n \ge n_0 > 0 and 1/n \le 1/n_0. So 1/n_0 is a greatest element of T. (e) False. Take the whole set. For each 1/n in it, 1/(n + 1) is in it too, and 1/(n + 1) < 1/n, so no element is least. (f) True. The integer -5 is a lower bound of S, since -5 < -	frac{13}{3} \le s for every s \in S. So @cor-well-ordering-integers applies. Items (c), (d) and (f) are well-ordering, sometimes after a change of view: (c) is a subset of 
N as it stands, (f) needs its bound -	frac{13}{3} replaced by the integer -5, and (d) passes from 1/n to n, where “greatest” becomes “least”. The false items are the warning after @thm-well-ordering in three costumes. C. Going deeper [C1: A greatest element from a least upper bound] Let S \subseteq 
N be non-empty, and suppose some M \in 
N satisfies s \le M for every s \in S. 1. Prove that S has a greatest element by applying @thm-well-ordering to the set U of upper bounds of S that lie in 
N, not by citing @cor-well-ordering-integers: show that the least element of U lies in S. 2. Show that the hypothesis “some M \in 
N bounds S above” cannot be dropped. [Hint 1] Consider U \coloneqq \{ u \in 
N : s \le u 	ext{ for every } s \in S \}. [Hint 2] U is non-empty because M \in U; let u be its least element, which exists by @thm-well-ordering. (a) Let U \coloneqq \{ u \in 
N : s \le u 	ext{ for every } s \in S \}. Then M \in U, so U is a non-empty subset of 
N, and @thm-well-ordering gives a least element u of U. We show u \in S. Suppose u 
otin S. Then every s \in S satisfies s \le u and s 
e u, so s < u, and s + 1 \le u by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (e); that is, s \le u - 1. Since S is non-empty, it has an element s_0, and 0 \le s_0 < u by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a), so u 
e 0. By @lem-naturals-arithmetic (c), u - 1 \in 
N. So u - 1 is an upper bound of S in 
N, that is, u - 1 \in U, and u - 1 < u, which contradicts the choice of u. Hence u \in S. Since u \in S and s \le u for every s \in S, u is a greatest element of S. (b) S = 
N is non-empty and has no greatest element: for every n \in 
N, also n + 1 \in 
N by (
NS), and n + 1 > n. In the proof, U is then empty, and @thm-well-ordering has nothing to apply to. The number u of (a) is the least upper bound of S among natural numbers, and the proof shows that it lies in S. Section 4.3 defines least upper bounds in any partially ordered set, and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 is about sets of real numbers whose least upper bound, when it exists, need not lie in the set. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: defines the set of upper bounds in 
N, shows it is non-empty, and takes its least element by @thm-well-ordering. - 2: handles u = 0 separately, or shows u 
e 0 using that S is non-empty, before using u - 1 \in 
N (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (c)). - 3: uses the minimality of u: either shows directly that u - 1 
otin U, so some s \in S has s > u - 1, or, supposing u 
otin S, derives u - 1 \in U and contradicts minimality. - 1: uses discreteness (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e)) to show that an element of S greater than u - 1 equals u, or to get s \le u - 1 in the contradiction route, and concludes that u \in S is a greatest element. - 2: (b) the witness S = 
N, with the reason it has no greatest element. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using u - 1 \in 
N without checking u 
e 0; taking a least element of U without showing U non-empty. A second route, through the least element M - s_0 of \{ M - s : s \in S \} \subseteq 
N (as in @exr-naturals-and-well-ordering-b3), proves the conclusion of (a) but not by the method the task names, so it earns at most 4 points for (a): 2 for showing that this set is a non-empty subset of 
N and taking its least element, and 2 for deducing s \le s_0 for every s \in S from M - s_0 \le M - s, with s_0 \in S; and (b) as above. [C2: A well-ordered set with gaps] Let X \coloneqq 
N \cup \{ n + 	frac12 : n \in 
N \}. Prove that every non-empty subset of X has a least element. Let T \subseteq X be non-empty, and put A \coloneqq T \cap 
N , \qquad B \coloneqq \{ t - 	frac12 : t \in T \setminus 
N \} . Every t \in T \setminus 
N is n + 	frac12 for some n \in 
N, since t \in X; so t - 	frac12 = n \in 
N, and B \subseteq 
N. Since T = A \cup (T \setminus 
N) is non-empty, A or B is non-empty. By @thm-well-ordering, A, if non-empty, has a least element a, and B, if non-empty, has a least element b. Define c \coloneqq  egin{cases} a & 	ext{if } B = \emptyset , \ b + 	frac12 & 	ext{if } A = \emptyset , \ \min\{ a, \, b + 	frac12 \} & 	ext{otherwise.} \end{cases} In each case c \in T: a \in A \subseteq T, and b = t - 	frac12 for some t \in T \setminus 
N, so b + 	frac12 = t \in T. Let t \in T. If t \in 
N, then t \in A, so A 
e \emptyset and t \ge a \ge c. If t 
otin 
N, then t - 	frac12 \in B, so B 
e \emptyset and t - 	frac12 \ge b, that is, t \ge b + 	frac12 \ge c. (In both chains, the last inequality holds in every case of the definition of c that can occur.) So c is a least element of T. The set X has the least-element property, contains 0 and is closed under n \mapsto n + 1, but it does not have the induction property (
N \subseteq X contains 0 and is closed, and 
N 
e X). That is the first witness after @thm-induction-iff-well-ordering: without the predecessor property, well-ordering does not give induction. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: splits T into its natural-number part and its half part, and shows the shifted half part lies in 
N. - 2: applies @thm-well-ordering to each non-empty part, saying that at least one part is non-empty. - 2: defines the candidate in all cases, including those where one part is empty, and checks it lies in T. - 3: checks the candidate is \le t for every t \in T, by cases on t \in 
N or not. - 1: concludes, with the quantifiers right: one least element for the given T. Fatal errors (0 for the step): applying @thm-well-ordering to T itself (it need not be a subset of 
N); taking a least element of an empty part. A second route, through the least element of \{ 2t : t \in T \} \subseteq 
N, earns the same points. It earns 4 for showing that this set lies in 
N, checking both 2n and 2n + 1 by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (b), and that it is non-empty, and for taking its least element 2t_0 with t_0 \in T by @thm-well-ordering. It earns 4 for deducing t_0 \le t from 2t_0 \le 2t for every t \in T, and 2 for the conclusion. The same fatal errors apply.

title: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and Divisibility
content:
Induction, Strong Induction and Divisibility Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 gave the principle of induction (@fd1:ax-induction), its strong form (@fd1:thm-strong-induction), and the first worked proofs: a sum (@fd1:exm-sum-consecutive-products), an inequality (@fd1:exm-power-inequality), and a strong induction with three base cases (@fd1:exm-threes-and-fives). Logic and Proof, Chapter 8 showed how an induction is written in prose (@fd1:exm-rhetoric-induction). This section is about the craft: which form of induction fits a claim, where it starts, how to find the induction hypothesis inside the step, and how an induction goes wrong, each failure located at one step. On the way it proves two facts that Logic and Proof took from school: a fraction can be reduced until numerator and denominator are not both even, and every integer n \ge 2 has a prime factor. Induction from any integer Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 already started inductions at numbers other than 0 (Logic and Proof, Section 4.2, “Starting from another number”), for a starting point b \in 
N. With 
Z and @prp-integers-closed in hand, the starting point may be any integer, negative ones included. To prove a statement for every integer from n_0 on, prove it at n_0 and show that it passes from each integer to the next. [Induction from a Base] Let n_0 be an integer, and for each integer n \ge n_0 let P(n) be a statement. Suppose 1. (base case) P(n_0) is true, and 2. (inductive step) for every integer n \ge n_0, if P(n) is true then P(n + 1) is true. Then P(n) is true for every integer n \ge n_0. Count from the base. The integers n \ge n_0 are exactly n_0 + k with k \in 
N, and moving from n to n + 1 moves k to k + 1. So the statement “P(n_0 + k)” about k \in 
N is ready for @fd1:ax-induction, and its base case is P(n_0). For k \in 
N, let Q(k) be the statement P(n_0 + k). This makes sense: n_0 + k is an integer by @prp-integers-closed (a), and n_0 + k \ge n_0 since k \ge 0 by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a). Base case. Q(0) is P(n_0), which holds by (i). Inductive step. Let k \in 
N, and suppose Q(k), that is, P(n_0 + k). The integer n \coloneqq n_0 + k satisfies n \ge n_0, so (ii) gives P(n + 1). Since n + 1 = n_0 + (k + 1), this is Q(k + 1). By @fd1:ax-induction, Q(k) holds for every k \in 
N. Now let n be an integer with n \ge n_0. Then k \coloneqq n - n_0 is an integer by @prp-integers-closed (a), and k \ge 0, so k \in 
N by @prp-integers-closed (b). Hence Q(k) holds, and Q(k) is P(n_0 + k) = P(n). This proves the theorem. For n_0 = 0 the theorem is @fd1:ax-induction itself, and for n_0 \in 
N it is Logic and Proof, Chapter 4’s induction started at n_0. In the inductive step, “P(n) is true” is the induction hypothesis: one implication, proved once, inside a ulename{{	o}I} box whose assumption is P(n) for one fixed but arbitrary integer n \ge n_0. The strong form moves to a base in the same way. [Strong Induction from a Base] Let n_0 be an integer, and for each integer n \ge n_0 let P(n) be a statement. Suppose that, for every integer n \ge n_0: if P(k) is true for every integer k with n_0 \le k < n, then P(n) is true. Then P(n) is true for every integer n \ge n_0. For j \in 
N, let Q(j) be P(n_0 + j), as in the proof of @thm-induction. We check the hypothesis of @fd1:thm-strong-induction for Q. Let j \in 
N, and suppose Q(i) holds for every i \in 
N with i < j. Put n \coloneqq n_0 + j, an integer with n \ge n_0. Let k be an integer with n_0 \le k < n. Then i \coloneqq k - n_0 is an integer with i \ge 0, so i \in 
N by @prp-integers-closed (b), and i < n - n_0 = j; so Q(i), which is P(k), holds. The hypothesis of the theorem at n now gives P(n), that is, Q(j). By @fd1:thm-strong-induction, Q(j) holds for every j \in 
N, and every integer n \ge n_0 is n_0 + j with j = n - n_0 \in 
N, as in the proof of @thm-induction. This proves the theorem. So @thm-strong-induction-from-base is a corollary of @fd1:thm-strong-induction, by the same shift. When n_0 \in 
N, it says what @fd1:exm-threes-and-fives achieved with a guard: there the property was “if n \ge 8, then …”, stated for every n \in 
N and vacuous below 8. Here the property is stated only for n \ge n_0, and the hypothesis speaks only about k \ge n_0. The two are the same argument in two notations, and the base cases sit in the same place: they are the n for which the step reaches below n_0. Every integer n \ge 24 is 5a + 7b for some integers a, b \ge 0. A proof by @thm-strong-induction-from-base writes n = (n - 5) + 5 in its step. How many base cases does it need, and which? Can the base 24 be lowered? The step uses P(n - 5), which the hypothesis supplies only when n - 5 \ge 24, that is, n \ge 29. So n = 24, 25, 26, 27, 28 are base cases, five of them, checked directly:  egin{aligned} 24 &= 5 \cdot 2 + 7 \cdot 2 , & 25 &= 5 \cdot 5 , & 26 &= 5 \cdot 1 + 7 \cdot 3 , \ 27 &= 5 \cdot 4 + 7 \cdot 1 , & 28 &= 7 \cdot 4 . \end{aligned} The base cannot be lowered: 23 is not of the form. With b = 0, 1, 2, 3 the difference 23 - 7b is 23, 16, 9, 2, none a multiple of 5, and b \ge 4 gives 23 - 7b < 0. Finding P(n) inside P(n + 1) In every induction the step is an implication P(n) \Rightarrow P(n + 1), proved for an arbitrary n. The work is to find, inside the statement P(n + 1), the statement P(n), so that the hypothesis can be used: one more term to split off, one more factor to take out, one more case to bound. The first example is about divisibility (@def-divides). [Scratch work] The claim is 7 \mid 9^n - 2^n for every n \in 
N, with the powers in their school meaning. The base is 9^0 - 2^0 = 0 = 7 \cdot 0. For the step, the hypothesis is about 9^n - 2^n, so write P(n + 1) out and look for that expression in it. The first try, 9^{n+1} - 2^{n+1} = 9 \cdot 9^n - 2 \cdot 2^n, does not contain it: the two powers have different factors in front, 9 and 2. Force the old expression in. Take 9 out of both terms, and pay back what that costs: 9 \cdot 9^n - 2 \cdot 2^n = 9(9^n - 2^n) + 9 \cdot 2^n - 2 \cdot 2^n, and the payment 9 \cdot 2^n - 2 \cdot 2^n is 7 \cdot 2^n, a multiple of 7 again. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal --------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------- P(n): 9^n - 2^n = 7k with k \in 
Z P(n + 1): 9^{n+1} - 2^{n+1} = 7m for some m \in 
Z 9^{n+1} = 9 \cdot 9^n, 2^{n+1} = 2 \cdot 2^n (school meaning) 9^{n+1} - 2^{n+1} rewritten so that 9^n - 2^n appears 9^{n+1} - 2^{n+1} = 9(9^n - 2^n) + 7 \cdot 2^n = 7(9k + 2^n) m \coloneqq 9k + 2^n \in 
Z: the gap is closed ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The old expression appears once, the hypothesis turns it into 7k, and what is left over is a multiple of 7 by computation. Divisibility claims about powers are a staple of induction, because the step can usually be arranged to contain the old expression once. Here is the proof the scratch work found. Claim: 7 \mid 9^n - 2^n for every n \in 
N, with 9^n and 2^n in their school meaning (a^0 = 1, a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a, and a^n is an integer for an integer a; Section 2.3 makes this a definition). Base case: 9^0 - 2^0 = 0 = 7 \cdot 0. Step: if 9^n - 2^n = 7k with k \in 
Z, then 9^{n+1} - 2^{n+1} = 9(9^n - 2^n) + 7 \cdot 2^n = 7(9k + 2^n) , and 9k + 2^n \in 
Z. By @fd1:ax-induction, the claim holds for every n \in 
N. [Method: finding P(n) inside P(n + 1)] Template. (1) Write P(n + 1) out in full. (2) Find P(n) inside it: split off the last term, take out one factor, or separate the new piece from the old. (3) Apply the induction hypothesis to the old part. (4) Close the rest by computation. (5) Choose the base: the first n the claim covers from which steps (2)–(4) work, with any smaller n the claim covers checked directly. When to use it. P(n + 1) is built from P(n) by one operation: a term added, a factor multiplied, an element added to a set. The usual failure. Starting from P(n + 1) and deriving something true, which proves the converse, entry (N5) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. A step that works only from some n on, with the base set lower (as in the gallery below). Using P(n + 1) inside its own step (N9). For a proof that 5 \mid 9^n - 4^n for every n \in 
N, write 9^{n+1} - 4^{n+1} so that 9^n - 4^n appears. 9^{n+1} - 4^{n+1} = 9 \cdot 9^n - 4 \cdot 4^n = 9(9^n - 4^n) + 5 \cdot 4^n. If 9^n - 4^n = 5k with k \in 
Z, this is 5(9k + 4^n), and 9k + 4^n \in 
Z. The fifth step of the template deserves an example of its own, because the place where the step starts working need not be the place where the claim starts being true. [Where the step starts working] Prove that 3^n \ge n^3 for every n \in 
N, with the powers in their school meaning. By @exm-method-induction-step, write P(n + 1) out: it contains 3^n as 3^{n+1} = 3 \cdot 3^n \ge 3n^3, so the step needs 3n^3 \ge (n + 1)^3. That holds from n = 3 on, and not before. So the base is 3, and 0, 1, 2 are checked directly. Small cases. 3^0 = 1 \ge 0 = 0^3, 3^1 = 3 \ge 1 = 1^3, and 3^2 = 9 \ge 8 = 2^3. From 3 on, by @thm-induction with base 3. Base case: 3^3 = 27 \ge 27 = 3^3. Step: let n \ge 3 be an integer with 3^n \ge n^3. Then 3^{n+1} = 3 \cdot 3^n \ge 3n^3. Since n \ge 3, 2n^3 \ge 6n^2 = 3n^2 + 3n^2 \ge 3n^2 + 9n \ge 3n^2 + 3n + 1 , so 3n^3 = n^3 + 2n^3 \ge n^3 + 3n^2 + 3n + 1 = (n + 1)^3. Hence 3^{n+1} \ge (n + 1)^3. The small cases and the induction together give 3^n \ge n^3 for every n \in 
N. The claim is true at 0, 1 and 2, but the argument of the step fails from 2 to 3: 3 \cdot 2^3 = 24 < 27 = 3^3. The base is where the step starts working, or the first n the claim covers if that is later. It need not be the first n at which the claim is true, and the cases below it are checked one by one. For which n \in 
N is 3n^3 \ge (n + 1)^3 false, and why does that make 3 the base although 3^n \ge n^3 holds at 0, 1 and 2? For n = 0, 1, 2: 0 < 1, 3 < 8 and 24 < 27. The step is proved only from 3 on, so the three smaller cases need their own checks; an induction from base 0 would have three unproved transitions. Divisibility and the division algorithm The next results are about divisibility. Divisibility and primes were defined in Section 1.1: for integers a and b, a \mid b means b = ka for some k \in 
Z (@def-divides), and a prime is an integer p \ge 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p (@def-prime); divisibility is transitive (@prp-divides-transitive). For instance, 3 \mid 12, with k = 4. Change 12 to 14: 3 
mid 14. The witness k would have to be 14/3, and 4 < 14/3 < 5, so 14/3 is not an integer, by the discreteness clause of @prp-integers-closed. The clause that fails is “k \in 
Z”: the equation 14 = k \cdot 3 has a real solution, just not an integer one. Section 1.1 worked the first examples of primes and non-primes after @def-prime. The clause p \ge 2 keeps 1 out so that factorizations into primes can be unique, a fact this chapter does not prove or use: Exercise B2 below is about existence only. Every integer, divided by a positive integer n, leaves a remainder between 0 and n - 1. This is school arithmetic, and it is the tool behind “even or odd”. [Division Algorithm] Let a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}. Then there are unique integers q and r with a = qn + r \quad 	ext{and} \quad 0 \le r < n . The hypothesis n > 0 matters: for n = 0 no r satisfies 0 \le r < 0. Try it first (ten minutes): which set of non-negative integers should have a least element, and why is that least element the remainder? The obvious attempt subtracts n from a again and again until what is left lies in [0, n), adding n instead when a is negative. “Again and again until” is a process, not yet a proof: why does it stop, and why at a number below n? Well-ordering replaces the process by its outcome. Among all the non-negative integers a - qn, take the least (the method of @exm-method-least-element: S the non-negative integers a - qn). If it were n or more, subtracting one more n would leave a smaller non-negative one. For uniqueness: two remainders differ by a multiple of n, yet lie less than n apart, so the multiple is 0. Existence. Let R \coloneqq \{ a - qn : q \in 
Z \} \cap \{ x \in 
Z : x \ge 0 \} , the set of non-negative integers of the form a - qn (each a - qn is an integer by @prp-integers-closed (a)). The set R is non-empty. [Every Integer at Least Two Has a Prime Factor] Every integer n \ge 2 has a prime factor. A prime is its own prime factor. otin \{1, n\} (@def-prime). Write n = ka with k \in 
Z. Since n > 0 and a > 0, also k > 0, so k \ge 1 and a \ge 1 by @prp-integers-closed (b). Hence a \le ka = n. With a 
e 1 and a

A gallery of broken inductions An induction proof has few moving parts: a property, a base case, a step, and a citation of the right principle. Each can fail, and each failure has a place in the proof where it can be pointed at. Two questions are kept apart throughout: is the conclusion true, and does the argument prove it? Each entry below names the part that breaks. [All Numbers Are Equal] Here is a “theorem” and a “proof”. Find the line that fails. “Theorem.” For every integer n \ge 1 and all real numbers x_1, \dots, x_n, we have x_1 = x_2 = \dots = x_n. “Proof.” For an integer n \ge 1, let P(n) be the statement “for all real numbers x_1, \dots, x_n, all the entries of the list x_1, \dots, x_n are equal”. We use @thm-induction with n_0 = 1. 1. Base case. A list x_1 of one number has only one entry, so all its entries are equal: P(1) holds. 2. Step. Let n \ge 1 be an integer, suppose P(n), and let x_1, \dots, x_{n+1} be real numbers. 3. The list x_1, \dots, x_n has n entries, so by P(n) its entries are all equal. 4. The list x_2, \dots, x_{n+1} has n entries, so by P(n) its entries are all equal. 5. The entry x_2 lies in both lists, so every entry of either list equals x_2. 6. Hence x_1 = x_2 = \dots = x_{n+1}, which is P(n + 1). By @thm-induction, P(n) holds for every n \ge 1. Is the conclusion true? No: the list x_1 = 0, x_2 = 1 has unequal entries, so P(2) is false. Does the argument prove it? No, and the failing line is (5) at n = 1. Then the two lists of lines (3) and (4) are x_1 and x_2, one entry each, and x_2 is not in the first. They share an entry exactly when the first list, x_1, \dots, x_n, contains x_2, that is, when n \ge 2. In the terms of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, line (5) cites a “fact” that is false in the case at hand: entry (N9). Everything else is correct. The base case (1) is true. For every n \ge 2 the step (2)–(6) is valid: if all lists of n reals had equal entries, so would all lists of n + 1. So the induction fails at exactly one transition, from 1 to 2, and the valid transitions from 2 on carry nothing, because P(2) is false and every later P(n) with it. A counterexample to the illegal step, as opposed to the conclusion: n = 1, x_1 = 0, x_2 = 1, where lines (3) and (4) hold and (5) does not. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- statement true? proved by the argument? --------------------------------------- ----------------------- ------------------------- P(1) yes yes, line (1) P(1) \Rightarrow P(2) no no: line (5) fails P(n) \Rightarrow P(n + 1) for n \ge 2 yes yes, lines (2)–(6) P(n) for every n \ge 1 no no ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- This is the failure that Logic and Proof, Chapter 4’s warning about 2^n \ge n^2 foreshadowed: a step that holds only from some point on, with a gap at the first transition. A step must be proved for every n \ge n_0, and the place to look for a gap is the smallest n, where the objects the step talks about are smallest. The other failures are quicker to state. The missing base case. “n = n + 1 for every n \in 
N.” The step is valid: if n = n + 1, adding 1 to both sides gives n + 1 = n + 2. But P(0), “0 = 1”, is false, and so is every P(n). The step is a true implication between false statements, and an induction with no true base proves nothing. The step run backwards. Claim: n^2 \ge 2n for every integer n \ge 2. "Step: (n + 1)^2 \ge 2(n + 1) gives n^2 + 2n + 1 \ge 2n + 2, so n^2 \ge 1, which is true." This starts from P(n + 1) and ends at a true statement, so it shows only that P(n + 1) implies something true, which every statement does (N5). Here each line can be reversed, and written forwards (n^2 \ge 1, so (n + 1)^2 = n^2 + 2n + 1 \ge 2n + 2) it is a valid step, though one that never uses P(n). In general a backward chain cannot be reversed: from the false 1 = -1, squaring gives the true 1 = 1. The hypothesis used out of range. A strong induction from a base n_0 may use P(k) only for n_0 \le k < n. A step that writes n in terms of n - 3 needs n - 3 \ge n_0, and for the first few n that fails. @fd1:exm-threes-and-fives handled this correctly, with three base cases; the exit check C1 below is a proof that did not. That conclusion is false at 17: with b = 0, 1, 2 the remainder 17 - 7b is 17, 10, 3, none a multiple of 4, and b \ge 3 makes it negative. The step that breaks is line (5) at n = 16: it takes P(13) from the hypothesis, but 13 < 14 is outside it, and 13 is not of the form (13 and 6 are not multiples of 4). At n = 16 the induction hypothesis is true (14 = 7 \cdot 2, 15 = 4 \cdot 2 + 7, 16 = 4 \cdot 4), and the step concludes the false P(17). So line (5) is an illegal step, not merely an unlucky one. (vi) Take four base cases, 18, 19, 20, 21, as in (i), and run the step only for n \ge 21, where n - 3 \ge 18. In the form of @thm-strong-induction-from-base: for n \in \{18, 19, 20, 21\}, P(n) holds directly; for n \ge 22, n - 4 \ge 18 and n - 4 < n, so the hypothesis gives n - 4 = 4a + 7b and n = 4(a + 1) + 7b. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: judges the conclusion true, with the small cases 18, 19, 20, 21 written as 4a + 7b. - 3: identifies the failing line exactly: the appeal to the hypothesis for n - 3, for n = 18, 19, 20. - 2: states the reason as a hypothesis used outside its range (ulename{ orall E} at a k with k < 18). - 2: gives a counterexample to the step: the same step carrying a true statement to a false one (for example, base 14 and the failure at 17), not merely a false conclusion. - 1: gives a correct repair (four base cases, or any equivalent). Fatal errors (0 for the item): calling the conclusion false; blaming the base case. [C2: Lowest terms, used later] Prove that every rational number can be written as p/q with p \in 
Z, q \in 
Z_{>0}, and no common divisor d \ge 2 of p and q: there is no integer d \ge 2 with d \mid p and d \mid q. [Hint 1] Follow the proof of @lem-lowest-terms, step by step. [Hint 2] Suppose r \in 
Q has no such representation, and let m be the least element of F \coloneqq \{ q \in 
Z_{>0} : r = p/q 	ext{ for some } p \in 
Z \}. Fix r \in 
Q, and suppose that r has no representation of the required kind. Let F be as in Hint 2. By the definition of 
Q, F is non-empty, and F \subseteq 
Z_{>0} \subseteq 
N, so by @thm-well-ordering it has a least element m. Write r = p/m with p \in 
Z. By the supposition, this representation fails: there is an integer d \ge 2 with d \mid p and d \mid m, say p = dp' and m = dm' with p', m' \in 
Z. Since m > 0 and d > 0, m' = m/d > 0, so m' \in 
Z_{>0} by @prp-integers-closed (b). Then r = dp'/(dm') = p'/m', so m' \in F. And m = dm' \ge 2m' > m', since d \ge 2 and m' > 0. So m' is an element of F smaller than its least element, a contradiction. Hence r has a representation p/q with no common divisor d \ge 2. The statement contains @lem-lowest-terms, since d = 2 is one of the excluded common divisors. The only change in the proof is the size of the step down: m' = m/d instead of m/2, and d \ge 2 is what makes it a step down. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: sets up the smallest counterexample: fixes r, supposes no good representation, and defines the set of denominators. - 2: shows that set is a non-empty subset of 
N and takes its least element by @thm-well-ordering. - 3: extracts the common divisor d \ge 2 and writes the reduced representation p'/m', checking m' \in 
Z_{>0}. - 2: shows m' < m, using d \ge 2 and m' > 0. - 1: concludes, with the contradiction to the choice of m. A strong induction on the denominator earns the same points step for step. Fatal errors (0 for the step): taking a least element of a set not shown to lie in 
N; dividing by d without d 
e 0. [C3: Smallest, not largest] 1. Prove that a set A \subseteq 
R has at most one least element. 2. Deduce that a claim “P(n) for every n \in 
N” that is false has exactly one smallest counterexample. 3. Show that a false claim about 
N need not have a largest counterexample, by examining the claim “n < 5 for every n \in 
N”. (a) Let m and m' be least elements of A. Since m' \in A and m is least, m \le m'; since m \in A and m' is least, m' \le m. Hence m = m'. (b) The smallest counterexamples are the least elements of the set F \coloneqq \{ n \in 
N : P(n) 	ext{ is false} \}. The claim is false, so F is non-empty, and @thm-well-ordering gives a least element. By (a), there is only one. (c) The claim is false, and its counterexamples form F = \{ n \in 
N : n \ge 5 \}, which is non-empty. It has no greatest element: for every n \in F, also n + 1 \in 
N by (
NS), and n + 1 \ge 5, so n + 1 \in F and n + 1 > n. So the claim has a smallest counterexample, 5, and no largest one. Well-ordering has no upward twin in 
N: a non-empty subset of 
N has a greatest element when it is bounded above (@exr-naturals-and-well-ordering-c1), and not in general.

title: 2.3 Definition by Recursion
content:
Definition by Recursion Since school we have defined powers by two clauses: u^0 = 1, and u^{n+1} = u^n u. Sums a_1 + \dots + a_n, factorials and many sequences are defined the same way: a starting value, and a rule that produces the next value from the last. Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 used induction to prove facts about such objects, such as 3^n \ge 2n + 1 in @fd1:exm-power-inequality. But induction proves facts about a function that already exists, and here the function is what we want to obtain. This section proves that two such clauses always define exactly one function on 
N, and then uses the theorem to define sums, products and powers properly and to prove their first laws. Definitions that define something Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 met the same question for formulas. A recursive definition on formulas gives a value for each atom and a rule for each way of building a compound formula, and @fd1:thm-structural-recursion showed that such clauses define exactly one function, because unique readability leaves no choice of clause. On 
N the clauses are simpler: one starting value at 0, and one rule for passing from n to n + 1. What we want to prove is this. A starting value and a rule for the next value determine exactly one sequence. [Recursion Theorem] Let X be a set, let a \in X, and let g \colon 
N 	imes X 	o X be a function. Then there is exactly one function f \colon 
N 	o X such that f(0) = a \quad 	ext{and} \quad f(n + 1) = g igl(n, f(n) igr) \ 	ext{ for every } n \in 
N . In words: a is the starting value, and g is the rule that turns the stage n and the current value f(n) into the next value. The rule may look at n as well as at f(n): the factorial needs this, since (n + 1)! = (n + 1) \cdot n! is g(n, x) = (n + 1)x at x = n!. The hypothesis that g maps into X is what lets the rule be applied again at the next stage. The conclusion has two halves: existence (some f obeys the two equations) and uniqueness (no two different functions do). Uniqueness is an ordinary induction: two solutions agree at 0, and if they agree at n, the second equation makes them agree at n + 1. Existence is harder, because induction cannot produce f; it can only prove statements. So we prove by induction a statement about finite pieces of f. The roadmap: ① Uniqueness, by induction on n. ② Claim: for every n \in 
N there is exactly one function on \{0, \dots, n\} obeying the two equations wherever they make sense (a partial solution). Its graph is the graph of the previous one with one pair added. ③ Glue: collect the graphs of all partial solutions in one set \sS and take the union. The partial solutions agree where they overlap, so the union is the graph of a function on all of 
N, and that function obeys the equations. Before reading on: self-explain the Claim’s inductive step. For n \in 
N, the set \{0, \dots, n\} = \{ k \in 
N : k \le n \} of Section 2.1 contains 0, since 0 \le n by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a). Call a function h \colon \{0, \dots, n\} 	o X a partial solution up to n if h(0) = a and h(k + 1) = g(k, h(k)) for every k \in 
N with k + 1 \le n. (For such k, both k and k + 1 lie in \{0, \dots, n\}, so the equation makes sense.) Step 1 (uniqueness). Let f, f' \colon 
N 	o X both satisfy the two equations, and let P(n) be “f(n) = f'(n)”. P(0) holds, since f(0) = a = f'(0). If P(n) holds, then f(n + 1) = g igl(n, f(n) igr) = g igl(n, f'(n) igr) = f'(n + 1) , so P(n + 1) holds. By @fd1:ax-induction, f(n) = f'(n) for every n \in 
N. The two functions have the same domain and the same codomain, so f = f' by @prp-function-equality. Step 2. For every n \in 
N there is exactly one partial solution up to n. We use @fd1:ax-induction on n. Base case. By @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a), every k \in 
N has k \ge 0, so k \le 0 holds only for k = 0, and \{0, \dots, 0\} = \{0\}. The graph \{(0, a)\} with codomain X is a function on \{0\}, since a \in X: the input 0 has the one output a. It is a partial solution up to 0: its value at 0 is a, and the second condition is vacuous, because k + 1 \ge 1 > 0 for every k \in 
N. Any partial solution up to 0 has value a at 0, so it equals this one by @prp-function-equality. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N, and suppose there is exactly one partial solution up to n; call it f_n, with graph G_n. Let G_{n+1} \coloneqq G_n \cup  igl\{  igl(n + 1, \ g(n, f_n(n)) igr)  igr\} . First, \{0, \dots, n + 1\} = \{0, \dots, n\} \cup \{n + 1\}: a natural number k \le n + 1 is either n + 1 or less than n + 1, and then k \le n, since no natural number lies strictly between n and n + 1 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e)). Also n + 1 
otin \{0, \dots, n\}, since n + 1 > n. We check the clauses of @def-function for G_{n+1} on \{0, \dots, n + 1\} with codomain X. Every pair of G_{n+1} lies in \{0, \dots, n + 1\} 	imes X, because g takes values in X. (Fn1): an input k \le n has the output f_n(k) in G_n, and the input n + 1 has the output g(n, f_n(n)). (Fn2): the pairs with first coordinate k \le n all lie in G_n, since the added pair has first coordinate n + 1 
e k, and G_n satisfies (Fn2); the only pair with first coordinate n + 1 is the added one, since the first coordinates in G_n are at most n. So f_{n+1} \coloneqq (G_{n+1}, X) is a function on \{0, \dots, n + 1\}, and it agrees with f_n on \{0, \dots, n\}. It is a partial solution up to n + 1. Its value at 0 is f_n(0) = a. Let k \in 
N with k + 1 \le n + 1, so k \le n. If k < n, then k + 1 \le n by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (e), and f_{n+1}(k + 1) = f_n(k + 1) = g(k, f_n(k)) = g(k, f_{n+1}(k)), because f_n is a partial solution. If k = n, then f_{n+1}(n + 1) = g(n, f_n(n)) = g(n, f_{n+1}(n)) by the choice of the added pair. It is the only one. Let h be a partial solution up to n + 1. Its restriction h|_{\{0, \dots, n\}} (Section 1.5) is a partial solution up to n, because the conditions on it are among the conditions on h. By the induction hypothesis it is f_n. So h(k) = f_n(k) = f_{n+1}(k) for k \le n, and h(n + 1) = g igl(n, h(n) igr) = g igl(n, f_n(n) igr) = f_{n+1}(n + 1) . By @prp-function-equality, h = f_{n+1}. This proves the claim. For each n \in 
N, let f_n be the partial solution up to n, and G_n its graph. If m \le n, then \{0, \dots, m\} \subseteq \{0, \dots, n\}, and the restriction of f_n to \{0, \dots, m\} is a partial solution up to m, so by the claim it is f_m. In terms of graphs, G_m = G_n \cap  igl(\{0, \dots, m\} 	imes X igr) \subseteq G_n \qquad (m \le n) . Step 3 (existence). Let \sS \coloneqq  igl\{ G \in \powerset{
N 	imes X} : G 	ext{ is the graph of a partial solution up to some } n \in 
N  igr\} , a set by @def-set-builder and @def-power-set. By the claim, the elements of \sS are exactly the graphs G_n. Let F \coloneqq  igcup \sS (@def-family-union-intersection), so a pair lies in F if and only if it lies in some G_n; in particular F \subseteq 
N 	imes X. We check the clauses of @def-function for F. (Fn1): for n \in 
N, the pair (n, f_n(n)) lies in G_n \in \sS, hence in F. (Fn2): let (k, y) \in F and (k, y') \in F, say (k, y) \in G_m and (k, y') \in G_n. If m \le n, then G_m \subseteq G_n, so both pairs lie in G_n, and y = y' because G_n satisfies (Fn2). If n < m, the same argument with m and n exchanged gives y = y'. So f \coloneqq (F, X) is a function 
N 	o X. For m \ge n, the pair (n, f_m(n)) lies in G_m \subseteq F, so f(n) = f_m(n). Hence f(0) = f_0(0) = a, and for every n \in 
N, f(n + 1) = f_{n+1}(n + 1) = g igl(n, f_{n+1}(n) igr) = g igl(n, f(n) igr) , where the middle equation holds because f_{n+1} is a partial solution. This proves existence, and with Step 1, the theorem. The starting value was used in both halves: Step 1 needs f(0) = f'(0) as its base case, and Step 2 needs it to fix the first partial solution. The set \sS is cut out of a power set by a condition, so no family n \mapsto f_n had to be formed before the union was taken. No choice is made anywhere: at every stage the claim leaves exactly one candidate. From now on, a definition of the form “f(0) \coloneqq a, f(n + 1) \coloneqq g(n, f(n))” is legitimate whenever a \in X and g is a function 
N 	imes X 	o X, and we say that f is defined by recursion. Because the rule may depend on n, the theorem also covers constructions in which the step uses outside data indexed by n. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 builds closed intervals I_{n+1} from I_n and the (n{+}1)-st number of a given list in exactly this way, with no choice principle involved. The values may be sets as well as numbers. With X = \powerset{
N}, A_0 \coloneqq 
N and A_{n+1} \coloneqq A_n \setminus \{n\} define a sequence of sets of the kind Section 1.3 promised, and an induction that follows the same two clauses shows A_n = \{ k \in 
N : k \ge n \}: the base is @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a), and the step removes n from \{ k : k \ge n \}, leaving \{ k : k > n \} = \{ k : k \ge n + 1 \} by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (e). Name X, a and g for the sequence 1, 3, 7, 15, \dots, in which each term is twice the previous one plus one. X = 
N (or 
R), a = 1 and g(n, x) = 2x + 1; the rule does not use n. Since 2x + 1 \in 
N for x \in 
N (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (b)), g is a function 
N 	imes X 	o X, so @thm-recursion applies. The clauses give f(1) = 2 \cdot 1 + 1 = 3, f(2) = 7, f(3) = 15, as listed. Starting elsewhere, looking two steps back Two variants come up constantly. Sequences are often indexed from 1, as in Section 1.5, and some recursions use the two previous values. Both reduce to the theorem. [Recursion from a Base] Let n_0 be an integer, D \coloneqq \{ n \in 
Z : n \ge n_0 \}, X a set, a \in X, and g \colon D 	imes X 	o X a function. Then there is exactly one function f \colon D 	o X with f(n_0) = a and f(n + 1) = g(n, f(n)) for every n \in D. Rename the index: k = n - n_0 turns D into 
N and the recursion on D into one on 
N, where @thm-recursion applies. For k \in 
N, the number n_0 + k is an integer (@prp-integers-closed (a)) and n_0 + k \ge n_0 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (a)), so it lies in D. Conversely, for n \in D, n - n_0 is an integer (@prp-integers-closed (a)) and \ge 0, so n - n_0 \in 
N by @prp-integers-closed (b). Define g' \colon 
N 	imes X 	o X by g'(k, x) \coloneqq g(n_0 + k, x). By @thm-recursion there is exactly one f' \colon 
N 	o X with f'(0) = a and f'(k + 1) = g(n_0 + k, f'(k)) for every k \in 
N. Existence. Let t \colon D 	o 
N, t(n) \coloneqq n - n_0, and f \coloneqq f' \circ t (@def-composition). Then f(n_0) = f'(0) = a, and for n \in D, with k = n - n_0, f(n + 1) = f'(k + 1) = g igl(n_0 + k, f'(k) igr) = g igl(n, f(n) igr) . Uniqueness. If 	ilde f \colon D 	o X also satisfies both equations, then k \mapsto 	ilde f(n_0 + k) satisfies the equations that define f', so it is f' by the uniqueness in @thm-recursion. Hence 	ilde f(n) = f'(n - n_0) = f(n) for every n \in D, and 	ilde f = f by @prp-function-equality. The renaming is the move that gave induction from a base (@thm-induction). The corollary covers every sequence (a_n)_{n \ge 1} given by a first term and a rule, and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1’s intervals, which are listed from 1. [Two-Step Recursion] Let X be a set, a, b \in X, and h \colon 
N 	imes (X 	imes X) 	o X a function (@def-cartesian-product); write h(n, x, y) for h(n, (x, y)). Then there is exactly one function f \colon 
N 	o X with f(0) = a, \quad f(1) = b, \quad f(n + 2) = h igl(n, f(n), f(n + 1) igr) \ 	ext{ for every } n \in 
N . A rule that looks two steps back is a rule that looks one step back at pairs. Carry the pair (f(n), f(n + 1)) along: the next pair is (f(n + 1), f(n + 2)), and both of its entries are computed from the current pair. Define G \colon 
N 	imes (X 	imes X) 	o X 	imes X by G(n, (x, y)) \coloneqq (y, h(n, x, y)). By @thm-recursion with the set X 	imes X and the starting value (a, b), there is exactly one p \colon 
N 	o X 	imes X with p(0) = (a, b) and p(n + 1) = G(n, p(n)). Write p(n) = (p_1(n), p_2(n)). The equation p(n + 1) = (p_2(n), h(n, p_1(n), p_2(n))) gives, by the characteristic property of pairs (@def-ordered-pair), p_1(n + 1) = p_2(n), \qquad p_2(n + 1) = h igl(n, p_1(n), p_2(n) igr) . Let f(n) \coloneqq p_1(n). Then f(0) = a, f(1) = p_2(0) = b, and f(n + 2) = p_2(n + 1) = h igl(n, p_1(n), p_2(n) igr) = h igl(n, f(n), f(n + 1) igr) . For uniqueness, let f' satisfy the three equations, and let p'(n) \coloneqq (f'(n), f'(n + 1)). Then p'(0) = (a, b) and p'(n + 1) =  igl(f'(n + 1), \ h(n, f'(n), f'(n + 1)) igr) = G igl(n, p'(n) igr) , so p' = p by the uniqueness in @thm-recursion, and f'(n) = p_1(n) = f(n) for every n. By @prp-function-equality, f' = f. Do a_0 = 1, a_1 = 1 and a_{n+2} = a_{n+1} a_n define a sequence of reals? What is it? Yes, by @cor-two-step-recursion with X = 
R and h(n, x, y) = yx, a function 
N 	imes (
R 	imes 
R) 	o 
R. Every term is 1: induct on the pair statement “a_n = 1 and a_{n+1} = 1”, as in the two-step example below, after @def-power. It holds at n = 0, and if it holds at n, then a_{n+2} = 1 \cdot 1 = 1, so it holds at n + 1. Sums, products and powers The symbols \sum and \prod are recursive definitions, and so are powers. Writing them as instances of @thm-recursion settles what they mean at the edges: the empty sum, the empty product and u^0. [Finite Sums and Products] Let (a_k)_{k \ge 1} be a sequence of real numbers. The sums \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k and products \prod_{k=1}^{n} a_k, for n \in 
N, are defined by recursion:  egin{aligned} \sum_{k=1}^{0} a_k &\coloneqq 0, & \sum_{k=1}^{n+1} a_k &\coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k + a_{n+1}, \ \prod_{k=1}^{0} a_k &\coloneqq 1, & \prod_{k=1}^{n+1} a_k &\coloneqq \Bigl(\prod_{k=1}^{n} a_k\Bigr) a_{n+1}. \end{aligned} The factorial of n \in 
N is n! \coloneqq \prod_{k=1}^{n} k. For integers m \le n + 1 and reals a_k given for every integer k \ge m, \sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^{n-m+1} a_{m-1+i}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^{n-m+1} a_{m-1+i} . In words: a sum starts at 0 and adds one term at each stage; a product starts at 1 and multiplies by one term at each stage. The sum is @thm-recursion with X = 
R, a = 0 and g(n, x) = x + a_{n+1}, a function 
N 	imes 
R 	o 
R because n + 1 \ge 1 is an index of the sequence (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (a), (
NS)); the product is a = 1, g(n, x) = x a_{n+1}. The letter k is a dummy: \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k and \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_j are the same number. In the general form, n - m + 1 is an integer \ge 0, hence in 
N (@prp-integers-closed (b)), and the terms a_{m-1+i}, for i \ge 1, run through a_m, a_{m+1}, \dots; when m = 1 it gives the first form back. The edge cases are the point of the definition. The empty sum is 0 and the empty product is 1: \sum_{k=m}^{m-1} a_k = 0 and 0! = 1. These are the only values that make the recursive clause true at the first stage for every sequence, since \sum_{k=1}^{1} a_k should be a_1 and \prod_{k=1}^{1} a_k should be a_1. So 1! = 1, 2! = 2, 3! = 6, 4! = 24. Three consequences are used constantly, and each is a short check from the definition. - Finite lists. \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k depends only on a_1, \dots, a_n. Precisely: if two sequences agree at 1, \dots, N, their sums up to n agree for every n \le N. Induct on n with the property “if n \le N, the two sums up to n are equal”. The base is 0 = 0. In the step, n + 1 \le N gives n \le N, so the sums up to n agree, and the added terms a_{n+1} agree because 1 \le n + 1 \le N. So a finite list a_1, \dots, a_N is summed by extending it in any way, say by a_k \coloneqq 0 for k > N, and the result does not depend on the extension. The same holds for products, and for the general bounds with a_m, \dots, a_n. - Shifting the index. For every integer p, \sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k = \sum_{k=m+p}^{n+p} a_{k-p}, because both sides unfold to \sum_{i=1}^{n-m+1} a_{m-1+i}. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1’s estimate of y^k - x^k uses the shift p = 1. - Splitting off the last term. For m \le n + 1, \sum_{k=m}^{n+1} a_k = \sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k + a_{n+1}. Unfold the left side to \sum_{i=1}^{n-m+2} a_{m-1+i} and apply the recursive clause; its last term is a_{m-1+(n-m+2)} = a_{n+1}. [Powers] Let u \in 
R. The powers u^n, for n \in 
N, are defined by recursion: u^0 \coloneqq 1, \qquad u^{n+1} \coloneqq u^n u . This is @thm-recursion with X = 
R, a = 1 and g(n, x) = xu. So u^1 = u^0 u = u, and u^2 = uu. The definition gives 0^0 = 1, in line with the empty product: u^n = \prod_{k=1}^{n} u, since both sides obey the same two clauses and so agree by the uniqueness in @thm-recursion. Only exponents in 
N are defined here; roots a^{1/n} come in Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1. A sequence that approaches \sqrt 2. Let X \coloneqq (0, \infty) and g(n, x) \coloneqq 	frac12 (x + 2/x). Before writing a recursion, check that g maps X into X: for x > 0, 2/x is defined and positive, so x + 2/x > 0, and half of it is positive. By @thm-recursion, a_0 \coloneqq 2 and a_{n+1} \coloneqq 	frac12 (a_n + 2/a_n) define a sequence in (0, \infty). Because the check was made on g, no separate induction is needed to show a_n > 0 before dividing by it. The first values are a_0 = 2, \qquad a_1 = 	frac12 (2 + 1) = 	frac32, \qquad a_2 = 	frac12 \Bigl(	frac32 + 	frac43\Bigr) = 	frac{17}{12} , and (17/12)^2 = 289/144, which exceeds 2 by 1/144. That the sequence converges to \sqrt 2 is a question for Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 2, where recursively defined sequences become objects of study. A two-step example. By @cor-two-step-recursion, a_0 = 2, a_1 = 3 and a_{n+2} = 3a_{n+1} - 2a_n define a unique sequence of reals (X = 
R, h(n, x, y) = 3y - 2x), and its first values are 2, 3, 5, 9, 17. These are 2^n + 1. To prove it, induct on the pair statement Q(n): “a_n = 2^n + 1 and a_{n+1} = 2^{n+1} + 1”. Q(0) is 2 = 1 + 1 and 3 = 2 + 1. The last result of this subsection is not about a recursive definition, but its induction runs over lists, and it is the fact Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 needs about finite sets. A maximum of a set A \subseteq 
R is a greatest element of A in the sense of Section 2.1, and a minimum is a least element. For reals x_1, \dots, x_n, we write \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} \coloneqq \{ x_k : k \in \{1, \dots, n\} \}. [Finite Sets Have a Maximum] For every integer n \ge 1 and all reals x_1, \dots, x_n, the set \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} has a maximum and a minimum. Add the elements one at a time. The maximum of the longer list is the old maximum or the new element, whichever is larger, and comparing the two is all the step needs. Let P(n) be “for all reals x_1, \dots, x_n, the set \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} has a maximum”. We prove P(n) for every n \ge 1 by @thm-induction with base 1. Base case. \{x_1\} has the maximum x_1. Inductive step. Let n \ge 1, suppose P(n), and let x_1, \dots, x_{n+1} be reals. Since \{1, \dots, n + 1\} = \{1, \dots, n\} \cup \{n + 1\} (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e), as in the proof of @thm-recursion), the set B \coloneqq \{x_1, \dots, x_{n+1}\} is A \cup \{x_{n+1}\}, where A \coloneqq \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}. By P(n), applied to the list x_1, \dots, x_n, the set A has a maximum M. By trichotomy, x_{n+1} \le M or M < x_{n+1}. Case 1: x_{n+1} \le M. Then M \in A \subseteq B, and every element of B is an element a \in A, with a \le M, or is x_{n+1} \le M. So M is a maximum of B. Case 2: M < x_{n+1}. Then x_{n+1} \in B, and every a \in A satisfies a \le M < x_{n+1}. So x_{n+1} is a maximum of B. In both cases P(n + 1) holds. By @thm-induction, P(n) holds for every n \ge 1. For the minimum, apply the result to -x_1, \dots, -x_n: if -x_j is a maximum of \{-x_1, \dots, -x_n\}, then -x_k \le -x_j, that is x_j \le x_k, for every k, so x_j is a minimum of \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}. The base is 1, not 0: for n = 0 the set is \emptyset, which has neither a maximum nor a minimum, since both must be elements. The proof used only order properties of \le: any two elements are comparable (trichotomy), \le is reflexive and transitive, and x \mapsto -x reverses \le. All of these hold in any ordered field, so the proof works word for word there; that is the setting in which Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 uses it. Passing from a finite set to a list x_1, \dots, x_n that enumerates it is what “finite” means in Section 2.5. When the claim is too weak to carry its step Sometimes the statement we want is true, but it cannot be proved by induction as it stands: its inductive step does not go through. The cure looks paradoxical. We prove more. Logic and Proof met this cure (@fd1:exm-strengthen-the-claim) with a sum that telescopes, where the stronger claim was an exact formula; here the sum has no closed form, and the stronger claim is an inequality with a margin. [Proving more to prove anything] Prove that \sum_{k=1}^{n}  rac{1}{k^2} < 2 for every integer n \ge 1. The direct attempt fails. Let S_n \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{n} 1/k^2, so S_{n+1} = S_n + 1/(n + 1)^2 by @def-sum-product. The base S_1 = 1 < 2 holds. For the step, all we may assume is S_n < 2, and that is too little: it allows S_n = 2 -  rac{1}{2(n + 1)^2}, and then S_n +  rac{1}{(n + 1)^2} > 2. The values of S_n never come so close to 2, but the induction hypothesis cannot know that. Prove more. We prove P(n): “S_n \le 2 -  rac1n” for every n \ge 1, by @thm-induction with base 1. It implies the claim, since 2 -  rac1n < 2. Base case. S_1 = 1 = 2 -  rac11. Inductive step. Let n \ge 1 and suppose S_n \le 2 -  rac1n. Then S_{n+1} = S_n +  rac{1}{(n + 1)^2} \le 2 -  rac1n +  rac{1}{(n + 1)^2} . It remains to show - rac1n +  rac{1}{(n + 1)^2} \le - rac{1}{n + 1}, that is,  rac{1}{(n + 1)^2} \le  rac1n -  rac{1}{n + 1} =  rac{1}{n(n + 1)}. Both denominators are positive, and n(n + 1) \le (n + 1)^2 because n \le n + 1 and n + 1 > 0; so the inequality holds. Hence S_{n+1} \le 2 -  rac{1}{n + 1}, which is P(n + 1). By @thm-induction, S_n \le 2 -  rac1n < 2 for every n \ge 1. The stronger statement carries its own step because its hypothesis says how far below 2 the sum is, and that margin pays for the next term. When a step fails, ask what the hypothesis would need to say, and prove that instead.
