Prove both together, and use F_n + F_{n+1} = F_{n+2} to merge terms. [Hint 2] In the step, start with F_{2n+3} = F_{2n+2} + F_{2n+1} and substitute both halves of P(n). The definition. @cor-two-step-recursion with X = 
R, a = 0, b = 1 and h(n, x, y) = x + y gives exactly one sequence with F_0 = 0, F_1 = 1 and F_{n+2} = F_n + F_{n+1}. Its first values are 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Small cases. P(0): F_1 = 1 = 0^2 + 1^2 and F_2 = 1 = 1 \cdot (0 + 1). P(1): F_3 = 2 = 1^2 + 1^2 and F_4 = 3 = 1 \cdot (1 + 2). P(2): F_5 = 5 = 1^2 + 2^2 and F_6 = 8 = 2 \cdot (1 + 3). Proof. We use @fd1:ax-induction. P(0) was checked. Suppose P(n). Using the recursion and then both halves of P(n),  egin{aligned} F_{2n+3} &= F_{2n+2} + F_{2n+1} \ &= F_{n+1} F_n + F_{n+1} F_{n+2} + F_n^2 + F_{n+1}^2 \ &= F_n (F_n + F_{n+1}) + F_{n+1} F_{n+2} + F_{n+1}^2 \ &= F_{n+2} (F_n + F_{n+1}) + F_{n+1}^2 = F_{n+2}^2 + F_{n+1}^2 , \end{aligned} where the last two lines use F_n + F_{n+1} = F_{n+2} twice. This is the first half of P(n + 1). For the second half,  egin{aligned} F_{2n+4} &= F_{2n+3} + F_{2n+2} \ &= F_{n+1}^2 + F_{n+2}^2 + F_{n+1} F_n + F_{n+1} F_{n+2} \ &= F_{n+1} (F_{n+1} + F_n) + F_{n+2}^2 + F_{n+1} F_{n+2} \ &= F_{n+2}  igl(2F_{n+1} + F_{n+2} igr) = F_{n+2}  igl(F_{n+1} + F_{n+3} igr) , \end{aligned} using the first half of P(n + 1) just proved, the second half of P(n), F_{n+1} + F_n = F_{n+2}, and finally F_{n+1} + F_{n+2} = F_{n+3}. So P(n + 1) holds, and by @fd1:ax-induction P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. The second identity is written with F_{n+2} rather than in the form F_{2n} = F_n (F_{n-1} + F_{n+1}), so that both identities make sense on all of 
N and no F_{-1} is needed. The two identities hold together, and together they carry a one-step induction that neither carries alone: this is “prove more” (@exm-strengthen-hypothesis) in the form of a pair, as in the two-step example after @def-power. (A two-step induction can prove the first identity alone; see the marking scheme.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: defines the sequence by @cor-two-step-recursion, naming X, a, b and h. - 1: checks the base case P(0), both halves. - 3: proves the first identity at n + 1 (or for all n): F_{2n+3} = F_{n+1}^2 + F_{n+2}^2. - 3: proves the second identity at n + 1 (or for all n): F_{2n+4} = F_{n+2}(F_{n+1} + F_{n+3}). - 1: concludes by induction (one-step or two-step), with a hypothesis that covers every value the step uses. Alternative route: 3 for proving F_{2n+1} = F_n^2 + F_{n+1}^2 alone by a two-step induction (via F_{k+2} = 3F_k - F_{k-2} for k \ge 2 and the matching recursion for F_n^2 + F_{n+1}^2, with both bases n = 0, 1 checked), and 3 for deriving the second identity as F_{2n+2} = F_{2n+3} - F_{2n+1} = F_{n+2}^2 - F_n^2 = F_{n+1}(F_n + F_{n+2}). Fatal errors (0 for the step): inducting on one identity alone while using the other at n unproved; using the identities at n + 1 to prove themselves.

title: 2.4 Contrapositive and Contradiction in Practice
content:
Contrapositive and Contradiction in Practice Section 1.1 proved statements straight from their definitions, and Section 1.2 met the first contradiction about sets. Logic and Proof, Section 8.1 sorted the arguments called “by contradiction” into three faces: refuting a statement (ulename{
eg I}), proving the contrapositive, and genuine reductio (ulename{RAA}), with the rule “use the weakest form that works, and say which one you use”. This section is about choosing. Which form a proof takes is decided by the shape of the claim and by what each assumption hands over to compute with. The section proves that there are infinitely many primes and that \sqrt[3]{2} is irrational, makes the smallest counterexample of Section 2.2 a method of its own, and ends with a word on existence proofs that name no witness. Choosing the form To prove “if P, then Q” there are three ways to start. Assume P and work towards Q: a direct proof (@exm-method-direct-proof). Assume 
eg Q and work towards 
eg P: the contrapositive, which proves the original by @fd1:prp-contrapositive-converse. Or assume P and 
eg Q together and work towards a contradiction. A claim that is itself a negation, such as “irrational”, “no solution” or “no bijection”, has one natural start, face (i): assume the positive statement, reach  ot, and conclude the negation by ulename{
eg I}. The choice is not a matter of taste. Unwind each candidate assumption by its definitions, and ask which one hands over something to compute with. [A negative hypothesis] Let n \in 
Z. Show that if n^2 + n + 1 is not divisible by 3, then n leaves remainder 0 or 2 on division by 3. [Scratch work] Direct. The hypothesis 3 
mid n^2 + n + 1 says that no integer k has n^2 + n + 1 = 3k. That is a “there is no”, and it gives nothing to compute with: no equation, no object. Contrapositive. The negation of “remainder 0 or remainder 2” is “remainder not 0 and not 2” (@fd1:prp-de-morgan). The remainder lies in \{0, 1, 2\} and is unique (@thm-division-algorithm), so this says: remainder 1. So the new assumption is n = 3q + 1, an equation, and the new goal 3 \mid n^2 + n + 1 asks for a witness, which the equation may produce. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ---------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------- 3 
mid n^2 + n + 1 the remainder of n is 0 or 2 (contrapositive) n = 3q + 1, q \in 
Z 3 \mid n^2 + n + 1 n^2 + n + 1 = 9q^2 + 9q + 3 n^2 + n + 1 = 3m: m = 3q^2 + 3q + 1, the gap is closed ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The direct start stalled at the first line; the contrapositive closed the gap in two. We prove the contrapositive: if n does not leave remainder 0 or 2 on division by 3, then 3 \mid n^2 + n + 1. Divide n by 3 (@thm-division-algorithm): n = 3q + r with q \in 
Z and r \in \{0, 1, 2\} (by discreteness, @prp-integers-closed (c)), and r is unique. By assumption r 
e 0 and r 
e 2, so r = 1. Then n^2 + n + 1 = (9q^2 + 6q + 1) + (3q + 1) + 1 = 9q^2 + 9q + 3 = 3(3q^2 + 3q + 1) , and 3q^2 + 3q + 1 \in 
Z, so 3 \mid n^2 + n + 1. The contrapositive turned a “not divisible” in the hypothesis into a witness to produce, and an “or” in the conclusion into a single case to compute with. The statement is not vacuous: n = 0 and n = 2 give n^2 + n + 1 = 1 and 7, neither divisible by 3. Write the contrapositive and the negation of the statement of @exm-contrapositive-mod-three. Which one is equivalent to it? Contrapositive: “if n leaves remainder 1 on division by 3, then 3 \mid n^2 + n + 1”; it is equivalent to the statement. Negation: “there is an integer n with 3 
mid n^2 + n + 1 that leaves remainder 1”; it is not equivalent, and it is false by the example. The example shows the questions to ask before any proof, and they are worth fixing as a method. [Method: choosing direct, contrapositive or contradiction] Template. Unwind P, Q, 
eg P and 
eg Q by their definitions. If P gives something to compute towards Q, go direct. If 
eg Q gives an equation, a case split or an object, and 
eg P is a statement you can reach, prove the contrapositive and announce it (“We prove the contrapositive”). If the claim is a negation (irrational, no solution, no bijection, no largest), assume the positive statement and derive a contradiction (ulename{
eg I}). Otherwise assume P and 
eg Q together, and use both. When to use it. Before every proof; at once when the direct attempt stalls, or when the conclusion is an “or”, a “not”, a “no” or “infinitely many”. The usual failure. A wrong negation: the negation of “A or B” is “not A and not B” (@fd1:prp-de-morgan). A “contradiction” that never uses its assumption 
eg Q, which is a direct proof in costume (@fd1:exm-costume-direct; for the contrapositive, @fd1:exm-costume-contrapositive). Not saying which form is used. Which form, and what first sentence, for the following? 1. For x \in 
R, if x^2 
e x, then x 
e 1. 2. There is no integer n with n^2 = 2. 3. For f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon Y 	o Z, if g \circ f is injective, then f is injective. (a) Contrapositive: “Suppose x = 1; then x^2 = 1 = x.” (b) Face (i), since the claim is a negation: “Suppose n \in 
Z and n^2 = 2.” (Then \abs{n} \le 1 gives n^2 \le 1, and \abs{n} \ge 2 gives n^2 \ge 4.) (c) Direct, by the method of @exm-method-injectivity: “Let x_1, x_2 \in X with f(x_1) = f(x_2).” Then g(f(x_1)) = g(f(x_2)), and injectivity of g \circ f gives x_1 = x_2. Infinitely many primes Logic and Proof, Section 8.1 met Euclid’s argument for a finite list of primes (@fd1:exr-connective-rhetoric-c1); here is a version that puts, for each n, a prime above n, and Exercise C2 turns the list argument into a bound of its own. @thm-prime-factor gives every integer n \ge 2 a prime factor. To show that the primes never run out, it is enough to build, for each n, a number all of whose prime factors exceed n. Multiplying 1, 2, \dots, n together and adding 1 does it. [There Are Infinitely Many Primes] For every n \in 
N there is a prime p with p > n. The number n! + 1 leaves remainder 1 on division by every k with 2 \le k \le n, so none of them divides it. Its prime factor (@thm-prime-factor) must therefore exceed n. The last step is a face (i) argument inside the proof: suppose p \le n. Step 1. For every n \in 
N, n! is a positive integer and k \mid n! for every k \in \{1, \dots, n\}. We use induction on n, following the clauses of n! (@def-sum-product). For n = 0, 0! = 1, and there is no k. Suppose the claim holds for n. Then (n + 1)! = n! \cdot (n + 1) is a positive integer. For k \le n, the hypothesis gives n! = kj with j \in 
Z, so (n + 1)! = k \cdot j(n + 1); and k = n + 1 divides (n + 1)! = n! \cdot (n + 1). Every k \in \{1, \dots, n + 1\} has k \le n or k = n + 1 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e)). Step 2. Let n \in 
N, and let N \coloneqq n! + 1. By Step 1 and @prp-integers-closed (b), n! \ge 1, so N \ge 2, and N has a prime factor p (@thm-prime-factor). Suppose p \le n. Since p \ge 2, p \in \{1, \dots, n\}, so p \mid n! by Step 1. From p \mid N and p \mid n!, p \mid N - n! = 1 (@exm-divides-combination). So 1 = kp with k \in 
Z; then k > 0, so k \ge 1, and p \le kp = 1, against p \ge 2. Hence p > n, by trichotomy. This proves the theorem. The proof does not say that n! + 1 is prime. For n = 4, n! + 1 = 25 = 5 \cdot 5. The proof uses only that n! + 1 has some prime factor, and shows that every one of them exceeds n. Run the proof at n = 5: compute N and a prime p > 5 dividing it. Is N prime? N = 5! + 1 = 121 = 11 \cdot 11, and p = 11 > 5. N is not prime. [Looking ahead] Section 2.5 defines infinite sets; with that definition, the set of primes is infinite. An irrational number by lowest terms Logic and Proof proved \sqrt 2 irrational (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational) with the fact (L), which @lem-lowest-terms now proves. The same lemma settles a cube root. Here \sqrt[3]{2} is the real number x with x^3 = 2; its existence and uniqueness are school facts, as in Section 1.6. [The Cube Root of 2 Is Irrational] \sqrt[3]{2} is irrational. The claim is a negation, so face (i): suppose \sqrt[3]{2} = p/q in the form of @lem-lowest-terms, and show that p and q are both even. One step, “p^3 even \Rightarrow p even”, is itself a contrapositive. A contrapositive first. For p \in 
Z, if p^3 is even, then p is even. Suppose p is not even. Then p is odd (@thm-even-or-odd), p = 2k + 1 with k \in 
Z, and p^3 = 8k^3 + 12k^2 + 6k + 1 = 2(4k^3 + 6k^2 + 3k) + 1 is odd, hence not even (@thm-even-or-odd). The claim. Suppose \sqrt[3]{2} is rational. By @lem-lowest-terms, \sqrt[3]{2} = p/q with p \in 
Z, q \in 
Z_{>0}, and p and q not both even. Cubing, p^3 = 2q^3, so p^3 is even, and p is even: p = 2s with s \in 
Z. Then 8s^3 = 2q^3, so q^3 = 4s^3 = 2(2s^3) is even, and q is even. So p and q are both even, a contradiction. Hence \sqrt[3]{2} is irrational (ulename{
eg I}). The outer frame is face (i), with no ulename{RAA}: the proof refutes “\sqrt[3]{2} is rational”. The step inside it is face (ii), a contrapositive whose conclusion “p even” is not a negation, so it rests on @fd1:prp-contrapositive-converse. (It could also avoid ulename{RAA}: by @thm-even-or-odd, p is even or odd, and the odd case closes by ulename{ ot E}.) The lemma’s “not both even” is the given that the contradiction breaks; without the lemma there would be nothing to contradict. Why does the same proof not show that \sqrt[3]{3} is irrational? p^3 = 3q^3 gives no parity contradiction: with q odd, p^3 is odd and p is odd, and “not both even” survives. The proof needs “no common divisor 3”, which Exercise C2 of Section 2.2 provides. The smallest counterexample Well-ordering gives the same power as strong induction, in a form that often reads more naturally. To prove a claim about every integer from n_0 on, suppose it fails somewhere. The failures form a non-empty set of integers with the integer lower bound n_0, so @cor-well-ordering-integers gives a least one. Below it the claim holds. If that is enough to produce a failure that is smaller still, or to show the claim at the least failure after all, we have a contradiction. To prove “P(n) for every integer n \ge n_0” by a smallest counterexample: - Suppose it fails: some integer n \ge n_0 has P(n) false. - Take the least failure: the set F of integers n \ge n_0 with P(n) false is non-empty and has the integer lower bound n_0, so it has a least element m (@cor-well-ordering-integers; @thm-well-ordering when n_0 \ge 0, since then F \subseteq 
N). - Use the claim below m: P(k) holds for every integer k with n_0 \le k < m, since such a k is not in F. - Produce a contradiction: a failure k < m, or P(m) itself. Then F is empty, and P(n) holds for every integer n \ge n_0. The method is strong induction with an ulename{RAA} box drawn around it. The work done inside the box, “if P(k) for every k with n_0 \le k < m, then P(m)”, is exactly the hypothesis of @thm-strong-induction-from-base at m; so any smallest-counterexample proof can be rewritten as a strong induction, and the reverse rewriting works too. Which one to write is a matter of which reads better. A smallest counterexample suits claims whose failure has a natural “smaller failure”, like a fraction that can be reduced, or a number with a factor. Section 2.2 used it in @lem-lowest-terms and in the proof sketched before @thm-prime-factor, and its Exercise B2 asks for one. [Method: the smallest counterexample] Template. The four steps of the list above, opening with “Suppose not, and let m be the least integer \ge n_0 for which P(m) fails”. The least failure is @exm-method-least-element applied to the set of failures. Worked examples: @lem-lowest-terms (Section 2.2) and @exm-three-power-factor below. When to use it. A failure would give a smaller failure: a number with a factor, a fraction that can be reduced, a representation that can be shortened. The usual failure. Not checking that the smaller object is still \ge n_0 (or positive), so that it lies in the set of failures. Forgetting the case in which no smaller object exists, which must be ruled out directly (in the example below, m not divisible by 3). [Taking out the threes] Show that every positive integer n is 3^a \cdot b with a \in 
N, b \in 
Z and 3 
mid b. [Scratch work] This is the argument of Exercise C1 of Section 2.3, with 3 in place of 2; here each step of the method is named. Suppose some positive integer has no such form, and let m be the least one. Unwind what m can be. If 3 \mid m, say m = 3m', then m' is a smaller positive integer, so it has the form, and one more factor 3 gives m the form too. If 3 
mid m, there is no smaller object to pass to; but then m = 3^0 \cdot m already has the form, so m was not a failure at all. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------- m the least positive integer with no form 3^a b, 3 
mid b; every k with 1 \le k < m has one a contradiction case 3 
mid m m = 3^0 \cdot m: m has the form after all case m = 3m': 1 \le m' < m, so m' = 3^a b with 3 
mid b m = 3^{a+1} b: m has the form; the gap is closed ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Suppose not, and let F be the set of positive integers with no such form. F is a non-empty subset of 
N, so it has a least element m (@thm-well-ordering). If 3 
mid m, then m = 3^0 \cdot m with 3 
mid m, so m 
otin F, a contradiction. So m = 3m' with m' \in 
Z; m' > 0 since m > 0, so m' \in 
Z_{>0} (@prp-integers-closed (b)), and m' < 3m' = m. As m is least in F, m' 
otin F: m' = 3^a b with a \in 
N, b \in 
Z and 3 
mid b. Then m = 3^{a+1} b (@def-power), so m 
otin F, a contradiction. Hence F = \emptyset. Write 54 and 45 in the form of @exm-three-power-factor, and say why m' 
otin F in the proof. 54 = 3^3 \cdot 2 and 45 = 3^2 \cdot 5. And m' is a positive integer smaller than the least element of F, so it cannot lie in F. Existence without a witness A proof of “there exists” by contradiction, an ulename{RAA} on a statement \exists x \, \varphi(x), may finish without naming any object. @thm-well-ordering was proved so, and the remark after its proof said what that means: the proof shows that a least element exists, not how to find one. Logic and Proof, Section 8.7 gave the classical example, an irrational power of an irrational number that is rational, shown to exist between two candidates without saying which one works (@fd1:thm-irrational-power-rational). It also gave the book’s position: classical rules are allowed, and a proof that names no witness is still a proof. The proof of @thm-primes-infinite and the contrapositive of @exm-contrapositive-mod-three went the other way. The proof of @thm-primes-infinite names its witness: a prime factor of n! + 1, and trying 2, 3, 4, \dots in turn finds the least one. The contrapositive in @exm-contrapositive-mod-three turned an existence goal into an explicit witness, m = 3q^2 + 3q + 1. (The smallest-counterexample proof of @exm-three-power-factor is formally an ulename{RAA}, but its two cases describe how to find a and b.) A named witness says more than bare existence, and it can be checked by computation. So the advice is: when a witness is cheap, name it. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write the converse, the contrapositive and the negation of “if n is prime and n \ge 3, then n is odd”. Which are true? 2. Name the form you would choose and write the first sentence (no proofs): (i) \sqrt[3]{3} is irrational; (ii) for a, b \in 
Z, if a^2 + b^2 is odd, then a is even or b is even; (iii) for sets A, B, if A \cup B = A \cap B, then A = B. 3. Run the proof of @thm-primes-infinite at n = 6: find N, its least prime factor, and check that it exceeds 6. 4. “Suppose p is the largest prime. Then p! + 1 has a prime factor q > p, a contradiction.” Which face of “by contradiction” is this, and does the proof name a prime larger than p? (a) Converse: if n is odd, then n is prime and n \ge 3. False: 9 = 3 \cdot 3. Contrapositive: if n is even, then n is not prime or n < 3. It is equivalent to the statement, and true: an even n \ge 3 has the divisor 2 
otin \{1, n\}. Negation: some prime n \ge 3 is even. False. (“Not odd” is “even” by @thm-even-or-odd.) (b) (i) Face (i): “Suppose \sqrt[3]{3} = p/q with p \in 
Z, q \in 
Z_{>0} and no common divisor d \ge 2” (Exercise C2 of Section 2.2; “not both even” is not enough, as the last Quick check of the subsection on \sqrt[3]{2} shows). (ii) Contrapositive: “Suppose a and b are both odd”, the negation of “a even or b even” by @fd1:prp-de-morgan and @thm-even-or-odd; then a^2 and b^2 are odd (@fd1:thm-odd-iff-square-odd), and a^2 + b^2 is even (@exm-parity-of-sums). (iii) Direct, by @exm-method-double-inclusion: “Let x \in A.” (c) N = 6! + 1 = 721. It is not divisible by 2, 3 or 5: 721 = 2 \cdot 360 + 1 = 3 \cdot 240 + 1 = 5 \cdot 144 + 1. And 721 = 7 \cdot 103. The least prime factor is 7 > 6, and 721 is not prime. (d) Face (i): it refutes “there is a largest prime”. Its body names q, so it can be rewritten without contradiction: for every prime p, a prime factor of p! + 1 is a larger prime (@thm-primes-infinite with n = p). This is the rewrite of @fd1:exr-connective-rhetoric-c1, applied to p! + 1 in place of Euclid’s product. B. Practice [B1: Contrapositive] Prove: 1. for all a, b \in 
Z, if 3 
mid a + b, then 3 
mid a or 3 
mid b; 2. for every x \in 
R, if x^2 > 2x + 8, then x > 4 or x < -2. (a) We prove the contrapositive: if 3 \mid a and 3 \mid b, then 3 \mid a + b; its hypothesis is the negation of “3 
mid a or 3 
mid b” by @fd1:prp-de-morgan. With a = 3k and b = 3l, a + b = 3(k + l) (@exm-divides-combination). (b) We prove the contrapositive. Suppose x \le 4 and x \ge -2 (the negation of the conclusion, by @fd1:prp-de-morgan and trichotomy). Then x - 4 \le 0 and x + 2 \ge 0, so x^2 - 2x - 8 = (x - 4)(x + 2) \le 0, that is, x^2 \le 2x + 8. [B2: Contradiction] Prove: 1. there is no rational number r with r^2 = r + 1; 2. there are no integers m, n with m^2 - 8n = 5. (a) Suppose r^2 = r + 1, with r = p/q as in @lem-lowest-terms. Multiplying by q^2, p^2 = pq + q^2. Two facts about products: odd times odd is odd, since (2k + 1)(2l + 1) = 2(2kl + k + l) + 1, and an even number times any integer is even. Since p and q are not both even, three cases remain. If p, q are odd: p^2 is odd, and pq + q^2 is odd plus odd, even (@exm-parity-of-sums). If p is even and q odd: p^2 is even, and pq + q^2 is even plus odd, odd. If p is odd and q even: p^2 is odd, and pq + q^2 is even. Each case equates an odd and an even integer, against @thm-even-or-odd. (b) Suppose m^2 = 8n + 5 = 2(4n + 2) + 1. Then m^2 is odd, so m is odd (@fd1:thm-odd-iff-square-odd), and m^2 = 8t + 1 with t \in 
Z by @exr-induction-in-practice-b3 (b). So 8(t - n) = 4, and 2(t - n) = 1: 1 would be even, against @thm-even-or-odd. [B3: Name the move, then complete it] Claim: n < 2^n for every integer n \ge 1. Here is a proof with its last step blank. Suppose not. Then the set F of integers n \ge 1 with n \ge 2^n is non-empty and has the integer lower bound 1, so it has a least element m (@cor-well-ordering-integers). Since 1 < 2 = 2^1, m 
e 1, so m \ge 2, and m - 1 is an integer with 1 \le m - 1 < m. \dots The move is the smallest counterexample (@exm-method-smallest-counterexample), and the blank is its last step. As m - 1 < m, m - 1 
otin F: m - 1 < 2^{m-1}. Since 2^{m-1} \in 
N (@prp-power-laws (d)), discreteness gives m \le 2^{m-1}. And 2^{m-1} < 2^{m-1} \cdot 2 = 2^m (@def-power, with m - 1 \in 
N, and 2^{m-1} > 0 by @prp-power-laws (e)). So m < 2^m, that is, m 
otin F, a contradiction. [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement; refute each false one with a concrete counterexample. 1. For every n \in 
Z: if n^2 - 1 is not divisible by 5, then n is divisible by 5. 2. For every n \in 
Z: if 4 
mid n^2, then n is odd. 3. For every x \in 
R: if x is irrational, then x^2 is irrational. 4. For every x \in 
R: if x^2 is irrational, then x is irrational. 5. For all positive integers a, b: a^2 - b^2 
e 10. 6. For every n \in 
N there is a prime p with n < p \le n + 6. (a) False. Take n = 2: n^2 - 1 = 3 is not divisible by 5, and neither is 2. (b) True. We prove the contrapositive. If n is not odd, it is even (@thm-even-or-odd), n = 2k, and n^2 = 4k^2, so 4 \mid n^2. (Its look-alike “if 4 \mid n^2, then 4 \mid n” is false at n = 2.) (c) False. Take x = \sqrt 2, irrational by @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational: x^2 = 2 is rational. (d) True. We prove the contrapositive: if x = p/q is rational, so is x^2 = p^2/q^2. (e) True, by contradiction (face (i)). Suppose a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b) = 10. Since a + b = (a - b) + 2b and 2b is even (@thm-even-or-odd), the two factors have the same parity (@exm-parity-of-sums). If both are odd, the product is odd, since (2k + 1)(2l + 1) = 2(2kl + k + l) + 1 as in B2 (a), but 10 is even. If both are even, 4 divides the product, but 10 = 4 \cdot 2 + 2 is not a multiple of 4 (uniqueness in @thm-division-algorithm). (f) False. Take n = 89. The numbers 90, \dots, 95 are not prime: 90, 92, 94 are even, 91 = 7 \cdot 13, 93 = 3 \cdot 31, 95 = 5 \cdot 19. (89 is the smallest counterexample.) Verdicts: three true, (b), (d), (e); three false. C. Going deeper [C1: Two proofs by contradiction] For each proof below: is the conclusion true? Is the argument valid? Name each flaw, and write a proof in the form that @exm-method-choosing-the-form recommends. Proof A. Claim: if n \in 
Z is odd, then n^2 + n is even. “Suppose n is odd and n^2 + n is odd. Write n = 2k + 1. Then n^2 + n = (2k + 1)(2k + 2) = 2(2k + 1)(k + 1) is even, which contradicts n^2 + n odd.” Proof B. Claim: for every n \in 
Z, if n^2 \ge 10, then n \ge 4 or n \le -4. 1. Suppose n^2 \ge 10. 2. Suppose, for a contradiction, that n < 4 or n > -4. 3. Say n < 4, so n \le 3. 4. If also n \ge -3, then n^2 \le 9 < 10; so n \le -4. 5. So n \le -4, which proves the claim. Proof A. The conclusion is true and the argument is valid, but the assumption “n^2 + n odd” is used only to clash with the result: a direct proof in costume (@fd1:exm-costume-direct). Written directly: “Let n = 2k + 1 with k \in 
Z; then n^2 + n = 2(2k + 1)(k + 1) is even.” The hypothesis is not even needed: n^2 + n = n(n + 1), and one of n, n + 1 is even. Proof B. The conclusion is true; the argument is not a proof. Line (2) negates “n \ge 4 or n \le -4” wrongly, entry (N11) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue: the negation is “n < 4 and n > -4” (@fd1:prp-de-morgan). Line (3) takes one disjunct of its own “or” and drops the other, a missing case (N7). Line (5) reaches no contradiction at all. A proof by the contrapositive: if n < 4 and n > -4, then -3 \le n \le 3 (@prp-integers-closed (c)), so \abs{n} \le 3 and n^2 \le 9 < 10. Or by cases: if n \ge 4, done; if n \le 3, then n \le -4 by the computation of line (4). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: judges A’s conclusion true and its argument valid, and names the assumption it never uses. - 1: rewrites A as a direct proof. - 3: names the wrong negation in line (2) and gives the correct one (citing (N11) is optional). - 1: names the missing case (N7). - 1: notes that B reaches no contradiction. - 2: gives a correct proof of B’s claim. [C2: A bound from Euclid’s list] Logic and Proof, Section 8.1 proved that for primes p_1, \dots, p_k, with k \ge 1, the number p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k + 1 has a prime factor different from each p_i (@fd1:exr-connective-rhetoric-c1). Here that argument becomes a bound. Let p_1 \coloneqq 2, and let p_{n+1} be the least prime greater than p_n; it exists by @thm-primes-infinite and @thm-well-ordering, and @cor-recursion-from-base makes (p_n)_{n \ge 1} a sequence. So p_2 = 3, p_3 = 5. 1. Prove that for every n \ge 1, every prime q \le p_n is one of p_1, \dots, p_n. 2. Prove that p_{n+1} \le p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n + 1 for every n \ge 1. 3. Deduce that p_n \le 2^{2^{n-1}} for every n \ge 1. 4. Compute P = p_1 \cdots p_k + 1 and its prime factors for the lists 3, 5 and 2, 7. Is P prime? (a) By @thm-induction with base 1. For n = 1: a prime q \le 2 has q \ge 2, so q = 2 = p_1. Suppose the claim for n, and let q \le p_{n+1} be prime. If q \le p_n, then q is one of p_1, \dots, p_n by the hypothesis. Otherwise q > p_n, by trichotomy; then q is a prime greater than p_n, so p_{n+1} \le q, as p_{n+1} is the least one, and q = p_{n+1}. (b) Let n \ge 1 and P \coloneqq p_1 \cdots p_n + 1. Each p_i \ge 2, so P \ge 3, and P has a prime factor q (@thm-prime-factor). Suppose q = p_i for some i \le n. Then p_i divides p_1 \cdots p_n, which is p_i times the product of the other entries (school arithmetic of finite products, @def-sum-product), so q \mid P - p_1 \cdots p_n = 1 (@exm-divides-combination), and q \le 1 as in the proof of @thm-primes-infinite, against q \ge 2. So q is none of p_1, \dots, p_n, and by (a) q 
ot\le p_n: q > p_n. Hence p_{n+1} \le q, by the choice of p_{n+1}. Finally P = kq with k \in 
Z, and k > 0 since P, q > 0, so k \ge 1 and q \le kq = P. (c) By @thm-strong-induction-from-base with base 1. For n = 1, p_1 = 2 = 2^{2^0}. Let n \ge 1, and suppose p_k \le 2^{2^{k-1}} for every k with 1 \le k \le n. By (b), multiplying these n inequalities between positive numbers, @prp-power-laws (a) and @prp-geometric-sum with r = 2, p_{n+1} \le p_1 \cdots p_n + 1 \le 2^{2^0 + 2^1 + \dots + 2^{n-1}} + 1 = 2^{2^n - 1} + 1 \le 2 \cdot 2^{2^n - 1} = 2^{2^n}, where the last inequality uses 1 \le 2^{2^n - 1}. (d) 3 \cdot 5 + 1 = 16 = 2^4, with prime factor 2. 2 \cdot 7 + 1 = 15 = 3 \cdot 5, with prime factors 3 and 5. Neither P is prime; each has a prime factor off its list, and neither list is an initial segment p_1, \dots, p_k, so (b) says nothing about them. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a), with the base case and the use of leastness of p_{n+1}. - 3: (b): a prime factor q of P off the list, q > p_n by (a), and p_{n+1} \le q \le P. - 3: (c): strong induction, the geometric sum in the exponent, and 2^{2^n - 1} + 1 \le 2^{2^n}. - 1: both computations in (d). [C3: Challenge: primes of the form 3k + 2] Prove that for every integer n \ge 1 there is a prime p > n with p = 3k + 2 for some k \in 
Z. Hint: consider N \coloneqq 3 \cdot n! - 1, and @exr-induction-in-practice-b2. N = 3(n! - 1) + 2 \ge 2, since n! \ge 1. By @exr-induction-in-practice-b2, N = q_1 \cdots q_r with primes q_i. Each q_i > n: if q_i \le n, then q_i \mid n! (Step 1 of the proof of @thm-primes-infinite), and q_i \mid N (school arithmetic of finite products, as in Exercise C2), so q_i \mid 3 \cdot n! - N = 1 (@exm-divides-combination), which is impossible. No q_i is 3, since N leaves remainder 2 on division by 3. Dividing q_i by 3 (@thm-division-algorithm) and using discreteness, each q_i is 3t, 3t + 1 or 3t + 2. So each q_i is 3t + 1 or 3t + 2: if q_i = 3t, then 3 \mid q_i, and q_i = 3 since q_i is prime. If every q_i were of the form 3t + 1, then N would be too, since (3a + 1)(3b + 1) = 3(3ab + a + b) + 1 and an induction on r carries this along the product; but N = 3(n! - 1) + 2, against the uniqueness in @thm-division-algorithm. So some q_i is 3t + 2, and q_i > n. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: shows N \ge 2 and a factorization into primes. - 2: shows each q_i > n via q_i \mid n!. - 1: shows q_i 
e 3. - 2: shows each q_i is 3t + 1 or 3t + 2. - 2: shows a product of factors 3t + 1 is 3t + 1, by induction. - 1: the contradiction with remainder 2.

title: 2.5 Equinumerous Sets and Finite Sets
content:
Equinumerous Sets and Finite Sets Section 1.1 left a puzzle half solved: among any five lattice points, two have a lattice point as midpoint, provided that five objects in four boxes always put two in one box. That principle sounds too obvious to need proof, but it is a statement about every finite collection, and “finite” has no definition yet. Section 1.6 supplied the tool: a bijection pairs the elements of two sets one for one. This section makes “the same size” mean “there is a bijection”, defines finite sets by pairing with \{1, \dots, n\}, proves the pigeonhole principle and comes back to the five points, and then proves the facts about finite sets on which counting rests. Whether 
Q is larger than 
N is the question of Chapter 3. Same size without counting So far we have compared functions; now we compare sets. The everyday word is “as many as”, and we can check it without knowing any numbers. Put two piles of coins on a table, and take one coin from each pile at a time, setting the two aside as a pair. If both piles run out at the same moment, they had the same number of coins. We know this before counting either pile, and a child who cannot count past ten can do it with piles of a thousand. Section 1.6 proved that the bijections are exactly the maps with a two-sided inverse (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse), and said that such a pairing is how this book says “the same size”. The pairing is a function from the first pile to the second. Different coins are paired with different coins, so it is injective; every coin of the second pile is used, so it is surjective. Pairing makes sense for any two sets, finite or not, and that is the definition. Same size means there is a pairing. [Equinumerous Sets] Let A and B be sets. We say that A and B are equinumerous, and write \card{A} = \card{B}, if there exists a bijection f \colon A 	o B. In symbols, \card{A} = \card{B} \iff \exists f \in B^A \ \ (f 	ext{ is injective} \wedge f 	ext{ is surjective}) . In words: the definition asks for one bijection, and it does not care which. Injectivity says that no two elements of A are paired with the same element of B; surjectivity says that no element of B is left over. The statement \card{A} = \card{B} is read as a whole, “A and B are equinumerous”. It is a relation between two sets. We do not define an object \card{A}, “the size of A”, standing alone, and a second-reading fold below explains why the obvious candidate is not available. For finite sets, the definition of a finite set below gives \card{A} a meaning as a natural number, and the two uses agree. Here are four examples, the degenerate one first. - The empty set. The empty function \emptyset 	o \emptyset of @prp-empty-function (a) is injective and surjective, vacuously: there are no two inputs to compare and no output to reach. So \card{\emptyset} = \card{\emptyset}. Conversely, if \card{A} = \card{\emptyset}, there is a function A 	o \emptyset, so A = \emptyset by @prp-empty-function (b). The empty set is equinumerous with itself and with nothing else. This case is the test case for every statement below about sets “with n elements”, at n = 0. - Three letters and three numbers. Let a, b, c be three different letters. The function \{a, b, c\} 	o \{1, 2, 3\} with a \mapsto 1, b \mapsto 2, c \mapsto 3 sends different letters to different numbers and reaches each of 1, 2, 3. So \card{\{a, b, c\}} = \card{\{1, 2, 3\}}. - Two intervals of different lengths. The function f \colon [0, 1] 	o [0, 2], f(x) = 2x, has the inverse y \mapsto y/2, since y/2 \in [0, 1] for y \in [0, 2], f(y/2) = y and f(x)/2 = x. By @thm-bijection-iff-inverse it is a bijection, so \card{[0, 1]} = \card{[0, 2]}. Length and size are different things. - The natural numbers and the positive integers. The function 
N 	o 
Z_{>0}, n \mapsto n + 1, is a bijection. It is the Quick check near the end of this section, where it shows that 
N is infinite. Decide, from @def-equinumerous: (a) \card{\emptyset} = \card{\{\emptyset\}}? (b) \card{\{1, 2\}} = \card{\{\{1, 2\}\}}? (c) \card{\{ x \in 
R : x^2 = -1 \}} = \card{\emptyset}? (a) No. The set \{\emptyset\} has the element \emptyset, and a function \emptyset 	o \{\emptyset\} has no values, so it is not surjective. (b) No. The set \{\{1, 2\}\} has one element, so every function \{1, 2\} 	o \{\{1, 2\}\} sends 1 and 2 to it and is not injective. (c) Yes. The set \{ x \in 
R : x^2 = -1 \} is empty, and the empty function \emptyset 	o \emptyset is a bijection. A non-example by a minimal change. Shrink \{1, 2, 3\} to \{1, 2\}. There is no bijection \{a, b, c\} 	o \{1, 2\}. Let g be any function \{a, b, c\} 	o \{1, 2\}. If g(a) = g(b), then g is not injective. Otherwise g(a) and g(b) are 1 and 2 in some order, and g(c), which is 1 or 2, equals one of them. In every case two different letters share a value. So the clause that fails is injectivity, and it fails for every function, which is what “not equinumerous” requires. Surjectivity can hold: a \mapsto 1, b \mapsto 2, c \mapsto 2 reaches both numbers. To show that two sets are not equinumerous, one map is never enough. The map x \mapsto x from [0, 1] to [0, 2] is not surjective, since 2 is not a value, and yet \card{[0, 1]} = \card{[0, 2]} by the map x \mapsto 2x above. “Not equinumerous” is a statement about all functions,  orall f \in B^A \, 
eg(f 	ext{ bijective}), and a proof of it must deal with an arbitrary f, as the non-example did. Why this definition. To count a set is to pair it with \{1, \dots, n\}: saying “one, two, three” while pointing at the coins is a bijection from \{1, 2, 3\} onto the pile. So the definition does not replace counting; it isolates the part of counting that still makes sense when the set is infinite. Each clause has a job. Without injectivity, the surjection \{1, 2, 3\} 	o \{1\} would make a three-element set as large as a one-element set. Without surjectivity, the inclusion \{1\} 	o \{1, 2, 3\} would do the same in the other direction. The first result says that equinumerosity behaves like equality: reflexive, symmetric and transitive. [Equinumerosity Is Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive] For all sets A, B and C: 1. \card{A} = \card{A}; 2. if \card{A} = \card{B}, then \card{B} = \card{A}; 3. if \card{A} = \card{B} and \card{B} = \card{C}, then \card{A} = \card{C}. (a) The identity \id_A is injective, since \id_A(x) = \id_A(y) says x = y, and surjective, since every x \in A is \id_A(x). (b) Let f \colon A 	o B be a bijection. By @thm-bijection-iff-inverse it has a two-sided inverse f^{-1} \colon B 	o A, with f^{-1} \circ f = \id_A and f \circ f^{-1} = \id_B. Read with the roles exchanged, these two equations say that f is a two-sided inverse of f^{-1} (@def-inverse-function). So f^{-1} is a bijection B 	o A, by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse again. (c) If f \colon A 	o B and g \colon B 	o C are bijections, then g \circ f \colon A 	o C is a bijection by @thm-composition-injective-surjective (c). This proves the proposition. Clauses (a)–(c) say that equinumerosity behaves like an equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric and transitive, as equality is. We do not call it one. Chapter 4 makes “equivalence relation” precise for relations on a set X, subsets of X 	imes X; equinumerosity relates any two sets whatever, and there is no set of all sets for it to live on (@thm-russell). That is also why the book writes \card{A} = \card{B} here and keeps the symbol \sim for later. Why not define \card{A} as “the collection of all sets equinumerous with A”? Because that collection is in general not a set. The next paragraph proves this for A = \{0\}. Take A = \{0\}. Every singleton \{x\} is equinumerous with \{0\}, by 0 \mapsto x. If the singletons formed a set \sS, its union  igcup \sS would be a set by (W3) of Section 1.2, and every object x would be an element of it, since x \in \{x\} \in \sS. That is a set of which every set is an element, which @thm-russell rules out. Finite sets Counting is pairing with \{1, \dots, n\}, so “finite” is defined by such a pairing. Recall from Section 2.1 that for n \in 
N, \{1, \dots, n\} \coloneqq \{ k \in 
N : 1 \le k \le n \} , so that \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset, since no k has 1 \le k \le 0. [Finite Set, Number of Elements] Let A be a set and n \in 
N. We say that A has n elements if \card{\{1, \dots, n\}} = \card{A}, that is, if there exists a bijection \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A. The set A is finite if it has n elements for some n \in 
N. In that case we write \card{A} = n. In words: \varphi numbers the elements of A as \varphi(1), \varphi(2), \dots, \varphi(n). Injectivity says that no element gets two numbers; surjectivity says that every element gets one. So a non-empty finite set is A = \{\varphi(1), \dots, \varphi(n)\}, a list without repetitions. By @prp-equinumerous-properties (b), “A has n elements” is the same as \card{A} = \card{\{1, \dots, n\}}, so the notation \card{A} = n is consistent with the relation of @def-equinumerous. There is a gap in the notation \card{A} = n. It presents n as the number of elements, but the definition only says that some n works. Could a set have 3 elements and also 4? It cannot, and a corollary of the pigeonhole principle below proves it. That corollary is the well-definedness step this definition needs. Until it is proved, read \card{A} = n as “A has n elements”. Examples: - The empty set has 0 elements: \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset, and the empty function \emptyset 	o \emptyset is a bijection. Conversely, a set with 0 elements is empty, since a bijection \emptyset 	o A is surjective and has no values. - \{1, \dots, n\} has n elements, by \id_{\{1, \dots, n\}}. - For n \in 
N, \{0, \dots, n\} has n + 1 elements: k \mapsto k - 1 maps \{1, \dots, n + 1\} to \{0, \dots, n\}, because k - 1 \in 
N for k 
e 0 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (c)) and k - 1 \le n. It has the inverse j \mapsto j + 1, so it is a bijection (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse). - The three-letter set \{a, b, c\} has 3 elements, by the inverse of the bijection of the second example after @def-equinumerous. How many elements does \{ n \in 
N : 3 \le n \le 7 \} have? Give the bijection. Five, by k \mapsto k + 2 from \{1, \dots, 5\}: for 1 \le k \le 5, 3 \le k + 2 \le 7. Its inverse is m \mapsto m - 2, which lies in \{1, \dots, 5\} for 3 \le m \le 7, since m - 2 \in 
N by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (d). The two maps undo each other, so the first is a bijection (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse). [Infinite Set] A set A is infinite if it is not finite: for every n \in 
N there is no bijection \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A. To prove a set infinite we must rule out every n at once, and for every n every candidate bijection. Nothing so far does that, not even for 
N. The tool is the pigeonhole principle, and the last theorem of this section turns it into a usable test. Shrinking the codomain. One small device is used in the rest of this section and in Chapter 3. Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function, and let C \subseteq Y contain every value f(x). The graph of f is then a subset of X 	imes C, and with the codomain C it is a function X 	o C with the same values (@def-function). We call it “f with codomain C”. It is injective if and only if f is, since injectivity speaks only of values. In particular, f with codomain f(X) is surjective (@def-image). So an injective f \colon X 	o Y is a bijection X 	o f(X) once its codomain is shrunk, and \card{X} = \card{f(X)}. Back to the pigeons Section 1.1 reduced its question (Q1) to one step: five points, each with one of four parity patterns, put two points on one pattern. In the language of functions, sending each point to its pattern is a map from a five-element set to a four-element set, and the step says that it is not injective. Chapter 1 also found one function from a three-element set to a two-element set that is not injective (@exm-injective-surjective-first (c)), and observed without proof that none can be. Here is the general fact, for the standard sets \{1, \dots, m\} and \{1, \dots, n\}. [Pigeonhole Principle] Let m, n \in 
N with m > n. Then there is no injection \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}. [Scratch work] Induct on the number n of holes. In the step there are n + 1 holes, and we look at the last one. If no pigeon sits in hole n + 1, all the pigeons sit in n holes, and the hypothesis applies at once. If pigeon j sits there, there is only one, by injectivity. Move pigeon j to the hole of pigeon m, and send pigeon m away. That leaves m - 1 pigeons in n holes, still one to a hole, and m - 1 > n. The hypothesis is used at m - 1, not at m, so the property we induct on must say “for every m”. On scrap paper, with n = 1 and m = 3: three pigeons in two holes; if hole 2 is empty, all three sit in hole 1; if pigeon 2 sits in hole 2, move it to pigeon 3’s place and send pigeon 3 away. As givens and goal, inside the step: -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- P(n); m > n + 1; f \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n + 1\} injective a contradiction Case 1: n + 1 is no value of f f with codomain \{1, \dots, n\} is injective, m > n: against P(n) Case 2: f(j) = n + 1 an injection \{1, \dots, m - 1\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}, with m - 1 > n: g \coloneqq f \circ \sigma -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Before reading on: self-explain the construction of the injection g in Case 2: why are its values in \{1, \dots, n\}, and why is it injective? For n \in 
N let P(n) be the statement for every m \in 
N with m > n, there is no injection \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}. We prove P(n) for every n \in 
N by @fd1:ax-induction. Base case P(0). Let m \in 
N with m > 0. Then m \ge 1 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (a)), so 1 \in \{1, \dots, m\} and the domain is non-empty, while \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset. By @prp-empty-function (b) there is no function \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \emptyset at all, so there is no injection. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N and suppose P(n). Let m \in 
N with m > n + 1, and suppose, for a contradiction, that f \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n + 1\} is injective. There are two cases. Case 1: n + 1 is not a value of f. For every i, f(i) \le n + 1 and f(i) 
e n + 1, so f(i) < n + 1, and f(i) \le n by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (e). So f with codomain \{1, \dots, n\} is an injection \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}, with m > n + 1 > n. This contradicts P(n). Case 2: f(j) = n + 1 for some j \in \{1, \dots, m\}. Since m > n + 1 \ge 1, we have m 
e 0, so m - 1 \in 
N by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (c); and m - 1 > n, by subtracting 1 from m > n + 1. Define \sigma \colon \{1, \dots, m - 1\} 	o \{1, \dots, m\} by \sigma(i) \coloneqq  egin{cases} i & 	ext{if } i 
e j , \ m & 	ext{if } i = j . \end{cases} (The second line applies only when j \le m - 1; if j = m, then \sigma(i) = i for every i.) The map \sigma is injective: two different inputs other than j keep their different values, and if one input is j, its value is m, while the other has value i \le m - 1 < m. Moreover \sigma(i) 
e j for every i: either \sigma(i) = i 
e j, or \sigma(i) = m, which happens only when j \le m - 1 < m. Let g \coloneqq f \circ \sigma. It is injective by @thm-composition-injective-surjective (a). For every i, \sigma(i) 
e j, and f is injective with f(j) = n + 1, so g(i) = f(\sigma(i)) 
e n + 1; as in Case 1, g(i) \in \{1, \dots, n\}. So g with codomain \{1, \dots, n\} is an injection \{1, \dots, m - 1\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}, with m - 1 > n. This contradicts P(n), applied to the number m - 1. In both cases the injection f cannot exist, so P(n + 1) holds. By @fd1:ax-induction, P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. This proves the theorem. The theorem is about the standard sets only, but bijections carry it to any finite sets. Part (b) below is its mirror image for surjections. [Pigeonhole for Finite Sets] Let m, n \in 
N, let A have m elements, and let B have n elements. 1. If m > n, there is no injection A 	o B. 2. If m < n, there is no surjection A 	o B. For (a), the bijections of @def-finite turn an injection A 	o B into an injection \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}, which @thm-pigeonhole forbids. For (b), a surjection g \colon A 	o B has a right inverse h, and h is an injection B 	o A, forbidden by (a). The right inverse is built by a rule: send b to the element of A with the smallest number among those that g sends to b (a least element, @exm-method-least-element). Let \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o A and \psi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o B be bijections (@def-finite). By @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, \psi has an inverse \psi^{-1} \colon B 	o \{1, \dots, n\}, which is a bijection: the equations \psi^{-1} \circ \psi = \id and \psi \circ \psi^{-1} = \id say that \psi is a two-sided inverse of \psi^{-1} (@def-inverse-function), so @thm-bijection-iff-inverse applies. (a) Suppose m > n and f \colon A 	o B is injective. Then \psi^{-1} \circ f \circ \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\} is injective by @thm-composition-injective-surjective (a), which contradicts @thm-pigeonhole. (b) Suppose m < n and g \colon A 	o B is surjective. For b \in B let S_b \coloneqq \{ i \in \{1, \dots, m\} : g(\varphi(i)) = b \} . Among any 3 different integers, two have an even sum. 3. Among any 5 different lattice points of space (points of 
Z^3), two have a lattice point as midpoint. 4. If A has 8 elements and f \colon A 	o \{1, 2, 3, 4\}, then some value of f is taken at least 3 times. 5. No function from the set of subsets of \{1, 2, 3\} to \{1, \dots, 7\} is injective. 6. Every injection \{1, \dots, n\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\} is surjective. (a) False. Take 0, 1, \dots, 11. Any two of them differ by an integer d with 1 \le \lvert d vert \le 11, which is not a multiple of 12. Thirteen integers would do, by the argument of the Quick check on 11 integers. (b) True. The pigeons are the three integers and the holes are the two parities (@thm-even-or-odd), a set with 2 elements. Since 3 > 2, two of the integers have the same parity (@cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a)), and their sum is even (@exm-parity-of-sums). (c) False. Take five of the eight points with all coordinates in \{0, 1\} (Exercise C3 of Section 1.1). Two different ones differ in some coordinate, where one has 0 and the other 1; the sum there is 1, so that coordinate of the midpoint is 	frac12. (d) False. Take A = \{1, \dots, 8\} and f(k) \coloneqq the integer part of (k + 1)/2, with values 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4: each value is taken exactly twice. Nine elements would force some value three times, as in Exercise B2 (b). (e) True. The set of subsets of \{1, 2, 3\} has 2^3 = 8 elements (@prp-power-set-count), and 8 > 7, so @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a) applies. (f) True. Let f be such an injection. With its codomain shrunk to its image, f is a bijection, so f(\{1, \dots, n\}) has n elements. It is a subset of \{1, \dots, n\}, so it is all of it, by the remark after @prp-subset-finite; that is, f is surjective. Three are true, (b), (e) and (f), and three are false. Each true item is the method of @exm-method-pigeonhole with the holes named; each false one either has too few pigeons or holes that do not give the property. C. Going deeper [C1: Infinite means arbitrarily large finite pieces] Prove that a set A is infinite if and only if for every n \in

[Hint 1] For (\Leftarrow), suppose A has m elements and use the hypothesis at one well-chosen n. For (\Rightarrow), induct on n. [Hint 2] For (\Rightarrow): let P(n) be “there is an injection \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A”; the base case is the empty function. (\Leftarrow) Suppose the condition holds and, for a contradiction, that A has m elements, with a bijection \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o A. Take n \coloneqq m + 1 and an injection f \colon \{1, \dots, m + 1\} 	o A. Then \varphi^{-1} \circ f \colon \{1, \dots, m + 1\} 	o \{1, \dots, m\} is injective (@thm-composition-injective-surjective (a)), which contradicts @thm-pigeonhole. So A is infinite. (\Rightarrow) Let A be infinite. For n \in

otin \{1, \dots, n\} (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e)). It is injective: two inputs \le n are separated by f, and g(n + 1) = a

Each x \in A' has exactly one partner, its h-value, because (a, b) has first coordinate a 
otin A'; and a has exactly one, b, because every pair of G has first coordinate in A'. So f \in B^A, and R(f) = (h, b). Hence R is a bijection. By @prp-equinumerous-properties (b) and (c), \card{\{1, \dots, n^{m+1}\}} = \card{B^A}, that is, B^A has n^{m+1} elements. By @fd1:ax-induction, Q(m) holds for every m. (c) For m = 0: B^{\emptyset} has one element by @prp-empty-function (a), and n^0 = 1, even for n = 0. For m \ge 1 and n = 0: A 
e \emptyset, so there is no function A 	o \emptyset by @prp-empty-function (b), and B^A = \emptyset has 0 elements; and 0^m = 0^{m-1} \cdot 0 = 0. Both agree with (b). With B = \{0, 1\}, (b) recovers the count 2^m of the paragraph after @prp-power-set-count. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: sets up each induction on m with B fixed, and handles m = 0 (the empty product; the empty function). - 2: in each step, takes an arbitrary A with m + 1 elements, removes one point by @cor-remove-point, and applies the hypothesis to the rest. - 2: (a) splits A 	imes B into two disjoint pieces and counts \{a\} 	imes B by a bijection with B. - 3: (b) gives a bijection between B^A and B^{A'} 	imes B, checking injectivity (equality of functions) and surjectivity (the extended graph is a function). - 1: (c) checks both degenerate cases against @prp-empty-function. - Direct route for (a): composing the given bijections with a bijection \{1, \dots, m\} 	imes \{1, \dots, n\} 	o \{1, \dots, mn\}, e.g. (i, j) \mapsto (i - 1)n + j, with injectivity and surjectivity checked (for example by @thm-division-algorithm) and the case m = 0 or n = 0 handled, earns the 2 points of the (a) line and the (a) halves (1 point each) of the two induction lines. Fatal errors (0 for the step): “each of the m elements has n possible values, so n^m” with no bijection or induction; a step that applies the hypothesis to a set not shown to have m elements. R. Review [R1] Decide whether each function is injective and whether it is surjective. Justify your answers. 1. g \colon

Z by @prp-integers-closed (a) (@def-parity), while 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 is odd, and no integer is both (@thm-even-or-odd). Not injective (@def-injective): g(3, -2) = 12 - 12 = 0 = g(0, 0), and (3, -2)

If 3n + 1 = 0 for some n \in

[R2] For a set X and a property R(x, y) of two elements of X, consider the statements 	ext{(S1)} \ \ \exists x \in X \  orall y \in X \ \, R(x, y), \qquad 	ext{(S2)} \ \  orall y \in X \ \exists x \in X \ \, R(x, y). 1. For X = \{2, \dots, 6\}, (S2) holds with x \coloneqq y, since y = 1 \cdot y. (S1) fails: its negation is  orall x \in X \ \exists y \in X \ \, x

Then R(x_0, y), so \exists x \in X \ R(x, y), with witness x_0 (ulename{\exists I}). As y was arbitrary, (S2) holds (ulename{ orall I}). [R3] Let v and w be valuations such that every atom true under v is true under w. Prove that every formula built from atoms with \wedge and \vee alone (no
