title: Countable and Uncountable Sets
content:
Countable and Uncountable Sets Are there more rational numbers than natural numbers? The rationals are dense, with a third between any two, while the naturals are spread out one unit apart; and yet the answer is no, because the rationals can be listed. Are there more real numbers than rationals? Yes: no list of real numbers, however cleverly it is made, contains them all. This chapter makes “more” exact, with bijections and injections in place of counting, and proves both answers. It then shows that there is no largest size at all: by Cantor’s theorem, the set of subsets of any set is strictly bigger than the set itself. A second motivating question comes from school: why does 0.999\ldots = 1 need a definition at all? The answer is in Section 3.3, where a decimal expansion is defined with finite sums only, and 0.999\ldots = 1 becomes true by that definition. Sections 3.1–3.4 teach one method of proof each on the way: list a set, name the choices a proof makes, run a diagonal, and compare sizes by injections both ways. The last section adds, multiplies and raises sizes to powers, and finds that the plane, the sequences of natural numbers and the subsets of 
N all have exactly as many elements as the line; it teaches two more methods, encode and decode, and prove a law of sizes by a bijection. On the way the chapter meets a principle that the rules of logic and the working rules for sets do not supply: making infinitely many arbitrary choices at once. The obvious proof that a countable union of countable sets is countable needs a list of every set of the family at the same time, and no rule produces one. The chapter states the missing principle as the axiom of choice, marks the line of each proof that uses it, and shows how often a rule (the least element, a formula) makes it unnecessary. It starts from the finite sets of Section 2.5 and the pigeonhole principle. What you need. Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–8, and Sets and Functions, Chapters 1–2. Induction (@fd1:ax-induction) from Logic and Proof, Chapter 4. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 5, the rule ulename{\exists E} (@fd1:def-rules-existential): Section 3.2 shows why one use of it names one object and cannot name infinitely many. From Logic and Proof, Chapters 2 and 6, excluded middle (@fd1:prp-excluded-middle) and the negation of quantifiers (@fd1:prp-quantifier-negation). From Logic and Proof, Chapter 8, the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue). The irrationality of \sqrt 2 (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational), used in one example of Section 3.1. From Chapter 1: the empty set and its uniqueness (@def-empty-set, @prp-empty-set-unique); sets cut out by a property (@def-set-builder) and Russell’s theorem (@thm-russell); power sets, families and their unions (@def-power-set, @def-indexed-family, @def-family-union-intersection); ordered pairs and products (@def-ordered-pair, @def-cartesian-product, @prp-product-set-laws); functions, the empty function and equality of functions (@def-function, @prp-empty-function, @prp-function-equality); injective, surjective and bijective maps and their composites (@def-injective, @def-surjective, @thm-composition-injective-surjective), with the methods for proving injectivity and surjectivity (@exm-method-injectivity, @exm-method-surjectivity); inverses (@def-left-right-inverse, @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective, @prp-right-inverse-surjective); images and preimages (@def-image, @def-preimage); the indicator function of a subset (Section 1.5, @exm-first-functions (d)) and associativity of composition (@prp-composition-associative). From Chapter 2: the arithmetic of 
N and 
Z (@lem-naturals-arithmetic, @prp-integers-closed), well-ordering (@thm-well-ordering), induction from any base (@thm-induction), the division algorithm (@thm-division-algorithm), definition by recursion (@thm-recursion), powers and sums (@def-power, @prp-power-laws, @def-sum-product, @prp-geometric-sum), and the largest element of a finite set of numbers (@prp-finite-max); equinumerous, finite and infinite sets (@def-equinumerous, @prp-equinumerous-properties, @def-finite, @def-infinite), removing a point and the uniqueness of the number of elements (@cor-remove-point, @cor-finite-size-unique), the pigeonhole principle (@thm-pigeonhole, @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets), subsets and disjoint unions of finite sets (@prp-subset-finite, @prp-disjoint-union-count), the 2^n subsets of an n-element set (@prp-power-set-count), the number of elements of a product (@exr-finite-sets-c2), and the fact that no finite set is equinumerous with a proper subset (@thm-finite-no-proper-copy, @exm-hilbert-hotel); and the methods of the least element and of pigeonhole (@exm-method-least-element, @exm-method-pigeonhole). The arithmetic and order of 
R are school facts in examples, as in the earlier chapters. Section 3.3 states three school facts about decimal expansions, (D1)–(D3), and Sections 3.3, 3.4 and 3.6 use them by name without proof; Section 3.2 uses one fact from school algebra, that a non-zero polynomial of degree d has at most d real roots. Time. About 35 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 55 hours for everything. Roadmap - Countable sets. Countable as listable with repetitions allowed (empty, or the image of 
N), the equivalent forms “an injection into 
N” and “finite or countably infinite”, closure under subsets, images, unions of two sets and finite products, and the countability of 
N 	imes 
N, 
Z and 
Q; the method: list a set, by a surjection from 
N or an injection into 
N. - Countable unions and the axiom of choice. The step in the proof for countable unions that no rule justifies, the axiom of choice that licenses it, the constructions that look like choice and are not, right inverses of surjections, countable unions of countable sets, and the countability of the algebraic numbers; the method: name each choice a proof makes. - Diagonal arguments: uncountable sets and Cantor’s theorem. The diagonal argument for 0–1 sequences, opening with the five-string game of Section 1.5, Cantor’s theorem that no map from a set onto its power set exists, decimal expansions defined with finite sums, the uncountability of 
R, and the existence of transcendental numbers; the method: the diagonal. - Comparing sizes: the Schröder–Bernstein theorem. Comparing sizes by injections, its exchange with surjections at the price of choice, the Schröder–Bernstein theorem proved without choice, and every interval with more than one point equinumerous with 
R; the method: injections both ways; whether any two sets are comparable is left open. - Infinite sets. Every infinite set contains a countably infinite subset (a stronger use of choice), so 
N is the smallest infinite size, and a set is infinite exactly when it is equinumerous with a proper subset of itself. - Cardinal arithmetic. Sums as disjoint unions, products and powers of sets compared by size; the laws \card{X^{Y \sqcup Z}} = \card{X^Y 	imes X^Z} and \card{(X^Y)^Z} = \card{X^{Y 	imes Z}} proved by bijections; subsets as 0–1 functions; no set of all sets, once more; and 
R, 
R 	imes 
R, 
N^{
N}, 
R^{
N} and \powerset{
N} all of one size; the methods: encode and decode, and prove a law of sizes by a bijection. The review exercises reach back across this volume and Logic and Proof. Named moves Each is a method box in the section named at the end of its line; the later sections use the move again. - List it (@exm-method-list-it). To show a set countable, give a surjection from 
N or an injection into 
N, whichever is cheaper to check; a list may repeat, and an injection only has to keep different elements apart. (Section 3.1) - Name the choice (@exm-method-name-the-choice). When a proof picks one object for each of infinitely many indices and no rule names it, say at that line that the axiom of choice is used; a least element or a formula is a rule, and needs no choice. (Section 3.2) - The diagonal (@exm-method-diagonal). Given any list, build an object that differs from the n-th entry at the n-th place; it is not on the list, and since the list was arbitrary, no list contains everything. (Section 3.3) - Injections both ways (@exm-method-injections-both-ways). To show \card{A} = \card{B}, find an injection A 	o B and an injection B 	o A and invoke the Schröder–Bernstein theorem, instead of hunting for the bijection. (Section 3.4) - Encode and decode (@exm-method-encode). To build a bijection, say what an element must record, write the code and the decoder, and check both round trips. (Section 3.6) - A law by a bijection (@exm-method-laws-by-bijection). To prove a law of sizes, write out an element of each side and regroup it into an element of the other side, never computing with \card{\cdot} as if it were a number. (Section 3.6) Threads - The five strings. Section 1.5 plants a game: write a string of five symbols not on a given list of five. Section 3.3 opens with the rule that always works (@exm-five-strings-diagonal), and the same rule, run on infinitely long strings, proves that the 0–1 sequences cannot be listed (@thm-binary-sequences-uncountable). - Russell to Cantor. Russell’s theorem (Section 1.2) built a set that disagrees with each candidate on the candidate itself; Cantor’s theorem (Section 3.3, @thm-cantor) is the same construction, as a theorem about sizes, and Section 3.6 proves the last clause of Russell’s theorem by sizes: a set of all sets would carry a surjection onto its power set (“No set of all sets, once more”). - Choice. Section 1.6 could not build a right inverse of an arbitrary surjection; Section 3.2 adds the axiom of choice that does (@ax-choice, @thm-surjection-right-inverse), Section 3.5 uses it again (@thm-infinite-countable-subset), and Chapter 6 states its strongest everyday form, Zorn’s lemma. - Comparability. Section 3.4 asks whether any two sets are comparable and leaves the question open; Section 6.2 answers it. - Same size. Section 2.5 defined it, Section 3.6 makes it arithmetic, and Section 4.2 names the requirement that arithmetic of sizes not depend on representatives: well-definedness. Summary Countable means listable (@def-countable), in three equivalent forms (@thm-countable-characterizations). Countable sets are closed under subsets, images, finite products and, with the axiom of choice, countable unions (@thm-countable-union), so 
Z, 
Q and the algebraic numbers are countable. The diagonal shows that the 0–1 sequences, 
R and every power set are too big to be listed (@thm-binary-sequences-uncountable, @thm-reals-uncountable-decimal, @thm-cantor), so transcendental numbers exist. Sizes are compared by injections, and injections both ways give a bijection, without choice (@thm-schroder-bernstein). Every infinite set contains a copy of 
N, by choice (@thm-infinite-countable-subset), and has a proper subset of its own size (@thm-infinite-iff-proper-subset). Sizes add, multiply and exponentiate by disjoint unions, products and sets of functions, with the laws of exponents proved by bijections (@thm-cardinal-laws); so \card{
R} = \card{\powerset{
N}} and the plane, 
N^{
N} and 
R^{
N} are the size of the line (@thm-reals-power-set-naturals, @thm-plane-equinumerous-line, @thm-baire-space-reals, @cor-real-sequences). What is open: are any two sets comparable? Chapter 6 answers it. Next, Chapter 4 studies relations, and “same size” returns there as an example. Terms - algebraic number: a real root of a non-zero polynomial with integer coefficients (Section 3.2, before @thm-algebraic-countable). - at most as big as, strictly smaller: \card{A} \le \card{B} if there is an injection A 	o B; \card{A} < \card{B} if moreover there is no bijection (@def-card-le). - choice function: a function c on the index set of a family with c(i) \in A_i for every i (@ax-choice). - countable: empty, or the image of a surjection 
N 	o A (@def-countable). - countably infinite: equinumerous with 
N (@def-countably-infinite). - decimal expansion of x \in [0, 1]: a digit sequence with t_n \le x \le t_n + 10^{-n} for every n \ge 1, where t_n is the finite sum of the first n digits (@def-decimal-expansion). - digit sequence: a function from 
Z_{>0} to \{0, 1, \dots, 9\} (@def-decimal-expansion). - disjoint union A \sqcup B: the set (A 	imes \{0\}) \cup (B 	imes \{1\}) (@def-disjoint-union). - transcendental number: a real number that is not algebraic (Section 3.3, before @cor-transcendental-exist). - uncountable: not countable (@def-countable).

title: 3.1 Countable Sets
content:
Countable Sets Section 2.5 made “the same size” exact and settled the finite sets. It also showed that 
N is infinite, because it is equinumerous with its proper subset 2
N (@exm-hilbert-hotel). The next question is which sets can be put into a list indexed by 
N. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 already uses the word for these sets, countable, in its proof that the real numbers cannot be listed. This section defines it, proves three equivalent forms of it, shows that countable sets are closed under subsets, images, unions of two sets and finite products, and lists the integers and the rationals. Lists Can we list the rational numbers as q_0, q_1, q_2, \dots so that every rational number appears somewhere? Density makes it look impossible. Between any two rationals p < q lies a third, (p + q)/2, so no rational has a next one, and a list in increasing order cannot even get from q_0 to q_1. And yet a list need not be in increasing order. It only has to reach every element at some finite position. The rationals can be listed in that sense, and so can many sets that look larger than 
N. A list indexed by 
N is a function on 
N, its n-th entry being the value at n. Reaching every element is surjectivity. Countable means listable, repetitions allowed. [Countable Set] A set A is countable if A = \emptyset or there exists a surjection f \colon 
N 	o A. In the second case A = f(
N) = \{ f(0), f(1), f(2), \dots \} , that is, the elements of A can be listed as x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots, with x_n \coloneqq f(n), repetitions allowed. A set that is not countable is uncountable. In symbols, A is countable if and only if A = \emptyset \ \vee \ \exists f \in A^{
N} \ \  orall a \in A \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \ f(n) = a . In words: a non-empty set is countable when some list x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots reaches every one of its elements, each at a finite position n \in 
N. The list may repeat an element as often as it likes, and it need not follow any order. The first clause is there because there is no function at all from 
N to \emptyset (@prp-empty-function (b)), so the second clause can never hold for the empty set; without the first clause, \emptyset would be uncountable. For a non-empty set the definition says that it is the image of some function from 
N, which is how Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 states it. Examples, starting from the smallest: - \emptyset is countable, by the first clause. - A non-empty finite set is countable. For three different objects a, b, c, the list a, b, c, c, c, \dots, that is f(0) \coloneqq a, f(1) \coloneqq b and f(n) \coloneqq c for n \ge 2, is a surjection 
N 	o \{a, b, c\}. Repetitions pad a short list out to the length of 
N. - 
N is countable: \id_{
N} is a surjection. - The set of squares \{ n^2 : n \in 
N \} is countable: it is the image of 
N under n \mapsto n^2, and a function is a surjection onto its image (Section 2.5, “Shrinking the codomain”). In the same way 2
N is countable. A non-example by a minimal change. The list n \mapsto 2n is a list of 2
N. Read it as a list of 
N, keeping the rule and changing only the target set, and it fails: the clause “for every a \in 
N there is an n with 2n = a” fails at a = 1. This shows that this list misses 1, not that 
N is uncountable; one map proves nothing about all maps (the warning after the non-example in Section 2.5). Sets that are genuinely uncountable appear in Section 3.3. Why repetitions are allowed. Two reasons. First, finite sets are then countable with no special case: pad the list by repeating an element, as above. Second, the closure proofs below become short. A function applied to a list gives a list of the image, which may have repetitions even if the first list had none; interleaving lists of two overlapping sets repeats their common elements. If repetitions were forbidden, every such proof would need a step that deletes them. The definition puts that work in one place, the theorem on three ways to say countable below, and does it once. Sometimes we need the stronger statement that a set has exactly the size of 
N. [Countably Infinite Set] A set A is countably infinite if \card{A} = \card{
N}, that is, if there is a bijection A 	o 
N (equivalently, by @prp-equinumerous-properties (b), a bijection 
N 	o A). So 
N, 2
N and 
Z_{>0} are countably infinite (Section 2.5), and a countably infinite set is countable, since a bijection is a surjection. In this book “countable” includes the finite sets and \emptyset. Some books use “countable” to mean “countably infinite” and say “at most countable” for our “countable”. Before quoting a theorem about countable sets from elsewhere, check which convention it uses. Here, \{0, 1\} is countable and is not countably infinite. Subsets of the natural numbers Every countable set will turn out to be finite or countably infinite, with nothing in between. The heart of that is a fact about subsets of 
N: an infinite one can be listed in increasing order without gaps. Subsets of the Natural Numbers Every subset S \subseteq 
N is finite or countably infinite. If S is infinite, list it in increasing order: s_0 is the least element of S, and s_{n+1} is the least element of S above s_n. Well-ordering supplies each least element, provided the set is non-empty, and it is non-empty because S has elements beyond any bound, being infinite. Recursion turns the rule into a function. The list misses nothing: if t \in S were skipped, it would lie strictly between two consecutive entries s_{n-1} < t < s_n, and then s_n would not be the least element of S above s_{n-1}. If S is finite there is nothing to prove, so let S be infinite. In particular S 
e \emptyset. Every x \in 
N has an element of S above it. Let x \in 
N, and suppose that no s \in S has s > x. Then S \subseteq \{0, \dots, x\}, a set with x + 1 elements (the third example after @def-finite), so S is finite by @prp-subset-finite, a contradiction. Hence T_x \coloneqq \{ s \in S : s > x \} is non-empty, and by @thm-well-ordering it has a least element. The list. Define g \colon 
N 	imes 
N 	o 
N by g(n, x) \coloneqq \min T_x; by the previous paragraph this is defined for every x \in 
N. By @thm-recursion, with X \coloneqq 
N and a \coloneqq \min S (which exists by @thm-well-ordering), there is a function n \mapsto s_n from 
N to 
N with s_0 = \min S , \qquad s_{n+1} = \min \{ s \in S : s > s_n \} \quad (n \in 
N) . Every s_n lies in S: s_0 \in S, and s_{n+1} \in T_{s_n} \subseteq S. Increasing. By construction s_{n+1} > s_n for every n. Hence s_m < s_n whenever m < n, by induction on n: there is no m < 0 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (a)), and if m < n + 1, then m \le n (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e)), so s_m \le s_n < s_{n+1}, using the hypothesis when m < n. In particular n \mapsto s_n is injective, since m 
e n gives m < n or n < m. Also s_n \ge n for every n: s_0 \ge 0 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (a)), and if s_n \ge n, then s_{n+1} > s_n \ge n, so s_{n+1} \ge n + 1 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e)). Onto S. Let t \in S. The set \{ n \in 
N : s_n \ge t \} is non-empty, since s_t \ge t, so it has a least element n by @thm-well-ordering. If n = 0, then s_0 = \min S \le t and s_0 \ge t, so s_0 = t. If n 
e 0, then n - 1 \in 
N (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (c)), and s_{n-1} < t by the minimality of n. So t \in T_{s_{n-1}}, and s_n = \min T_{s_{n-1}} \le t. With s_n \ge t this gives s_n = t. So n \mapsto s_n, with codomain S, is a bijection 
N 	o S, and S is countably infinite. Three ways to say countable Being countable (empty or listable by 
N), having an injection into 
N, and being finite or the size of 
N all describe the same sets. Having the three forms side by side is what makes countability easy to prove: we may use whichever is cheapest for the set in hand. [Characterizations of Countable Sets] For every set A, the following are equivalent. 1. A is countable. 2. There is an injection A 	o 
N. 3. A is finite or countably infinite. From a list to an injection: send each element to the first position at which it appears. From an injection to (iii): the injection makes A equinumerous with a subset of 
N, and @lem-subsets-of-naturals sorts those. From (iii) back to a list: pad a finite list by repetition, as in the examples above. (i) \Rightarrow (ii). If A = \emptyset, the empty function \emptyset 	o 
N is injective, vacuously. Otherwise let g \colon 
N 	o A be a surjection. For a \in A, the preimage g^{-1}(\{a\}) \subseteq 
N is non-empty, since g is onto, so it has a least element by @thm-well-ordering. Define h \colon A 	o 
N by h(a) \coloneqq \min g^{-1}(\{a\}) . Then g(h(a)) = a for every a \in A, that is, g \circ h = \id_A, so h is injective by @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (a). (ii) \Rightarrow (iii). Let h \colon A 	o 
N be injective. With its codomain shrunk to h(A), it is a bijection A 	o h(A) (Section 2.5), so \card{A} = \card{h(A)}. By @lem-subsets-of-naturals, h(A) \subseteq 
N is finite or countably infinite. If h(A) has n elements, there is a bijection \{1, \dots, n\} 	o h(A), and following it by the inverse of A 	o h(A) gives a bijection \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A (@prp-equinumerous-properties (b) for the inverse, @thm-composition-injective-surjective (c)); so A has n elements. If \card{h(A)} = \card{
N}, then \card{A} = \card{
N} by @prp-equinumerous-properties (c). (iii) \Rightarrow (i). If A is countably infinite, a bijection 
N 	o A is a surjection. Let A be finite with n elements. If n = 0, then A = \emptyset, which is countable. If n \ge 1, let \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A be a bijection and define f \colon 
N 	o A by f(k) \coloneqq  egin{cases} \varphi(k) & 	ext{if } 1 \le k \le n , \ \varphi(1) & 	ext{if } k = 0 	ext{ or } k > n . \end{cases} Every a \in A is \varphi(k) = f(k) for some k \in \{1, \dots, n\}, so f is a surjection. This proves the theorem. The step (i) \Rightarrow (ii) picks one element h(a) of g^{-1}(\{a\}) for every a \in A at once, and it needs no new principle for that, because there is a rule that names the element: the least one. That works because the preimages are subsets of 
N, which is well-ordered. Section 3.2 meets a step that looks the same and has no such rule, and it is the point at which the book adds the axiom of choice. Which form to use is the first decision in every countability proof: [Method: list it] Template. To show A countable, give one map and check it. (S) A surjection onto A from 
N or a countable set: check that every a \in A is a value (repetitions are free; split off A = \emptyset), and cite @def-countable (or, from a countable set, the result on images proved below). (I) An injection of A into 
N or a countable set: check that equal values come from equal elements, and cite @thm-countable-characterizations, (ii) \Rightarrow (i), composing if needed. When to use it. (S) for “all objects of the form \varphi(m, n, \dots)”: list the parameters. (I) when each element carries a code that can be read back, above all when a parametrization would leave A. The usual failure. A list that runs through an infinite block before the next (@exm-rows-first-listing). An “injection” never checked to be injective. Which route of the method would you take for (a) the set of numbers n^2 + 3n with n \in 
N; (b) the set of n \in 
N with n^2 + 1 even? (a) Route (S): the set is the image of 
N under n \mapsto n^2 + 3n, and a function is a surjection onto its image (Section 2.5), so @def-countable applies and nothing is left to check. (b) Route (I): the inclusion into 
N is an injection with nothing to check, so the set is countable by @thm-countable-characterizations, (ii) \Rightarrow (i). No parametrization of the set is needed, and nobody has to work out which n qualify. Closure properties Three closure properties follow at once, each from the form of countability that suits it. [Subsets of Countable Sets] Every subset of a countable set is countable. Let B be countable and A \subseteq B. By @thm-countable-characterizations, (i) \Rightarrow (ii), there is an injection h \colon B 	o 
N. Its restriction h|_A \colon A 	o 
N is injective, since it has the same values. By (ii) \Rightarrow (i), A is countable. [Images of Countable Sets] Let A be countable and f \colon A 	o B a function. Then f(A) is countable. In particular, if f is surjective, then B is countable. If A = \emptyset, then f(A) = \emptyset, which is countable. Otherwise let g \colon 
N 	o A be a surjection. The function f with codomain f(A) is surjective (Section 2.5), so its composite with g is a surjection 
N 	o f(A) by @thm-composition-injective-surjective (b). If f is surjective, then f(A) = B. For unions we interleave two lists, taking the entries of the first list at the even positions and those of the second at the odd positions. That needs the fact that every natural number is even or odd, in exactly one way. [Union of Two Countable Sets] If A and B are countable, then A \cup B is countable. Two lists a_0, a_1, \dots and b_0, b_1, \dots merge into one, a_0, b_0, a_1, b_1, \dots: the entry at position 2q comes from the first list and the entry at position 2q + 1 from the second. For this to define a function, every position must be even or odd, and not both. If A = \emptyset, then A \cup B = B, and if B = \emptyset, then A \cup B = A; both are countable. So let g \colon 
N 	o A and h \colon 
N 	o B be surjections. Every a \in 
N can be written as a = 2q + r with q \in 
N and r \in \{0, 1\}, and the pair (q, r) is unique. In particular, no natural number is both of the form 2q and of the form 2q' + 1 with q, q' \in 
N. By @thm-division-algorithm with divisor 2, there are unique integers q, r with a = 2q + r and 0 \le r < 2. Then r \in 
N by @prp-integers-closed (b), and r \le 1 by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (e), so r \in \{0, 1\}. If q < 0, then q + 1 \le 0 by the discreteness clause @prp-integers-closed (c), so q \le -1 and a = 2q + r \le -2 + 1 < 0, which contradicts a \ge 0 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (a)). So q \ge 0, and q \in 
N by @prp-integers-closed (b). Uniqueness among pairs with q \in 
N follows from uniqueness among all integer pairs. The last sentence is the uniqueness of r. Define k \colon 
N 	o A \cup B by k(2q) \coloneqq g(q) , \qquad k(2q + 1) \coloneqq h(q) \qquad (q \in 
N) . By the claim, each a \in 
N falls under exactly one of the two clauses, with exactly one q, so k is a function. It is onto: an element of A is g(q) = k(2q) for some q, and an element of B is h(q) = k(2q + 1) for some q, where 2q and 2q + 1 lie in 
N by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (b). So A \cup B is countable. If A and B overlap, the interleaved list repeats their common elements, and the definition does not mind. By induction on the number of sets, a union of finitely many countable sets is countable. A union of infinitely many is a different matter, and Section 3.2 is about it. Pairs of natural numbers The set 
N 	imes 
N looks two-dimensional, and a first attempt to list it shows where the difficulty lies. [Listing the rows one after another] Arrange 
N 	imes 
N in rows, the m-th row being (m, 0), (m, 1), (m, 2), \dots. Consider the “list” (0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2), \dots , \ 	ext{then} \ (1, 0), (1, 1), \dots , \ 	ext{then} \ (2, 0), \dots Is it a surjection 
N 	o 
N 	imes 
N? No. A list indexed by 
N gives each entry a position n \in 
N. Here position n holds (0, n), for every n \in 
N: that already defines a function f(n) \coloneqq (0, n) on all of 
N. No position is left for (1, 0): there is no n \in 
N with f(n) = (1, 0), since the first coordinate of every value is 0. The word “then” asks for positions after all the natural numbers, and there are none. So the claim that this is a list of 
N 	imes 
N is false. It is a list of the first row only. A list must give every entry a finite position. “First all of row 0, then all of row 1” never reaches row 1, because row 0 uses up every position. The same mistake hides in any listing that runs through an infinite block before starting the next one. The conclusion that 
N 	imes 
N is countable is nevertheless true. [The Plane of Natural Numbers Is Countable] The map p \colon 
N 	imes 
N 	o 
N, p(m, n) \coloneqq 2^m 3^n, is injective. Hence 
N 	imes 
N is countable. Try it first (ten minutes): list 
N 	imes 
N, or inject it into 
N. Which is less work to write down and check? [Scratch work] The rows-first list fails, as we saw. A list that works runs along the diagonals m + n = 0, 1, 2, \dots, each of which is finite; but writing a formula for the position of (m, n) and checking that every position is used takes real work. Route (I) of @exm-method-list-it is cheaper. By @thm-countable-characterizations it is enough to inject 
N 	imes 
N into 
N, and an injection only has to be a code from which m and n can be read back. As givens and goal: ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- — 
N 	imes 
N countable @thm-countable-characterizations, (ii) \Rightarrow (i) an injection p \colon 
N 	imes 
N 	o 
N p(m, n) \coloneqq 2^m 3^n, and 2^m 3^n = 2^{m'} 3^{n'} m = m' and n = n' suppose m > m' (symmetry); cancel 2^{m'}: 2^{m - m'} 3^n = 3^{n'} gap: an even number equals an odd one, which is impossible (the claim in the proof of @prp-union-two-countable); so m = m', and then n = n' because k \mapsto 3^k is increasing ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- In 2^m 3^n, the power of 2 records m and the power of 3 records n. To read them back we do not cite unique factorization into primes, which we have not proved. Parity closes the gap: cancel the smaller power of 2; if any factor 2 is left on one side, that side is even and the other is odd. First, p(m, n) \in 
N by @prp-power-laws (d) and @lem-naturals-arithmetic (b). Next, every power 3^k with k \in 
N is odd, that is, 3^k = 2j + 1 for some j \in 
N: by @fd1:ax-induction, 3^0 = 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1, and if 3^k = 2j + 1, then 3^{k+1} = 3^k \cdot 3 = 2(3j + 1) + 1 (@def-power). Let (m, n), (m', n') \in 
N 	imes 
N with 2^m 3^n = 2^{m'} 3^{n'}. Suppose m 
e m'. The hypothesis is symmetric in the two pairs, so we may assume m > m'. Then m - m' \in 
N and m - m' \ge 1 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (d), (e)), and 2^m = 2^{m'} 2^{m - m'} by @prp-power-laws (a). Canceling 2^{m'}, which is positive by @prp-power-laws (e), gives 2^{m - m'} 3^n = 3^{n'} . The left side is even: 2^{m - m'} = 2^{m - m' - 1} \cdot 2 by @def-power, where m - m' - 1 \in 
N by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (c), so the left side is 2 times the natural number 2^{m - m' - 1} 3^n. The right side is odd, as shown above. No natural number is both even and odd, by the uniqueness of the remainder in @thm-division-algorithm with divisor 2 (the claim in the proof of @prp-union-two-countable). This contradiction shows m = m'. Canceling 2^m now gives 3^n = 3^{n'}. By @prp-power-laws (e) with u = 3 > 1, n < n' would give 3^n < 3^{n'}, and n' < n would give 3^{n'} < 3^n; so n = n'. Hence (m, n) = (m', n'), and p is injective. By @thm-countable-characterizations, (ii) \Rightarrow (i), 
N 	imes 
N is countable. Alternatively, one can list 
N 	imes 
N along its diagonals: first the one pair with m + n = 0, then the two pairs with m + n = 1, then the three with m + n = 2, and so on. Each diagonal is finite, so every pair is reached after finitely many steps, and the list never stalls on an infinite block. Some readers find this picture more convincing than the code 2^m 3^n. The injection is shorter to write out and to check, which is why the proof uses it. The theorem passes to products of any countable sets. Chapter 1 defines X^n for one set X; for several sets we first say what the product is. For an integer k \ge 2 and sets A_1, \dots, A_k, let U \coloneqq  igcup_{i \in \{1, \dots, k\}} A_i and A_1 	imes \dots 	imes A_k \coloneqq \{ x \in U^k : x = (x_1, \dots, x_k) 	ext{ with } x_i \in A_i 	ext{ for every } i \} , the k-tuples whose i-th coordinate lies in A_i. It is a set by (W3), (W5) and (W1) of Section 1.2. For k = 2 it is A_1 	imes A_2 of @def-cartesian-product, a pair being a 2-tuple, and if every A_i is the same set X, it is X^k. [Products of Countable Sets] 1. If A and B are countable, then A 	imes B is countable. 2. Let k \ge 2 be an integer. If A_1, \dots, A_k are countable, then A_1 	imes \dots 	imes A_k is countable. For two factors, injections A 	o 
N and B 	o 
N turn A 	imes B into a subset of 
N 	imes 
N, and the code 2^m 3^n does the rest. More factors are added one at a time: a (k + 1)-tuple is a k-tuple followed by one more coordinate. (a) By @thm-countable-characterizations, (i) \Rightarrow (ii), there are injections i \colon A 	o 
N and j \colon B 	o 
N. The map A 	imes B 	o 
N 	imes 
N, (a, b) \mapsto (i(a), j(b)), is injective: if (i(a), j(b)) = (i(a'), j(b')), then i(a) = i(a') and j(b) = j(b') by @def-ordered-pair, so a = a' and b = b'. Following it by the injection p of @thm-product-countable gives an injection A 	imes B 	o 
N (@thm-composition-injective-surjective (a)), and (ii) \Rightarrow (i) concludes. No case split is needed: if A = \emptyset or B = \emptyset, then A 	imes B = \emptyset (@prp-product-set-laws), so the map (a, b) \mapsto (i(a), j(b)) and its composite with p are empty functions (@prp-empty-function (a)), which are injective vacuously. (b) We use @thm-induction with n_0 = 2 on the statement “for all countable sets A_1, \dots, A_k, the set A_1 	imes \dots 	imes A_k is countable”. Base case k = 2. This is (a). Step. Let k \ge 2, suppose the statement for k, and let A_1, \dots, A_{k+1} be countable. The map  igl( (a_1, \dots, a_k), a_{k+1}  igr) \mapsto (a_1, \dots, a_{k+1}) is a function, since a k-tuple determines its coordinates (Section 1.4), and it sends (A_1 	imes \dots 	imes A_k) 	imes A_{k+1} onto A_1 	imes \dots 	imes A_{k+1}: a (k + 1)-tuple with x_i \in A_i is the image of ((x_1, \dots, x_k), x_{k+1}). By the hypothesis, A_1 	imes \dots 	imes A_k is countable, so the domain is countable by (a), and the (k + 1)-fold product is countable by @prp-countable-image. By @thm-induction the statement holds for every k \ge 2. The map in the step is in fact a bijection, by the characteristic property of tuples (Section 1.4). The proof uses that property only to see that the map is well defined, and of the map it uses only that it is onto; injectivity is never needed. Tuples of different lengths are different objects, and the book has no 1-tuples, so the corollary starts at k = 2; a single countable set needs no corollary. Let L be the set of the 26 letters a–z. Is the set of all strings of exactly 5 letters, that is L^5, countable? Which results do you use? Yes. The set L is finite, so it is countable by @thm-countable-characterizations, (iii) \Rightarrow (i). The strings of length 5 are the 5-tuples of letters, L^5 = L 	imes L 	imes L 	imes L 	imes L, which is countable by @cor-product-countable (b) with k = 5. (It is in fact finite, with 26^5 elements: the map in the step of the proof of @cor-product-countable (b) is a bijection L^k 	imes L 	o L^{k+1} (the remark above), so @exr-finite-sets-c2 (a), applied for k = 2, 3, 4 after L^2 = L 	imes L, counts it. N} exists by specification. We build an injection \sigma \colon \sF 	o

Splitting off the last term (Section 2.3), for F \subseteq \{0, \dots, N + 1\}, S_{N+1}(F) = S_N igl(F \cap \{0, \dots, N\} igr) + \ind_F(N + 1) \, 2^{N+1} . For the step, let F, G \subseteq \{0, \dots, N + 1\} with S_{N+1}(F) = S_{N+1}(G), and write F' \coloneqq F \cap \{0, \dots, N\}, G' \coloneqq G \cap \{0, \dots, N\}. If N + 1 \in F and N + 1 
otin G, then Steps 2 and 1 give S_{N+1}(F) \ge 2^{N+1} > 2^{N+1} - 1 \ge S_N(G') = S_{N+1}(G) , a contradiction; the case N + 1 \in G \setminus F is the same with F and G exchanged. So N + 1 lies in both or in neither, the last terms in Step 2 agree, and S_N(F') = S_N(G'). By the hypothesis, F' = G'. Since \{0, \dots, N + 1\} = \{0, \dots, N\} \cup \{N + 1\}, it follows that F = G. Step 4: the injection. Every F \in \sF lies in some \{0, \dots, N\}: if F = \emptyset, take N = 0; otherwise F is a non-empty finite set of real numbers, so it has a maximum M \in F \subseteq 
N (@prp-finite-max, as in the remark at the end of Section 2.5), and F \subseteq \{0, \dots, M\}. Define \sigma(F) \coloneqq S_N(F) for any such N; by Step 2 this does not depend on N. So \sigma is injective, and \sF is countable by @thm-countable-characterizations, (ii) \Rightarrow (i). For example \sigma(\emptyset) = 0 (the empty set contributes no terms), \sigma(\{0, 2\}) = 1 + 4 = 5 and \sigma(\{1, 3\}) = 2 + 8 = 10: \sigma(F) is the number whose binary numeral has a 1 exactly in the places listed in F. Step 3 is the uniqueness of binary numerals, and Step 4 uses no principle of choice: every value is given by a formula. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: defines a map from the finite subsets to 
N explicitly, including the value at \emptyset, and checks that its values are natural numbers. - 2: makes the map well defined, either by a bound-independent definition (as in Step 2) or by summing over the elements of F listed in increasing order. - 4: proves injectivity, either by comparing the terms at the largest element at which F and G differ, using \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} 2^k < 2^m, or by an induction on the bound as in Step 3, or by an equivalent proved uniqueness argument for binary numerals. - 2: concludes with @thm-countable-characterizations, (ii) \Rightarrow (i). - Route by surjection: an explicit map

e \emptyset, so there is a surjection g \colon

otin A the formula offers no value in A at all. Counterexample to line (3): B = 
N, g = \id_{
N}, A = \{1\}. Then “h(2) = g(2) = 2”, and 2 
otin A, so h is not a function into A. Lines (1), (2) and (4) are correct, and (5) would follow if h were a function 
N 	o A. Repair. In the case A 
e \emptyset, fix one element a_0 \in A (one ulename{\exists E}) and define h(n) \coloneqq  egin{cases} g(n) & 	ext{if } g(n) \in A , \ a_0 & 	ext{if } g(n) 
otin A . \end{cases} Now h is a function

title: 3.2 Countable Unions and the Axiom of Choice
content:
Countable Unions and the Axiom of Choice Section 3.1 listed 
N 	imes 
N, 
Z and 
Q, and showed that a union of two countable sets is countable (@prp-union-two-countable). The next question is a union of countably many countable sets. The natural proof is short, and it contains one step that none of the rules met so far can justify. This section isolates that step, adds the principle that licenses it, the axiom of choice, and then shows how to tell a proof that needs the axiom from one that only seems to. A union of countably many lists Let A_0, A_1, A_2, \dots be countable sets, a family (A_n)_{n \in 
N} in the sense of @def-indexed-family. We want to prove that  igcup_{n \in 
N} A_n is countable. Here is the proof most people write first. List each set: A_n = \{ a_{n,0}, a_{n,1}, a_{n,2}, \dots \}. Put a_{n,m} in row n and column m of an infinite grid. Every element of the union stands somewhere in the grid, and the grid is indexed by 
N 	imes 
N, which is countable (@thm-product-countable). So the union is the image of a countable set, and it is countable. Every step but the first, “list each set”, is a result of Section 3.1. Where do the lists come from? The obstacle, rule by rule For a non-empty A_n, “A_n is countable” says that there exists a surjection 
N 	o A_n (@def-countable). To use it we apply ulename{\exists E} (@fd1:def-rules-existential): we name the object and argue inside the box of that name. One ulename{\exists E} names one surjection, for one n. - Finitely many sets. The proof of @prp-union-two-countable used two ulename{\exists E}’s; for A_0, \dots, A_9 we could nest ten boxes. - All n \in 
N at once. The grid needs a list of A_n for every n, assembled into one object: a function that sends each n to a surjection 
N 	o A_n. A proof is a finite object. It cannot contain one ulename{\exists E} for each of infinitely many indices, and no rule of Logic and Proof, Chapter 5 makes infinitely many choices in one step. Two escape routes fail. Recursion (@thm-recursion) defines a function on all of 
N at once, but from a rule g given in advance, each value determined by the previous one. The list of A_{n+1} is not determined by the list of A_n, and a rule producing a list of every A_{n+1} would already be the missing object. Induction on k, with @prp-union-two-countable at each step, proves “for every k, A_0 \cup \dots \cup A_k is countable” (Exercise C3 writes it out), but that is a statement about each k separately; nothing makes the lists for different k fit together. Section 1.6 met the same wall: a right inverse of a surjection must pick a preimage of every point at once, and the rules could do that only for finitely many points, or when a rule names the preimage. The axiom of choice None of the working rules (W1)–(W6) of Section 1.2 forms a set out of infinitely many arbitrary picks. The principle we add is the simplest statement that does. From any family of non-empty sets, one may pick one element from each set, all at once. [Axiom of Choice] Let I be a set, and let (A_i)_{i \in I} be a family of sets such that A_i is non-empty for every i \in I. Then there exists a function c \colon I 	o  igcup_{i \in I} A_i \quad 	ext{with} \quad c(i) \in A_i \ 	ext{ for every } i \in I . Such a function c is called a choice function for the family. title: 3.3 Diagonal Arguments: Uncountable Sets and Cantor's Theorem
content:
Diagonal Arguments: Uncountable Sets and Cantor’s Theorem Every infinite set met so far has turned out to be countable: 
N, 
Z, 
Q, finite products of countable sets, countable unions of them (@thm-countable-union), and even the algebraic numbers (@thm-algebraic-countable). Is every infinite set countable? This section shows that the answer is no, by one argument, which starts from the game of Section 1.5 and is then used three times. Given any list, it builds an object that the list misses. The argument proves that the set of 0–1 sequences is uncountable, that no set can be mapped onto the set of its subsets (Cantor’s theorem), and, with decimals, that 
R is uncountable. Back to the five strings Section 1.5 left a game open: one player lists five strings of five symbols 0 or 1, and the other must write a string that is not on the list. Searching all 32 strings works; a rule is better. Back to the five strings Find a rule that, from any list s_1, \dots, s_5 of strings of five symbols 0 or 1, builds a string not on the list. Run it on 00000, 11111, 01010, 10101, 00111, and prove that it always works. Let the new string g have, as its k-th symbol, the flip of the k-th symbol of the k-th string: g(k) \coloneqq 1 - s_k(k) \qquad (k = 1, \dots, 5) (strings are functions \{1, \dots, 5\} 	o \{0, 1\}, Section 1.5). On the given list, the symbols s_1(1), \dots, s_5(5) are 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, so g = 10110. It differs from 00000 in place 1, from 11111 in place 2, from 01010 in place 3, from 10101 in place 4 and from 00111 in place 5. For any list: for each k, g(k) 
e s_k(k), since 1 - b 
e b for b \in \{0, 1\}. So g 
e s_k (@prp-function-equality), for k = 1, \dots, 5. The k-th step looks only at the k-th string, in its own place k. The rule never used the number 32. It used one place for each string on the list. Give the strings infinitely many places, indexed by 
N, and let the list be infinite too, and the same rule still applies. Can the rule handle a list of six strings of five symbols? Does that contradict anything? No. The sixth string has no sixth place to be flipped in. Nothing is contradicted: a list of 32 strings may contain every string. The rule needs as many places as strings, and in the next subsection both are indexed by 
N. A sequence that is not on the list Recall from Section 1.5 that \{0, 1\}^{
N} is the set of all functions 
N 	o \{0, 1\}: the sequences of zeros and ones, indexed from 0. These are the strings of the game with places indexed by 
N. It is infinite, and it looks no bigger than 
N 	imes 
N, which is countable. To show that it is not countable we must show, by @def-countable, that it is non-empty and that no function f \colon 
N 	o \{0, 1\}^{
N} is onto. So we take an arbitrary list f(0), f(1), f(2), \dots of sequences and look for a sequence that is not on it. Write the list as a table: row n is the sequence f(n), and the entry in row n and column k is the number f(n)(k). Here is the start of one such table, with the entries in places (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) boxed: The boxed entries run down the diagonal of the table. The bottom row g is the diagonal with every entry flipped: g(n) = 1 - f(n)(n). It cannot be row 0, because it differs from f(0) in place 0; it cannot be row 1, because it differs from f(1) in place 1; and so on down the table. Nothing in this reasoning used the particular entries. [The 0–1 Sequences Are Uncountable] The set \{0, 1\}^{
N} of all sequences of zeros and ones is uncountable. [Scratch work] By @def-countable, “uncountable” has two parts: the set is non-empty, and no map from 
N onto it exists. The second is a statement about every f, so take f arbitrary and look for a sequence it misses. As givens and goal: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------- f \colon 
N 	o \{0, 1\}^{
N} arbitrary f is not onto; and \{0, 1\}^{
N} 
e \emptyset — some g \in \{0, 1\}^{
N} with g 
e f(n) for every n g 
e f(n) as soon as g and f(n) differ at one place (@prp-function-equality) pick the place for each n: place n, as in the game gap: g(n) 
e f(n)(n) for every n closed by g(n) \coloneqq 1 - f(n)(n) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The proof writes this forwards. Let f \colon 
N 	o \{0, 1\}^{
N} be any function. Define g \colon 
N 	o \{0, 1\} by g(n) \coloneqq 1 - f(n)(n) \qquad (n \in 
N) ; its values lie in \{0, 1\}, since 1 - 0 = 1 and 1 - 1 = 0. So g \in \{0, 1\}^{
N}. For every n \in 
N, g(n) 
e f(n)(n), since no b \in \{0, 1\} has 1 - b = b. Hence g 
e f(n): if g = f(n), then g(n) = f(n)(n), which is false; the two functions differ at place n [ulename{{=}E}, ulename{
eg I}; @prp-function-equality]. So g is not a value of f, and f is not surjective. Since f was arbitrary, no function 
N 	o \{0, 1\}^{
N} is surjective. The set \{0, 1\}^{
N} is non-empty, since it contains the zero sequence. By @def-countable, \{0, 1\}^{
N} is not countable. This is the move of the section. [Method: the diagonal] Template. To show that no map from I onto X exists (for “uncountable”: I = 
N, and check X 
e \emptyset), let f \colon I 	o X be arbitrary. Build d \in X whose entry at i differs from the entry of f(i) at i, for every i \in I. Then d 
e f(i) for each i, so f is not onto. Since f was arbitrary, no such map exists. When to use it. The elements of X are themselves functions or subsets on the index set of the list: sequences, digit strings, subsets of I. The usual failure. A d that falls outside X (a decimal ending in 9s, met below; a sequence of the wrong kind). A difference at place i that is not a real difference (two expansions of one number). Running the construction on one list only (the warning below). Would the unflipped diagonal, g(n) \coloneqq f(n)(n), do? Test it on the list whose every entry is the zero sequence. No. There g is the zero sequence, which is f(0). The new object must differ from the n-th entry at place n, for every n. Run the proof on the list f(n) \coloneqq \ind_{\{n\}}, the sequence with a 1 in place n and 0 elsewhere. What is g? Is it on the list? Here f(n)(n) = \ind_{\{n\}}(n) = 1 for every n, so g(n) = 1 - 1 = 0 for every n: g is the zero sequence. It is indeed not on the list, since every f(n) has a 1 in place n. The diagonal object depends on the list. “The diagonal sequence” is not one sequence: each list has its own, and a different list may well contain the g built from this one (the list g, f(0), f(1), \dots does). And the conclusion “uncountable” needs the list to be arbitrary. Running the construction on one list, or on a few, shows only that those lists miss something; concluding “so no list works” from them is the error (N1) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. The proof above starts from “let f be any function”, and that is what makes its conclusion universal. [A function that outgrows a list] Let f_0, f_1, f_2, \dots be any list of functions 
N 	o 
N. Find g \colon 
N 	o 
N such that, for every k \in 
N, g(n) > f_k(n) for every n \ge k. Idea. The flipped diagonal beats f_n at place n only. To beat f_k from place k on, let place n beat f_0, \dots, f_n at once: finitely many, so a maximum exists. Let g(n) \coloneqq \max \{ f_0(n), \dots, f_n(n) \} + 1 \qquad (n \in 
N) . The set is \{x_1, \dots, x_{n+1}\} with x_{k+1} \coloneqq f_k(n), so the maximum exists by @prp-finite-max; it is one of the x_j, so g(n) \in 
N. For k \in 
N and n \ge k, f_k(n) is one of the numbers in the set, so f_k(n) \le \max \{ f_0(n), \dots, f_n(n) \} < g(n). The example asks more of g than a diagonal does, and each step still looks at finitely many entries at one place. Back to Russell: Cantor’s theorem Section 1.2 proved Russell’s theorem (@thm-russell): the set R_A disagrees with each candidate x \in A about x itself, so it is not in A. Here the same disagreement becomes a theorem about sizes. The table had a row for each n \in 
N and a column for each place k \in 
N. Nothing about the diagonal needs the rows and the columns to be indexed by 
N: it needs only that they are indexed by the same set. A subset S of a set X is a row with one entry for each x \in X, “in” or “out”, the values of \ind_S. So the argument applies to any set and the set of its subsets. [Cantor’s Theorem] Let X be a set. Then there is no surjection X 	o \powerset{X}. Try it first (ten minutes): given a function f \colon X 	o \powerset{X}, which subset of X could be missed by f? Try X = \{1, 2, 3\} with a function of your own first. The first attempts look for a subset that is “too big” or “too small” to be a value, such as X itself or \emptyset, and fail: f may well take both values. Size is the wrong idea. A set D differs from f(x) as soon as the two disagree about one element, and the only element we know anything about in connection with f(x) is x itself. So we make D disagree with f(x) at x: put x into D exactly when x 
otin f(x). This is the diagonal of the table, flipped. It is the method of @exm-method-diagonal, with the rows and the places both indexed by X. Before reading on: where is surjectivity used? Let f \colon X 	o \powerset{X} be a function, and let D \coloneqq \{ x \in X : x 
otin f(x) \} , a subset of X by @def-set-builder, so D \in \powerset{X} (@def-power-set). Suppose f is surjective. Then there is d \in X with f(d) = D (@def-surjective). If d \in D, then d 
otin f(d) by the definition of D, that is, d 
otin D, a contradiction. Hence d 
otin D. Then d 
otin f(d), and since d \in X, the definition of D gives d \in D, a contradiction again. So f is not surjective. This proves the theorem. Surjectivity was used once, to obtain d; everything else holds for every function f. Read without the supposition, the proof shows that D 
e f(x) for every x \in X: the two sets disagree about x. Three consequences follow. (i) Russell’s theorem is the same argument. In @thm-russell, the set R_A = \{ x \in A : x 
otin x \} is the set D built from the rule f(x) \coloneqq x: each x \in A is tested against itself. The proof that D differs from every f(x) becomes the proof that R_A differs from every element of A, that is, R_A 
otin A. (The rule x \mapsto x need not map into \powerset{A}, but the argument never used that f(x) \subseteq X, only the test “x \in f(x)”.) (ii) The power set is strictly bigger. The map x \mapsto \{x\} is an injection X 	o \powerset{X}, since \{x\} = \{y\} gives x = y. So \powerset{X} has at least as many elements as X, in the sense that X is in bijection with a subset of it, and by the theorem it is not equinumerous with X, since a bijection would be a surjection. Section 3.4 names this relation: X is strictly smaller than \powerset{X}. (iii) There is no largest size. 
N, \powerset{
N}, \powerset{\powerset{
N}}, …: each set in this sequence is strictly bigger than the one before. [The Subsets of the Naturals] The power set \powerset{
N} is uncountable. The set \powerset{
N} is non-empty, since \emptyset \in \powerset{
N}, and by @thm-cantor with X = 
N there is no surjection 
N 	o \powerset{
N}. By @def-countable, \powerset{
N} is not countable. The two diagonal proofs are one. By the correspondence of Section 1.5, S \mapsto \ind_S is a bijection \powerset{
N} 	o \{0, 1\}^{
N}, with inverse b \mapsto \{ n \in 
N : b(n) = 1 \} (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse). Given f \colon 
N 	o \powerset{
N}, the sequence g(n) = 1 - \ind_{f(n)}(n) of @thm-binary-sequences-uncountable is 1 exactly when n 
otin f(n), so g = \ind_D for the set D of Cantor’s proof. Decimal expansions The real numbers should be next. A real number in [0, 1) is written as a decimal 0.d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots, a sequence of digits, so the diagonal suggests itself: list the numbers, write their decimals as the rows of a table, and change the diagonal digits. Two questions must be answered first. What does it mean that a sequence of digits is the decimal of x? And what is 0.999\ldots? School says it equals 1, and a diagonal that produces 0.4999\ldots when 0.5000\ldots is on the list has produced a number that is on the list. An infinite sum would answer the first question, but this book has not yet defined one. Finite sums are enough. The first n digits of x should pin x down to within 10^{-n}. A digit sequence is a decimal of x when each of its finite truncations is within one unit of its last place below x. [Decimal Expansion] A digit sequence is a function k \mapsto d_k from 
Z_{>0} to \{0, 1, \dots, 9\}. For n \ge 1 let t_n \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{n} d_k 10^{-k} (@def-sum-product), where 10^{-k} \coloneqq (1/10)^k (@def-power). The digit sequence is a decimal expansion of x \in [0, 1] if for every n \ge 1, t_n \le x \le t_n + 10^{-n} . In words: t_n is the number written with the first n digits, 0.d_1 \ldots d_n, and the condition says that x lies in the closed interval of length 10^{-n} starting at t_n, for every n. The digits are indexed from 1, so that d_k is the digit in the k-th place after the point. No infinite sum appears: every t_n is a finite sum. Examples. 1. Zero. The all-zero sequence has t_n = 0, and 0 \le 0 \le 10^{-n}; it is an expansion of 0. 2. One half, twice. The sequence 5, 0, 0, \dots has t_n =  rac12 for every n \ge 1, and  rac12 \le  rac12 \le  rac12 + 10^{-n}. The sequence 4, 9, 9, \dots has t_n =  rac{4}{10} + \sum_{k=2}^{n} 9 \cdot 10^{-k} =  rac12 - 10^{-n}, by @prp-geometric-sum, so t_n \le  rac12 \le t_n + 10^{-n} =  rac12. Both are expansions of  rac12. 3. One. The all-nine sequence has t_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} 9 \cdot 10^{-k} = 1 - 10^{-n} (@prp-geometric-sum), so t_n \le 1 \le t_n + 10^{-n} = 1: it is an expansion of 1. A non-example by minimal change. Keep the sequence 5, 0, 0, \dots and move x from  rac12 to 0.51. The inequalities still hold for n = 1 (0.5 \le 0.51 \le 0.6) and for n = 2 (0.50 \le 0.51 \le 0.51), and they fail at n = 3: 0.51 > 0.500 + 0.001. So 5, 0, 0, \dots is not an expansion of 0.51; the clause “for every n \ge 1” is what fails. Why this definition. Both inequalities are non-strict. With a strict right inequality, x < t_n + 10^{-n}, the all-nine sequence would be an expansion of no number at all: it would need x < 1 together with 1 - 10^{-n} \le x for every n, and no real number satisfies both, by the Archimedean property (a school fact; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves it). The non-strict form is what makes 0.999\ldots = 1 true, and true by the definition: the inequalities for x = 1 are checked in Example 3, and no other number satisfies them, since 1 - 10^{-n} \le x \le 1 for every n forces x = 1, again by the Archimedean property (this is the uniqueness half of (D2) below). Example 2 shows that the price is two expansions for some numbers. What this book does not prove are the facts that make expansions behave as school says. We state them once and use them in this section and the next, always by name. 1. Every x \in [0, 1) has a decimal expansion that does not end in all 9s. 2. Every digit sequence is a decimal expansion of exactly one x \in [0, 1]. 3. If two different digit sequences are expansions of the same x, then one of them ends in all 9s and the other ends in all 0s. Here a digit sequence ends in all 9s if there is N \ge 1 with d_k = 9 for every k \ge N, and likewise for 0s. By the uniqueness in (D2), we may write x = 0.d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots for “x is the number of which d_1, d_2, d_3, \dots is an expansion”. So 0.4999\ldots = 0.5000\ldots =  rac12, as in (D3). Neither (D1) nor (D2) follows from what we have so far. (D3) does, by a finite computation at the first place where the two sequences differ (@thm-well-ordering, @prp-geometric-sum); we state it with the others to quote it by name. The existence half of (D2), that some x satisfies all the inequalities at once, is where the completeness of 
R hides, and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 takes completeness as an axiom. The uniqueness half of (D2) and the “not ending in all 9s” of (D1) rest on the Archimedean property: two numbers x, x' with \abs{x - x'} \le 10^{-n} for every n must be equal, which Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 also proves. Until then we use them as school facts, and each use names the fact it uses. One consequence is used below. A digit sequence with no digit 0 and no digit 9 is the only expansion of its number. Indeed, by (D3) a second expansion of the same number would force one of the two to end in all 9s and the other in all 0s; the given sequence ends in neither, since it has no 9s and no 0s at all. The real numbers are uncountable With the facts in hand, the diagonal runs on digits. Two precautions are built in. Each number on the list gets its expansion by a rule, so that no choosing is needed. And the new digits avoid 0 and 9, so that the new number has only one expansion. [The Reals Are Uncountable, by Decimals] The interval [0, 1) is uncountable. Hence 
R is uncountable. Take an arbitrary list of numbers in [0, 1), write each as its expansion with no tail of 9s, and change the n-th digit of the n-th number to 4 or 5. The resulting digit sequence is an expansion of some y, by (D2). If y were the n-th number, it would have two different expansions, one with no 0s or 9s, against (D3). Let f \colon 
N 	o [0, 1) be any function. For n \ge 1 let x_n \coloneqq f(n - 1), so that the list x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots has the same values as f. Let (d_{n,k})_{k \ge 1} be this expansion. It is named by a rule, “the expansion of x_n not ending in all 9s”, so no choice is involved. title: 3.4 Comparing Sizes: the Schröder–Bernstein Theorem
content:
Comparing Sizes: the Schröder–Bernstein Theorem We have (0, 1) \subseteq [0, 1] \subseteq 
R. Are the three sets the same size? Section 2.5 made “same size” mean “there is a bijection”, and for these sets a bijection is fiddly to write down: [0, 1] has two endpoints that (0, 1) lacks, and 
R is unbounded. An injection, on the other hand, is easy in both directions: the inclusion goes one way, and squeezing [0, 1] into the middle of (0, 1) goes the other. This section turns injections into a way of comparing sizes, and proves the theorem that makes the comparison useful: injections both ways give a bijection. Comparing sizes with injections An injection A 	o B places a copy of A inside B: distinct elements of A go to distinct elements of B, so B has room for all of A. For finite sets this is the pigeonhole principle read the other way round (@cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets). It deserves a name for all sets. A is at most as big as B when A fits into B without collisions. [Comparing Sizes] Let A and B be sets. We write \card{A} \le \card{B}, and say that A is at most as big as B, if there exists an injection A 	o B. We write \card{A} < \card{B}, and say that A is strictly smaller than B, if \card{A} \le \card{B} and not \card{A} = \card{B}: there is an injection A 	o B, and there is no bijection A 	o B. In words: “\le” asks for one injection, of our choosing. “<” asks for an injection and rules out every bijection, which is a statement about all functions A 	o B at once. As with \card{A} = \card{B} in Section 2.5 (@def-equinumerous), the symbols \card{A} \le \card{B} and \card{A} < \card{B} are relations between the sets A and B. No object \card{A} is defined for an infinite set, and nothing here compares two numbers. Examples. - Subsets. If A \subseteq B, the inclusion a \mapsto a is an injection A 	o B, so \card{A} \le \card{B}. In particular \card{(0, 1)} \le \card{[0, 1]} \le \card{
R}. - The degenerate case. For every set B, \card{\emptyset} \le \card{B}: the empty function \emptyset 	o B (@prp-empty-function (a)) is injective, vacuously, since there are no x_1, x_2 \in \emptyset to test. - Finite sets. Let A have m elements and B have n elements (@def-finite). Then \card{A} \le \card{B} exactly when m \le n. If m \le n, take bijections \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o A and \psi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o B; the inclusion \iota \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\} is injective, so \psi \circ \iota \circ \varphi^{-1} \colon A 	o B is injective by @thm-composition-injective-surjective (a), \varphi^{-1} being a bijection (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse). If \card{A} \le \card{B} and \card{B} \le \card{A}, then \card{A} = \card{B}. Let f \colon A 	o B and g \colon B 	o A be the two injections. We want a bijection h \colon A 	o B, and at each a \in A there are two candidates: go forward, h(a) = f(a), or go back along g: let h(a) be the unique b with g(b) = a. title: 3.5 Infinite Sets
content:
Infinite Sets Section 3.4 compared sizes with injections. Here we ask where 
N sits in that comparison. Every infinite set we have met contains a copy of 
N, and it is tempting to say that this must always happen by picking new elements one at a time; this section makes that picking exact. It turns out to need @ax-choice again, this time applied to a family with one set for each non-empty subset of the given set, and it gives two results: 
N is the smallest infinite size, and a set is infinite exactly when it is the same size as a proper part of itself. Every infinite set contains a copy of the natural numbers The question has a goal theorem: we want to show that an infinite set X has a countably infinite subset, that is, a subset equinumerous with 
N (@def-countably-infinite). Equivalently, we want an injection 
N 	o X: its image is then such a subset. [Infinite Sets Contain a Countably Infinite Subset] Every infinite set X has a countably infinite subset. Equivalently, there is an injection 
N 	o X. The natural attempt picks x_0 \in X, then x_1 \in X \setminus \{x_0\}, then x_2 \in X \setminus \{x_0, x_1\}, and so on. Each pick is possible, because a finite set cannot exhaust the infinite X, and each single pick is one ulename{\exists E}. But “and so on” is a definition by recursion, and @thm-recursion needs a function g that says, once and for all, which new element to take after any finite stage. That function must pick an element from every non-empty set of the form X \setminus F at once, with no rule for doing so when X is arbitrary. So we let @ax-choice supply a choice function c on all non-empty subsets of X first, and then the recursion is an ordinary one, with c as its rule. Let X be infinite. The family (S)_{S \in \powerset{X} \setminus \{\emptyset\}}, indexed by the non-empty subsets of X with each index as its own member, consists of non-empty sets, and its union is X: every index is a subset of X, and each x \in X lies in the index \{x\}. By @ax-choice there is a function c \colon \powerset{X} \setminus \{\emptyset\} 	o X with c(S) \in S \quad 	ext{for every non-empty } S \subseteq X . This is the one line of the proof that uses the axiom. Define g \colon 
N 	imes \powerset{X} 	o \powerset{X} by g(n, F) \coloneqq F \cup \{ c(X \setminus F) \} if F 
e X, and g(n, F) \coloneqq F if F = X. In the first case X \setminus F is non-empty, so c(X \setminus F) is defined; so g is a function. By @thm-recursion, applied with the set \powerset{X}, the starting value \emptyset and this g, there are sets F_n \subseteq X, for n \in 
N, with F_0 = \emptyset and F_{n+1} = g(n, F_n). We show by induction (@fd1:ax-induction) that F_n has exactly n elements, for every n \in 
N. For n = 0, F_0 = \emptyset has 0 elements (@def-finite). Suppose F_n has n elements. Then F_n is finite and X is not, so F_n 
e X, and F_{n+1} = F_n \cup \{ c(X \setminus F_n) \} with c(X \setminus F_n) \in X \setminus F_n. This is a union of disjoint sets with n elements and 1 element, so F_{n+1} has n + 1 elements by @prp-disjoint-union-count. In particular F_n 
e X for every n \in 
N, so we may define x_n \coloneqq c(X \setminus F_n) \in X \setminus F_n , \qquad	ext{and then}\qquad F_{n+1} = F_n \cup \{x_n\} . Hence F_n \subseteq F_{n+1} for every n, and by induction on k, F_m \subseteq F_{m+k} for all m, k \in 
N. Now let m, n \in 
N with m < n. Then x_m \in F_{m+1} \subseteq F_n, because m + 1 \le n (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e)), so k \coloneqq n - (m + 1) \in 
N (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (d)) and F_{m+1} \subseteq F_{(m+1)+k} = F_n; and x_n 
otin F_n. So x_m 
e x_n. Hence n \mapsto x_n is an injection 
N 	o X. Its image \{ x_n : n \in 
N \} \subseteq X is equinumerous with 
N, since n \mapsto x_n is a bijection from 
N onto it. This proves the theorem. The proof shows where the axiom enters and why one ulename{\exists E} per step is not enough: ulename{\exists E} names one element for one set, while the recursion needs g as a single function defined on every stage at once. Each F_n is then determined by c; the only arbitrary thing is c itself. A non-example by a minimal change. Run the same construction on the finite set X = \{a, b\}, with a 
e b. The choice function c and the recursion still make sense, since g is defined on every F \subseteq X. But F_1 = \{ c(X) \} has one element, F_2 adds the other, so F_2 = X, and from then on g leaves F_n unchanged. So x_2 = c(X \setminus F_2) = c(\emptyset) is not defined. The step that fails is “F_n is finite and X is not, so F_n 
e X”, exactly where the hypothesis that X is infinite is used. Compare Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1’s proof that the real numbers cannot be listed. There, a given list is used to build nested closed intervals, and each interval is obtained from the previous one by an explicit rule (keep an outer third that misses the next point of the list), so no choice principle is involved. Here X is an arbitrary infinite set, and there is no rule available for picking an element of an arbitrary non-empty subset of it; the choice function is the rule. For a particular X a rule may exist: for X \subseteq 
N, “the least element” is one (@thm-well-ordering), and then the proof needs no axiom. That the theorem cannot be proved in general from the other rules of set formation alone is a result of set theory; we state it without proof, and nothing depends on it. Consequences: the smallest infinite size The theorem says \card{
N} \le \card{X} for every infinite X (@def-card-le). Three consequences follow at once. - 
N is the smallest infinite size. If X is infinite and \card{X} \le \card{
N}, then \card{X} = \card{
N}, by @thm-schroder-bernstein and the theorem. So no infinite set is strictly smaller than 
N. - Countable sets are exactly the sets of size at most \card{
N}, by @thm-countable-characterizations, (i) \iff (ii). Combining with the first point: a countable set is finite or equinumerous with 
N, which @thm-countable-characterizations (iii) already said. - An uncountable set is strictly bigger than 
N. If X is uncountable, then X is infinite (a finite set is countable, by @thm-countable-characterizations), so \card{
N} \le \card{X}; and \card{
N} = \card{X} would make X countable. So \card{
N} < \card{X}. For example \card{
N} < \card{
R}, since 
R is uncountable (@thm-reals-uncountable-decimal). “Infinite” and “uncountable” are different words. 
Q is infinite (it contains 
N, which is infinite by @exm-hilbert-hotel, and a subset of a finite set is finite, by @prp-subset-finite) and countable (@thm-integers-rationals-countable). Likewise “X contains a copy of 
N” is not “X is equinumerous with 
N”: 
R contains 
N, and \card{
N} < \card{
R} (as above). Let X be uncountable. Is X \setminus \{x\} uncountable for every x \in X? Why must X have an element at all? X 
e \emptyset, because \emptyset is countable by @def-countable. For x \in X, if X \setminus \{x\} were countable, then X = (X \setminus \{x\}) \cup \{x\} would be a union of two countable sets, countable by @prp-union-two-countable. So X \setminus \{x\} is uncountable. Infinite sets are the same size as a proper part Section 2.5 proved that a finite set is never equinumerous with a proper subset (@thm-finite-no-proper-copy), and @exm-hilbert-hotel showed 
N doing exactly that. With @thm-infinite-countable-subset, the hotel can be built inside any infinite set: run it on the copy of 
N, and leave everything else alone. [Infinite Sets and Proper Subsets] A set X is infinite if and only if \card{X} = \card{Y} for some proper subset Y \subsetneq X. One direction is already done: Section 2.5 showed that finite sets have no proper subset of their own size. For the other, take the copy x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots of 
N inside X and move every guest one room up, x_n \mapsto x_{n+1}, as n \mapsto n + 1 does in the Quick check after @exm-hilbert-hotel. Room x_0 is vacated, and every point outside the copy stays where it is. (\Leftarrow) This is the contrapositive of @thm-finite-no-proper-copy: a finite set is not equinumerous with any proper subset, so a set that is equinumerous with one is not finite. (\Rightarrow) Let X be infinite. By @thm-infinite-countable-subset there is an injection n \mapsto x_n from 
N to X; let S \coloneqq \{ x_n : n \in 
N \}. Each element of S is x_n for exactly one n \in 
N, by injectivity. Define h \colon X 	o X \setminus \{x_0\} by h(x) \coloneqq  egin{cases} x_{n+1} & 	ext{if } x = x_n 	ext{ with } n \in 
N, \ x & 	ext{if } x 
otin S . \end{cases} This is a function into X \setminus \{x_0\}: x_{n+1} 
e x_0 because n + 1 
e 0, and an x 
otin S is not x_0. h is injective. Two points of S: x_{m+1} = x_{n+1} gives m + 1 = n + 1, so m = n. Two points outside S: h is the identity there. One of each: h(x_n) = x_{n+1} \in S, while h(x) = x 
otin S, so the values differ. h is onto X \setminus \{x_0\}. Let y \in X \setminus \{x_0\}. If y 
otin S, then y = h(y). If y \in S, then y = x_m with m 
e 0, so n \coloneqq m - 1 \in 
N (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (c)) and y = x_{n+1} = h(x_n). So h is a bijection, and Y \coloneqq X \setminus \{x_0\} is a proper subset of X, as x_0 \in X \setminus Y, with \card{X} = \card{Y}. This proves the theorem. Together with Section 2.5, this gives a characterization of “infinite” that never mentions 
N or counting: a set is infinite precisely when some proper part of it is as big as the whole. The finite intuition “a part is smaller than the whole” is exactly the property that separates finite sets from infinite ones. The direction (\Rightarrow) used @ax-choice, through @thm-infinite-countable-subset; the direction (\Leftarrow) did not. Name a proper subset of 
R that is equinumerous with 
R, and give a bijection. (-1, 1), with the bijection x \mapsto x/(1 + \abs{x}) of @exm-reals-open-interval. (Any interval with more than one point other than 
R itself works, by the same example.) No choice is needed for 
R: the bijection is a formula. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Where does the proof of @thm-infinite-countable-subset use @ax-choice? Why is one ulename{\exists E} per step not enough? 2. True or false, with a reason: every infinite subset of 
R contains a countably infinite subset; every uncountable set contains an uncountable proper subset. 3. Write down the bijection X 	o X \setminus \{x_0\} of the proof of @thm-infinite-iff-proper-subset for X = 
Z and x_n = n for n \in 
N. 4. For X = 
N, is choice needed to find a countably infinite subset? (a) At the line “By @ax-choice there is a function c with c(S) \in S for every non-empty S \subseteq X.” One ulename{\exists E} names one element of one non-empty set; that would give x_0, then x_1, and any finite number of steps. But @thm-recursion needs the step as a function g, defined once for every stage F at once, before the sequence exists. Defining g means picking an element of X \setminus F for every such F simultaneously, and that is what the axiom provides. (b) Both are true. The first is @thm-infinite-countable-subset applied to the infinite subset. For the second, let X be uncountable; then X 
e \emptyset, and for x \in X, X \setminus \{x\} is an uncountable proper subset, by the Quick check after the warning above. (c) h(n) = n + 1 for n \in 
N, and h(k) = k for k < 0. It maps 
Z onto 
Z \setminus \{0\}: a positive m is h(m - 1), and a negative k is h(k). (d) No. 
N itself is countably infinite, via \id_{
N}. (More generally, an infinite X \subseteq 
N can be listed in increasing order by @lem-subsets-of-naturals, a rule.) B. Practice [B1: Removing finitely many points] Let X be infinite and let F \subseteq X be finite. Prove that \card{X \setminus F} = \card{X}. First, X \setminus F is infinite: otherwise X = (X \setminus F) \cup F would be a union of two disjoint finite sets, finite by @prp-disjoint-union-count. By @thm-infinite-countable-subset applied to X \setminus F (this uses @ax-choice), there is an injection n \mapsto s_n from 
N to X \setminus F; let S \coloneqq \{ s_n : n \in 
N \}. Let F have k elements, and let \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, k\} 	o F be a bijection (@def-finite). No two of X \setminus (F \cup S), F and S meet, and together they make up X; and X \setminus F is the union of the disjoint sets X \setminus (F \cup S) and S. By @thm-infinite-countable-subset (using @ax-choice) there is a countably infinite S \subseteq X. Define h \colon X \cup C 	o X by h(x) \coloneqq x for x \in X \setminus S and h(x) \coloneqq \psi(x) for x \in S \cup C. It is a bijection on each piece, onto the corresponding piece, so it is a bijection, and \card{X \cup C} = \card{X}. N with g(0) = f_0(0) + 1, \qquad g(n + 1) = \max\{ g(n), f_{n+1}(n + 1) \} + 1 . \underline{\hspace{8em}} [Hint 1] Two things must be shown about g: that it lies in I, and that it differs from each f_n somewhere. Where? [Hint 2] The second half begins: “For every n \in 
N, g(n + 1) \ge g(n) + 1 > g(n).” The move is the diagonal: given any list, build an object that differs from the n-th entry at the n-th place. Here the object must also stay inside I, which is why g(n + 1) is pushed above g(n) as well as above f_{n+1}(n + 1). Completion. For every n \in 
N, g(n + 1) = \max\{ g(n), f_{n+1}(n + 1) \} + 1 \ge g(n) + 1 > g(n). From this, g(m) < g(n) whenever m < n, by induction on n (@thm-induction with base m + 1): g(m) < g(m + 1), and g(m) < g(n) < g(n + 1). So g \in I. Next, g(n) > f_n(n) for every n \in 
N: for n = 0, g(0) = f_0(0) + 1; for n = k + 1, g(k + 1) \ge f_{k+1}(k + 1) + 1. So g(n) 
e f_n(n), and hence g 
e f_n, for every n \in 
N. So g \in I is not a value of n \mapsto f_n, and no function 
N 	o I is onto. Since I 
e \emptyset (it contains \id_{
N}), I is not countable. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: names the diagonal move. - 4: shows g is strictly increasing: 2 for the step g(n) < g(n + 1) for every n, and 2 for the passage to all m < n. - 3: shows g(n) > f_n(n) for every n, treating n = 0 and n = k + 1 separately, and concludes g 
e f_n. - 2: concludes that no function 
N 	o I is onto and, noting I 
e \emptyset (\id_{
N} \in I), that I is not countable. Fatal errors (0 for the part concerned): taking g(n) < g(n + 1) alone as strict increase, with no passage to all m < n; inferring g 
e f_n without exhibiting a point where they differ, or exhibiting one only for n \ge 1. The max in g is needed: the plain diagonal g(n) \coloneqq f_n(n) + 1 need not be strictly increasing (for f_0(n) = 5 + n and f_1(n) = n, it gives g(0) = 6 > g(1) = 2). [C2: The irrationals] Deduce from @exr-infinite-sets-b2 that \card{
