title: 3.6 Cardinal Arithmetic
content:
Cardinal Arithmetic Section 2.5 counted finite sets, and Section 2.3 proved the laws of powers m^{n+k} = m^n m^k and (m^n)^k = m^{nk} by induction (@prp-power-laws). For finite sets these numbers count functions: Y^X has m^n elements when Y has m and X has n (Section 1.5, before @exm-function-set-small). This section asks what is left of that arithmetic when the sets are infinite and all we have are bijections. The plane and the line A square has two dimensions and a segment has one. Surely the plane 
R 	imes 
R has more points than the line? The injection x \mapsto (x, 0) gives \card{
R} \le \card{
R 	imes 
R}, and it seems that the other half of the plane should be left over. A second question. Is 
N^{
N}, the set of sequences of natural numbers, bigger than 
R? A real number in [0, 1) is only a sequence of digits below 10, while a sequence in 
N^{
N} may use any natural number at every place, so 
N^{
N} looks bigger. Guess both answers before reading on. The plane is a product, 
N^{
N} is a power, and the line will turn out to be a power too: a power of 2. Adding sizes: disjoint unions For finite sets that do not meet, Section 2.5 added sizes by taking the union (@prp-disjoint-union-count). So define the sum of two sets as their union? With A = B = \{0\} we want two elements, and A \cup B = \{0\} has one. The union counts the shared element once. The cure is to tag every element with the name of the set it came from, so that the two copies cannot overlap. A disjoint union keeps a labeled copy of each set, so nothing is counted twice. [Disjoint Union] Let A and B be sets. Their disjoint union is A \sqcup B \coloneqq (A 	imes \{0\}) \cup (B 	imes \{1\}) . The maps \iota_A \colon A 	o A \sqcup B, \iota_A(a) \coloneqq (a, 0), and \iota_B \colon B 	o A \sqcup B, \iota_B(b) \coloneqq (b, 1), are the inclusions. In words: every element of A \sqcup B is (a, 0) with a \in A or (b, 1) with b \in B, and not both, since (a, 0) = (b, 1) would give 0 = 1 by the characteristic property of pairs (@def-ordered-pair). By the same property each inclusion is injective, the two images are disjoint, and together they make up A \sqcup B. So a function on A \sqcup B may be defined by giving its values on the two tagged parts separately: these are the two cases that cannot overlap, as in the proof of @prp-union-two-countable. [Two copies of ℕ] Show that \card{
N \sqcup 
N} = \card{
N}. This is the merging of two lists from the proof of @prp-union-two-countable, now as a bijection. Let e(n, 0) \coloneqq 2n and e(n, 1) \coloneqq 2n + 1, for n \in 
N; by the unwinding above this defines e \colon 
N \sqcup 
N 	o 
N. For the decoder, let d(m) \coloneqq (q, r), where m = 2q + r with q \in 
N and r \in \{0, 1\}; the pair exists and is unique by the claim in that proof, and (q, r) \in 
N \sqcup 
N. Then d(e(n, r)) = (n, r) by the uniqueness, and e(d(m)) = 2q + r = m. By @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, e is a bijection. This is the first encoding of the section: e writes a pair as one number, and d reads it back. The method box comes with the next one. (a) With a 
e b, list the elements of \{a, b\} \sqcup \{a\} and of \{a, b\} \cup \{a\}. (b) What is \emptyset \sqcup B? (c) If A \cap B = \emptyset, give a bijection A \cup B 	o A \sqcup B. (a) \{a, b\} \sqcup \{a\} = \{ (a, 0), (b, 0), (a, 1) \}, three elements; \{a, b\} \cup \{a\} = \{a, b\}, two. (b) \emptyset \sqcup B = B 	imes \{1\}, since \emptyset 	imes \{0\} = \emptyset; and b \mapsto (b, 1) is a bijection B 	o \emptyset \sqcup B. (c) Send x to (x, 0) if x \in A and to (x, 1) if x \in B. The cases do not overlap, since A \cap B = \emptyset, so this is a function. Its inverse sends (a, 0) \mapsto a and (b, 1) \mapsto b. No subtraction. For numbers, m + k = n + k gives m = n. For sets, \card{\{0\} \sqcup 
N} = \card{\emptyset \sqcup 
N} although \card{\{0\}} 
e \card{\emptyset}: the map sending (0, 0) \mapsto 0 and (n, 1) \mapsto n + 1 is a bijection \{0\} \sqcup 
N 	o 
N, and (n, 1) \mapsto n is a bijection \emptyset \sqcup 
N 	o 
N (Exercise B4 (a) has the details). Every law below is proved by a bijection, never borrowed from the numbers. Multiplying, raising to powers, and comparing Products A 	imes B (@def-cartesian-product) and sets of functions Y^X (Section 1.5) are the other two operations. If A has m elements and B has n, then A 	imes B has mn elements and B^A has n^m, as Exercise C2 of Section 2.5 counts. The base is written on the line and the exponent is the domain: Y^X is the set of functions from X to Y. Before any law, we check that the three operations see only sizes. [Sums, Products and Powers Respect Size] Let A, A', B, B' be sets with \card{A} = \card{A'} and \card{B} = \card{B'}. Then 1. \card{A \sqcup B} = \card{A' \sqcup B'}; 2. \card{A 	imes B} = \card{A' 	imes B'}; 3. \card{A^B} = \card{A'^{B'}}. Carry each element across along the bijections: on each tagged part for (a), on each coordinate for (b), and for (c) by composing a function with the bijections on both sides. The inverses carry everything back. Let \alpha \colon A 	o A' and  eta \colon B 	o B' be bijections, with two-sided inverses \alpha^{-1} and  eta^{-1} (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse). (a) Send (a, 0) \mapsto (\alpha(a), 0) and (b, 1) \mapsto ( eta(b), 1); this is a function by the two-part rule after @def-disjoint-union. The same rule with \alpha^{-1} and  eta^{-1} undoes it on each part, so it is a two-sided inverse. (b) Send (a, b) \mapsto (\alpha(a),  eta(b)). The map (a', b') \mapsto (\alpha^{-1}(a'),  eta^{-1}(b')) is a two-sided inverse, by @def-ordered-pair. (c) For f \in A^B, the composite \alpha \circ f \circ  eta^{-1} is a function B' 	o A'. Let \Theta(f) \coloneqq \alpha \circ f \circ  eta^{-1} and \Lambda(g) \coloneqq \alpha^{-1} \circ g \circ  eta for g \in A'^{B'}. By @prp-composition-associative and \alpha^{-1} \circ \alpha = \id_A,  eta^{-1} \circ  eta = \id_B, \Lambda(\Theta(f)) = (\alpha^{-1} \circ \alpha) \circ f \circ ( eta^{-1} \circ  eta) = f , and \Theta(\Lambda(g)) = g in the same way. In each part, @thm-bijection-iff-inverse gives a bijection. The proposition lets us replace either set by an equinumerous one without changing the size of the result. An answer computed from representatives must not depend on which representatives we used. Compare “send p/q to p” in Section 1.5 (@exm-not-a-function), which fails exactly this test. The comparison \le of @def-card-le is respected as well, with one exception. [Monotonicity] Let A, A', B, B' be sets with \card{A} \le \card{A'} and \card{B} \le \card{B'}. Then 1. \card{A \sqcup B} \le \card{A' \sqcup B'}; 2. \card{A 	imes B} \le \card{A' 	imes B'}; 3. if A' 
e \emptyset, then \card{A^B} \le \card{A'^{B'}}. Carry the injections across, as in the previous proof. For powers, a function on B must be extended to all of B', and the extension needs a value to put on the points that B does not reach. Let u \colon A 	o A' and v \colon B 	o B' be injections. (a), (b): the maps of the previous proof with u, v in place of \alpha,  eta are injective, by @def-ordered-pair. (c) Fix a_0 \in A'. For f \in A^B define F(f) \colon B' 	o A' by F(f)(b') \coloneqq  egin{cases} u(f(b)) & 	ext{if } b' = v(b) 	ext{ for some } b \in B , \ a_0 & 	ext{if } b' 
otin v(B) . \end{cases} In the first case b is unique, since v is injective, so F(f) is a function. If F(f) = F(g), then for every b \in B, u(f(b)) = F(f)(v(b)) = F(g)(v(b)) = u(g(b)) , so f(b) = g(b), since u is injective. Hence f = g (@prp-function-equality), and F is an injection A^B 	o A'^{B'}. A non-example by minimal change. Drop “A' 
e \emptyset” from (c), and take A = A' = \emptyset, B = \emptyset, B' = \{0\}. Then \card{B} \le \card{B'}, but \emptyset^{\emptyset} has one element, the empty function (@prp-empty-function), while \emptyset^{\{0\}} = \emptyset; there is no injection from a one-element set into \emptyset. The proof used a_0 exactly once, and here there is no a_0. (If A' = \emptyset, then A = \emptyset too, since a function into \emptyset has empty domain.) Where does the proof of (c) use that v is injective? Where does it use that u is injective? Injectivity of v makes F(f) a function: the point b with v(b) = b' must be unique. Injectivity of u makes F injective: u(f(b)) = u(g(b)) must give f(b) = g(b). Encoding: the diagonals of ℕ × ℕ Section 3.1 showed 
N 	imes 
N countable by an injection. At the scratch work for @thm-product-countable it set aside the list along the diagonals, because writing a formula for the position of (m, n) and checking that every position is used takes real work. The Quick check before 3.4’s Looking-ahead remark got \card{
N 	imes 
N} = \card{
N} from @thm-schroder-bernstein without ever seeing a bijection. Here is the work, done. For s \in 
N, the triangular number 	au_s \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^{s} i (@def-sum-product) has 	au_0 = 0 and 	au_{s+1} = 	au_s + s + 1. It counts the points on the diagonals m + n = 0, 1, \dots, s - 1, which hold 1, 2, \dots, s points. [The diagonal pairing of ℕ × ℕ with ℕ] Show that \pi(m, n) \coloneqq 	au_{m+n} + n is a bijection 
N 	imes 
N 	o 
N. [Scratch work] What must the code record? Which diagonal the point is on, s = m + n, and its place on that diagonal, n \in \{0, \dots, s\}; from s and n we read back m = s - n. The diagonals before diagonal s hold 1 + 2 + \dots + s = 	au_s points, so the code counts them and adds the place. Small values: diagonal 0 gives 0; diagonal 1 gives 1, 2; diagonal 2 gives 3, 4, 5. The decoder must find, for each k, the diagonal it falls on. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Givens Goal ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ (m, n) \in 
N 	imes 
N \pi(m, n) \in 
N k \in 
N exactly one (m, n) with 	au_{m+n} + n = k gap every k \in 
N is 	au_s + n with s, n \in 
N, n \le s, in exactly one way ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Existence by induction on k: stepping from k to k + 1 moves one place along the diagonal, or, at its end, to the start of the next one. Uniqueness: diagonal s fills the block 	au_s, \dots, 	au_s + s, just below 	au_{s+1}, so different diagonals give different numbers. For every k \in 
N there are s, n \in 
N with n \le s and k = 	au_s + n, and the pair (s, n) is unique. Existence, by @thm-induction from 0. First, 0 = 	au_0 + 0. Suppose k = 	au_s + n with n \le s. If n < s, then k + 1 = 	au_s + (n + 1) with n + 1 \le s. If n = s, then k + 1 = 	au_s + s + 1 = 	au_{s+1} + 0. Uniqueness. First, 	au_{j+1} = 	au_j + j + 1 > 	au_j for every j, so if s < s', then 	au_{s+1} \le 	au_{s'}, by @thm-induction on s' from s + 1. Now let 	au_s + n = 	au_{s'} + n' with n \le s and n' \le s', and suppose s 
e s'; by symmetry s < s'. Then 	au_s + n \le 	au_s + s < 	au_{s+1} \le 	au_{s'} \le 	au_{s'} + n' , a contradiction. So s = s', and then n = n'. The bijection. \pi(m, n) \in 
N, since 	au_{m+n} \in 
N, by @thm-induction on s from 	au_0 = 0 and 	au_{s+1} = 	au_s + s + 1 with @lem-naturals-arithmetic (b). For k \in 
N, write k = 	au_s + n by the claim and set \delta(k) \coloneqq (s - n, n), where s - n \in 
N because n \le s (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (d)); the uniqueness in the claim makes \delta a function. Then \pi(\delta(k)) = 	au_{(s - n) + n} + n = 	au_s + n = k. And \delta(\pi(m, n)) = (m, n), by the uniqueness applied to k = 	au_{m+n} + n, where s = m + n \ge n. By @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, \pi is a bijection. A table of the first values: \pi(0, 0) = 0, \pi(1, 0) = 1, \pi(0, 1) = 2, \pi(2, 0) = 3, \pi(1, 1) = 4, \pi(0, 2) = 5. Decoding 11: 	au_4 = 10 \le 11 < 15 = 	au_5, so 11 = 	au_4 + 1 and \delta(11) = (3, 1). [Method: build a bijection by encoding and decoding] Template. (1) Say what an element of the source must record for nothing to be lost. (2) Choose a code: a rule sending each element to an element of the target, and check that it lands there. (3) Write the decoder: a rule reading an element of the source back from each element of the target, and check that it is a function, with exactly one answer for each input. (4) Check both round trips and cite @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. When to use it. The two sets carry the same information arranged differently: two numbers in one, a pair of sequences in one sequence, a function of two variables as a function with function values. The usual failure. Checking one round trip only: \delta \circ \pi = \id alone shows only that \pi is injective (@thm-left-inverse-iff-injective). A decoder that is not a function, with two readings of one code or none (the interleaving of decimals, later in this section). If the decoder works on part of the target only, keep the injection and use @exm-method-injections-both-ways. An injective code is not yet a bijection. The code 2^m 3^n of @thm-product-countable is injective, but 5 is not a value, and no decoder is defined at 5. Step (3) of the method, a decoder defined on the whole target, is what makes \pi a bijection. Compute \pi(3, 2) and \delta(47). \pi(3, 2) = 	au_5 + 2 = 15 + 2 = 17. For 47: 	au_9 = 45 \le 47 < 55 = 	au_{10}, so 47 = 	au_9 + 2, and \delta(47) = (9 - 2, 2) = (7, 2). Check: \pi(7, 2) = 	au_9 + 2 = 47. The laws of exponents, for all sets For numbers, m^{n+k} = m^n m^k and (m^n)^k = m^{nk}. Read through the sets these numbers count, each law says that two sets of functions are the same size, and for sets we must find the bijection. [Laws of Cardinal Arithmetic] For all sets A, B, C, X, Y, Z: 1. \card{A \sqcup B} = \card{B \sqcup A}, \card{(A \sqcup B) \sqcup C} = \card{A \sqcup (B \sqcup C)}, \card{A 	imes B} = \card{B 	imes A} and \card{(A 	imes B) 	imes C} = \card{A 	imes (B 	imes C)}; 2. \card{A 	imes (B \sqcup C)} = \card{(A 	imes B) \sqcup (A 	imes C)}; 3. X^{\emptyset} has exactly one element, and \card{X^{\{0\}}} = \card{X}; 4. \card{X^{Y \sqcup Z}} = \card{X^Y 	imes X^Z}; 5. \card{(X 	imes Y)^Z} = \card{X^Z 	imes Y^Z}; 6. \card{(X^Y)^Z} = \card{X^{Y 	imes Z}}. [Scratch work] For (d): what is an element of each side? On the left, a function h defined on the tagged copies of Y and Z. On the right, a pair (f, g) with f \colon Y 	o X and g \colon Z 	o X. A function on two disjoint pieces is the same thing as a function on each piece. So cut h into its two pieces by composing with the inclusions, and glue a pair back together piece by piece. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ----------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- h \in X^{Y \sqcup Z} an element of X^Y 	imes X^Z: (h \circ \iota_Y, h \circ \iota_Z) (f, g) \in X^Y 	imes X^Z one h with h \circ \iota_Y = f and h \circ \iota_Z = g gap h(y, 0) \coloneqq f(y), h(z, 1) \coloneqq g(z) is a function: the parts do not overlap (after @def-disjoint-union) -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (d) Let \Phi(h) \coloneqq (h \circ \iota_Y, h \circ \iota_Z) for h \in X^{Y \sqcup Z}. For (f, g) \in X^Y 	imes X^Z, let \Psi(f, g) be the function h \colon Y \sqcup Z 	o X with h(y, 0) \coloneqq f(y), \qquad h(z, 1) \coloneqq g(z) \qquad (y \in Y, \ z \in Z) . This is a function, because every element of Y \sqcup Z has exactly one of the two forms. Then \Phi(\Psi(f, g)) = (f, g): for y \in Y, h(\iota_Y(y)) = h(y, 0) = f(y), so h \circ \iota_Y = f by @prp-function-equality, and likewise h \circ \iota_Z = g; the pairs are equal by @def-ordered-pair. And \Psi(\Phi(h)) = h: the two functions agree at every (y, 0) and every (z, 1), which are all the points of Y \sqcup Z, so they are equal by @prp-function-equality. By @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, \Phi is a bijection. (e) For g \in (X^Y)^Z, each g(z) is a function Y 	o X. Let \Phi(g) \colon Y 	imes Z 	o X, \Phi(g)(y, z) \coloneqq g(z)(y). For h \in X^{Y 	imes Z} and z \in Z, the rule y \mapsto h(y, z) is an element of X^Y; let \Psi(h) \colon Z 	o X^Y send z to it. Then \Phi(\Psi(h))(y, z) = \Psi(h)(z)(y) = h(y, z) for all (y, z), so \Phi(\Psi(h)) = h. And \Psi(\Phi(g))(z) is the function y \mapsto g(z)(y), which is g(z); so \Psi(\Phi(g)) = g. Here @prp-function-equality is used twice: first for functions on Y, then for functions on Z. By @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, \Phi is a bijection. The remaining parts are proved by the same kind of regrouping; the maps are in the fold below. Each map below has the stated inverse, and each round trip is one line of @prp-function-equality and @def-ordered-pair. As a sample, the associativity of \sqcup has three cases, one for each form of element; on ((b, 1), 0) the map gives ((b, 0), 1), and the inverse, reading the tag 1 outside and the tag 0 inside, returns ((b, 1), 0). (a) A \sqcup B 	o B \sqcup A: (a, 0) \mapsto (a, 1), (b, 1) \mapsto (b, 0); it is its own inverse, with the roles of A and B exchanged. (A \sqcup B) \sqcup C 	o A \sqcup (B \sqcup C): ((a, 0), 0) \mapsto (a, 0), ((b, 1), 0) \mapsto ((b, 0), 1), (c, 1) \mapsto ((c, 1), 1); the three forms of the source do not overlap, and the inverse reads the three forms of the target back. A 	imes B 	o B 	imes A: (a, b) \mapsto (b, a). (A 	imes B) 	imes C 	o A 	imes (B 	imes C): ((a, b), c) \mapsto (a, (b, c)), with inverse (a, (b, c)) \mapsto ((a, b), c). (b) A 	imes (B \sqcup C) 	o (A 	imes B) \sqcup (A 	imes C): (a, (b, 0)) \mapsto ((a, b), 0) and (a, (c, 1)) \mapsto ((a, c), 1); the inverse moves the tag back inside. (c) X^{\emptyset} = \{ (\emptyset, X) \}, the empty function, by @prp-empty-function (a). The map f \mapsto f(0) is a bijection X^{\{0\}} 	o X, with inverse sending x to the function 0 \mapsto x. (d) Let p_1(x, y) \coloneqq x and p_2(x, y) \coloneqq y on X 	imes Y. The map h \mapsto (p_1 \circ h, p_2 \circ h) from (X 	imes Y)^Z to X^Z 	imes Y^Z has the inverse (f, g) \mapsto  igl(z \mapsto (f(z), g(z)) igr). Law (f) is called currying: a function of two variables becomes a function whose values are functions. For finite sets with m, n and k elements, the theorem gives back m^{n+k} = m^n m^k and (m^n)^k = m^{nk} with no induction in sight; the induction has moved into the counting of Section 2.5. Nothing in the proof used finiteness. [Method: prove a law of sizes by a bijection of sets] Template. (1) Write out what an element of each side is: a tagged element, a pair, a function, a function with function values. (2) Find the map that only regroups: compose with the inclusions, pair the coordinates, or curry. (3) Write the reverse regrouping. (4) Check both round trips with @prp-function-equality and @def-ordered-pair, and cite @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. When to use it. A law familiar from numbers, such as m^{n+k} = m^n m^k, is claimed for sets of any size; or a size is to be computed by rewriting a set step by step. The usual failure. Computing with symbols, as in “\card{X}^{\card{Y} + \card{Z}} = \card{X}^{\card{Y}} \card{X}^{\card{Z}}”, when no number \card{X} exists and the step is the law itself: (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. Dropping the tags: with \cup in place of \sqcup the law fails: for X = \{0, 1\} and Y = Z = \{0\}, X^{Y \cup Z} has 2 elements and X^Y 	imes X^Z has 4 (Exercise B4 (b)). Let X = \{0, 1\}, Y = \{a\} and Z = \{b, c\}. How many elements has each side of (d)? Let h(a, 0) = 1, h(b, 1) = 0, h(c, 1) = 1. What is \Phi(h)? Y \sqcup Z = \{ (a, 0), (b, 1), (c, 1) \} has three elements, and a function from it to \{0, 1\} is fixed by three values, each 0 or 1: 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8 functions. On the right, X^Y has 2 elements and X^Z has 4, so the product has 2 \cdot 4 = 8. And \Phi(h) = (f, g) with f(a) = 1, g(b) = 0, g(c) = 1. title: Relations: Equivalence and Order
content:
Relations: Equivalence and Order This chapter is about relations. When is “the same” a legitimate way to identify different things, as a clock identifies 2 with 14, or a function identifies two points with the same value? And what does “larger” mean when not everything can be compared, as with sets under inclusion or natural numbers under divisibility? The motivating problem: in what sense is “9 + 5 = 2 on a clock” a true statement? The answer is an equivalence relation, the partition it cuts its set into, and a check that arithmetic on the pieces does not depend on which integer names a piece. For orders the answer is that “largest” splits into two notions, greatest and maximal, which agree only when every two elements are comparable. The last section reaches least upper bounds in a general partially ordered set (Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1’s supremum is the case of \le on 
R, and its axiom says that such suprema exist) and closes with well-ordered sets, the order-theoretic name for what Section 2.1 proved about 
N. Two methods of proof are new. Section 4.1 decides a property of a relation by a proof for all elements or by one witness against it, and records the verdicts in a table. Section 4.2 checks that a definition made through a representative does not depend on the representative: the check called well-definedness, promised in Section 1.5. Section 4.3 uses the methods of Chapters 1 and 2 without new scaffolding. What you need. Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–8, and Sets and Functions, Chapters 1–3. From Logic and Proof: the rules for “there exists” (@fd1:def-rules-existential), equality (@fd1:def-rules-equality, @fd1:prp-equality-symmetric-transitive), negating bounded quantifiers and implications (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication), De Morgan and double negation (@fd1:prp-de-morgan, @fd1:prp-double-negation), the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), squares and order (@fd1:thm-squares-order), and induction (@fd1:ax-induction). From Chapter 1: subsets, set equality and sets cut out by a property (@def-subset, @def-set-equality, @def-set-builder, @prp-empty-set-unique, @prp-subset-antisymmetric, @prp-subset-transitive); power sets and unions of families (@def-power-set, @def-family-union-intersection); ordered pairs and relations as sets of pairs (@def-ordered-pair, @def-relation); functions, their equality, and rules that are not functions (@def-function, @prp-function-equality, @exm-not-a-function); surjections and two-sided inverses (@def-surjective, @thm-bijection-iff-inverse); preimages (@def-preimage, @prp-image-preimage); Russell’s theorem (@thm-russell); divisibility and parity (@def-divides, @prp-divides-transitive, @thm-even-or-odd); and the methods direct proof, cases, counterexample, double inclusion, uniqueness, injectivity and construct-and-verify (@exm-method-direct-proof, @exm-method-cases, @exm-method-counterexample, @exm-method-double-inclusion, @exm-method-uniqueness, @exm-method-injectivity, @exm-method-construct-and-verify). From Chapter 2: well-ordering and the least-element method (@thm-well-ordering, @cor-well-ordering-integers, @exm-method-least-element); the arithmetic of the integers (@prp-integers-closed, @lem-naturals-arithmetic); induction from a base (@thm-induction); the division algorithm and prime factors (@thm-division-algorithm, @thm-prime-factor); powers (@def-power, @prp-power-laws); finite maxima (@prp-finite-max); choosing between direct proof, contrapositive and contradiction (@exm-method-choosing-the-form); equinumerous, finite and infinite sets (@def-equinumerous, @prp-equinumerous-properties, @cor-finite-size-unique, @def-finite, @def-infinite, @prp-subset-finite, @exm-hilbert-hotel). From Chapter 3: images of countable sets and the countability of 
Z (@prp-countable-image, @thm-integers-rationals-countable), for one review exercise, and the axiom of choice (@ax-choice), for one remark. The arithmetic and order of 
R are school facts, as before. Time. About 20 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit check 4.2 C1); about 25 hours for everything. Roadmap - Properties of relations. Reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive; deciding each one by a proof for all elements or by a single witness, with the verdicts collected in a table of eight relations; divisibility as the relation whose antisymmetry depends on the set. - Equivalence relations and partitions. Relations that behave like equality, the proof that their classes partition the set and that every partition arises from exactly one of them (a correspondence proved in both directions), the integers modulo n, sizes of subsets as a last example, and the method for checking that a definition on classes is well defined. - Partial orders, maximal and greatest elements. Relations that behave like \le, greatest elements against maximal ones and when the two agree, uniqueness from antisymmetry, least upper bounds in a partially ordered set, and well-ordered sets. Named moves The first two are method boxes; Chapters 1–3’s boxes are cited where they are used. - Prove or disprove each property (@exm-method-relation-properties). A property that holds is a “for all”: take arbitrary related elements and unwind. A property that fails needs one witness: an element, a pair or a triple. (Section 4.1) - Well-definedness (@exm-method-well-definedness). For a rule that reads a representative, take two representatives of one class and show that the outputs agree. (Section 4.2) - Classes from a relation, a relation from classes. Pass between an equivalence relation and its partition, whichever description makes the next step easier. - Uniqueness by antisymmetry. Two candidates, each below the other, are equal: the method of @exm-method-uniqueness with (PO2) closing the gap. (Section 4.3) Threads - Same size. The bijections of Section 1.6 say when two sets have the same size; Section 2.5 makes this a definition (@def-equinumerous); Section 4.2 meets it as an equivalence relation on the subsets of one set (@exm-same-size-subsets), and explains why it is not one on all sets. - The clock. The arithmetic of 
Z/n in Section 4.2 returns in Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 3.4, where 
Z/n becomes a ring. - Maximal elements and chains. Section 4.3 ends by asking when a partially ordered set must have a maximal element; Chapter 6 answers with Zorn’s lemma. Summary A relation on a set may be reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric or transitive (@def-relation-properties); each property is proved for all elements or refuted by one witness. The relations with the first, second and fourth are the equivalence relations (@def-equivalence-relation); their classes partition the set (@thm-classes-partition), and every partition comes from exactly one of them (@thm-partition-equivalence). Congruence modulo n gives 
Z/n = \{[0], \dots, [n - 1]\} (@prp-integers-mod-n), whose sum and product are well defined (@prp-congruence-arithmetic), while some rules on classes are not functions at all (@exm-ill-defined-class-map). The relations with the first, third and fourth are the partial orders (@def-partial-order). A greatest element is unique (@prp-greatest-unique) and maximal, and the converse needs totality (@prp-greatest-maximal); a supremum is the least upper bound (@def-order-supremum), and under divisibility it is the least common multiple (@exm-divisibility-lcm). What is open: in a partially ordered set where every chain has an upper bound, must there be a maximal element? Nothing proved so far decides it. Chapter 6 states the principle that does, Zorn’s lemma, and puts it to work. Next, Chapter 5 uses quotient sets and well-definedness to build functions: every function factors through the quotient by “same value”. Terms - antisymmetric: x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x give x = y (@def-relation-properties). - block: one of the sets of a partition (@def-partition). - bounded: bounded above and below, that is, with an upper and a lower bound (@def-order-bounds). - comparable: x \preceq y or y \preceq x (@def-partial-order). - congruent modulo n: a \equiv b \pmod{n}, that is, n \mid a - b (@def-congruence). - equivalence class: [a] = \{ x \in X : x \sim a \} (@def-equivalence-class). - equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric and transitive (@def-equivalence-relation). - greatest element: an element of A above every element of A (@def-greatest-element). - infimum: a greatest lower bound (@def-order-supremum). - least element: an element of A below every element of A (@def-greatest-element). - lower bound: an element of X below every element of A (@def-order-bounds). - maximal element: an element of A with nothing in A strictly above it (@def-maximal-element). - minimal element: an element of A with nothing in A strictly below it (@def-maximal-element). - partially ordered set: a set with a reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive relation (@def-partial-order). - partition: a set of non-empty, pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is the whole set (@def-partition). - quotient map: x \mapsto [x], from X onto X/{\sim} (@def-quotient-set). - quotient set: the set X/{\sim} of all equivalence classes (@def-quotient-set). - reflexive: x \mathrel{R} x for every x \in X (@def-relation-properties). - representative: an element of a class, which names the class (@def-equivalence-class). - strict part: x \prec y, that is, x \preceq y and x 
e y (@def-partial-order). - supremum: a least upper bound (@def-order-supremum). - symmetric: x \mathrel{R} y gives y \mathrel{R} x (@def-relation-properties). - total: every two elements are comparable (@def-partial-order). - transitive: x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} z give x \mathrel{R} z (@def-relation-properties). - upper bound: an element of X above every element of A (@def-order-bounds). - well defined: a rule on classes whose output does not depend on the representative (@exm-method-well-definedness). - well-ordered set: a partially ordered set whose order is total and in which every non-empty subset has a least element (@def-well-ordered-set).

title: 4.1 Properties of Relations
content:
Properties of Relations Chapter 1 made relations into sets: a relation on a set X is a subset R \subseteq X 	imes X, and x \mathrel{R} y means (x, y) \in R (@def-relation). It named the properties that make a relation an order or an equivalence and left them to this chapter. Equality, \le, inclusion \subseteq, divisibility \mid, and “leaves the same remainder on division by 3” are all relations, and they behave alike in some ways and differently in others. This section names four properties that sort them, proves the ones that divisibility has, and collects witnesses for every failure. Each property is decided by the same method: a proof for all elements when it holds, one witness when it fails. Sections 4.2 and 4.3 then study the two combinations that matter most. Four properties Start from equality. Every x equals itself; if x = y, then y = x; and if x = y and y = z, then x = z. The relation \le on 
R keeps the first and third of these and loses the second, but it has a substitute: x \le y and y \le x together force x = y. Each of these is a property a relation may or may not have. Each property is one rule for what the relation must contain, given what it already contains. [Properties of a Relation] Let X be a set and R a relation on X. Then R is - reflexive on X if x \mathrel{R} x for every x \in X:  orall x \in X \ \ x \mathrel{R} x ; - symmetric if x \mathrel{R} y implies y \mathrel{R} x, for all x, y \in X:  orall x \in X \  orall y \in X \ \  igl( x \mathrel{R} y 	o y \mathrel{R} x  igr) ; - antisymmetric if x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x together imply x = y, for all x, y \in X:  orall x \in X \  orall y \in X \ \  igl( (x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} x) 	o x = y  igr) ; - transitive if x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} z together imply x \mathrel{R} z, for all x, y, z \in X:  orall x \in X \  orall y \in X \  orall z \in X \ \  igl( (x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} z) 	o x \mathrel{R} z  igr) . In words: reflexive says every element is related to itself. Symmetric says the relation can be read backwards: whenever it relates x to y, it also relates y to x. Antisymmetric says it can be read both ways only between an element and itself. Transitive says two steps can always be replaced by one. Three of the four are implications, so a relation has them unless some related pair (or triple) makes the conclusion false: for symmetry and transitivity a pair is missing from R, and for antisymmetry two different elements are related both ways. Negating with @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation and @fd1:prp-negated-implication turns each failure into a witness:  egin{aligned} 	ext{not reflexive:} \quad & \exists x \in X \ \ 
eg (x \mathrel{R} x) , \ 	ext{not symmetric:} \quad & \exists x \in X \ \exists y \in X \ \  igl( x \mathrel{R} y \wedge 
eg (y \mathrel{R} x)  igr) , \ 	ext{not antisymmetric:} \quad & \exists x \in X \ \exists y \in X \ \  igl( (x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} x) \wedge x 
e y  igr) , \ 	ext{not transitive:} \quad & \exists x \in X \ \exists y \in X \ \exists z \in X \ \  igl( (x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} z) \wedge 
eg (x \mathrel{R} z)  igr) . \end{aligned} So “not symmetric” is shown by one pair related in one direction only, and “not transitive” by one triple. A single witness settles a failure; a success needs an argument for all elements. Reading a relation as a picture. Draw the elements of X as points and an arrow from x to y whenever x \mathrel{R} y. The relation \le on \{1, 2, 3\} is \{ (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3) \}: Reflexive means a loop at every point. Symmetric means every arrow has a return arrow. Antisymmetric means no two different points are joined in both directions. Transitive means every path of two arrows has a direct arrow from its start to its end. In the picture there are loops everywhere, no return arrows, and the two-arrow path 1 	o 2 	o 3 has its shortcut 1 	o 3; so \le on \{1, 2, 3\} is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, and not symmetric, with witness the pair (1, 2). A path may also return to its start: x 	o y 	o x. Transitivity then demands the loop at x. That case is the source of the warning below. Why “reflexive on X”. The other three properties mention elements only when they are related, so they depend on the set R alone. Reflexivity depends on X too. The relation \{(0, 0)\} is reflexive on \{0\}, and the same set of pairs, viewed as a relation on \{0, 1\}, is not reflexive on \{0, 1\}, with witness 1. That is why the definition names the set. Prove or disprove, property by property A relation given by a formula has each property or not, and nothing tells us in advance which. So the first step is to test small elements and guess; the second is a proof if the guess is “yes”, and a witness, checked clause by clause, if it is “no”. [Deciding four properties] On 
Z, let x \mathrel{R} y mean 7 \mid 3x + 4y. Decide which of the four properties of @def-relation-properties R has. [Scratch work] Test small elements first. 1 \mathrel{R} 1, since 3 + 4 = 7. Also 0 \mathrel{R} 7 (0 + 28 = 28) and 7 \mathrel{R} 0 (21 + 0 = 21), with 0 
e 7: antisymmetry fails, and the pair 0, 7 is the witness. Reflexivity looks true in general: 3x + 4x = 7x. [B2: Example generation] Give an example of a relation on \{1, 2, 3\} that is reflexive and transitive, but neither symmetric nor antisymmetric. Check each property. Then list the properties that every correct answer must have. One answer: R = \{ (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 3), (2, 3) \} . Reflexive: the three loops are in R. Not symmetric: 1 \mathrel{R} 3 and not 3 \mathrel{R} 1. Not antisymmetric: 1 \mathrel{R} 2, 2 \mathrel{R} 1 and 1 
e 2. Transitive: we check every two-step path x \mathrel{R} y \mathrel{R} z with x 
e y and y 
e z (a step along a loop changes nothing). They are 1 	o 2 	o 1, 1 	o 2 	o 3, 2 	o 1 	o 2 and 2 	o 1 	o 3, and their shortcuts (1, 1), (1, 3), (2, 2), (2, 3) are all in R. Element 3 has no arrow out except its loop, so no other path exists. Every correct answer must: - contain the three pairs (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3); - contain two different elements related both ways (to fail antisymmetry); - contain a pair related one way only (to fail symmetry); - contain the shortcut of every two-arrow path. The second and fourth items together force more: if a \mathrel{R} b, b \mathrel{R} a and b \mathrel{R} c, transitivity puts a \mathrel{R} c in. First, there is only one two-way pair: two of them, say \{a, b\} and \{b, c\}, give a \mathrel{R} c and c \mathrel{R} a by transitivity, so R is the full relation, which is symmetric. Call the two-way pair \{a, b\} and the third element c. Every arrow between a and b is two-way, so a one-way arrow must have c at one end, and one such arrow is never enough: transitivity relates c to the other element of the pair too, in the same direction. For example, \{(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 1), (3, 1)\} fails transitivity, since 3 \mathrel{R} 1 \mathrel{R} 2 and not 3 \mathrel{R} 2. If c \mathrel{R} a, then c \mathrel{R} a \mathrel{R} b gives c \mathrel{R} b, and neither a \mathrel{R} c nor b \mathrel{R} c can hold, since that would make a second two-way pair; so both arrows point out of c. Likewise a \mathrel{R} c forces b \mathrel{R} c, and both arrows point into c. Conversely, each of these six relations is a correct answer. Those with c above the pair are the answer above with the elements renamed. Those with c below are obtained from them by reversing every arrow, which keeps the loops, the two-way pair and the one-way arrows, and keeps transitivity: a path z 	o y 	o x of the reversed relation is the reverse of a path x 	o y 	o z, and the reverse of its shortcut (x, z) is (z, x). So \{1, 2, 3\} carries exactly six correct answers: one for each choice of the two-way pair (three choices) and of whether the third element lies above the pair or below it (two choices); the answer above has 3 above the pair \{1, 2\}. [B3: Intersections and unions] Let R and S be transitive relations on a set X. Prove that R \cap S is transitive. Show by an example on \{1, 2, 3\} that R \cup S need not be transitive. Let x, y, z \in X with (x, y) \in R \cap S and (y, z) \in R \cap S. Then (x, y), (y, z) \in R, so (x, z) \in R because R is transitive; likewise (x, z) \in S. Hence (x, z) \in R \cap S. For the union, let R = \{(1, 2)\} and S = \{(2, 3)\}. Each is transitive, vacuously: in R a two-step path would need a pair starting at 2, and there is none; in S one would need a pair ending at 2. But R \cup S = \{ (1, 2), (2, 3) \} contains (1, 2) and (2, 3) and not (1, 3), so it is not transitive. The intersection keeps both relations’ shortcuts; the union creates paths that neither relation contains, so neither supplies their shortcuts. [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove or disprove each statement. Here R and S are relations on a set X, and R^{-1} is the inverse relation (@def-relation). 1. If R is reflexive on X and transitive, then R \cap R^{-1} is an equivalence relation on X (reflexive on X, symmetric and transitive). 2. If R and S are symmetric, then R \cup S is symmetric. 3. If R and S are antisymmetric, then R \cup S is antisymmetric. 4. If R is transitive, then R^{-1} is transitive. 5. On 
N, the relation “x + y is a multiple of 3” is transitive. (a) True. Write E \coloneqq R \cap R^{-1}; so (x, y) \in E means x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x. Reflexive. For x \in X, x \mathrel{R} x by reflexivity, so (x, x) \in E. Symmetric. The definition of E is symmetric in x and y. Transitive. Let (x, y), (y, z) \in E. From x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} z, transitivity gives x \mathrel{R} z; from z \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x, it gives z \mathrel{R} x. So (x, z) \in E. (b) True. If (x, y) \in R \cup S, say (x, y) \in R, then (y, x) \in R by symmetry of R, so (y, x) \in R \cup S; likewise if (x, y) \in S. (c) False. On X = \{1, 2\}, R = \{(1, 2)\} and S = \{(2, 1)\} are antisymmetric (vacuously: neither relates two elements both ways), but R \cup S contains (1, 2) and (2, 1), and 1 
e 2. (d) True. Let x \mathrel{R^{-1}} y and y \mathrel{R^{-1}} z, that is, y \mathrel{R} x and z \mathrel{R} y. By transitivity of R, from z \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x, z \mathrel{R} x, that is, x \mathrel{R^{-1}} z. (e) False. Take x = 1, y = 2, z = 1: 1 + 2 = 3 and 2 + 1 = 3 are multiples of 3, but 1 + 1 = 2 is not: 2 = 3k fails for every integer k, since k \le 0 gives 3k \le 0, and k > 0 gives k \ge 1 by @prp-integers-closed (c), hence 3k \ge 3. (A triple with x = z is allowed: transitivity quantifies over all x, y, z.) C. Going deeper [C1: Properties as equations between sets] Let R be a relation on X, let R^{-1} be its inverse relation (@def-relation), and let \Delta_X \coloneqq \{ (x, x) : x \in X \} be the diagonal. 1. Prove that R is symmetric if and only if R = R^{-1}, and that R is antisymmetric if and only if R \cap R^{-1} \subseteq \Delta_X. 2. Deduce that a relation that is both symmetric and antisymmetric satisfies R \subseteq \Delta_X. Is every subset of \Delta_X both symmetric and antisymmetric? Recall that (x, y) \in R^{-1} if and only if (y, x) \in R. (a) Symmetric. (\Rightarrow) Let R be symmetric. If (x, y) \in R, then (y, x) \in R, that is, (x, y) \in R^{-1}; so R \subseteq R^{-1}. If (x, y) \in R^{-1}, then (y, x) \in R, so (x, y) \in R by symmetry; so R^{-1} \subseteq R. By @prp-subset-antisymmetric, R = R^{-1}. (\Leftarrow) If R = R^{-1} and x \mathrel{R} y, then (x, y) \in R^{-1}, so (y, x) \in R. Antisymmetric. A pair (x, y) lies in R \cap R^{-1} exactly when x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x, and it lies in \Delta_X exactly when x = y (by the characteristic property of pairs, @def-ordered-pair). So “R \cap R^{-1} \subseteq \Delta_X” says: for all x, y \in X, if x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x, then x = y. That is antisymmetry, word for word. (b) If R is symmetric and antisymmetric, then by (a), R = R \cap R = R \cap R^{-1} \subseteq \Delta_X. Conversely, every R \subseteq \Delta_X is symmetric (each of its pairs is (x, x), which is its own reverse) and antisymmetric (x \mathrel{R} y already forces x = y). So the relations with both properties are exactly the subsets of the diagonal; equality, \Delta_X itself, is the largest of them, and \emptyset the smallest. [C2: What symmetry and transitivity do give] Let R be a symmetric and transitive relation on X, and let D \coloneqq \{ x \in X : \exists y \in X \ \ x \mathrel{R} y \} be its domain. Prove that R \subseteq D 	imes D and that R, as a relation on D, is reflexive on D, symmetric and transitive. R \subseteq D 	imes D. Let (x, y) \in R. Then x \in D, with witness y. By symmetry y \mathrel{R} x, so y \in D, with witness x. Hence (x, y) \in D 	imes D. Reflexive on D. Let x \in D. By the definition of D there is y \in X with x \mathrel{R} y; fix one (an ulename{\exists E}, legitimate now, because x \in D is exactly the statement \exists y \in X \ x \mathrel{R} y). By symmetry y \mathrel{R} x, and by transitivity, from x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x, x \mathrel{R} x. Symmetric and transitive on D. These are implications about related elements, and every related pair lies in D 	imes D; so they hold on D because they hold on X. This is the correct version of the false theorem in the warning: its argument proves reflexivity exactly on the set of elements for which “take y with x \mathrel{R} y” is available. Elements outside D are related to nothing, and there reflexivity fails. In the language of Section 4.2, R is an equivalence relation on D. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: shows R \subseteq D 	imes D, using symmetry to put the second coordinate in D. - 4: for reflexivity on D, obtains y with x \mathrel{R} y from x \in D, and says why this step is now legitimate. - 2: applies symmetry and then transitivity, in that order, to get x \mathrel{R} x. - 2: explains why symmetry and transitivity restrict to D. Fatal errors (0 for the step): taking y with x \mathrel{R} y for an arbitrary x \in X rather than x \in D (the error of the warning); applying transitivity to x \mathrel{R} y and x \mathrel{R} y.

title: 4.2 Equivalence Relations and Partitions
content:
Equivalence Relations and Partitions Section 4.1 sorted relations by four properties: reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive (@def-relation-properties). This section studies the relations that have the first, second and fourth. They are the relations that say two things are “the same” in some respect, and each of them cuts its set into disjoint pieces of mutually “same” elements. We prove that the pieces always form a partition, and that every partition arises from exactly one such relation. Then we build the integers modulo n, and meet the check that every definition on pieces needs: that it does not depend on which element names the piece. Section 1.5 promised that check for functions defined on classes; here it is, with a method for making it. Arithmetic on a clock On a twelve-hour clock, five hours after nine o’clock it is two o’clock. People say “9 + 5 = 2 on a clock”, and nobody is confused. Read as a statement about integers, it is false: 9 + 5 = 14. So what is it a statement about? The clock does not distinguish 2 from 14, or from 26 or -10: all of them put the hand in the same place. Two integers name the same hour when they differ by a multiple of 12. The sentence “9 + 5 = 2” is then about hours, and an hour is not one integer but a whole collection of them, \{ \dots, -10, 2, 14, 26, \dots \}. The addition adds collections: take any integer from the first, any from the second, add them, and see which collection the sum lands in. Two things have to be checked before this is mathematics. First, “differ by a multiple of 12” must behave like “is the same as”: it must cut the integers into separate collections, and no integer may land in two of them. Second, the answer must not depend on the choice: if we take 21 for “nine” and -7 for “five”, the sum 14 must still name two o’clock. It does, since 21 + (-7) = 14. The first check is the theory of equivalence relations and partitions. The second is called well-definedness, and it comes at the end of the section. Equivalence relations Equality has three properties that every argument with “=” uses silently: x = x; if x = y, then y = x; and if x = y and y = z, then x = z (@fd1:prp-equality-symmetric-transitive). They are exactly what lets us replace a thing by an equal thing, as often as we like, in either direction. “Same hour on the clock”, “same remainder on division by 3” and “same absolute value” all have the same three properties, although none of them is equality. They deserve a common name. An equivalence relation declares things the same in a way that behaves like equality. [Equivalence Relation] Let X be a set. An equivalence relation on X is a relation \sim on X (@def-relation) that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive on X (@def-relation-properties): 1. for every x \in X, x \sim x; 2. for all x, y \in X, if x \sim y, then y \sim x; 3. for all x, y, z \in X, if x \sim y and y \sim z, then x \sim z. When x \sim y, we say that x is equivalent to y (under \sim). In words: (Eq1) says everything is the same as itself. (Eq2) says “the same” has no direction: if x counts as the same as y, then y counts as the same as x. (Eq3) says sameness passes along a chain: two things that are each the same as a third are linked through it. Then 1 \sim 2 with P = \{1, 2\}, and 2 \sim 3 through \{2, 3\}; line (3) concludes 3 \in \{1, 2\}, which is false, and the argument “proves” 1 \sim 3, although no set of the cover contains 1 and 3. e \emptyset, and P = Q by (P2). Hence x \in P and z \in P, so x \sim z.”

title: 4.3 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content:
Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements Section 4.2 studied the relations that behave like equality. This section studies the ones that behave like \le: reflexive and transitive like an equivalence relation, but antisymmetric instead of symmetric, so that they have a direction. For numbers, “the largest element of a set” is clear. For sets under \subseteq, or for natural numbers under divisibility, two elements can be incomparable, neither below the other, and “largest” splits into two different notions. We separate them, prove what links them, and then take a first look at least upper bounds. That is the vocabulary Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 needs for the supremum. Partial orders Section 4.1 found three relations with the same three properties: \le on 
R, \subseteq on \powerset{X} (@exm-relation-table), and \mid on 
N (@prp-divides-partial-order). Each is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. Each says “below” in its own sense: smaller, contained in, a divisor of. What they share is what “being below” needs, and it deserves a name, so that a fact proved once holds for all three. A partial order says which elements lie below which, without requiring every two to be comparable. [Partial Order] Let X be a set. A partial order on X is a relation \preceq on X that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive on X (@def-relation-properties): 1. for every x \in X, x \preceq x; 2. for all x, y \in X, if x \preceq y and y \preceq x, then x = y; 3. for all x, y, z \in X, if x \preceq y and y \preceq z, then x \preceq z. The pair (X, \preceq) is a partially ordered set. Elements x, y \in X are comparable if x \preceq y or y \preceq x. The partial order is total if every two elements of X are comparable. The strict part of \preceq is the relation \prec on X given by x \prec y \iff x \preceq y \ 	ext{ and } \ x 
e y . We also write y \succeq x for x \preceq y. In words: (PO1) everything is below itself. (PO2) is the clause that gives an order its direction: two elements below each other are the same element, so “below” cannot run both ways between different things. (PO3) lets “below” pass along a chain. “Total” adds that any two elements can be compared; “partial” is the word for not requiring it. The symbol \preceq is a letter for an arbitrary partial order, chosen so that \le keeps its meaning on numbers. The strict part is irreflexive and transitive. No x has x \prec x, since that would need x 
e x. If x \prec y and y \prec z, then x \preceq z by (PO3); and x 
e z, because x = z would give x \preceq y and y \preceq x, hence x = y by (PO2), contradicting x 
e y. So x \prec z. Examples. - (
R, \le) is a partially ordered set, and it is total: for real numbers x \le y or y \le x. Its strict part is <. The same holds for (
N, \le) and (
Z, \le), since restricting a total order to a subset keeps all four properties: each is a statement about all elements, and holds in particular for the elements of the subset. - (
N, \mid) is a partially ordered set by @prp-divides-partial-order, and it is not total: 2 
mid 3 and 3 
mid 2, so 2 and 3 are incomparable. - (\powerset{X}, \subseteq) is a partially ordered set; the example after this list decides when it is total. - Degenerate cases: equality on any set X is a partial order, in which no two different elements are comparable; and the empty relation is a partial order on \emptyset, vacuously. Non-examples by minimal change. Divisibility on 
Z is reflexive and transitive, but not antisymmetric: 2 \mid -2 and -2 \mid 2, and 2 
e -2 (@prp-divides-partial-order). Passing from 
N to 
Z loses exactly (PO2). The relation < on 
R is antisymmetric (vacuously: x < y and y < x never both hold) and transitive, but not reflexive, since 0 < 0 fails. It is the strict part of \le, not a partial order. Why these clauses. Without (PO2), two different elements could each be below the other, and “the largest element” of a set could fail to be unique; the uniqueness proof in the next subsection uses (PO2) and nothing else. A relation that keeps (PO1) and (PO3) and drops (PO2) is often called a preorder; \mid on 
Z is one. Totality is left out because the important examples, \subseteq and \mid, do not have it, and much of the interest lies in what changes without it. [Inclusion is a partial order, rarely total] Let X be a set. Show that \subseteq is a partial order on \powerset{X}, and that it is total if and only if X has at most one element. A partial order. (PO1) A \subseteq A for every set A. (PO2) If A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A, then A = B by @prp-subset-antisymmetric. (PO3) is @prp-subset-transitive. (These are the entries of @exm-relation-table.) Total exactly when X has at most one element. Suppose X has two different elements a 
e b. Then \{a\}, \{b\} \in \powerset{X}, and \{a\} 
ot\subseteq \{b\}, since a \in \{a\} and a 
otin \{b\}; likewise \{b\} 
ot\subseteq \{a\}. So \{a\} and \{b\} are incomparable, and \subseteq is not total. For X = \{1, 2\}, the incomparable pair is \{1\}, \{2\}. Conversely, suppose any two elements of X are equal. Let A \subseteq X. If A 
e \emptyset, take a \in A; then every x \in X equals a, so x \in A, and A = X. So every subset of X is \emptyset or X. Any two of these are comparable, since \emptyset \subseteq X (Section 1.2, after @prp-empty-set-unique) and each is a subset of itself. So \subseteq is total on \powerset{X}. In a partial order, “x \preceq y fails” does not give “y \prec x”. In (\powerset{\{1, 2\}}, \subseteq), \{1\} 
ot\subseteq \{2\}, and \{2\} \subsetneq \{1\} is false too: the two are incomparable. The habit from numbers, “not \le means >”, is the totality of \le on 
R, and it must not be carried into a partial order. Bounds, greatest and maximal elements From now on, (X, \preceq) is a partially ordered set and A \subseteq X. The bounds come first, because both kinds of “largest” are measured against them. [Upper and Lower Bounds] An element u \in X is an upper bound of A if a \preceq u for every a \in A, and a lower bound of A if u \preceq a for every a \in A. The set A is bounded above if it has an upper bound in X, bounded below if it has a lower bound in X, and bounded if both. An upper bound lives in X and need not belong to A: in (
R, \le), 5 is an upper bound of [0, 1]. Every element of X is an upper bound of \emptyset, vacuously. In (
N, \mid), an upper bound of \{4, 6\} is a common multiple of 4 and 6, such as 12, 24 or 0. Now the two notions of “largest”. The first is the familiar one: an element of the set that is above everything in the set. The second asks less: an element with nothing in the set strictly above it. [Greatest and Least Elements] An element g is a greatest element of A if g \in A and a \preceq g for every a \in A. An element l is a least element of A if l \in A and l \preceq a for every a \in A. [Maximal and Minimal Elements] An element m is a maximal element of A if m \in A and there is no a \in A with m \prec a. An element m is a minimal element of A if m \in A and there is no a \in A with a \prec m. In words: a greatest element is an upper bound of A that belongs to A. A maximal element is one that cannot be beaten inside A, which is weaker: an element can be unbeaten simply because it is incomparable with its rivals. In symbols the difference is where the negation sits:  egin{aligned} g 	ext{ greatest:} &\quad g \in A \wedge  orall a \in A \ \, a \preceq g , \ m 	ext{ maximal:} &\quad m \in A \wedge 
eg \exists a \in A \ \, m \prec a . \end{aligned} By @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (b), 
eg \exists a \in A \ \, m \prec a is  orall a \in A \ \, 
eg (m \prec a), and 
eg (m \prec a) says that m \preceq a implies m = a. So “maximal” reads: everything in A that is above m is m. “Greatest” reads: everything in A is below g. The first only forbids elements above; the second demands that every element be compared. For numbers the two coincide. In (
R, \le), the set \{1, 4, 9\} has greatest element 9, its only maximal element, and least element 1. The interval [0, 1) has least element 0 and neither a greatest nor a maximal element: for each a \in [0, 1), the number (a + 1)/2 lies in [0, 1) and is strictly above a. A one-point set \{x\} has x as greatest, least, maximal and minimal element, and \emptyset has none of the four, since each definition requires an element of A. The first result explains the article in “the greatest element”. [Greatest and Least Elements Are Unique] A subset A of a partially ordered set has at most one greatest element and at most one least element. The method of @exm-method-uniqueness, uniqueness half: take two greatest elements, about which nothing else is assumed. Each is in A, so each is below the other, and (PO2) closes the gap. Let g and g' be greatest elements of A. Since g' \in A and g is greatest, g' \preceq g; since g \in A and g' is greatest, g \preceq g'. By (PO2), g = g'. For least elements the same argument applies with the inequalities reversed. So we may speak of the greatest element and the least element of A when they exist. In (
R, \le), the greatest element of a set is its maximum, \max A, and the least element its minimum, \min A. This settles a point left open in Section 1.5: the least q_0 \in 
Z_{>0} with r q_0 \in 
Z in @exm-not-a-function exists by @thm-well-ordering: the set of such q lies in 
Z_{>0} \subseteq 
N, and it is non-empty, since writing r = p/q with q \in 
Z_{>0} (as the solution of (b) there notes) gives rq = p \in 
Z. It is unique by the least-element half of the proposition, so the rule there names one value. Divisibility on 
Z is reflexive and transitive but not antisymmetric, so it is not a partial order. Read the formula of @def-greatest-element in (
Z, \mid) anyway, and run the proof of @prp-greatest-unique for A = \{2, -2\}: which elements of A satisfy the formula, and which line of the proof fails? Both: 2 \mid 2, -2 \mid 2 (2 = (-1)(-2)), 2 \mid -2 and -2 \mid -2. Every line of the proof goes through except the last, “By (PO2), g = g'”: 2 \mid -2 and -2 \mid 2, yet 2 
e -2. The second result compares the two notions. [Greatest and Maximal Elements] Let (X, \preceq) be a partially ordered set and A \subseteq X. 1. A greatest element of A is a maximal element of A. 2. If \preceq is total, then a maximal element of A is a greatest element of A. The same holds for least and minimal elements. For (a), anything strictly above the greatest element would also be below it, and antisymmetry forbids that. For (b), a maximal element m must be compared with each a \in A, and totality says it can be: either a \preceq m, as wanted, or m \preceq a, and then maximality forces a = m. Part (a) proves a negative claim, “no element strictly above”, so it starts by supposing one (@exm-method-choosing-the-form); part (b) is a proof by cases on the two outcomes of comparability (@exm-method-cases). (a) Let g be a greatest element of A. Then g \in A. Suppose some a \in A has g \prec a, so g \preceq a and g 
e a. Since g is greatest, a \preceq g. By (PO2), a = g, contradicting g 
e a. So no such a exists, and g is maximal. (b) Let \preceq be total and m a maximal element of A, and let a \in A. By totality, a \preceq m or m \preceq a. Case 1: a \preceq m. This is what we want. Case 2: m \preceq a. If m 
e a, then m \prec a with a \in A, which maximality excludes. So m = a, and a \preceq m by (PO1). In either case a \preceq m. Since a \in A was arbitrary and m \in A, m is a greatest element. For least and minimal elements, apply (a) and (b) to the partial order \succeq: its greatest and maximal elements are the least and minimal elements for \preceq, and it is total when \preceq is. (That \succeq satisfies (PO1)–(PO3), and is total when \preceq is, comes from reading those clauses with the two variables exchanged. Its strict part is x \succ y \iff y \prec x, since x 
e y is symmetric in x and y. So “no a \in A with m \succ a” is “no a \in A with a \prec m”, and “a \succeq l for every a \in A” is “l \preceq a for every a \in A”.) Part (b) uses totality once, in the case split of its second sentence, and the case split is where it fails without it. The proof of @prp-finite-max in Section 2.3 compares two elements at a time and keeps the larger. Its maximum half uses nothing about \le on 
R beyond reflexivity, transitivity and the comparability of any two elements, so it works word for word in any totally ordered set. The minimum half passes to -x_1, \dots, -x_n, which needs an ordered field; in a totally ordered set, apply the maximum half to the reverse order \succeq instead, which is total by the last paragraph of the proof above. In particular the whole proposition holds in any ordered field, which is how Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 reads it. Without totality, (b) fails, and maximal elements need not be greatest. Each failure is shown by a counterexample (@exm-method-counterexample). [Maximal elements that are not greatest] Find the maximal elements of each set, and decide whether it has a greatest element: (a) A = \{2, 3, 4, 5, 6\} in (
N, \mid); (b) \sB = \{ \{1\}, \{2\} \} in (\powerset{\{1, 2\}}, \subseteq). (a) Within A, the only strict divisibilities are 2 \mid 4, 2 \mid 6 and 3 \mid 6. So 2 \prec 4 and 3 \prec 6, and 2, 3 are not maximal. Nothing in A is strictly above 4, 5 or 6: every element of A is positive, and a positive multiple k n of n \in \{4, 5, 6\} other than n has k > 0 and k 
e 1, so k \ge 2 (@prp-integers-closed (c)), and then k n \ge 2n \ge 8, while every element of A is at most 6. So the maximal elements are 4, 5 and 6. There is no greatest element. By @prp-greatest-maximal (a), a greatest element would be maximal, so it would be 4, 5 or 6. But 5 
mid 4, 4 
mid 5 and 4 
mid 6, so none of the three is above every element of A. (b) \{1\} and \{2\} are incomparable (@exm-subset-order-not-total), so neither is strictly above the other: both are maximal. Neither is greatest, since neither contains the other. In (a), the minimal elements are 2, 3 and 5, and there is no least element either. The example is the minimal change from \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}, which has the least element 1 and still no greatest. “Maximal” is not “greatest”. A set can have many maximal elements and no greatest, as in @exm-maximal-not-greatest; and a set can have no maximal element at all: 
N under \le, where n + 1 \in 
N (by (
NS)) is strictly above n. The answer also depends on the order, not just on the set: under divisibility, 
N has a greatest element, 0, since every a \in 
N divides 0 = 0 \cdot a. In \powerset{\{1, 2, 3\}} \setminus \{ \{1, 2, 3\} \}, ordered by \subseteq, name the maximal elements. Is there a greatest element? The maximal elements are the three two-element sets \{1, 2\}, \{1, 3\}, \{2, 3\}: the only subset of \{1, 2, 3\} strictly containing a two-element set is \{1, 2, 3\}, which was removed, and every set with at most one element lies strictly inside some two-element set. There is no greatest element: it would be maximal (@prp-greatest-maximal (a)), hence a two-element set, and no two-element set contains the other two. Least upper bounds, a first look Here is the notion that the rest of the book is built on. When a set has no greatest element, its upper bounds may still have a least one, and that element plays the part of “the top of the set” from outside. The supremum is the best upper bound: the least element of the set of upper bounds. [Supremum and Infimum] Let (X, \preceq) be a partially ordered set and A \subseteq X. An element s \in X is a least upper bound, or supremum, of A in X if 1. s is an upper bound of A, and 2. s \preceq u for every upper bound u of A. An element i \in X is a greatest lower bound, or infimum, of A in X if i is a lower bound of A and u \preceq i for every lower bound u of A. In other words, a supremum of A is a least element of the set of upper bounds of A, and an infimum a greatest element of the set of lower bounds. By @prp-greatest-unique, applied to those sets, each is unique when it exists, and we write \sup A and \inf A. The words “in X” matter: the upper bounds are taken in X, and enlarging or shrinking X can create or destroy a supremum. The definition also carries no promise that \sup A exists, or that it belongs to A. Two quick consequences. If A has a greatest element g, then g = \sup A: g is an upper bound, and every upper bound u has g \preceq u because g \in A. And a supremum that belongs to A is a greatest element of A, by (S1). So a supremum is a greatest element exactly when it lies in the set; the new cases are the ones where it lies outside. Suprema of sets. In (\powerset{X}, \subseteq), let A, B \subseteq X. Then \sup \{A, B\} = A \cup B. (S1): A \subseteq A \cup B and B \subseteq A \cup B, and A \cup B \in \powerset{X}. (S2): let C \in \powerset{X} be an upper bound, so A \subseteq C and B \subseteq C; every element of A \cup B lies in A or in B, hence in C, so A \cup B \subseteq C. The supremum A \cup B belongs to \{A, B\} only when one of the two sets contains the other; for \{ \{1\}, \{2\} \} it is \{1, 2\}, which is not in the set. Exercise B1 extends this to every family of subsets, and adds the infimum. Suprema under divisibility. In (
N, \mid), an upper bound of \{a, b\} is a common multiple of a and b. The least upper bound turns out to be the least common multiple, and proving that it is least in the divisibility order, not merely the smallest number, is a job for the division algorithm and for the least-element method (@exm-method-least-element): the least common multiple is a least element, and a smaller common multiple would contradict it. [The supremum under divisibility is the least common multiple] Let a, b \in 
N. Find \sup \{a, b\} in (
N, \mid). Deduce that an integer divisible by 2 and by 3 is divisible by 6. Case a, b \in 
Z_{>0}. Let M \coloneqq \{ m \in 
Z_{>0} : a \mid m 	ext{ and } b \mid m \}, the positive common multiples. It is non-empty: ab \in 
N by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (b), ab > 0 as a product of positive numbers, so ab \in 
Z_{>0} (@prp-integers-closed (b)), and ab = b \cdot a = a \cdot b is a multiple of both. Since M \subseteq 
Z_{>0} \subseteq 
N, M has a least element L (@thm-well-ordering), the least common multiple of a and b. We show that L divides every integer common multiple c of a and b. By @thm-division-algorithm, c = qL + r with q, r \in 
Z and 0 \le r < L. Write c = as, L = at with s, t \in 
Z; then r = c - qL = a(s - qt) with s - qt \in 
Z (@prp-integers-closed (a)), so a \mid r, and in the same way b \mid r. If r > 0, then r \in 
Z_{>0} (@prp-integers-closed (b)), so r \in M and r < L, contradicting the choice of L. Hence r = 0, and c = qL: L \mid c. The argument never used c \ge 0. Now L = \sup \{a, b\}. (S1): a \mid L and b \mid L, since L \in M. (S2): an upper bound c \in 
N of \{a, b\} is a common multiple, so L \mid c by the previous paragraph. Case a = 0 or b = 0. Say a = 0. An upper bound c has 0 \mid c, that is, c = k \cdot 0 = 0 for some k \in 
Z. And 0 is an upper bound, since n \mid 0 = 0 \cdot n for every n \in 
N. So 0 is the only upper bound, and \sup \{a, b\} = 0, the greatest element of (
N, \mid). The instance. For a = 2, b = 3: 6 \in M, and none of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 is a multiple of both 2 and 3 (1, 3, 5 are odd, and 2, 4 lie strictly between consecutive multiples of 3). So L = 6, and every integer n with 2 \mid n and 3 \mid n has 6 \mid n, by the second paragraph with c = n. The instance gives a second proof, through the least common multiple, of the fact that Section 1.3 used as a school fact and Section 2.2 proved in Exercise B3 (c) (@exr-induction-in-practice-b3): an integer divisible by 2 and by 3 is divisible by 6. It also shows the two orders on 
N disagreeing: \sup \{4, 6\} is 12 under divisibility and 6 under \le. A supremum that does not exist. In (
Q, \le), the set \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \} is non-empty and bounded above (by 2, for instance: a rational x > 2 has x^2 > 4). It has no least upper bound in 
Q. We do not prove this here. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves it, and then takes the existence of suprema in 
R as its axiom: the supremum of Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1, defined in an ordered field, is @def-order-supremum for the order \le of that field; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 uses it in 
Q and in 
R. The ambient set decides: the same set has a supremum in (
R, \le), namely \sqrt 2. Well-ordered sets Section 2.1 proved that every non-empty subset of 
N has a least element (@thm-well-ordering). In the language of this section, that is a property of the partially ordered set (
N, \le), and it has a name. [Well-Ordered Set] A partially ordered set (X, \preceq) is well-ordered, and \preceq is a well-order on X, if \preceq is total and every non-empty subset of X has a least element. (
N, \le) is well-ordered: \le is total, and @thm-well-ordering supplies the least elements. (
Z, \le) is not: 
Z itself has no least element, since for every n \in 
Z also n - 1 \in 
Z (@prp-integers-closed (a)) and n - 1 < n. Nor is the set of positive rationals, which has no least element (q/2 < q). The word “non-empty” is needed because \emptyset has no least element in any order. Totality is in fact automatic: any two elements x, y form a non-empty set \{x, y\}, whose least element is below the other one. Upper bounds work too: in (
N, \le) a non-empty set bounded above has a greatest element (@cor-well-ordering-integers). Exercise C1 gives a well-ordered set that does not look like 
N. In a general partially ordered set, one may ask: if every chain (a subset on which \preceq is total) has an upper bound, must there be a maximal element? For a non-empty partially ordered set the answer “yes” is Zorn’s lemma, and it cannot be proved from what we have: it is equivalent to the axiom of choice, which Section 3.2 states (@ax-choice). Chapter 6 states Zorn’s lemma and uses it, and Axiomatic Set Theory, Chapter 4 proves it equivalent to the axiom of choice, together with the other equivalents, among them the claim that every set has a well-order. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Let (X, \preceq) be a partially ordered set and A \subseteq X. Write “g is a greatest element of A” and “m is a maximal element of A” in symbols, and negate each. 2. True or false, with a witness: every finite non-empty subset of a partially ordered set has a greatest element. 3. Find \sup \{4, 6\} in (
N, \mid) and in (
N, \le). 4. On 
N 	imes 
N, the lexicographic order is (a, b) \preceq (c, d) if a < c, or a = c and b \le d. Given that it is a partial order, is it total? (a) g greatest: g \in A \wedge  orall a \in A \ \, a \preceq g. Its negation, by @fd1:prp-de-morgan and @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a): g 
otin A \vee \exists a \in A \ \, 
eg (a \preceq g). m maximal: m \in A \wedge 
eg \exists a \in A \ \, m \prec a. Its negation: m 
otin A \vee \exists a \in A \ \, m \prec a, by @fd1:prp-de-morgan and @fd1:prp-double-negation. In words: g fails to be greatest if some element of A is not below it; m fails to be maximal if some element of A is strictly above it. The first failure can happen through incomparability; the second cannot. (b) False. In (\powerset{\{1, 2\}}, \subseteq), the set \{ \{1\}, \{2\} \} is finite and non-empty and has no greatest element (@exm-maximal-not-greatest (b)). What is true is that it has a maximal element: it can be listed as \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}, which is what “finite” means (@def-finite, Section 2.5), so it has one by Exercise R4. (c) Under divisibility, \sup \{4, 6\} = 12, the least common multiple (@exm-divisibility-lcm): 12 is a common multiple, and none of 1, \dots, 11 is (the positive multiples of 6 below 12 are just 6, and 4 
mid 6). Under \le, \sup \{4, 6\} = 6, the greatest element. (d) Yes. Let (a, b), (c, d) \in 
N 	imes 
N. If a < c, then (a, b) \preceq (c, d); if c < a, then (c, d) \preceq (a, b); if a = c, then b \le d or d \le b, by totality of \le, and the pairs are comparable. By trichotomy these cases cover everything. B. Practice [B1: Suprema of families of sets] Let X be a set and (A_i)_{i \in I} a family of subsets of X. In (\powerset{X}, \subseteq), prove that the set \{ A_i : i \in I \} has supremum  igcup_{i \in I} A_i and infimum  igcap_{i \in I} A_i, the intersection taken in X. What are they when I = \emptyset? Write U \coloneqq  igcup_{i \in I} A_i and N \coloneqq  igcap_{i \in I} A_i (@def-family-union-intersection). Both are subsets of X, so they lie in \powerset{X}. Supremum. (S1) For each i \in I, every element of A_i lies in U, so A_i \subseteq U. (S2) Let C \in \powerset{X} be an upper bound: A_i \subseteq C for every i \in I. Let x \in U. Then x \in A_i for some i \in I; name it i. Since A_i \subseteq C, x \in C. So U \subseteq C. Infimum. N is a lower bound: for each i \in I, every x \in N lies in A_i, so N \subseteq A_i. Let D \in \powerset{X} be a lower bound: D \subseteq A_i for every i. Let x \in D. Then x \in X, and x \in A_i for every i \in I, so x \in N. Hence D \subseteq N. Empty index set. If I = \emptyset, then U = \emptyset and N = X, since an intersection in X of no sets is X. This agrees with the definitions: every element of \powerset{X} is an upper bound of the empty set, and the least of them is \emptyset; every element is a lower bound, and the greatest is X. The arguments above cover this case, since their “for every i” clauses hold vacuously. [B2: Two maximal elements and a least one] Give an example of a partially ordered set that has exactly two maximal elements and a least element, and check each property. Then list the properties that every answer must have. An example. X = \{ \emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\} \} ordered by \subseteq. It is a partial order, as a subset of (\powerset{\{1, 2\}}, \subseteq). The least element is \emptyset, since \emptyset \subseteq A for every A \in X (Section 1.2, after @prp-empty-set-unique). The maximal elements are \{1\} and \{2\}: neither is strictly contained in an element of X. And \emptyset is not maximal, since \emptyset \subsetneq \{1\}. So there are exactly two. Another answer: \{1, 2, 3\} under divisibility, with least element 1 and maximal elements 2, 3. What every answer must have. Let l be the least element and m_1 
e m_2 the maximal elements. - m_1 and m_2 are incomparable: if m_1 \preceq m_2, then m_1 \prec m_2, since m_1 
e m_2, and m_1 would not be maximal; symmetrically for m_2 \preceq m_1. - So the order is not total, and there is no greatest element: a greatest element g would have m_1 \preceq g, and maximality of m_1 gives m_1 = g; likewise m_2 = g, contradicting m_1 
e m_2. - l, m_1, m_2 are three different elements: if l = m_1, then m_1 = l \preceq m_2, which the first point excludes; likewise l 
e m_2. So an answer has at least three elements and two incomparable maximal ones above a common least element. A candidate failing any of these is not an answer. [B3: Minimal is least in a total order] Let (X, \preceq) be a totally ordered set and A \subseteq X. Prove that a minimal element of A is a least element of A, by applying @prp-greatest-maximal (b) to the reverse order \succeq. Check each fact about \succeq that you use. The reverse order. \succeq is the relation x \succeq y \iff y \preceq x. (PO1): x \preceq x, so x \succeq x. (PO2): if x \succeq y and y \succeq x, then y \preceq x and x \preceq y, so x = y. (PO3): if x \succeq y and y \succeq z, then z \preceq y and y \preceq x, so z \preceq x, that is, x \succeq z. Totality: for x, y \in X, x \preceq y or y \preceq x, that is, y \succeq x or x \succeq y. Its strict part is x \succ y \iff y \prec x, since x 
e y is symmetric in x, y. Translating. In the order \succeq, “x lies below y” is written x \succeq y, and “strictly below” is x \succ y. Now m is minimal for \preceq: m \in A and no a \in A has a \prec m, that is, no a \in A has m \succ a. That is exactly “m is maximal for \succeq”. Then m is maximal in A for the total order \succeq, so it is greatest for \succeq by @prp-greatest-maximal (b), hence least for \preceq. C. NS), and a < a + 1. For A = \{1, \dots, 5\} the negation holds, with a = 5: every b \in A has b \le 5. [R3] Let X be a countable set and \sim an equivalence relation on X. Prove that X/{\sim} is countable. Give an example with X countable, not finite, and X/{\sim} finite. The quotient map q \colon X 	o X/{\sim}, q(a) = [a], is surjective (@def-quotient-set and the paragraph after it). By @prp-countable-image, the image of a countable set under a function is countable, and here the image is all of X/{\sim}. Example: X =

Z/2 = \{[0], [1]\} (@prp-integers-mod-n) has two elements. [R4] Let (X, \preceq) be a partially ordered set, let n \ge 1 be an integer, and let x_1, \dots, x_n \in X. Show that the set \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} has a maximal element. The tool is induction from base 1 (@thm-induction with n_0 = 1), in the shape of @prp-finite-max: add one element at a time and keep track of a maximal element. Let P(n) say: for all x_1, \dots, x_n \in X, the set \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} has a maximal element. Base. \{x_1\}: no element a of it has x_1 \prec a, since the only candidate is x_1 and x_1 \prec x_1 never holds. So x_1 is maximal. Step. Let n \ge 1, assume P(n), and let x_1, \dots, x_{n+1} \in X. Put A \coloneqq \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} and A' \coloneqq \{x_1, \dots, x_{n+1}\}, where, as in Section 2.3, \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} \coloneqq \{ x_k : k \in \{1, \dots, n\} \}, now for elements of X. Since \{1, \dots, n + 1\} = \{1, \dots, n\} \cup \{n + 1\} (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e), as in the proof of @prp-finite-max), A' = A \cup \{x_{n+1}\}. By P(n), A has a maximal element m. Case 1: m \prec x_{n+1} fails. Then m is maximal in A': m \in A'; no a \in A has m \prec a, by maximality in A; and a = x_{n+1} is excluded by the case. Case 2: m \prec x_{n+1}. Then x_{n+1} is maximal in A'. Suppose x_{n+1} \prec a with a \in A'. Then a 
e x_{n+1}, so a \in A; and m \prec x_{n+1} \prec a gives m \prec a, since the strict part of a partial order is transitive. This contradicts the maximality of m in A. In either case A' has a maximal element, so P(n + 1) holds, and @thm-induction gives P(n) for every n \ge 1. The look-alikes. “Take the greatest element” fails, because a finite set need not have one (@exm-maximal-not-greatest). “Take the largest, as in @prp-finite-max” fails for the same reason: that proof keeps the larger of M and x_{n+1}, which needs the two to be comparable; here Case 1 covers incomparable elements by keeping m. “Take x_n, the last one” confuses the order of the list with the order \preceq: nothing makes x_n large.

title: Building Functions
content:
Building Functions Chapter 1 made a function a set of pairs, and Chapter 4 cut sets into classes. This chapter builds new functions from old ones: cut a function down to a smaller domain, extend it, glue several together, factor it through the quotient by “has the same value”, combine functions by an operation, and apply one function again and again. The motivating problem: shuffle a deck of twelve cards by a fixed rule and repeat the shuffle; must the deck come back to its starting order, and after how many shuffles? The answer is in Section 5.4, and it comes from the orbits of a permutation, which are the classes of an equivalence relation. Along the way, the subsets of a set turn out to be functions with values 0 and 1, and a function turns out to be a quotient map, followed by a bijection between its fibers and its image, followed by an inclusion. Each section teaches one method of proof. Section 5.1 defines a function by pieces and checks that the pieces agree where they overlap. Section 5.2 defines a function on a quotient by a rule on representatives and checks that the rule is constant on classes, which is the well-definedness check of Section 4.2 turned into a theorem.
