Section 5.3 proves that two objects are equal by computing one expression in two ways. Section 5.4 follows a point under repeated application of a map until the sequence repeats. The operations of Section 5.3 and the permutations of Section 5.4 are the first examples of the structures that Algebraic Preliminaries studies, and this chapter proves facts that book can cite. What you need. Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–8, and Sets and Functions, Chapters 1–4 and Section 3.6. From Logic and Proof: induction (@fd1:ax-induction), squares and order (@fd1:thm-squares-order) and the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue). From Chapter 1: equality of sets and subsets (@def-set-equality, @def-subset), the operations on sets, families and the laws of set algebra (@def-set-operations, @def-family-union-intersection, @thm-set-algebra), the method of uniqueness (@exm-method-uniqueness), and divisibility is transitive (@prp-divides-transitive); functions, the empty function, equality of functions and what is not a function (@def-function, @prp-empty-function, @prp-function-equality, @exm-first-functions, @exm-not-a-function); injective, surjective and bijective maps and composition (@def-injective, @def-surjective, @def-bijective, @def-composition, @prp-composition-associative, @thm-composition-injective-surjective); inverses (@def-inverse-function, @prp-inverse-unique, @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, @exr-inverses-b2); images and preimages (@def-image, @def-preimage, @thm-image-union, @thm-image-intersection). From Chapter 2: the integers are closed under the operations (@prp-integers-closed), well-ordering and induction (@thm-well-ordering, @thm-induction), the division algorithm (@thm-division-algorithm), definition by recursion, powers and sums (@thm-recursion, @def-power, @def-sum-product), and finite sets: equinumerous and finite sets, the uniqueness of the number of elements and the pigeonhole principle (@def-equinumerous, @def-finite, @cor-finite-size-unique, @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets), subsets and disjoint unions of finite sets (@prp-subset-finite, @prp-disjoint-union-count), and Hilbert’s hotel (@exm-hilbert-hotel). From Chapter 3: the default-value repair in the find-the-error exercise on subsets of countable sets (@exr-countable-sets-c2), the axiom of choice and right inverses of surjections (@ax-choice, @thm-surjection-right-inverse), the diagonal (@thm-binary-sequences-uncountable, @thm-cantor, @exr-diagonal-arguments-c2), the Schröder–Bernstein theorem (@thm-schroder-bernstein), and, from Section 3.6, subsets as 0–1 functions (@thm-power-set-two-power, @cor-cantor-two-power). From Chapter 4: relations and their properties (@exm-method-relation-properties), equivalence relations, classes, partitions and quotient sets (@def-equivalence-relation, @def-equivalence-class, @def-partition, @def-quotient-set, @thm-classes-partition), congruence (@def-congruence, @prp-congruence-arithmetic, @prp-integers-mod-n), the fibers of a function as classes (@exm-fibres-of-function), the check that a definition does not depend on the representative (@exm-method-well-definedness), the reals modulo the integers and equal-size subsets as quotients (@exm-reals-mod-integers, @exm-same-size-subsets), a quotient built from fractions (@exr-equivalence-relations-b1), and the least common multiple as an order example (@exm-divisibility-lcm). The arithmetic and order of 
R are school facts in examples, as in the earlier chapters. Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 35 hours for everything. Roadmap - Restriction, extension and gluing. Restriction to a subset, extension, the inclusion map; a function defined on the pieces of a cover is one function exactly when the pieces agree on the overlaps; indicator functions, with the set operations as arithmetic of indicators and the subsets of X as the functions X 	o \{0, 1\}; the method: define a function by gluing. - Fibers and the canonical factorization. The fibers of a function partition its domain, and every function is a quotient map, then a bijection onto its image, then an inclusion; a function constant on classes factors through the quotient in exactly one way; the method: define a function on a quotient. - Binary operations. An operation on a set, closure, associativity, commutativity, identities and inverses, with the uniqueness proofs; the operations on the set of functions Y^X defined pointwise, and composition as an operation on X^X; an operation that is constant on classes descends to the quotient; the method: compute one expression in two ways. - Permutations and iteration. The permutations of a set and their composites and inverses, iterates by recursion, orbits as the classes of an equivalence relation, fixed points, the decomposition of a permutation of a finite set into disjoint cycles, the number of shuffles after which a deck returns, and the eventually periodic orbits of a self-map of a finite set; the method: follow an orbit. Named moves Each is a method box in the section named at the end of its line; later sections, and the later chapters of this volume, use the move again. The first four below are this chapter’s; the last bullet names three earlier moves reused here as tools: Chapter 4’s well-definedness, Chapter 1’s uniqueness and Chapter 2’s pigeonhole principle. - Define a function by gluing (@exm-method-gluing). Name the pieces, check that they cover the domain, check that the formulas agree on each overlap, and conclude by the gluing theorem; prove injectivity across pieces too, not only inside each piece. (Section 5.1) - Define a function on a quotient (@exm-method-factor-through-quotient). Write the function on X that the rule computes from a representative, check that it is constant on classes, and conclude that the induced function exists, is unique, and agrees with the rule. (Section 5.2) - Compute one expression in two ways (@exm-method-two-ways). To equate two objects known only through equations, reduce both to one expression and cite a hypothesis at each step. (Section 5.3) - Follow an orbit (@exm-method-follow-the-orbit). List the forward orbit of a point, use the pigeonhole principle to find a repeat in a finite set, take the first repeat, and carry the repeat through the structure of the map. (Section 5.4) - Well-definedness (@exm-method-well-definedness), from Section 4.2, is step 2 of the quotient box, and uniqueness (@exm-method-uniqueness), from Section 1.4, is the shape of the uniqueness proofs in Section 5.3. The pigeonhole principle (@cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets) is step 2 of the orbit box. Threads - Same value, same class. Section 4.2 observed that the fibers of a function are the classes of an equivalence relation (@exm-fibres-of-function). Section 5.2 turns the observation into a factorization theorem (@thm-canonical-factorization), and Section 5.3 runs the same well-definedness check on pairs of classes to define an operation on a quotient (@prp-operation-on-quotient). - Subsets are functions. Section 1.5 introduced the indicator of a subset, Section 3.6 proved that A \mapsto \ind_A is a bijection (@thm-power-set-two-power), and Section 5.1 makes it a calculus: intersections and complements of subsets are products and differences of indicators, and the indicator of a union is \ind_A + \ind_B - \ind_A \ind_B (a sum when the sets are disjoint) (@prp-indicator-arithmetic). - Inverses. Section 1.6 showed that a function has at most one inverse. Section 5.3 shows that an element has at most one inverse for any associative operation with an identity (@prp-operation-inverse-unique), of which composition of bijections is the case, and Section 5.4 puts this to work on the set of permutations. - Orbits. The classes of “can be reached from” are the orbits of a permutation (@thm-orbits-partition), and each is a cycle (@prp-orbit-cycle). The same idea, without invertibility, gives tails and cycles for an arbitrary self-map of a finite set (@prp-eventually-periodic). Summary A function can be restricted to a subset, extended, and glued from functions on the pieces of a cover that agree on the overlaps (@thm-gluing). Subsets of X correspond to indicator functions, and the set operations become arithmetic (@prp-indicator-arithmetic). The fibers of a function partition its domain (@prp-fibres-partition), and every function factors as a quotient map, a bijection and an inclusion (@thm-canonical-factorization); a function that is constant on the classes of an equivalence relation factors through the quotient in exactly one way (@thm-functions-out-of-quotient). The identity of an associative operation and the inverse of an element are unique (@prp-operation-identity-unique, @prp-operation-inverse-unique), pointwise operations on Y^X inherit the properties of the operation on Y (@prp-pointwise-operations), and an operation that respects an equivalence relation descends to the quotient (@prp-operation-on-quotient). The permutations of a set are closed under composition and inverses (@prp-permutations-closed), the orbits of a permutation partition the set (@thm-orbits-partition), and a permutation of a finite set is a product of disjoint cycles (@thm-permutation-cycles), so some power of it is the identity (@cor-permutation-power-identity). What is open: Zorn’s lemma, in Chapter 6. The permutations of a set with composition are the first example of the structures that Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 2 will study. Next, Chapter 6 states and uses Zorn’s lemma. Terms - associative, commutative: properties of an operation \ast with (x \ast y) \ast z = x \ast (y \ast z), respectively x \ast y = y \ast x, for all x, y, z (@def-operation-properties). - binary operation on a set X: a function X 	imes X 	o X; the operation is closed on a subset A if x \ast y \in A for all x, y \in A (@def-binary-operation). - cycle: the permutation (x_1\ x_2\ \cdots\ x_k) that sends x_j \mapsto x_{j+1}, x_k \mapsto x_1 and fixes every other point; disjoint cycles have disjoint sets of entries (@def-permutation-cycle). - extension, restriction: g extends f \colon A 	o Y if g|_A = f; f|_A is the function f with its domain cut down to A (@def-restriction-extension). - fiber of a function f \colon X 	o Y over y: the set \{ x \in X : f(x) = y \} (@exm-fibres-of-function, @prp-fibres-partition). - fixed point of f \colon X 	o X: a point with f(x) = x (@def-orbit). - identity (left, right, two-sided) of an operation; inverse of an element and invertible element (@def-operation-properties). - inclusion map \iota_A \colon A 	o X, a \mapsto a (@def-restriction-extension). - indicator function \ind_A \colon X 	o \{0, 1\} of A \subseteq X: 1 on A, 0 off A (@def-indicator). - iterate f^n: the n-th composite of a self-map f, by recursion; for a permutation, also \sigma^{-n} (@def-iterate). - orbit of x under a permutation \sigma: \{ \sigma^k(x) : k \in 
Z \}; its length is its number of elements (@prp-orbit-cycle); the forward orbit of x under any self-map is \{ f^n(x) : n \in 
N \} (@def-orbit). - permutation of X: a bijection X 	o X; S_X is the set of them (@def-permutation). - symmetric difference A 	riangle B: the elements in exactly one of A and B (Section 5.1, before @prp-indicator-arithmetic).

title: 5.1 Restriction, Extension and Gluing
content:
Restriction, Extension and Gluing Chapter 1 made a function a graph with a codomain, and Chapter 4 cut sets into classes. This chapter builds new functions out of old ones. Here we take the three simplest constructions: cutting a function down to a smaller domain, enlarging its domain, and assembling one function from pieces defined on parts of the domain. The last of these is behind every definition “by cases”, and the section ends with the functions that take only the values 0 and 1, with which an equation between sets becomes a computation with numbers. A function in two pieces The proof of the Schröder–Bernstein theorem (@thm-schroder-bernstein) defined its bijection h by one formula on a set C and by another off C, and then said: each a falls under exactly one case, and in each case the value exists and is unique, so h is a function. That sentence carried the whole definition. It is worth asking what it really needed. Here is a familiar definition by cases: \abs{x} =  egin{cases} x & 	ext{if } x \ge 0, \ -x & 	ext{if } x \le 0 . \end{cases} This time a point falls under both cases: 0 \ge 0 and 0 \le 0. So the sentence from Schröder–Bernstein does not apply. Is \abs{\cdot} still a function? Most readers would say yes at once, because both formulas give 0 at 0. Now try r(x) =  egin{cases} x & 	ext{if } x \ge 0, \ x + 1 & 	ext{if } x \le 0 . \end{cases} At 0 the first line gives 0 and the second gives 1. The “rule” offers two values at one input, and by (Fn2) of @def-function it is not a function. So whether “one formula on this piece, another on that piece” defines a function depends on two things: whether the pieces leave any point out, and what the formulas do where the pieces meet. Before reading on: write down the condition on two formulas, on two pieces, that makes the definition a function. The gluing theorem below answers this, for any number of pieces. Restriction and extension Section 1.5 cut a function down: the restriction of f \colon X 	o Y to a subset A \subseteq X keeps the pairs of f whose input lies in A. The reverse question is just as natural. A function is known on part of a set, say g(x) = 1/x on (0, 1]; can it be extended to a larger set, and in how many ways? A restriction forgets part of the domain; an extension fills in the part that was missing. [Restriction, Extension, Inclusion] Let X and Y be sets and A \subseteq X. 1. For f \colon X 	o Y, the restriction of f to A is the function f|_A \colon A 	o Y, f|_A(a) \coloneqq f(a), as in Section 1.5. 2. For g \colon A 	o Y, an extension of g to X is a function f \colon X 	o Y with f|_A = g. 3. The inclusion map of A into X is \iota_A \colon A 	o X, \iota_A(a) \coloneqq a. In words: the restriction keeps the codomain and forgets the inputs outside A. An extension is any function on the larger set that agrees with g at every point of A; by @prp-function-equality, f|_A = g says exactly that f(a) = g(a) for every a \in A, since both functions have domain A and codomain Y. The inclusion map is the identity of A with its codomain enlarged to X; it is not \id_A unless A = X, because the codomains differ. The article in (b) is “a”, not “the”, and the naive expectation that an extension is determined by g fails at once. The function g \colon (0, 1] 	o 
R, g(x) = 1/x, has an extension to [0, 1] for every choice of a value at 0: sending 0 to 0 and sending 0 to 5 give two different extensions, since they differ at 0. The formula 1/x suggests no value at all there. Nor need an extension keep a property that g has. Let a 
e b, and let g \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{a, b\} send 1 \mapsto a and 2 \mapsto b, a bijection. An extension to \{1, 2, 3\} with codomain \{a, b\} is a function from a set of three elements to a set of two, and by @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a) no such function is injective. So the bijection g has extensions, but no injective one. Restriction, by contrast, is predictable. The next proposition lists what it does. [Restrictions] Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function and B \subseteq A \subseteq X. 1. f|_A = f \circ \iota_A. 2. (f|_A)|_B = f|_B. 3. For every function g \colon Y 	o Z, (g \circ f)|_A = g \circ (f|_A). 4. If f is injective, then so is f|_A. 5. f|_A(B) = f(B). Parts (a)–(c) are equations between functions, so we compare domains, codomains and values. Parts (d) and (e) only unwind @def-injective and @def-image, using f|_A(a) = f(a). For (a)–(c) we use @prp-function-equality: in each part both sides have the same domain and codomain, and we compare values. (a) Both sides are functions A 	o Y (@def-composition). For a \in A, (f \circ \iota_A)(a) = f(\iota_A(a)) = f(a) = f|_A(a). (b) Both sides are functions B 	o Y. For b \in B, (f|_A)|_B(b) = f|_A(b) = f(b) = f|_B(b), where the middle step uses b \in A. (c) Both sides are functions A 	o Z. For a \in A, (g \circ f)|_A(a) = g(f(a)) = g(f|_A(a)) = (g \circ (f|_A))(a). (d) Let a, a' \in A with f|_A(a) = f|_A(a'). Then f(a) = f(a'), so a = a' because f is injective (@def-injective). (e) By @def-image, f|_A(B) = \{ f|_A(b) : b \in B \} = \{ f(b) : b \in B \} = f(B), since f|_A(b) = f(b) for every b \in B \subseteq A. Part (e) with B = A says that the restriction has the same image as f on A: f|_A(A) = f(A). Part (d) has no partner for surjectivity, and the next check asks why. Is a restriction of a surjection always surjective? No. The function f \colon 
R 	o [0, \infty), f(x) = x^2, is surjective (every t \ge 0 is (\sqrt{t})^2). Its restriction f|_{[1, 2]} \colon [1, 2] 	o [0, \infty) has image f([1, 2]) = [1, 4], so 0 is not a value. The restriction keeps the codomain while the domain shrinks, so it can lose surjectivity. It can also gain injectivity: f|_{[0, \infty)} is injective, although f is not. Gluing Restriction takes a function apart: it hands us the pieces f|_{A_i} on the parts A_i of the domain. Gluing is the reverse. We are given functions on the parts and want one function on the whole set. The hook named the two ways this can go wrong: a point may lie in no part, and a point may lie in two parts whose formulas disagree there. Only the second failure appeared there; the first is easy to picture. [Gluing Functions] Let (A_i)_{i \in I} be a family of subsets of a set X with  igcup_{i \in I} A_i = X, and let (f_i)_{i \in I} be a family of functions f_i \colon A_i 	o Y. Suppose the f_i agree on overlaps: f_i(x) = f_j(x) \quad 	ext{for all } i, j \in I 	ext{ and every } x \in A_i \cap A_j . Then there is exactly one function f \colon X 	o Y with f|_{A_i} = f_i for every i \in I. [Scratch work] A function is a graph satisfying (Fn1) and (Fn2), together with a codomain (@def-function). We must produce a graph, and the only graphs in sight are the graphs G_i of the f_i. The obvious candidate is their union. The plan, as givens and goal: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Givens Goal --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- graphs G_i \subseteq A_i 	imes Y, each with (Fn1) and (Fn2) on A_i;  igcup_i A_i = X; agreement on overlaps a function f \colon X 	o Y whose restriction to each A_i is f_i, and only one G \coloneqq  igcup_{i} G_i \subseteq X 	imes Y (Fn1) and (Fn2) for G on X x \in X, so x \in A_i for some i (the cover) (Fn1): (x, f_i(x)) \in G_i \subseteq G (x, y) \in G_i, (x, y') \in G_j; so y = f_i(x), y' = f_j(x) and x \in A_i \cap A_j (Fn2): y = y'; this is the gap, and agreement on overlaps closes it ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ In the existence part each hypothesis has one job: the cover gives (Fn1), agreement gives (Fn2). Uniqueness is easier: two functions with the right restrictions both take the value f_i(x) at a point x \in A_i. For each i \in I, let G_i \subseteq A_i 	imes Y be the graph of f_i, and let G \coloneqq  igcup_{i \in I} G_i (@def-family-union-intersection). Since A_i \subseteq X, each G_i \subseteq X 	imes Y, so G \subseteq X 	imes Y. (Fn1). Let x \in X. Since  igcup_{i \in I} A_i = X, there is i \in I with x \in A_i. Then (x, f_i(x)) \in G_i \subseteq G. (Fn2). Let (x, y) \in G and (x, y') \in G. Then (x, y) \in G_i and (x, y') \in G_j for some i, j \in I. Since G_i \subseteq A_i 	imes Y and G_j \subseteq A_j 	imes Y, we have x \in A_i \cap A_j, and by (\ast\ast) of Section 1.5, y = f_i(x) and y' = f_j(x). Agreement on overlaps gives y = y'. So f \coloneqq (G, Y) is a function X 	o Y. Let i \in I. Both f|_{A_i} and f_i are functions A_i 	o Y, and for x \in A_i we have (x, f_i(x)) \in G, so f(x) = f_i(x) by (\ast\ast); that is, f|_{A_i}(x) = f_i(x). By @prp-function-equality, f|_{A_i} = f_i. Uniqueness. Let g \colon X 	o Y also satisfy g|_{A_i} = f_i for every i \in I. Let x \in X, and choose i with x \in A_i. Then g(x) = g|_{A_i}(x) = f_i(x) = f|_{A_i}(x) = f(x). By @prp-function-equality, g = f. This proves the theorem. In the existence part, the proof used the cover only for (Fn1) and agreement only for (Fn2). Each hypothesis is needed. If a point x lies in no A_i, the union graph has no pair with first coordinate x, and (Fn1) fails; the theorem fails too: for X = Y = \{0, 1\}, A_1 = \{0\} and f_1(0) = 0, both ways of choosing the value at 1 give a function f with f|_{A_1} = f_1, so “exactly one” fails. The rule r of the hook shows two pieces that cover 
R and disagree at 0, where (Fn2) fails. The theorem is used so often that its use deserves a template. Step (4) below is the one most often forgotten. [Method: define a function by gluing] Template. (1) Name the pieces and check that they cover the domain. (2) For each two pieces, find the overlap and check that the formulas agree on it; disjoint pieces need nothing. (3) Conclude by @thm-gluing. (4) Prove further properties piece by piece and across pieces: for injectivity, compare a value from one piece with a value from another. When to use it. Definitions by cases, piecewise formulas, a default value off a subset, constructions such as Schröder–Bernstein’s. The usual failure. Checking the cover and forgetting the overlaps (a boundary point lies in two pieces); checking injectivity inside each piece only. [Piecewise definitions are gluings] Decide whether each definition glues to a function 
R 	o 
R. 1. x on [0, \infty) and -x on (-\infty, 0]. 2. x on [0, \infty) and x + 1 on (-\infty, 0]. 3. x on [0, \infty) and x + 1 on (-\infty, 0). If it glues, is the result injective? (a) Step (1): the pieces cover 
R, since every real number is \ge 0 or \le 0. Step (2): the overlap is \{0\}, where the formulas give 0 and -0 = 0. They agree, so by @thm-gluing there is exactly one function with these restrictions: the absolute value \abs{\cdot}. (b) The pieces cover 
R and overlap in \{0\}, where the values are 0 and 1. Agreement fails, so the hypothesis of @thm-gluing fails; and no function can have both restrictions, since its value at 0 would be 0 and 1. This is the rule r of the hook, which is not a function. (c) A minimal change to (b): the second piece loses the point 0. Now the pieces are disjoint and still cover 
R, so step (2) has nothing to check, and they glue to a function k \colon 
R 	o 
R. Inside each piece k is injective (x = x' and x + 1 = x' + 1 each force x = x'). Across the pieces, step (4) finds a collision: k(	frac12) = 	frac12 and k(-	frac12) = -	frac12 + 1 = 	frac12. So k is not injective. Back to Schröder–Bernstein. In the proof of @thm-schroder-bernstein, the pieces were C and A \setminus C: disjoint, and covering A. So the definition of h is a gluing, with nothing to check in step (2), and “each a falls under exactly one case” is steps (1) and (2) at once: the pieces cover A, and there is no overlap to check. The proof’s Case 3 of injectivity, one point in C and one outside, is step (4)’s comparison across pieces; Cases 1 and 2 are the checks inside each piece. Default values. Let A \subseteq X, g \colon A 	o Y and y_0 \in Y. “Take g on A and the value y_0 on X \setminus A” glues g with the constant function X \setminus A 	o Y with value y_0: the pieces A and X \setminus A are disjoint and cover X. The “Repair” in the solution of Section 3.1’s @exr-countable-sets-c2 was a default-value definition of this kind, with the default a_0 on the inputs that had no value of the right kind. The indicator functions of the next subsection are default-value definitions too. A boundary point usually lies in two pieces. “x^2 on (-\infty, 1], 3x on [1, \infty)” covers 
R, and each formula is a function on its piece, but at 1 the values are 1 and 3, so nothing glues. Check every overlap, not just the cover. Glue x^2 on (-\infty, 1] and 2x - 1 on [1, \infty). Does it glue? Is the result injective? The pieces cover 
R and overlap in \{1\}, where 1^2 = 1 = 2 \cdot 1 - 1; so the definitions glue to a function f \colon 
R 	o 
R. It is not injective, and the failure is inside the first piece: f(-1) = 1 = f(1). Indicator functions A subset A of X can be described by a function that answers, for each x \in X, the question “is x in A?” with 1 for yes and 0 for no. Section 1.5 met this function in @exm-first-functions (d). It now gets its own label, because it turns statements about sets into arithmetic. [Indicator Function] Let X be a set and A \subseteq X. The indicator function of A is \ind_A \colon X 	o \{0, 1\}, \ind_A(x) \coloneqq  egin{cases} 1 & 	ext{if } x \in A, \ 0 & 	ext{if } x \in X \setminus A . \end{cases} It is a default-value definition: the constant 1 on A glued with the constant 0 on X \setminus A, over a disjoint cover of X. The function depends on X as well as on A, since X is its domain; throughout this subsection one set X is fixed and every set named is a subset of it. Two small cases: \ind_X is the constant function 1, and \ind_{\emptyset} is the constant function 0. Section 3.6 proved that A \mapsto \ind_A is a bijection \powerset{X} 	o \{0, 1\}^X, with inverse f \mapsto \{ x \in X : f(x) = 1 \} = f^{-1}(\{1\}) (@thm-power-set-two-power). Only one consequence is needed here, and it can be read off directly: A is recovered from its indicator as the set of points where the value is 1. So \ind_A = \ind_B \quad 	ext{implies} \quad A = B . This is what lets a computation with indicators prove an equation between sets: show that the two sides have the same indicator, and they are equal. To compute, we need to know what the set operations do to indicators. Besides the operations of @def-set-operations we use one more. The symmetric difference of A and B is A 	riangle B \coloneqq (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A) , the set of points that lie in exactly one of A and B. [Set Operations as Arithmetic of Indicators] Let A, B \subseteq X. For every x \in X, write u \coloneqq \ind_A(x) and v \coloneqq \ind_B(x). Then: 1. \ind_{A \cap B}(x) = uv; 2. \ind_{X \setminus A}(x) = 1 - u; 3. \ind_{A \cup B}(x) = u + v - uv; 4. \ind_{A 	riangle B}(x) = u + v - 2uv; 5. A \subseteq B if and only if \ind_A(x) \le \ind_B(x) for every x \in X. For (a), (b) and (d), membership of x in the left-hand set is decided by which of x \in A, x \in B hold: four cases, one table. Part (c) need not be tabled at all: De Morgan turns a union into a complement of an intersection, and (a), (b) compute that. Fix x \in X. By @def-indicator, u = 1 if x \in A and u = 0 otherwise, and likewise for v and B. (a), (b), (d). There are four cases, and in each we read membership from @def-set-operations and the definition of 	riangle: ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- x \in A? x \in B? u v x \in A \cap B? uv x \in X \setminus A? 1 - u x \in A 	riangle B? u + v - 2uv ---------- ---------- ------- ------- ----------------- ------- ---------------------- ------- ---------------------- ------------- yes yes 1 1 yes 1 no 0 no 0 yes no 1 0 no 0 no 0 yes 1 no yes 0 1 no 0 yes 1 yes 1 no no 0 0 no 0 yes 1 no 0 ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- In every row, the number in each formula column is 1 exactly when the membership column before it says yes, and 0 otherwise. That is (a), (b) and (d). (c) By @thm-set-algebra (d) with X in the place of A, X \setminus (A \cup B) = (X \setminus A) \cap (X \setminus B). Applying (a) to the sets X \setminus A and X \setminus B, whose indicators at x are 1 - u and 1 - v by (b), gives \ind_{X \setminus (A \cup B)}(x) = (1 - u)(1 - v). Applying (b) to the set A \cup B \subseteq X, \ind_{A \cup B}(x) = 1 - \ind_{X \setminus (A \cup B)}(x) = 1 - (1 - u)(1 - v) = u + v - uv . (d) (\Rightarrow) Suppose A \subseteq B and let x \in X. If \ind_A(x) = 1, then x \in A, so x \in B and \ind_B(x) = 1. If \ind_A(x) = 0, then \ind_A(x) \le \ind_B(x) since \ind_B(x) \in \{0, 1\}. (\Leftarrow) Suppose the inequality holds at every point, and let x \in A. Then 1 = \ind_A(x) \le \ind_B(x) \le 1, so \ind_B(x) = 1 and x \in B. By @def-subset, A \subseteq B. Part (e) says the only pattern of values that A \subseteq B forbids is u = 1, v = 0: a point of A outside B. Express \ind_{A \setminus B}(x) in terms of u = \ind_A(x) and v = \ind_B(x). By @def-set-operations, A \setminus B = A \cap (X \setminus B), since both consist of the points of A not in B. By (a) and (b), \ind_{A \setminus B}(x) = u(1 - v) = u - uv. Check on the row u = 1, v = 0: the value is 1, and indeed such an x lies in A \setminus B. Compute with indicators. To prove an equation L = R between sets built from subsets A, B, C of X, fix x \in X, write u, v, w for the values of \ind_A, \ind_B, \ind_C at x, and translate each side into a polynomial in u, v, w by @prp-indicator-arithmetic. Simplify both, using u^2 = u, v^2 = v, w^2 = w, which hold because 0^2 = 0 and 1^2 = 1. If the two polynomials agree for all values in \{0, 1\}, then \ind_L = \ind_R, and L = R because a set is recovered from its indicator. The method replaces a case analysis on memberships by algebra, and it pays most when the case analysis is long. [Symmetric difference is associative] Show that (A 	riangle B) 	riangle C = A 	riangle (B 	riangle C) for all A, B, C \subseteq X. Fix x \in X and let u, v, w be the values of \ind_A, \ind_B, \ind_C at x. By @prp-indicator-arithmetic (d), \ind_{A 	riangle B}(x) = u + v - 2uv. Applying (d) again, to the sets A 	riangle B and C,  egin{aligned} \ind_{(A 	riangle B) 	riangle C}(x) &= (u + v - 2uv) + w - 2(u + v - 2uv)w \ &= u + v + w - 2uv - 2uw - 2vw + 4uvw . \end{aligned} The final expression does not change when u, v, w are permuted. The right-hand side gives u + (v + w - 2vw) - 2u(v + w - 2vw), which expands to the same expression. So the two sets have the same indicator, and they are equal. The common value is 1 exactly when an odd number of u, v, w equal 1: with one of them equal to 1 it is 1, with two it is 2 - 2 = 0, with three 3 - 6 + 4 = 1. So both sides are the set of points lying in an odd number of A, B, C. An element chase would split into eight cases, one for each pattern of memberships; the indicator computation did all eight at once. Cantor, re-read. The set D = \{ x \in X : x 
otin f(x) \} in the proof of @thm-cantor has indicator \ind_D(x) = 1 - \ind_{f(x)}(x): it is the flipped diagonal of the proof of @thm-binary-sequences-uncountable in Section 3.3, and Section 3.3, after @thm-cantor, already joined the two arguments for X = 
N. Exercise C3 runs the argument for an arbitrary set, with 0–1 functions first and subsets second. Let X = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}, A = \{1, 2\} and B = \{2, 3\}. List the values \ind_{A 	riangle B}(1), \dots, \ind_{A 	riangle B}(4), first from the formula u + v - 2uv and then from the definition of 	riangle. The values of \ind_A are (1, 1, 0, 0) and those of \ind_B are (0, 1, 1, 0). The formula gives 1 + 0 - 0 = 1, 1 + 1 - 2 = 0, 0 + 1 - 0 = 1, 0: the list (1, 0, 1, 0). From the definition, A 	riangle B = \{1\} \cup \{3\} = \{1, 3\}, whose indicator is the same list. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = x^2. What is the image of f|_{[-1, 2]}? 2. Let a, b, c be distinct and let g \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{a, b\} send 1 \mapsto a, 2 \mapsto b. Does g have an injective extension to \{1, 2, 3\} with codomain \{a, b\}? With codomain \{a, b, c\}? 3. Let A \subseteq X and g \colon A 	o Y. Show that g has an extension to X if and only if A = X or Y 
e \emptyset. 4. For X = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}, write \ind_{\{1, 3\}} as the list of its values at 1, 2, 3, 4, and name the subset of X whose indicator has the values (0, 1, 1, 0). (a) By @prp-restriction-properties (e), the image is f([-1, 2]). For x \in [-1, 2], 0 \le x^2 \le 4; conversely each t \in [0, 4] is (\sqrt{t})^2 with \sqrt{t} \in [0, 2]. So the image is [0, 4]. (b) No: a function from a set of three elements to a set of two elements is not injective, by @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a). Yes: send 3 \mapsto c; the three values a, b, c are distinct, so the extension is injective. (c) (\Leftarrow) If A = X, then g is an extension of itself, since g|_X = g. If Y 
e \emptyset, choose y_0 \in Y and glue g with the constant function X \setminus A 	o Y with value y_0: the pieces A and X \setminus A are disjoint and cover X, so @thm-gluing gives f \colon X 	o Y with f|_A = g. (\Rightarrow) Suppose A 
e X and Y = \emptyset. Since A \subseteq X and A 
e X, some x_0 \in X is not in A; so X is non-empty, and by @prp-empty-function (b) there is no function X 	o \emptyset, let alone an extension of g. By contraposition, an extension forces A = X or Y 
e \emptyset. (d) (1, 0, 1, 0); the subset \{2, 3\}, the set of points where the value is 1. B. Practice [B1: Three pieces] Let f_1(x) = -x on (-\infty, -1], f_2(x) = x^2 on [-1, 1] and f_3(x) = x on [1, \infty), each with codomain 
R. Show that they glue to a function f \colon 
R 	o 
R. Find f(
R) and f^{-1}(\{	frac14\}), and decide whether f is injective. The three intervals cover 
R. The overlaps are (-\infty, -1] \cap [-1, 1] = \{-1\}, where f_1(-1) = 1 = f_2(-1); [-1, 1] \cap [1, \infty) = \{1\}, where f_2(1) = 1 = f_3(1); and (-\infty, -1] \cap [1, \infty) = \emptyset. So the pieces agree on overlaps and glue, by @thm-gluing. Since 
R is the union of the three pieces, @thm-image-union gives f(
R) as the union of the images of the pieces, and by @prp-restriction-properties (e) the image of a piece is the image of the corresponding f_i. These are f_1((-\infty, -1]) = [1, \infty), f_2([-1, 1]) = [0, 1] and f_3([1, \infty)) = [1, \infty). Hence f(
R) = [0, \infty). On the first and third pieces every value is \ge 1, so a solution of f(x) = 	frac14 lies in [-1, 1], where it solves x^2 = 	frac14. Hence f^{-1}(\{	frac14\}) = \{ -	frac12, 	frac12 \}. Two different points have the same value, so f is not injective. [B2: Injective across pieces] Let f \colon X 	o Y and X = A \cup B. Prove that f is injective if and only if f|_A and f|_B are injective and f(A) \cap f(B) = f(A \cap B). (\Rightarrow) The restrictions are injective by @prp-restriction-properties (d), and f(A) \cap f(B) = f(A \cap B) by @thm-image-intersection (b), since f is injective. (\Leftarrow) Let x, x' \in X with f(x) = f(x'). If both lie in A, then f|_A(x) = f|_A(x') and x = x' since f|_A is injective; likewise if both lie in B. Otherwise, since X = A \cup B, one lies in A and the other in B; by symmetry say x \in A and x' \in B. Then y \coloneqq f(x) = f(x') lies in f(A) \cap f(B) = f(A \cap B), so y = f(z) for some z \in A \cap B (@def-image). Now x, z \in A with f|_A(x) = y = f|_A(z), so x = z; and x', z \in B with f|_B(x') = f|_B(z), so x' = z. Hence x = x', and f is injective. [B3: By indicators] Let A, B, C \subseteq X. Prove by computing with indicators: 1. A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C); 2. A \cap (B 	riangle C) = (A \cap B) 	riangle (A \cap C). Fix x \in X and write u, v, w for the values of \ind_A, \ind_B, \ind_C at x. For any S \subseteq X, A \setminus S = A \cap (X \setminus S), so @prp-indicator-arithmetic (a), (b) give \ind_{A \setminus S}(x) = u(1 - \ind_S(x)). (a) By @prp-indicator-arithmetic (c), \ind_{B \cup C}(x) = v + w - vw, so the left side has indicator value u(1 - v - w + vw) = u(1 - v)(1 - w). The right side has, by @prp-indicator-arithmetic (a), u(1 - v) \cdot u(1 - w) = u^2 (1 - v)(1 - w) = u(1 - v)(1 - w), using u^2 = u. The indicators agree at every x, so the sets are equal. (b) By @prp-indicator-arithmetic (a) and (d), the left side has u(v + w - 2vw) = uv + uw - 2uvw. The sets A \cap B and A \cap C have indicator values uv and uw, so by @prp-indicator-arithmetic (d) the right side has uv + uw - 2(uv)(uw) = uv + uw - 2u^2 vw = uv + uw - 2uvw. The indicators agree, so the sets are equal. [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement and refute each false one with a counterexample. 1. If X = A \cup B with A \cap B = \emptyset, and f \colon A 	o Y, g \colon B 	o Y are functions, then there is exactly one h \colon X 	o Y with h|_A = f and h|_B = g. 2. If f \colon X 	o Y, X = A \cup B, and f|_A and f|_B are injective, then f is injective. 3. If f \colon X 	o Y and f|_A \colon A 	o Y is surjective for some A \subseteq X, then f is surjective. 4. The definition h(x) = x for x \in 
Q, h(x) = 2x for x \in 
R \setminus 
Q gives a bijection h \colon 
R 	o 
R. 5. Gluing x on [0, 1] and 2 - x on [1, 2] gives an injective function [0, 2] 	o 
R. (a) True. The family A, B covers X, and the only overlap A \cap B is empty, so agreement holds vacuously. By @thm-gluing there is exactly one such h. (b) False. Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = x^2, A = [0, \infty) and B = (-\infty, 0]. Then X = A \cup B, and both restrictions are injective (on each piece, x^2 = x'^2 with x, x' of the same sign gives x = x'), but f(1) = 1 = f(-1). The collision is across the pieces. (c) True. Let y \in Y. Since f|_A is surjective, y = f|_A(a) = f(a) for some a \in A \subseteq X. So y is a value of f. (d) True. The pieces 
Q and 
R \setminus 
Q are disjoint and cover 
R, so h is a function by @thm-gluing. Injective. Inside the pieces: x = x' and 2x = 2x' each give x = x'. Across the pieces: if x \in 
Q, x' 
otin 
Q and h(x) = h(x'), then x = 2x', so x' = x/2 \in 
Q, a contradiction. Surjective. A rational y is h(y). An irrational y is h(y/2): here y/2 
otin 
Q, since otherwise y = 2 \cdot (y/2) \in 
Q. (e) False. The pieces agree at the overlap \{1\} (both give 1), so they glue to a function f; but f(	frac12) = 	frac12 = 2 - 	frac32 = f(	frac32). C. Going deeper [C1: Counting extensions] Let A \subseteq X and g \colon A 	o Y, and let E be the set of all extensions of g to X. Show that f \mapsto f|_{X \setminus A} is a bijection from E to Y^{X \setminus A}. Write ho(f) \coloneqq f|_{X \setminus A}, a function E 	o Y^{X \setminus A}. For k \in Y^{X \setminus A}, the pieces A and X \setminus A are disjoint and cover X, so by @thm-gluing there is exactly one \gamma(k) \colon X 	o Y with \gamma(k)|_A = g and \gamma(k)|_{X \setminus A} = k. In particular \gamma(k) \in E, so \gamma \colon Y^{X \setminus A} 	o E. Round trip on Y^{X \setminus A}. ho(\gamma(k)) = \gamma(k)|_{X \setminus A} = k, by the choice of \gamma(k). Round trip on E. Let f \in E. Both f and \gamma(ho(f)) restrict to g on A and to f|_{X \setminus A} on X \setminus A. By the uniqueness in @thm-gluing, \gamma(ho(f)) = f. So \gamma is a two-sided inverse of ho, and ho is a bijection by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. In words: an extension of g is the same thing as an arbitrary choice of values off A. For finite sets this counts the extensions: if X \setminus A has m elements and Y has n, there are as many extensions as functions from an m-element set to an n-element set. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: defines \gamma by gluing, checking the pieces cover and are disjoint. - 2: ho(\gamma(k)) = k. - 3: \gamma(ho(f)) = f by uniqueness in @thm-gluing. - 2: concludes that ho is a bijection. [C2: Find the error] Here is a proposed proof of the existence part of @thm-gluing. “Given x \in X, pick i with x \in A_i, and set f(x) \coloneqq f_i(x). Then f|_{A_i} = f_i for every i \in I.” Which hypothesis of the theorem is never used? Where does the argument fail, and which check is missing? Is the conclusion true? The conclusion is true: it is @thm-gluing. The argument does not prove it. Agreement on overlaps is never used. The failure is in the definition of f: the rule reads a chosen index i from the set \{ i \in I : x \in A_i \}, and it defines a function only if the value f_i(x) does not depend on which such i is picked. That is the well-definedness check of @exm-method-well-definedness, with “an index i with x \in A_i” in the role of a representative; it is exactly agreement on overlaps. Without it, the second sentence fails too: at a point x \in A_i \cap A_j where i was picked, f|_{A_j}(x) = f_i(x), which need not equal f_j(x). @exm-piecewise-as-gluing (b) at x = 0 is a case: picking the first piece gives f(0) = 0, and then f|_{(-\infty, 0]} is not x \mapsto x + 1, which has the value 1 at 0. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: names agreement on overlaps as the unused hypothesis. - 4: locates the failure either in the definition of f (the value depends on the choice of i, so a well-definedness check is missing) or in the claim f|_{A_j} = f_j at a point of A_i \cap A_j where another index was picked, and says that agreement on overlaps is what is missing. - 3: gives a concrete case where the choice matters and f|_{A_j} = f_j fails. Fatal errors (0 for the step): claiming the conclusion is false; locating the error in the cover (every x does lie in some A_i). [C3: Cantor through indicators] Let X be a set and g \colon X 	o \{0, 1\}^X a function. Define d \colon X 	o \{0, 1\} by d(x) \coloneqq 1 - g(x)(x). 1. Prove that d is not a value of g. 2. Deduce @thm-cantor. Hint: for f \colon X 	o \powerset{X}, use g(x) \coloneqq \ind_{f(x)}. (a) Since g(x)(x) \in \{0, 1\}, also d(x) \in \{0, 1\}, so d \in \{0, 1\}^X. Suppose d = g(a) for some a \in X. Then d(a) = g(a)(a), and by the definition of d, d(a) = 1 - g(a)(a). Hence 2 g(a)(a) = 1, which is impossible for g(a)(a) \in \{0, 1\}. So d is not a value of g. (b) Let f \colon X 	o \powerset{X} be a function, and put g(x) \coloneqq \ind_{f(x)} \in \{0, 1\}^X. Let D \coloneqq \{ x \in X : d(x) = 1 \}. Since d takes only the values 0 and 1, \ind_D = d. If D = f(a) for some a \in X, then g(a) = \ind_{f(a)} = \ind_D = d, against (a). So D is not a value of f, and f is not surjective. Unwinding, d(x) = 1 exactly when \ind_{f(x)}(x) = 0, so D = \{ x \in X : x 
otin f(x) \}, the set of the proof in Section 3.3. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: checks that d \in \{0, 1\}^X. - 4: assumes d = g(a) and reaches the contradiction 2 g(a)(a) = 1. - 4: shows \ind_D = d and transfers the argument to f via g(x) = \ind_{f(x)}. - 1: concludes that f is not surjective. Section 3.6’s @cor-cantor-two-power went the other way, from Cantor’s theorem to 0–1 functions; here the argument about 0–1 functions comes first, and the statement about subsets follows from it.

title: 5.2 Fibers and the Canonical Factorization
content:
Fibers and the Canonical Factorization Section 4.2 cut a set into classes, and Section 5.1 cut functions down and glued them together. This section joins the two threads. Every function sorts its domain into piles by value, the fibers, and we prove that the piles carry all the information the function has, apart from the names of the values: every function is a quotient map, then a bijection, then an inclusion. Read in reverse, the same argument says exactly which functions on a set pass to a function on a quotient set, and gives a method for defining one. Functions on the clock Section 4.2 built the clock 
Z/12, whose elements are the twelve hours [0], [1], \dots, [11]. Some questions about an integer are really questions about its hour. “Is a even?” is one: 14 and 2 name the same hour, and both are even; 13 and 1 name the same hour, and both are odd. In general, let g \colon 
Z 	o Y be a function with g(a) = g(a') \quad 	ext{whenever } 12 \mid a - a' , so that g takes one value on each class modulo 12. Then g “is” a function of the hour: to compute it at an hour, pick any integer naming that hour and apply g. The condition is stated for all pairs in one class at once. A condition such as g(a + 12) = g(a) for every a says the same thing in the end, but getting from it to g(a + 12k) = g(a) for every k \in 
Z takes an induction in each direction. Other functions are not functions of the hour. “Is a positive?” gives different answers at 2 and at -10, which name the same hour, so no function on 
Z/12 can answer it. There is a second way into the same idea, from the side of an arbitrary function. A function f \colon X 	o Y sorts its domain: put two points in one pile when f gives them the same value. Section 4.2 met these piles as the classes of the relation \sim_f (@exm-fibres-of-function). So every function produces a quotient set of its domain. Two questions organize the section. - (Q1) Given an equivalence relation \sim on X, when does a function on X pass to a function on X/{\sim}, and is the function it passes to unique? - (Q2) What does a function look like once its domain has been sorted by value? We answer (Q2) first, because its answer contains the answer to (Q1). The fibers of a function Recall the relation of @exm-fibres-of-function. For f \colon X 	o Y and x, x' \in X, x \sim_f x' means f(x) = f(x'). It is an equivalence relation on X, and the class of a \in X is the fiber of f over f(a), [a] = \{ x \in X : f(x) = f(a) \} = f^{-1}(\{ f(a) \}) , a preimage in the sense of @def-preimage. A fiber over a point of Y that f never takes is empty, and so is not a class. The fibers of a function are the piles it sorts its domain into, one pile for each value it takes. The Fibers of a Function Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function. 1. The fibers f^{-1}(\{y\}) over the points y \in f(X) are exactly the classes of \sim_f, and they form a partition of X. 2. The rule y \mapsto f^{-1}(\{y\}) is a bijection f(X) 	o X/{\sim_f}. Hence \card{f(X)} = \card{X/{\sim_f}}. Part (a) is already proved: @exm-fibres-of-function identified the classes with the fibers, and @thm-classes-partition says the classes partition X. For (b), a fiber over a value is a class, so the rule lands in X/{\sim_f}; every class is the fiber over the value at its representative, which is surjectivity; and two different values have different fibers, because a point of the first fiber is not in the second. (a) Let y \in f(X), say y = f(a) with a \in X (@def-image). Then f^{-1}(\{y\}) = f^{-1}(\{f(a)\}) = [a], by the computation in @exm-fibres-of-function; so each such fiber is a class. Conversely, each class is [a] for some a \in X, and [a] = f^{-1}(\{f(a)\}) with f(a) \in f(X). So the fibers over the points of f(X) are the elements of X/{\sim_f}, and these form a partition of X by @thm-classes-partition (d). (b) By (a), each y \in f(X) is sent to an element of X/{\sim_f}, and to only one, so the rule is a function \Phi \colon f(X) 	o X/{\sim_f} (@def-function). It is surjective: an element of X/{\sim_f} is [a] for some a \in X, and [a] = \Phi(f(a)) by (a). It is injective: let y, y' \in f(X) with y 
e y', and write y = f(a) with a \in X. Then a \in f^{-1}(\{y\}), while a 
otin f^{-1}(\{y'\}) because f(a) = y 
e y'. So \Phi(y) 
e \Phi(y'), and different values have different fibers. Hence \Phi is a bijection (@def-bijective), and \card{f(X)} = \card{X/{\sim_f}} by @def-equinumerous. So a function takes exactly as many values as it has fibers, in the sense of equinumerosity: the values and the piles can be paired off. The partition remembers which points share a value, and forgets only what the values are called. List the classes of \sim_f for f(n) = n^2 - 2n on \{-1, 0, 1, 2, 3\}, and match each class with its value. The values are f(-1) = 3, f(0) = 0, f(1) = -1, f(2) = 0, f(3) = 3. So the classes are \{-1, 3\} (value 3), \{0, 2\} (value 0) and \{1\} (value -1): three classes for the three values in f(X) = \{-1, 0, 3\}. The proposition explains a computation of Section 4.2. In @exm-same-size-subsets, the subsets of \{1, 2, 3\} were sorted by “same number of elements”. That relation is \sim_f for the function f \colon \powerset{\{1, 2, 3\}} 	o \{0, 1, 2, 3\} sending each subset to its number of elements, a function by @prp-subset-finite (every subset has some number of elements, at most 3) and @cor-finite-size-unique (only one). Its four fibers are \{\emptyset\}, the three singletons, the three pairs, and \{\{1, 2, 3\}\}, and its image is all of \{0, 1, 2, 3\}. Part (c) of that example, the well-defined map from classes to numbers, is the bijection of (b) read backwards. List the fibers of f \colon \{1, \dots, 6\} 	o \{0, 1, 2\}, where f(n) is the remainder of n on division by 3. f^{-1}(\{0\}) = \{3, 6\}, f^{-1}(\{1\}) = \{1, 4\}, f^{-1}(\{2\}) = \{2, 5\}. Three fibers, three values; every value is taken, so f(X) is the whole codomain. Every function factors Now (Q2). The quotient map q \colon X 	o X/{\sim_f}, q(x) = [x] (@def-quotient-set), sends each point to its fiber. The bijection of @prp-fibres-partition (b) goes from values to fibers; turn it around, and it sends the fiber [x] to the value f(x). Finally, a value of f lies in the image f(X), and the inclusion map \iota \colon f(X) 	o Y, \iota(y) = y (@def-restriction-extension), puts it back into the codomain. Composed, the three maps take x to [x], to f(x), to f(x). That is f. [Canonical Factorization] Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function, let q \colon X 	o X/{\sim_f} be the quotient map, and let \iota \colon f(X) 	o Y be the inclusion map. There is exactly one function  ar f \colon X/{\sim_f} 	o f(X) with f = \iota \circ  ar f \circ q . It is given by  ar f([x]) = f(x), and it is a bijection. [Scratch work] The only candidate is forced. If \iota( ar f(q(x))) = f(x), then  ar f([x]) = f(x), since \iota changes no value. So uniqueness costs nothing, and the work is to show that the forced rule is a function and a bijection. The rule [x] \mapsto f(x) reads a representative, so the first check is well-definedness, by the method of @exm-method-well-definedness. The twist is in the table’s third row: injectivity is the well-definedness line read backwards. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------- [x] = [x'] \iff x \sim_f x' (@thm-classes-partition (b)), and x \sim_f x' \iff f(x) = f(x')  ar f a function, bijective, f = \iota \circ  ar f \circ q, unique [x] = [x'] f(x) = f(x'): one class, one value, (Fn2), well defined f(x) = f(x') [x] = [x']: injective, the same equivalence read right to left y \in f(X), so y = f(a) with a \in X y =  ar f([a]): surjective -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Uniqueness: q is onto, so every class is [x] for some x; a second  ar f' with \iota \circ  ar f' \circ q = f has  ar f'([x]) = f(x) at every class. The proof writes this forwards. A function. Every element of X/{\sim_f} is [x] for some x \in X, and f(x) \in f(X) by @def-image; this gives (Fn1). Let [x] = [x']. By @thm-classes-partition (b), x \sim_f x', that is, f(x) = f(x'). So all representatives of one class give one value, which is (Fn2), and  ar f([x]) \coloneqq f(x) defines a function  ar f \colon X/{\sim_f} 	o f(X) (@def-function). Injective. Let  ar f([x]) =  ar f([x']), that is, f(x) = f(x'). Then x \sim_f x', and [x] = [x'] by @thm-classes-partition (b). Surjective. Let y \in f(X). By @def-image there is a \in X with f(a) = y, and then  ar f([a]) = f(a) = y. The factorization. Both f and \iota \circ  ar f \circ q have domain X and codomain Y, and for every x \in X, (\iota \circ  ar f \circ q)(x) = \iota igl(  ar f([x])  igr) = \iota igl( f(x)  igr) = f(x) , by @def-composition. Hence f = \iota \circ  ar f \circ q by @prp-function-equality. Uniqueness. Let  ar f' \colon X/{\sim_f} 	o f(X) satisfy f = \iota \circ  ar f' \circ q. Every element of X/{\sim_f} is [x] = q(x) for some x \in X, and  ar f'([x]) = \iota igl(  ar f'(q(x))  igr) = f(x) =  ar f([x]) , where the first equality holds because \iota sends each point to itself. The two functions have the same domain and codomain, so  ar f' =  ar f by @prp-function-equality. This proves the theorem. Read the factorization from left to right: every function is a surjection (q, onto by @def-quotient-set), followed by a bijection ( ar f), followed by an injection (\iota, which sends each point to itself, so different points stay different). All the identifying is done by q, all the renaming by  ar f, and all the enlarging of the target by \iota. The two properties of Section 1.5 sit at the two ends. The function f is injective exactly when q is: if f is injective and q(x) = q(x'), then x \sim_f x' by @thm-classes-partition (b), so f(x) = f(x') and x = x'; if q is injective and f(x) = f(x'), then x \sim_f x', so q(x) = q(x') by @thm-classes-partition (b), and x = x'. And f is surjective exactly when f(X) = Y, that is, when \iota = \id_Y. The middle map is a bijection onto the image, not onto the codomain. With target Y, the rule [x] \mapsto f(x) is still a well-defined injection, but it is surjective only when f is. For f(x) = x^2 on 
R, the rule [x] \mapsto x^2 maps the classes \{-x, x\} onto [0, \infty) and reaches no negative number of the codomain 
R. The factorization also explains a failure from Section 1.5. [Fractions as classes] Let f \colon 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} 	o 
Q, f(a, b) \coloneqq a/b. Describe \sim_f, the three maps of @thm-canonical-factorization, and decide whether “send a/b to its numerator a” passes through q. The relation. (a, b) \sim_f (c, d) means a/b = c/d, and since b, d 
e 0 this holds exactly when ad = bc, by the arithmetic of fractions. It is the relation of Exercise B1 in Section 4.2 (@exr-equivalence-relations-b1), now seen as the fiber relation of a function; that it is an equivalence relation is also immediate from @exm-fibres-of-function. The class of (1, 2) is the fiber over 	frac12: the pairs (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), \dots, all the ways of writing one half as a fraction. The three maps. The quotient map q sends a pair to its class, “the fraction a/b up to rewriting”. The map  ar f sends a class to the rational number its pairs all name. And f is onto 
Q, since every rational number is a/b for some a \in 
Z and b \in 
Z_{>0}; so f(X) = 
Q and \iota = \id_
Q. By @thm-canonical-factorization,  ar f is a bijection from the set of classes onto 
Q: a rational number “is” a class of fractions, and nothing is lost by identifying the two. The numerator. Let p(a, b) \coloneqq a. If p were g \circ q for some function g on the classes, then (a, b) \sim_f (c, d) would force p(a, b) = g([(a, b)]) = g([(c, d)]) = p(c, d). But (1, 2) \sim_f (2, 4), since 1 \cdot 4 = 2 \cdot 2, while p(1, 2) = 1 
e 2 = p(2, 4). So p does not pass through q, and no function on the classes, hence none on 
Q, sends each fraction to its numerator. This is the failure of @exm-not-a-function (b), located: the numerator is a function of the pair, not of its fiber. In @exm-fraction-map-factorization, which of q,  ar f, \iota are injective, and which are surjective? q is surjective, and not injective, since q(1, 2) = q(2, 4).  ar f is both, by @thm-canonical-factorization. \iota is injective, as every inclusion is; here it is \id_
Q, so it is also surjective. Functions out of a quotient Now (Q1). The canonical factorization built a function on the classes of \sim_f from f itself. Nothing in its first step needed the relation to come from f: what made [x] \mapsto f(x) a function was only that equivalent points have equal values. So the same argument works for any equivalence relation, as long as the function is constant on its classes. Functions out of a Quotient Let \sim be an equivalence relation on a set X, let q \colon X 	o X/{\sim} be its quotient map, and let g \colon X 	o Z be a function. 1. There is a function  ar g \colon X/{\sim} 	o Z with  ar g \circ q = g if and only if g is constant on classes: for all x, x' \in X, if x \sim x', then g(x) = g(x'). In that case  ar g is unique, and  ar g([x]) = g(x). 2. Suppose g is constant on classes. Then  ar g is injective if and only if, for all x, x' \in X, g(x) = g(x') implies x \sim x'. 3. Suppose g is constant on classes. Then  ar g is surjective if and only if g is surjective. This is the argument of @thm-canonical-factorization with \sim in place of \sim_f (@exm-method-well-definedness for the existence, q onto for the uniqueness). The new part is the forward direction of (a): if  ar g exists, equivalent points have one class, so g =  ar g \circ q gives them one value. For (b) and (c), translate statements about classes into statements about representatives with @thm-classes-partition (b). (a) (\Rightarrow) Suppose  ar g \circ q = g, and let x \sim x'. Then q(x) = [x] = [x'] = q(x') by @thm-classes-partition (b), so g(x) =  ar g(q(x)) =  ar g(q(x')) = g(x') . (\Leftarrow) Suppose g is constant on classes. Every element of X/{\sim} is [x] for some x \in X, with g(x) \in Z, which is (Fn1). If [x] = [x'], then x \sim x' by @thm-classes-partition (b), so g(x) = g(x'), which is (Fn2). Hence  ar g([x]) \coloneqq g(x) defines a function  ar g \colon X/{\sim} 	o Z (@def-function). Both  ar g \circ q and g have domain X and codomain Z, and ( ar g \circ q)(x) =  ar g([x]) = g(x) for every x \in X, so  ar g \circ q = g by @prp-function-equality. Uniqueness. If h \colon X/{\sim} 	o Z also satisfies h \circ q = g, then each element of X/{\sim} is q(x) for some x \in X, since q is onto (@def-quotient-set), and h(q(x)) = g(x) =  ar g(q(x)). So h =  ar g by @prp-function-equality. (b) By @def-injective,  ar g is injective when  ar g(C) =  ar g(D) implies C = D for all C, D \in X/{\sim}. Every class is [x] for some x \in X, and  ar g([x]) = g(x); so the condition reads: for all x, x' \in X, g(x) = g(x') implies [x] = [x']. By @thm-classes-partition (b), [x] = [x'] is x \sim x'. (c) By @def-surjective,  ar g is surjective when every z \in Z is  ar g(C) for some class C. Since every class is [x] for some x \in X, and  ar g([x]) = g(x), this says that every z \in Z is g(x) for some x \in X: that g is surjective. The canonical factorization is the case where \sim is \sim_f, with g the function X 	o f(X), x \mapsto f(x). That g is constant on the classes of \sim_f by the definition of \sim_f; the converse condition of (b) holds for the same reason, so  ar g is injective; and g is onto f(X) by @def-image, so  ar g is surjective by (c). The map  ar g is  ar f. “Constant on classes” runs from equivalence to equal values: x \sim x' \Rightarrow g(x) = g(x'). Its converse, g(x) = g(x') \Rightarrow x \sim x', is the injectivity condition of (b), and checking it instead proves nothing about existence. For congruence modulo 12 and g(a) = [a]_{24}, the converse holds, since 24 \mid a - a' gives 12 \mid a - a'; but 0 \equiv 12 \pmod{12} while [0]_{24} 
e [12]_{24}, so “[a]_{12} \mapsto [a]_{24}” is not a function. The theorem turns the check of @exm-method-well-definedness into a complete method: it says what the check buys, and how to read off injectivity and surjectivity afterwards. [Method: define a function on a quotient] Template. (1) Write the function g on X that the rule computes from a representative. (2) Check that g is constant on classes (@exm-method-well-definedness). (3) Conclude by @thm-functions-out-of-quotient:  ar g exists, is unique, and  ar g \circ q = g. (4) Read injectivity of  ar g as “equal values force equivalence”, and surjectivity of  ar g as surjectivity of g. When to use it. Maps out of 
Z/n, out of classes of fractions, out of any “the same in some respect”. The usual failure. Proving (4)’s converse condition instead of (2); a g not defined on all of X; running the check for a map into a quotient, which needs none: compose with q. Here is the method three times, twice on the clock and once on 
Z/2. As in Section 4.2, the subscript in [a]_n names the modulus: it is the class of a in 
Z/n. [Maps out of the clock] (a) Let r \colon 
Z 	o \{0, 1\} send each integer to its remainder on division by 2. Show that “[a]_{12} \mapsto r(a)” is a function 
Z/12 	o \{0, 1\}, and decide whether it is injective and whether it is surjective. (b) Do the same for “[a]_2 \mapsto r(a)”, from 
Z/2. (c) Show that “[a]_{12} \mapsto [a + 1]_{12}” is a bijection t \colon 
Z/12 	o 
Z/12. The remainder r(a) is well defined by the uniqueness in @thm-division-algorithm. We use the remainder test of Section 4.2, after @prp-integers-mod-n: a \equiv a' \pmod{n} if and only if a and a' leave the same remainder on division by n. (a) Step (1). The rule computes r(a) from the representative a, so g = r. Step (2). Let a \equiv a' \pmod{12}, so a - a' = 12k with k \in 
Z. Then a - a' = 2(6k) with 6k \in 
Z, so a \equiv a' \pmod 2, and r(a) = r(a') by the remainder test. Step (3). By @thm-functions-out-of-quotient (a),  ar r([a]_{12}) \coloneqq r(a) is a function 
Z/12 	o \{0, 1\}: “is the hour even?” is a question about the hour. Step (4). It is surjective by @thm-functions-out-of-quotient (c), since r(0) = 0 and r(1) = 1. It is not injective, by part (b) of the theorem: r(0) = r(2), but 0 
ot\equiv 2 \pmod{12}, since 2 - 0 = 2 lies strictly between 0 and 12 and so is not a multiple of 12 (@prp-integers-closed (c)). So  ar r([0]_{12}) =  ar r([2]_{12}) with [0]_{12} 
e [2]_{12}. (b) Step (2). If a \equiv a' \pmod 2, then r(a) = r(a') by the remainder test. Step (4). Conversely, r(a) = r(a') gives a \equiv a' \pmod 2, again by the remainder test, so the induced map 
Z/2 	o \{0, 1\} is injective by @thm-functions-out-of-quotient (b), and surjective by part (c), as in (a). It is a bijection: the two classes of 
Z/2 are the even and the odd integers, matched with the remainders 0 and 1. (c) Steps (1)–(3). Here g(a) \coloneqq [a + 1]_{12}, a function 
Z 	o 
Z/12. If a - a' = 12k, then (a + 1) - (a' + 1) = a - a' = 12k, so [a + 1]_{12} = [a' + 1]_{12} (@thm-classes-partition (b)). So t([a]_{12}) \coloneqq [a + 1]_{12} is a function 
Z/12 	o 
Z/12, the tick of the clock. A bijection. In the same way, (a - 1) - (a' - 1) = a - a', so s([a]_{12}) \coloneqq [a - 1]_{12} is a function 
Z/12 	o 
Z/12. For every a \in 
Z, s(t([a])) = s([a + 1]) = [a] and t(s([a])) = t([a - 1]) = [a]; so s \circ t and t \circ s are the identity of 
Z/12 (@prp-function-equality), and t is a bijection with inverse s (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse). In (c) the codomain is itself a quotient set, and the check compared outputs as classes. In (a) and (b) the codomain is \{0, 1\}, and outputs were compared as numbers. Step (2) of the method is the same check in both cases; only the meaning of “equal outputs” changes with the codomain. If f \colon X 	o Y is onto, then \iota = \id_Y, and @thm-canonical-factorization reads f =  ar f \circ q with  ar f \colon X/{\sim_f} 	o Y a bijection. So every surjection is a quotient map up to renaming the classes: to give an onto map out of X is to give an equivalence relation on X and names for its classes. In the other direction, q itself is onto, so it has a right inverse c \colon X/{\sim} 	o X by @thm-surjection-right-inverse, which uses @ax-choice. Then q(c(C)) = C, that is, c(C) \in C for every class C: a right inverse of a quotient map is a choice of one representative from each class. For 
Z/n no axiom is needed, since the remainder picks one, c([a]) \coloneqq the remainder of a on division by n (@prp-integers-mod-n). Is the rule [a]_{10} \mapsto [a]_5 a well-defined function 
Z/10 	o 
Z/5? Is it injective? Is it surjective? Take g \colon 
Z 	o 
Z/5, g(a) = [a]_5. Well defined: yes. If a - a' = 10k with k \in 
Z, then a - a' = 5(2k), so g(a) = g(a') (this was Exercise B3 (c) of Section 4.2). Injective: no. g(0) = [0]_5 = [5]_5 = g(5), but 0 
ot\equiv 5 \pmod{10}, since 0 < 5 < 10; by @thm-functions-out-of-quotient (b), the classes [0]_{10} 
e [5]_{10} have one image. Surjective: yes, by (c), because g is the quotient map of congruence modulo 5, which is onto. [Looking ahead] Later in this chapter, in the section on permutations and iteration, the tick t of @exm-clock-maps is applied again and again; its iterates carry each hour once round the whole clock. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. For f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = x^2 - 1, find the fibers over 3, over -1 and over -2. Which of them are classes of \sim_f? 2. Let f \colon \{a, b, c, d\} 	o \{1, 2, 3\} send a and c to 1, and b and d to 3. Write down X/{\sim_f}, f(X),  ar f and \iota of @thm-canonical-factorization. 3. Which of the functions a \mapsto [a]_2, a \mapsto [a]_8 and a \mapsto [a^2]_8, from 
Z, are constant on the classes of congruence modulo 4? (a) x^2 - 1 = 3 means x^2 = 4, so the fiber over 3 is \{-2, 2\}. x^2 - 1 = -1 means x^2 = 0, so the fiber over -1 is \{0\}. x^2 - 1 = -2 would need x^2 = -1, and no real square is negative, so the fiber over -2 is \emptyset. The first two are classes, since 3 = f(2) and -1 = f(0) lie in f(
R); the empty fiber is not a class, because -2 
otin f(
R) and every class is non-empty (@thm-classes-partition (a)). (b) The fibers over the values are \{a, c\} and \{b, d\}, so X/{\sim_f} = \{ \{a, c\}, \{b, d\} \}. The image is f(X) = \{1, 3\}. The bijection is  ar f(\{a, c\}) = 1,  ar f(\{b, d\}) = 3, and \iota \colon \{1, 3\} 	o \{1, 2, 3\} sends 1 \mapsto 1 and 3 \mapsto 3. The value 2 is in the codomain but outside the image, which is why \iota is not surjective. (c) Let a' = a + 4k with k \in 
Z, the general element of the class of a modulo 4. a \mapsto [a]_2: yes, since a' - a = 4k = 2(2k). a \mapsto [a]_8: no. 0 \equiv 4 \pmod 4, but [0]_8 
e [4]_8, since 4 - 0 = 4 lies strictly between 0 and 8. a \mapsto [a^2]_8: yes, since a'^2 - a^2 = 8ak + 16k^2 = 8(ak + 2k^2), with ak + 2k^2 \in 
Z. B. Practice [B1: The absolute value, factored] Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = \abs{x}. Describe the classes of \sim_f, the image f(
R) and the bijection  ar f. Then show that [x] \mapsto x^2 is a well-defined injective function 
R/{\sim_f} 	o 
R. The pieces. \abs{x} = \abs{x'} holds exactly when x' = x or x' = -x, so the class of x is \{-x, x\}, which is \{0\} for x = 0. Every value \abs{x} is \ge 0, and every t \ge 0 is \abs{t}, so f(
R) = [0, \infty). The bijection of @thm-canonical-factorization is  ar f(\{-x, x\}) = \abs{x}, from the set of classes onto [0, \infty). Well defined. Let g(x) \coloneqq x^2. Since x^2 = \abs{x}^2, x \sim_f x' gives x^2 = \abs{x}^2 = \abs{x'}^2 = x'^2. So g is constant on classes, and [x] \mapsto x^2 is a function by @thm-functions-out-of-quotient (a). Injective. Let x^2 = x'^2. Then \abs{x}^2 = \abs{x'}^2 with \abs{x}, \abs{x'} \ge 0, and @fd1:thm-squares-order, applied in both orders, gives \abs{x} \le \abs{x'} and \abs{x'} \le \abs{x}. So \abs{x} = \abs{x'}, that is, x \sim_f x'. By @thm-functions-out-of-quotient (b), the induced function is injective. (It is not surjective onto 
R: no class goes to -1.) [B2: Same fibers] Let f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon X 	o Z be functions. Prove that \sim_f = \sim_g if and only if there is a bijection h \colon f(X) 	o g(X) with g(x) = h(f(x)) for every x \in X. (\Leftarrow) Let h be such a bijection, and let x, x' \in X. If f(x) = f(x'), then g(x) = h(f(x)) = h(f(x')) = g(x'). If g(x) = g(x'), then h(f(x)) = h(f(x')), and f(x) = f(x') because h is injective. So x \sim_f x' \iff x \sim_g x': the two relations contain the same pairs, and are equal (@def-set-equality). (\Rightarrow) Suppose \sim_f = \sim_g; write \sim for both, so the two quotient sets are one set X/{\sim}. By @thm-canonical-factorization there are bijections  ar f \colon X/{\sim} 	o f(X) and  ar g \colon X/{\sim} 	o g(X) with  ar f([x]) = f(x) and  ar g([x]) = g(x). The inverse  ar f^{-1} \colon f(X) 	o X/{\sim} is a bijection (@def-inverse-function, @thm-bijection-iff-inverse), so h \coloneqq  ar g \circ  ar f^{-1} \colon f(X) 	o g(X) is a bijection by @thm-composition-injective-surjective (c). For every x \in X,  ar f^{-1}(f(x)) = [x], since  ar f([x]) = f(x); so h(f(x)) =  ar g([x]) = g(x). [B3: A coarser relation] Let \sim and \approx be equivalence relations on a set X such that x \sim x' implies x \approx x'. Show that [x]_\sim \mapsto [x]_\approx is a well-defined surjection X/{\sim} 	o X/{\approx}. Give the instance 
Z/12 	o 
Z/4. Apply @thm-functions-out-of-quotient to the relation \sim and to g \coloneqq q_\approx \colon X 	o X/{\approx}, the quotient map of \approx. It is constant on \sim-classes: if x \sim x', then x \approx x' by hypothesis, so [x]_\approx = [x']_\approx by @thm-classes-partition (b). By part (a), [x]_\sim \mapsto [x]_\approx is a function, and by part (c) it is surjective, since q_\approx is onto (@def-quotient-set). For 
Z/12 	o 
Z/4, the hypothesis is: 12 \mid a - a' implies 4 \mid a - a'. This holds by @prp-divides-transitive, since 4 \mid 12 (12 = 3 \cdot 4). So [a]_{12} \mapsto [a]_4 is a well-defined surjection: each hour is sent to its position within a block of four hours (0, 4 and 8 go to [0]_4). [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove or disprove each statement. 1. If g \colon X 	o Z is constant on the classes of an equivalence relation \sim on X and g is surjective, then  ar g \colon X/{\sim} 	o Z is a bijection. 2. For every function f \colon X 	o Y, \card{f(X)} = \card{X/{\sim_f}}. 3. If f \colon X 	o Y is injective, then the quotient map X 	o X/{\sim_f} is a bijection. 4. The rule [a]_4 \mapsto [3a]_{12} is a bijection 
Z/4 	o 
Z/12. 5. If f, g \colon X 	o Y satisfy \sim_f = \sim_g, then f = g. (a) False. Let X = \{1, 2\}, let \sim be equality, and let g \colon X 	o \{0\} be the constant function. It is constant on classes (every function is, for equality) and surjective. But  ar g([1]) = 0 =  ar g([2]) with [1] = \{1\} 
e \{2\} = [2], so  ar g is not injective. Surjectivity of g gives surjectivity of  ar g only, by @thm-functions-out-of-quotient (c). (b) True. This is @prp-fibres-partition (b). (c) True. If x \sim_f x', then f(x) = f(x'), so x = x' by injectivity; hence [x] = \{x\} for every x. The quotient map q is injective: q(x) = q(x') gives x \sim_f x' by @thm-classes-partition (b), so x = x'. And q is onto by @def-quotient-set. (d) False. Let g(a) \coloneqq [3a]_{12}. It is constant on classes modulo 4: if a - a' = 4k, then 3a - 3a' = 12k. The induced map is injective by @thm-functions-out-of-quotient (b): if [3a]_{12} = [3a']_{12}, then 3(a - a') = 12k for some k \in 
Z, so a - a' = 4k after cancelling 3. But it is not surjective, so by part (c) of the theorem, look for a class that g misses. If [1]_{12} = [3a]_{12}, then 1 - 3a = 12k for some k \in 
Z, so 1 = 3(a + 4k) and 3 \mid 1. That is impossible: 1 = 0 \cdot 3 + 1 with 0 \le 1 < 3, so by the uniqueness in @thm-division-algorithm the remainder of 1 on division by 3 is 1, not 0. So [1]_{12} is missed. (e) False. Take X = Y = 
R, f = \id_
R and g(x) = 2x. Both are injective, so \sim_f and \sim_g are both equality on 
R, but f(1) = 1 
e 2 = g(1). Equal fiber relations make the functions differ only by a renaming of values, which is Exercise B2. C. Going deeper [C1: Equal fibers] Let k, m, n \in 
N, let X be a set with n elements, and let f \colon X 	o \{1, \dots, k\} be a function such that the fiber f^{-1}(\{i\}) has exactly m elements for every i \in \{1, \dots, k\}. Prove that n = km. For k \in 
N, let P(k) be the statement: for every n \in 
N, every set X with n elements, and every f \colon X 	o \{1, \dots, k\} all of whose fibers over 1, \dots, k have m elements, n = km. We prove P(k) for every k by @fd1:ax-induction, with m fixed. Base case P(0). Here \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset, so f is a function X 	o \emptyset, and X = \emptyset by @prp-empty-function (b). Then n = 0: for n \ge 1, a bijection \{1, \dots, n\} 	o \emptyset would give 1 a value in \emptyset. So n = 0 = 0 \cdot m. Inductive step. Suppose P(k), and let X have n elements and f \colon X 	o \{1, \dots, k + 1\} have every fiber of m elements. Put X' \coloneqq f^{-1}(\{1, \dots, k\}) and F \coloneqq f^{-1}(\{k + 1\}). Every x \in X has f(x) \le k or f(x) = k + 1, and not both, so X = X' \cup F and X' \cap F = \emptyset. By @prp-subset-finite, X' has j elements for some j \in 
N. Let f' \colon X' 	o \{1, \dots, k\}, f'(x) \coloneqq f(x); this is a function, because f(x) \in \{1, \dots, k\} for x \in X'. For i \le k, its fiber is f'^{-1}(\{i\}) = \{ x \in X' : f(x) = i \} = f^{-1}(\{i\}), since every x with f(x) = i lies in X'; so it has m elements. By P(k), j = km. The fiber F has m elements by hypothesis, so @prp-disjoint-union-count gives that X = X' \cup F has km + m = (k + 1)m elements. Since X also has n elements, n = (k + 1)m by @cor-finite-size-unique. This proves P(k + 1). The statement says that a function whose fibers all have one size cuts X into equal piles, so the size of X is the number of piles times the pile size. With fibers of different sizes the same induction gives the sum of the fiber sizes. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: states the induction hypothesis with X and f quantified inside it. - 2: the base case k = 0: X = \emptyset and n = 0. - 3: the step: X' and F are disjoint with union X, the fibers of f' are fibers of f, and j = km. - 3: the conclusion by @prp-disjoint-union-count and @cor-finite-size-unique. Fatal errors (0 for the step): induction with X fixed; applying P(k) to a function whose fibers were not shown to have m elements. [C2: Find the error] A student proves the uniqueness clause of @thm-functions-out-of-quotient (a) as follows. (1) Suppose  ar g \colon X/{\sim} 	o Z and h \colon X/{\sim} 	o Z both satisfy  ar g \circ q = g and h \circ q = g. (2) Then  ar g \circ q = h \circ q. (3) The quotient map q is injective, so q can be cancelled on the right, and  ar g = h. Is the conclusion true? Which line fails, and why? Give a counterexample to the failing step, and repair the proof. The conclusion is true: it is the uniqueness clause, proved in the text. Lines (1) and (2) are correct. Line (3) fails twice. First, q is injective only when every class is a single point (the second reading after @thm-classes-partition), which the theorem does not assume. Second, even for an injective map p, u \circ p = v \circ p need not give u = v. Counterexample to the step. For congruence modulo 12 on 
Z, q(0) = [0] = [12] = q(12) with 0 
e 12, so q is not injective, and the claim “q is injective” is false in the very case the clock needs. Counterexample to the inference. The inclusion \iota \colon \{0\} 	o \{0, 1\} is injective; let u = \id_{\{0, 1\}} and v be the constant function 0. Then u \circ \iota = v \circ \iota but u 
e v. Repair. What cancels q on the right is that q is onto. Replace (3) by: “Let C \in X/{\sim}. Since q is surjective (@def-quotient-set), C = q(x) for some x \in X, and then  ar g(C) =  ar g(q(x)) = h(q(x)) = h(C) by (2). The two functions have the same domain and codomain, so  ar g = h by @prp-function-equality.” Injectivity of q would let one cancel q on the left, in q \circ u = q \circ v, which is a different situation. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says the conclusion is true. - 3: identifies line (3), and says either that q need not be injective or that injectivity does not license cancelling on the right (surjectivity does). - 2: gives a concrete non-injective quotient map, such as q(0) = q(12) modulo 12. - 3: repairs the proof by surjectivity of q: every class is q(x), where both functions take the value g(x). Fatal errors (0 for the step): calling the conclusion false; a repair that assumes classes are singletons. [C3: Exit check: depends only on f] Let f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon X 	o Z be functions such that, for all x, x' \in X, f(x) = f(x') implies g(x) = g(x'). 1. Prove that there is exactly one function h \colon f(X) 	o Z with g(x) = h(f(x)) for every x \in X. 2. For f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = x^2, decide whether g(x) = x^4 and whether g(x) = x^3 are of the form h \circ f for some function h \colon f(
R) 	o 
R. (a) Existence. The hypothesis says that g is constant on the classes of \sim_f. By @thm-functions-out-of-quotient (a), there is a function  ar g \colon X/{\sim_f} 	o Z with  ar g([x]) = g(x). By @thm-canonical-factorization,  ar f \colon X/{\sim_f} 	o f(X),  ar f([x]) = f(x), is a bijection, so it has an inverse  ar f^{-1} \colon f(X) 	o X/{\sim_f} (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse), and  ar f^{-1}(f(x)) = [x] for every x \in X. Put h \coloneqq  ar g \circ  ar f^{-1}. Then, for every x \in X, h(f(x)) =  ar g igl(  ar f^{-1}(f(x))  igr) =  ar g([x]) = g(x) . Uniqueness. Let h, h' \colon f(X) 	o Z both satisfy the condition. Let y \in f(X); by @def-image, y = f(x) for some x \in X. Then h(y) = g(x) = h'(y). The two functions have the same domain and codomain, so h = h' by @prp-function-equality. (b) g(x) = x^4 is of this form: x^4 = (x^2)^2, so h(t) \coloneqq t^2 on f(
R) works, and by (a) it is the only such h. g(x) = x^3 is not: if x^3 = h(x^2) for every x, then 1 = 1^3 = h(1) = h((-1)^2) = (-1)^3 = -1, which is false. The hypothesis of (a) fails at the pair 1, -1: f(1) = f(-1), while g(1) 
e g(-1). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: recognizes the hypothesis as “g is constant on the classes of \sim_f” and obtains  ar g with  ar g([x]) = g(x) (or defines h(f(x)) \coloneqq g(x) directly and checks it is well defined). - 2: uses the bijection  ar f onto f(X), or an equivalent argument, so that h is defined at every point of f(X) and only there. - 2: verifies h(f(x)) = g(x) for every x. - 2: uniqueness, using that every point of f(X) is a value f(x). - 2: part (b): h(t) = t^2 for x^4; the witness pair 1, -1 for x^3. A direct proof that defines h(y) \coloneqq g(x) for any x with f(x) = y earns the first two steps if it checks that the value does not depend on the choice of x (that is the hypothesis) and that every y \in f(X) has such an x. Fatal errors (0 for the step): defining h on all of Y without a value for points outside f(X); proving the converse implication g(x) = g(x') \Rightarrow f(x) = f(x') instead of using the hypothesis.

title: 5.3 Binary Operations
content:
Binary Operations Sections 5.1 and 5.2 built new functions from old ones by cutting, gluing and factoring. This section looks at functions of a special shape: functions that take two elements of a set and return a third element of the same set, such as + on 
Z, \cup on \powerset{X} and \circ on the functions from a set to itself. We name the properties such an operation may have, one at a time, and ask what each property buys on its own. The central answers, uniqueness of identities and of inverses, are short proofs by one method, computing a single expression in two ways; the rest are proved by checking candidates. All of them work at once for numbers, for sets, for functions and for the hours of the clock. Brackets Nobody writes brackets in 2 + 3 + 4: whether we add 2 + 3 first or 3 + 4 first, the answer is 9. Subtraction is different. Reading 2 - 3 - 4 from the left gives (2 - 3) - 4 = -5, and from the right gives 2 - (3 - 4) = 3. Powers behave like subtraction: 2^{(3^2)} = 2^9 = 512, while (2^3)^2 = 8^2 = 64. School arithmetic settles this by convention (subtraction from the left, towers of powers from the top), and a convention is needed exactly because the bracketing changes the answer. The same questions arise far from numbers. For subsets of a set X, is (A \cup B) \cup C the same set as A \cup (B \cup C)? For functions from X to itself, is h \circ (g \circ f) the same function as (h \circ g) \circ f? On the clock 
Z/12 of Section 4.2, is there an hour that changes nothing when added, as 0 does for integers, and can every hour be undone? Each of these questions asks whether some rule of arithmetic holds for some way of combining two things into a third. The aim of this section is to separate the rules and to find out what each rule gives on its own.
