Here is a test question to keep in mind: can a set with an operation have two different elements that both behave like 0? For + on

[Associative, Commutative, Identity, Inverse] Let \ast be an operation on a set X. 1. \ast is associative if (x \ast y) \ast z = x \ast (y \ast z) for all x, y, z \in X. 2. \ast is commutative if x \ast y = y \ast x for all x, y \in X. 3. An element e \in X is a left identity of \ast if e \ast x = x for every x \in X; a right identity if x \ast e = x for every x \in X; and an identity if it is both. 4. Suppose \ast has an identity e, and let x \in X. An element y \in X is an inverse of x if x \ast y = e and y \ast x = e. The element x is invertible if it has an inverse. (d) To prove a = b for objects known only through equations, find one expression that the equations about a reduce to a and those about b reduce to b, and write a = \dots = m = \dots = b with a reason at each step (@exm-method-two-ways). In @prp-operation-inverse-unique the expression is (y \ast x) \ast z, which equals z as written and, regrouped as y \ast (x \ast z), equals y. B. Practice [B1: Deciding properties] On 
R, let x \ast y \coloneqq x + y - xy. Determine whether \ast is associative and whether it is commutative, find its identity, and find which elements are invertible, with their inverses. Justify your answer. Associative. Expanding both sides,  egin{aligned} (x \ast y) \ast z &= (x + y - xy) + z - (x + y - xy)z \ &= x + y + z - xy - xz - yz + xyz , \ x \ast (y \ast z) &= x + (y + z - yz) - x(y + z - yz) \ &= x + y + z - xy - xz - yz + xyz . \end{aligned} The two results agree, so \ast is associative. (Both are unchanged by any rearrangement of x, y, z.) Commutative. x + y - xy = y + x - yx. Identity. 0 \ast x = 0 + x - 0 = x, and x \ast 0 = x by commutativity; so 0 is the identity, unique by @prp-operation-identity-unique. Inverses. We need y with x + y - xy = 0 (the other side follows by commutativity), that is, y(1 - x) = -x. If x 
e 1, this has the solution y = x/(x - 1): indeed x + 	frac{x}{x - 1} - 	frac{x^2}{x - 1} = 	frac{x(x - 1) + x - x^2}{x - 1} = 0. If x = 1, then 1 \ast y = 1 + y - y = 1 
e 0 for every y, so 1 has no inverse. So every x 
e 1 is invertible, with inverse x/(x - 1) under \ast, and 1 is not. A remark. 1 - x \ast y = (1 - x)(1 - y). For u, v \in \{0, 1\}, u \ast v = u + v - uv is the indicator rule for a union, @prp-indicator-arithmetic (c): \ind_{A \cup B}(x) = \ind_A(x) \ast \ind_B(x). [B2: Every square is the identity] Let \ast be an associative operation on a set X with identity e, such that x \ast x = e for every x \in X. Prove that \ast is commutative. Check the hypothesis for 	riangle on \powerset{X}. Let x \in X. The equation x \ast x = e says that x is an inverse of itself, from both sides; by @prp-operation-inverse-unique, x^{-1} = x. Now let x, y \in X. By the hypothesis applied to x \ast y, and by @prp-operation-inverse-rules (c), x \ast y = (x \ast y)^{-1} = y^{-1} \ast x^{-1} = y \ast x . For 	riangle: it is associative (@exm-symmetric-difference-associative) with identity \emptyset, and A 	riangle A = \emptyset for every A \subseteq X (the Quick check after @prp-operation-inverse-rules). So 	riangle is commutative, which can also be read off its definition, since (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A) is symmetric in A and B. [B3: Two kinds of inverse] In 
R^{
R}, find, if they exist, the inverses of f(x) = x^3 + 1 under composition and under pointwise +, and the inverses of g(x) = x^2 under composition and under pointwise \cdot. Justify each answer. f under \circ. Let h(x) \coloneqq \sqrt[3]{x - 1}, the real cube root. Then f(h(x)) = (x - 1) + 1 = x and h(f(x)) = \sqrt[3]{x^3} = x, so h is the inverse (@prp-composition-operation). f under +. The identity is c_0, and x \mapsto -x^3 - 1 is the inverse: (x^3 + 1) + (-x^3 - 1) = 0 at every x (@prp-pointwise-operations (c)). g under \circ. None: g(1) = 1 = g(-1), so g is not injective, hence not bijective, hence not invertible under \circ by @prp-composition-operation. g under \cdot. None: the value g(0) = 0 has no inverse under multiplication of reals (0 \cdot y = 0 
e 1), so by @prp-pointwise-operations (c) g is not invertible. [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove or disprove each statement. Throughout, \ast is an operation on a set X. 1. Every left identity of \ast equals every right identity of \ast. 2. \ast has at most one left identity. 3. If \ast is associative with identity, x is invertible and x \ast y = x \ast z, then y = z. 4. If \ast is associative with identity e and x \ast y = e, then y \ast x = e. 5. A commutative operation with an identity is associative. (a) True. This is @prp-operation-identity-unique. (b) False. For x \ast y \coloneqq y on X = \{1, 2\}, both 1 and 2 are left identities, as in Exercise A1 (c). (c) True, by computing (x^{-1} \ast x) \ast y, regrouped as x^{-1} \ast (x \ast y), in two ways (@exm-method-two-ways), with associativity at the second and fourth steps: y = (x^{-1} \ast x) \ast y = x^{-1} \ast (x \ast y) = x^{-1} \ast (x \ast z) = (x^{-1} \ast x) \ast z = z . (d) False. Take X = 
N^{
N} under composition, associative with identity \id_{
N} (@prp-composition-operation). Let s(n) \coloneqq n + 1, and p(n) \coloneqq n - 1 for n \ge 1, p(0) \coloneqq 0: the successor map of Section 1.6 and a left inverse of it. Then p \circ s = \id_{
N}, since p(n + 1) = n. But (s \circ p)(0) = s(0) = 1 
e 0, so s \circ p 
e \id_{
N}. With x = p and y = s, x \circ y = e and y \circ x 
e e. (e) False. The operation of @exm-two-inverses is commutative with identity e, and not associative. C. Going deeper [C1: Four factors] Let \ast be an associative operation on a set X, and let a, b, c, d \in X. Writing uv for u \ast v, show that the five bracketings ((ab)c)d, \quad (a(bc))d, \quad (ab)(cd), \quad a((bc)d), \quad a(b(cd)) are all equal. We show that each equals ((ab)c)d. Each step is one use of associativity, (xy)z = x(yz), with x, y, z chosen as stated. - (a(bc))d = ((ab)c)d: associativity with x = a, y = b, z = c gives a(bc) = (ab)c, and then both sides are that element times d. - (ab)(cd) = ((ab)c)d: associativity with x = ab, y = c, z = d. - a((bc)d) = (a(bc))d: associativity with x = a, y = bc, z = d; and (a(bc))d = ((ab)c)d by the first item. - a(b(cd)) = (ab)(cd): associativity with x = a, y = b, z = cd; and (ab)(cd) = ((ab)c)d by the second item. So all five bracketings are equal. That every bracketing of any finite number of factors gives the same element is true as well; its proof is an induction on the number of factors, not carried out here, and this chapter regroups longer composites only by repeated use of the three-factor law. [C2: Find the error] Let \ast be an operation on a set X with identity e. A student argues: (1) Let y and z be inverses of x. (2) Then x \ast y = e and x \ast z = e, so x \ast y = x \ast z. (3) Cancelling x on the left, y = z. (4) Hence an element has at most one inverse. 1. Which line fails, and which hypothesis does it hide? 2. Show that without that hypothesis the step of the failing line is false. (a) Line (3) fails. “Cancelling x” is the statement of Exercise B4 (c), which holds when \ast is associative and x is invertible; its proof regroups x^{-1} \ast (x \ast y) as (x^{-1} \ast x) \ast y, and that is associativity. The statement here does not assume associativity, so line (3) cites a fact that is not available: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. Lines (1) and (2) are correct, and with associativity added the argument becomes a correct proof of @prp-operation-inverse-unique. (b) In @exm-two-inverses, which has an identity and is not associative, a \ast a = e = a \ast b, so a \ast a = a \ast b, and yet a 
e b. Cancelling a on the left is false there, and so is the conclusion (4): a has the two inverses a and b. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: names line (3) as the step that fails. - 3: names associativity as the hidden hypothesis, and says where cancellation uses it. - 4: gives an operation with identity, not associative, and an invertible element x with x \ast y = x \ast z and y 
e z (for instance y, z two inverses of x), each equation checked. A different counterexample to cancellation earns the 4 points if its table is given and the failure of associativity is shown. Fatal errors (0 for the step): naming line (2) or line (4); a counterexample that is associative, or that has no identity, or whose element x is not invertible. [C3: Transport by a bijection] Let \varphi \colon X 	o Y be a bijection, and let \ast be an operation on Y. For x, x' \in X, define x \star x' \coloneqq \varphi^{-1} igl(\varphi(x) \ast \varphi(x') igr) . 1. Show that \star is an operation on X with \varphi(x \star x') = \varphi(x) \ast \varphi(x') for all x, x' \in X. 2. Show that \star is associative if and only if \ast is. 3. Compute \star for X = Y = 
R, \varphi(x) = 1 - x and \ast = \cdot. (a) The inverse function \varphi^{-1} \colon Y 	o X exists by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, so the right-hand side is one element of X for each pair, and \star is an operation on X. Applying \varphi and using \varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = \id_Y (@def-inverse-function) gives \varphi(x \star x') = \varphi(x) \ast \varphi(x'). (b) (\Leftarrow) Let \ast be associative and x, y, z \in X. By (a), applied twice on each side, \varphi igl((x \star y) \star z igr) = (\varphi(x) \ast \varphi(y)) \ast \varphi(z) = \varphi(x) \ast (\varphi(y) \ast \varphi(z)) = \varphi igl(x \star (y \star z) igr) , and \varphi is injective, so (x \star y) \star z = x \star (y \star z). (\Rightarrow) Let \star be associative and u, v, w \in Y. Since \varphi is surjective, u = \varphi(x), v = \varphi(y), w = \varphi(z) for some x, y, z \in X, and the same display read from the outside in gives (u \ast v) \ast w = \varphi((x \star y) \star z) = \varphi(x \star (y \star z)) = u \ast (v \ast w). (c) \varphi \circ \varphi = \id_{
R}, since 1 - (1 - x) = x, so \varphi^{-1} = \varphi (@def-inverse-function). Hence x \star x' = 1 - (1 - x)(1 - x') = x + x' - xx' , the operation of Exercise B1. Its identity 0 = \varphi(1) and its one non-invertible element 1 = \varphi(0) are the images of the identity 1 and of the non-invertible 0 of multiplication.

title: 5.4 Permutations and Iteration
content:
Permutations and Iteration Sections 5.1–5.3 built new functions from old ones: by cutting a domain down, by gluing pieces together, by passing to a quotient, and by combining two functions with an operation. This section does the simplest thing that can be done with a function whose codomain is its own domain: it applies the function again, and again. For a bijection, going forwards and backwards sorts the set into orbits, and on a finite set each orbit is a cycle. We prove that a bijection of a finite set, repeated often enough, gives back the identity, and we say after how many steps. Then we see what is left of this when the map is not a bijection. Shuffling twelve cards Lay twelve cards in a row and number the positions 0, 1, \dots, 11. Cut the row into three piles of four: positions 0–3, positions 4–7, positions 8–11. Now deal them back: take the first card of each pile in turn, then the second card of each pile, and so on. The new row holds the cards from the old positions 0, \ 4, \ 8, \ 1, \ 5, \ 9, \ 2, \ 6, \ 10, \ 3, \ 7, \ 11 , in that order. So the card that was at position 4 is now at position 1, and the card that was at position 1 is now at position 3. The card at old position i moves to the new position \sigma(i), where \sigma(i) =  egin{cases} 3i & 	ext{if } 0 \le i \le 3, \ 3i - 11 & 	ext{if } 4 \le i \le 7, \ 3i - 22 & 	ext{if } 8 \le i \le 11 . \end{cases} Check one card from each pile: card 2 lands at 6, card 5 at 15 - 11 = 4, card 10 at 30 - 22 = 8, as the row above says. The three pieces \{0, \dots, 3\}, \{4, \dots, 7\}, \{8, \dots, 11\} are disjoint and cover the positions, so \sigma is a gluing with nothing to check on overlaps (@exm-method-gluing). Now shuffle again by the same rule. After two shuffles the card from position i is at \sigma(\sigma(i)). Follow card 1 through the shuffles: it goes to 3, then 9, then 27 - 22 = 5, then 15 - 11 = 4, then 12 - 11 = 1. Card 2 goes to 6, 7, 10, 8, and back to 2. Cards 0 and 11 never move. These are 1 + 1 + 5 + 5 = 12 cards, every card of the deck, and each is back in its place after five shuffles. The deck is in its starting order. Was that luck? Three questions organize the section. Does every shuffle of a finite deck, repeated, bring the deck back? After how many shuffles? And what is left of the answer when the rule is not a shuffle, for instance when it sends two positions to one? Permutations and iterates A shuffle sends every position to a position, sends no two positions to the same one, and fills every position. That is a bijection from the set of positions to itself. [Permutation] Let X be a set. A permutation of X is a bijection \sigma \colon X 	o X. The set of all permutations of X is written S_X; it is a subset of X^X, the set of all functions X 	o X. For a finite set, a function X 	o X can be written as a two-line table: the elements of X in the top row, and under each element its image. For instance,  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} is the function on \{1, 2, 3\} with 1 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 3, 3 \mapsto 1. It is a table, not a matrix: nothing is multiplied. Such a function is a permutation exactly when its bottom row lists every element of X once: “every element appears” is surjectivity, and “no element twice” is injectivity. The hook’s shuffle is the table with top row 0, \dots, 11 and bottom row 0, 3, 6, 9, 1, 4, 7, 10, 2, 5, 8, 11. The two permutations of \{1, 2\} are the identity and the swap 1 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 1. Section 5.3 made composition an operation on X^X (@prp-composition-operation). The permutations are closed under it, and they keep everything that operation has. [Permutations under Composition] Let X be a set. 1. If \sigma, 	au \in S_X, then \sigma \circ 	au \in S_X. 2. \id_X \in S_X. 3. If \sigma \in S_X, then \sigma^{-1} \in S_X, and \sigma \circ \sigma^{-1} = \id_X = \sigma^{-1} \circ \sigma. Hence S_X is closed under \circ, and \circ is an associative operation on S_X with identity \id_X, in which every element \sigma is invertible, with inverse \sigma^{-1}. (a) is @thm-composition-injective-surjective (c). (b) \id_X \circ \id_X = \id_X, so \id_X is a two-sided inverse of itself, and it is bijective by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. (c) Since \sigma is bijective, it has the inverse \sigma^{-1} with \sigma^{-1} \circ \sigma = \id_X and \sigma \circ \sigma^{-1} = \id_X (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse, @def-inverse-function). Read the other way round, the same two equations say that \sigma is a two-sided inverse of \sigma^{-1}, so \sigma^{-1} is bijective by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. By (a), S_X is closed under \circ, so \circ restricted to S_X 	imes S_X is an operation on S_X (@def-binary-operation). Associativity holds on all of X^X (@prp-composition-operation), so in particular on S_X; \id_X lies in S_X by (b) and is an identity there; and by (c) each \sigma \in S_X has an inverse \sigma^{-1} that lies in S_X. So everything Section 5.3 proved for an associative operation with an identity applies to S_X. For instance, @prp-operation-inverse-rules (c) gives (\sigma \circ 	au)^{-1} = 	au^{-1} \circ \sigma^{-1}: undo the second shuffle first. Composing a function with itself needs only that its codomain is its domain; bijectivity is not needed. Shuffling twice is \sigma \circ \sigma, and “apply f a total of n times” is a definition by recursion. [Iterates] Let X be a set and f \colon X 	o X. The iterates f^n \colon X 	o X, for n \in 
N, are defined by f^0 \coloneqq \id_X , \qquad f^{n+1} \coloneqq f \circ f^n . For \sigma \in S_X and n \in 
N, we also set \sigma^{-n} \coloneqq (\sigma^{-1})^n. The definition is an instance of @thm-recursion, applied to the set X^X with the starting value \id_X and the step g \colon 
N 	imes X^X 	o X^X, g(n, h) \coloneqq f \circ h: there is exactly one sequence n \mapsto f^n in X^X with these two properties. Unwinding, f^1 = f \circ \id_X = f, f^2 = f \circ f, f^3 = f \circ (f \circ f), and f^n(x) is “apply f to x, n times”. For a permutation the two clauses do not clash: \sigma^{-0} = (\sigma^{-1})^0 = \id_X = \sigma^0, and (\sigma^{-1})^1 = \sigma^{-1} is the inverse function. So \sigma^k has one meaning for every k \in 
Z. As Section 5.3 warned, f^n is always an iterate in this book, never the pointwise power x \mapsto f(x)^n. The definition adds one f at a time, on the left. The first thing to prove is that blocks of f’s can be moved around as the notation suggests. [Laws of Iterates] Let X be a set, f \colon X 	o X, and m, n \in 
N. 1. f^{m+n} = f^m \circ f^n. 2. (f^m)^n = f^{mn}. 3. If \sigma \in S_X, then \sigma^k \in S_X for every k \in 
Z; \sigma^n \circ \sigma^{-n} = \id_X = \sigma^{-n} \circ \sigma^n; and \sigma^{k + l} = \sigma^k \circ \sigma^l for all k, l \in 
Z. Each law is an equation between iterates, and the definition only tells us how to peel one f off the left. So we induct on the exponent that appears first, peel one f, and use the induction hypothesis on what is left. For (c) the new feature is the sign: \sigma^{-n} undoes \sigma^n, and a mixed sum k + l is handled by canceling the overlap. (a) Fix n and induct on m (@fd1:ax-induction). For m = 0, f^{0+n} = f^n = \id_X \circ f^n = f^0 \circ f^n by @prp-composition-associative. Suppose f^{m+n} = f^m \circ f^n. Then, by @def-iterate, the induction hypothesis and @prp-composition-associative, f^{(m+1)+n} = f \circ f^{m+n} = f \circ (f^m \circ f^n) = (f \circ f^m) \circ f^n = f^{m+1} \circ f^n . (b) Induct on n. For n = 0, (f^m)^0 = \id_X = f^0 = f^{m \cdot 0}. If (f^m)^n = f^{mn}, then (f^m)^{n+1} = f^m \circ (f^m)^n = f^m \circ f^{mn} = f^{m + mn} by (a), and m + mn = m(n + 1). (c) First, \sigma^n \in S_X for n \in 
N, by induction: \sigma^0 = \id_X \in S_X, and \sigma^{n+1} = \sigma \circ \sigma^n \in S_X by @prp-permutations-closed (a). Since \sigma^{-1} \in S_X (@prp-permutations-closed (c)), the same induction gives \sigma^{-n} = (\sigma^{-1})^n \in S_X. So \sigma^k \in S_X for every k \in 
Z. Next, \sigma^n \circ \sigma^{-n} = \id_X, by induction on n. For n = 0 both factors are \id_X. If it holds for n, then \sigma^{n+1} = \sigma^n \circ \sigma by (a) with the exponents n and 1, and \sigma^{-(n+1)} = \sigma^{-1} \circ \sigma^{-n} by @def-iterate, so \sigma^{n+1} \circ \sigma^{-(n+1)} = \sigma^n \circ (\sigma \circ \sigma^{-1}) \circ \sigma^{-n} = \sigma^n \circ \sigma^{-n} = \id_X , by @prp-composition-associative and @prp-permutations-closed (c). The equation \sigma^{-n} \circ \sigma^n = \id_X is the same induction with the roles of \sigma and \sigma^{-1} exchanged. Finally, \sigma^{k+l} = \sigma^k \circ \sigma^l. When k, l \ge 0 this is (a). When k, l \le 0, it is (a) for the map \sigma^{-1} with the exponents -k and -l. The cases with k and l of opposite signs reduce to these two by canceling, as the second reading below shows. Let k and l have opposite signs. All equalities below use @prp-composition-associative, the cases of (c) already proved, and \sigma^n \circ \sigma^{-n} = \id_X = \sigma^{-n} \circ \sigma^n for n \in 
N. Case k \ge 0, l = -b with b > 0. If k \ge b, then \sigma^k = \sigma^{k-b} \circ \sigma^b by (a), so \sigma^k \circ \sigma^{-b} = \sigma^{k-b} \circ (\sigma^b \circ \sigma^{-b}) = \sigma^{k-b}. If k < b, then \sigma^{-b} = \sigma^{-k} \circ \sigma^{-(b-k)} by (a) for \sigma^{-1}, so \sigma^k \circ \sigma^{-b} = (\sigma^k \circ \sigma^{-k}) \circ \sigma^{-(b-k)} = \sigma^{k-b}. In both cases \sigma^k \circ \sigma^l = \sigma^{k+l}. Case k = -a with a > 0, l \ge 0. If l \ge a, then \sigma^l = \sigma^a \circ \sigma^{l-a} by (a), so \sigma^{-a} \circ \sigma^l = (\sigma^{-a} \circ \sigma^a) \circ \sigma^{l-a} = \sigma^{l-a}. If l < a, then \sigma^{-a} = \sigma^{-(a-l)} \circ \sigma^{-l} by (a) for \sigma^{-1}, so \sigma^{-a} \circ \sigma^l = \sigma^{-(a-l)} \circ (\sigma^{-l} \circ \sigma^l) = \sigma^{l-a}. Again \sigma^k \circ \sigma^l = \sigma^{k+l}. In particular \sigma^{-n} is the inverse of \sigma^n, by the middle clause of (c) and @def-inverse-function: shuffling backwards n times undoes shuffling forwards n times. For f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = x + 3, find f^n and prove your answer. f^n(x) = x + 3n. By induction on n: f^0(x) = x = x + 3 \cdot 0; and if f^n(x) = x + 3n, then f^{n+1}(x) = f(f^n(x)) = (x + 3n) + 3 = x + 3(n + 1) by @def-iterate. Here f^n is not the power (x + 3)^n. Orbits In the hook, the cards fell into sets that move among themselves: \{1, 3, 9, 5, 4\}, \{2, 6, 7, 10, 8\}, \{0\} and \{11\}. The natural guess for “in the same set” is “one card reaches the other”: y = f^n(x) for some n \in 
N. This relation is reflexive (n = 0) and transitive (add the exponents, @prp-iterate-laws (a)). It is not symmetric. For f \colon 
N 	o 
N, f(n) = n + 1, the point 0 reaches 1 = f(0), but 1 never reaches 0, since f^n(1) = 1 + n \ge 1. So reachability does not cut a set into pieces. For a permutation the repair is to allow negative exponents: walk backwards as well as forwards. The orbit of a point is everywhere a permutation can take it, forwards or backwards. [Orbit, Forward Orbit, Fixed Point] Let X be a set and \sigma \in S_X. For x, y \in X, let x \sim_\sigma y mean that y = \sigma^k(x) for some k \in 
Z. The orbit of x under \sigma is O_\sigma(x) \coloneqq \{ \sigma^k(x) : k \in 
Z \} . For an arbitrary function f \colon X 	o X, the forward orbit of x is \{ f^n(x) : n \in 
N \}. A fixed point of f is an x \in X with f(x) = x. In words: the orbit collects every point reached from x by applying \sigma or \sigma^{-1} any number of times; the forward orbit uses f only, so it makes sense for every self-map. For a permutation, the forward orbit of x is contained in O_\sigma(x), since 
N \subseteq 
Z; on a finite set the two are equal, as the next subsection proves. A fixed point is a point the map does not move, the sense in which Section 3.4 called 0 a fixed point of a bijection. For the hook’s shuffle, O_\sigma(1) = \{1, 3, 9, 5, 4\}: since \sigma^5(1) = 1, the negative powers give nothing new (\sigma^{-1}(1) = \sigma^4(1), and so on; @prp-orbit-cycle proves this in general), and 0 and 11 are the fixed points. Forward orbits need not cut a set into pieces. For f(n) = n + 1 on 
N, the forward orbit of 0 is 
N and that of 1 is \{ n \in 
N : n \ge 1 \}: they overlap and are not equal. Only orbits of a permutation, with k running over 
Z, are guaranteed to be disjoint or equal. The guarantee is the next theorem: \sim_\sigma is an equivalence relation, and the orbits are its classes. [The Orbits of a Permutation Partition the Set] Let X be a set and \sigma \in S_X. Then \sim_\sigma is an equivalence relation on X, and the class of each x \in X is O_\sigma(x). Hence the orbits of \sigma form a partition of X. Moreover, x is a fixed point of \sigma if and only if O_\sigma(x) = \{x\}. We check (Eq1)–(Eq3) of @def-equivalence-relation, using @prp-iterate-laws (c) throughout. (Eq1): x = \sigma^0(x), so x \sim_\sigma x. (Eq2): if y = \sigma^k(x), then \sigma^{-k}(y) = \sigma^{-k}(\sigma^k(x)) = \sigma^{-k + k}(x) = \sigma^0(x) = x, so y \sim_\sigma x. (Eq3): if y = \sigma^k(x) and z = \sigma^l(y), then z = \sigma^l(\sigma^k(x)) = \sigma^{l+k}(x) and l + k \in
