If f^n \circ g = g \circ f^n, then, by @def-iterate and @prp-composition-associative, f^{n+1} \circ g = f \circ (f^n \circ g) = f \circ (g \circ f^n) = (f \circ g) \circ f^n = (g \circ f) \circ f^n = g \circ f^{n+1} . [B3: Orbits are invariant] Let \sigma \in S_X and x \in X. Prove that \sigma(O_\sigma(x)) = O_\sigma(x). (\subseteq) A point of \sigma(O_\sigma(x)) is \sigma(\sigma^k(x)) = \sigma^{k+1}(x) for some k \in 
Z (@def-image, @prp-iterate-laws (c)), and k + 1 \in 
Z. (\supseteq) For k \in 
Z, \sigma^k(x) = \sigma(\sigma^{k-1}(x)) by @prp-iterate-laws (c), and \sigma^{k-1}(x) \in O_\sigma(x). [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove or disprove each statement. 1. If X is finite and f \colon X 	o X is injective, then every x \in X has f^k(x) = x for some k \ge 1. 2. If f \colon X 	o X and f^N = \id_X for some N \ge 1, then f is a permutation. 3. Every function from a finite non-empty set to itself has a fixed point. 4. Every orbit of a permutation is finite. 5. If X is finite and every orbit of \sigma \in S_X has length 1 or 2, then \sigma \circ \sigma = \id_X. (a) True. The proof of @prp-orbit-cycle used only that \sigma^i is injective. Here f^i is injective for every i \in 
N, by induction with @thm-composition-injective-surjective (a) (f^0 = \id_X, f^{i+1} = f \circ f^i). So pigeonhole gives f^i(x) = f^j(x) with i < j; by @prp-iterate-laws (a), f^j = f^i \circ f^{j-i}, and canceling f^i gives f^{j-i}(x) = x, with j - i \ge 1. (b) True. By @prp-iterate-laws (a), f \circ f^{N-1} = f^N = \id_X and f^{N-1} \circ f = f^{(N-1) + 1} = \id_X. So f^{N-1} is a two-sided inverse of f, and f is bijective by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. (c) False. The swap of \{0, 1\}, 0 \mapsto 1, 1 \mapsto 0, moves both points. (d) False. \sigma \colon 
Z 	o 
Z, \sigma(n) = n + 1, is a permutation with inverse n \mapsto n - 1, and \sigma^k(0) = k for every k \in 
Z (induction in each direction), so O_\sigma(0) = 
Z. This is not finite: it contains 
N, which is infinite (@exm-hilbert-hotel, @prp-subset-finite). (e) True. Each orbit length k_x divides 2, so \sigma^2(x) = x by @prp-orbit-cycle (c), for every x; and \sigma^2 = \sigma \circ \sigma by @def-iterate. So \sigma \circ \sigma = \id_X by @prp-function-equality. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: fifteen cards] Fifteen cards lie at positions 0, \dots, 14. Cut them into three piles of five and deal them back in turn, as in the hook, so that \sigma(i) =  egin{cases} 3i & 	ext{if } 0 \le i \le 4, \ 3i - 14 & 	ext{if } 5 \le i \le 9, \ 3i - 28 & 	ext{if } 10 \le i \le 14 . \end{cases} Show that \sigma is a permutation, decompose it into disjoint cycles, and find the least N \ge 1 with \sigma^N = \id. A permutation. The three pieces have images \{0, 3, 6, 9, 12\}, \{1, 4, 7, 10, 13\} and \{2, 5, 8, 11, 14\}: the positions with remainder 0, 1, 2 on division by 3. Each piece is injective (3i - c = 3i' - c gives i = i'), and the images are disjoint and cover \{0, \dots, 14\} by @thm-division-algorithm. So two different cards in one piece land in different places, two cards in different pieces land in different images, and every position is hit: \sigma is bijective. (This is the cross-piece check of @exm-method-gluing.) Arithmetic modulo 14. Write i = 5p + r with 0 \le r < 5; the card lands at \sigma(i) = 3r + p, and 3i - \sigma(i) = 15p - p = 14p, so \sigma(i) \equiv 3i \pmod{14}. Since 3r + p = 14 only for r = 4, p = 2, that is i = 14, \sigma maps \{0, \dots, 13\} into itself, with \sigma(i) the remainder of 3i on division by 14, and \sigma(14) = 14. By induction and @prp-congruence-arithmetic, \sigma^k(i) \equiv 3^k i \pmod{14} for i \le 13. Cycles. 0, 7 (21 \equiv 7) and 14 are fixed. Following orbits (@exm-method-follow-the-orbit):  egin{aligned} &1 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 9 \mapsto 13 \mapsto 11 \mapsto 5 \mapsto 1 &&(27 \equiv 13, \ 39 \equiv 11, \ 33 \equiv 5, \ 15 \equiv 1), \ &2 \mapsto 6 \mapsto 4 \mapsto 12 \mapsto 8 \mapsto 10 \mapsto 2 &&(18 \equiv 4, \ 36 \equiv 8, \ 24 \equiv 10, \ 30 \equiv 2). \end{aligned} These account for 3 + 6 + 6 = 15 positions, so \sigma = (1\ 3\ 9\ 13\ 11\ 5)(2\ 6\ 4\ 12\ 8\ 10) by @thm-permutation-cycles. The return. The orbit lengths are 1, 1, 1, 6, 6. By @cor-permutation-power-identity, \sigma^N = \id exactly when 6 \mid N; the least N \ge 1 is 6. Check: 3^6 = 729 = 52 \cdot 14 + 1, so six shuffles multiply every position below 14 by 1 modulo 14. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: proves \sigma bijective, including the check across pieces (or by an explicit inverse). - 2: reduces \sigma to multiplication by 3 modulo 14 on \{0, \dots, 13\} with 14 fixed, or follows the orbits directly from the three formulas. - 3: finds the two 6-cycles and the fixed points 0, 7, 14, with the arithmetic shown. - 3: concludes N = 6 and shows that no smaller N works, either from the orbit lengths by @cor-permutation-power-identity or directly (3^6 \equiv 1 \pmod{14} and \sigma^k(1) 
e 1 for 1 \le k \le 5). Fatal errors (0 for the step): claiming bijectivity from injectivity of each piece alone; taking N as the sum, rather than a common multiple, of the orbit lengths. [C2: Find the error] Here is a claim and a proof. Claim. For every function f from a finite set X to itself and every x \in X, there is k \ge 1 with f^k(x) = x. Proof. By pigeonhole, f^i(x) = f^j(x) for some i < j. Apply f^{-i} to both sides: x = f^{j-i}(x). Take k = j - i. Is the claim true? Find the line that fails, say why, and state what the argument does prove. The claim is false. The line that fails is “apply f^{-i}”: f^{-i} is defined only for a permutation (@def-iterate), and the claim is about every self-map. A counterexample to that step, and to the claim, is @exm-squaring-mod-eleven with x = [2]: s^1([2]) = s^5([2]) = [4], but no s^k([2]) with k \ge 1 is [2]. The correct conclusion from the pigeonhole repeat is @prp-eventually-periodic: after a tail, the forward orbit is periodic. For a permutation, or more generally an injective f (B4 (a)), the cancellation is legitimate and the claim holds. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: says the claim is false, with a counterexample. - 4: names the failing line, “apply f^{-i}”, and the reason: f need not be invertible, or even injective. - 3: states the correct conclusion (tail then cycle, @prp-eventually-periodic), or the extra hypothesis under which the proof is right. Fatal errors (0 for the step): accepting the proof because the claim holds for permutations; objecting to the pigeonhole step, which is correct. [C3: Each point, its own clock] Let X be a finite set and \sigma \in S_X. Show that the length of O_\sigma(x) is the same for all points x of one orbit. Show also that if \sigma has exactly two orbits, then the number of elements of X is the sum of their lengths. Let y \in O_\sigma(x). Then x \sim_\sigma y, so O_\sigma(y) = O_\sigma(x) by @thm-orbits-partition and @thm-classes-partition (b). By @prp-orbit-cycle (b), the length of an orbit is its number of elements, so the length at y is the number of elements of O_\sigma(y) = O_\sigma(x), which is the length at x. If \sigma has exactly two orbits O and O', they are disjoint and their union is X (@thm-orbits-partition, @def-partition). By @prp-orbit-cycle (b), O and O' have as many elements as their lengths k and k', so X = O \cup O' has k + k' elements by @prp-disjoint-union-count. R. Review [R1] On 
R, let x \sim y mean x - y \in 
Z. Show that [x] \mapsto [2x] is a well-defined surjection 
R/{\sim} 	o 
R/{\sim} that is not injective. Here \sim is the equivalence relation of @exm-reals-mod-integers. Let g \colon 
R 	o 
R/{\sim}, g(x) \coloneqq [2x]. If x \sim x', then 2x - 2x' = 2(x - x') \in 
Z, so g is constant on classes, and @thm-functions-out-of-quotient (a) gives the function [x] \mapsto [2x] (@exm-method-factor-through-quotient). It is onto: every class [y] is the image of [y/2]. It is not injective: [0] \mapsto [0] and [	frac12] \mapsto [1] = [0], while [0] 
e [	frac12] by @exm-reals-mod-integers. The method is the well-definedness check of Section 4.2 (@exm-method-well-definedness). [R2] Let \varphi \colon X 	o Y be a bijection. Show that \sigma \mapsto \varphi \circ \sigma \circ \varphi^{-1} is a bijection from S_X to S_Y, and that x is a fixed point of \sigma if and only if \varphi(x) is a fixed point of \varphi \circ \sigma \circ \varphi^{-1}. For \sigma \in S_X, \varphi \circ \sigma \circ \varphi^{-1} \colon Y 	o Y is a composite of bijections (\varphi^{-1} is bijective by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, since \varphi is a two-sided inverse of it, @def-inverse-function), so it lies in S_Y (@thm-composition-injective-surjective (c)); so the rule is a function c \colon S_X 	o S_Y. In the same way d(	au) \coloneqq \varphi^{-1} \circ 	au \circ \varphi defines d \colon S_Y 	o S_X. By @prp-composition-associative and \varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi = \id_X, \varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = \id_Y (@def-inverse-function), d(c(\sigma)) = \varphi^{-1} \circ  igl((\varphi \circ \sigma) \circ \varphi^{-1} igr) \circ \varphi =  igl(\varphi^{-1} \circ (\varphi \circ \sigma) igr) \circ (\varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi) =  igl((\varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi) \circ \sigma igr) \circ \id_X = \sigma , with @prp-composition-associative at each regrouping, and likewise c(d(	au)) = 	au. So c has a two-sided inverse and is bijective (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse). For the fixed points, c(\sigma)(\varphi(x)) = \varphi igl(\sigma(\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(x))) igr) = \varphi(\sigma(x)) , which equals \varphi(x) if and only if \sigma(x) = x, since \varphi is injective. The tools are the composites and inverses of Sections 1.5 and 1.6. (Section 3.3’s @exr-diagonal-arguments-c2 used bijections of 
N for a different purpose.) [R3] Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = 2x + 1. Prove that f^n(x) = 2^n x + 2^n - 1 for every n \in 
N and x \in 
R. By induction on n (@fd1:ax-induction), with the powers of @def-power. For n = 0: f^0(x) = x = 1 \cdot x + 1 - 1. If f^n(x) = 2^n x + 2^n - 1, then by @def-iterate f^{n+1}(x) = 2 igl(2^n x + 2^n - 1 igr) + 1 = 2^{n+1} x + 2^{n+1} - 1 , since 2 \cdot 2^n = 2^n \cdot 2 = 2^{n+1}. The method is the induction of Section 2.2 on a sequence defined by recursion (@thm-recursion). [R4] Let f \colon X 	o Y, A \subseteq X and B \subseteq Y. Show that (f|_A)^{-1}(B) = A \cap f^{-1}(B). For every a, by @def-preimage applied to f|_A \colon A 	o Y and to f, and f|_A(a) = f(a) for a \in A (@def-restriction-extension), a \in (f|_A)^{-1}(B) \iff a \in A \wedge f(a) \in B \iff a \in A \cap f^{-1}(B) , where the second step uses A \subseteq X. The two sets have the same elements, so they are equal. This is the element-chasing of Section 1.7 applied to a function built in Section 5.1. The tool is the preimage definition (@def-preimage), tested pointwise. The look-alike tools fail: image rules such as @prp-restriction-properties compare images, not preimages, and f(A \cap C) can be strictly smaller than f(A) \cap f(C); and (f|_A)^{-1} here is a preimage, not an inverse function, which f|_A need not have.

title: Zorn's Lemma
content:
Zorn’s Lemma Some objects are built one piece at a time: an injection one pair at a time, a set of representatives one class at a time, a total order one comparison at a time. When the pieces can be listed, induction finishes the job, one step for each natural number. When they cannot, as for the elements of 
R, the words “and so on” stand in for a step that is never given, and that is not a proof. Zorn’s lemma is the principle that replaces them. If every unfinished partial object can be enlarged, and every growing chain of partial objects has a partial object above it, then there is one that cannot be enlarged, and it is complete. The chapter states the lemma and says why it is not proved here: it is equivalent to the axiom of choice of Chapter 3, and this volume proves only the half that gives choice. It turns the lemma into a single method of proof, the maximality template, and runs the template four times. The third run settles the question Section 3.4 left open: any two sets are comparable in size. What you need. Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–8, in particular the rule ulename{\exists E} (@fd1:def-rules-existential) and the catalogue of what is not allowed (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), above all (N13), “an ‘and so on’ needs its step”. From this volume: Section 4.3 on orders (@def-partial-order, @exm-subset-order-not-total, @def-order-bounds, @def-greatest-element, @def-maximal-element, @prp-greatest-maximal, @exm-maximal-not-greatest, @prp-greatest-unique); Section 4.2 on equivalence relations (@def-equivalence-relation, @def-equivalence-class, @thm-classes-partition, @exm-reals-mod-integers); Chapter 3 on sizes and choice (@ax-choice, Section 3.2’s method box @exm-method-name-the-choice, @def-card-le, @thm-schroder-bernstein, @prp-card-le-surjection, @prp-countable-image, @prp-union-two-countable, @thm-reals-uncountable-decimal); Section 2.5 on finite sets (@prp-subset-finite, @exm-hilbert-hotel, @prp-disjoint-union-count, @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets, @prp-equinumerous-properties); Sections 2.1–2.2 (@thm-well-ordering, @thm-induction); Chapter 1 (@def-divides, @def-relation, @def-function). Proof methods: proof by contradiction (@exm-method-choosing-the-form, Chapter 2) and disproof by counterexample (@exm-method-counterexample, Chapter 1). Time. About 10 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 15 hours for everything. Roadmap - Chains and Zorn’s lemma. A pair-by-pair matching that cannot finish; chains in a partially ordered set, and why finitely many elements of the union of a chain of sets lie in one member; Zorn’s lemma, why each hypothesis is needed, and why it is stated and not proved; the axiom of choice from Zorn’s lemma, as the first run of the maximality template; a set of representatives for any equivalence relation. - Using Zorn’s lemma. Any two sets are comparable, so sizes satisfy trichotomy; every partial order extends to a total order, one added comparison at a time; and, in an optional last subsection, how the same template gives every vector space a basis (Linear Algebra, Section 1.8). Named moves - The maximality template (@exm-method-maximality). Partial objects ordered by extension; the union of a chain is again a partial object, since each defining condition mentions finitely many elements and these lie in one member of the chain (@lem-chain-union); Zorn’s lemma gives a maximal one; a maximal one is complete, since a missing piece would give a strictly larger partial object. (Section 6.1) Threads - Comparing sizes. Section 3.4 asked whether any two sets are comparable. Section 6.1 opens with a pair-by-pair matching that does not finish, and Section 6.2 finishes it with Zorn’s lemma (@thm-cardinal-comparability). - Choice. Chapter 3 stated the axiom of choice. Section 6.1 derives it from Zorn’s lemma (@thm-choice-from-zorn), and Axiomatic Set Theory, Chapter 4 proves the converse. Summary A chain is a subset of a partially ordered set on which the order is total (@def-chain), and finitely many elements of the union of a chain of sets lie in one member (@lem-chain-union). Zorn’s lemma (@thm-zorn): a non-empty partially ordered set in which every non-empty chain has an upper bound has a maximal element, usually one of many and not a greatest one. It is stated without proof; it implies the axiom of choice (@thm-choice-from-zorn), and the converse belongs to Axiomatic Set Theory, Chapter 4. The maximality template (@exm-method-maximality) gives a set of representatives for any equivalence relation (@exm-zorn-representatives), shows that any two sets are comparable in size (@thm-cardinal-comparability), so that exactly one of \card{A} < \card{B}, \card{A} = \card{B}, \card{B} < \card{A} holds (@cor-cardinal-trichotomy), and extends every partial order to a total order (@thm-order-extension), by adding one comparison at a time (@lem-one-step-order-extension). Every object built in this chapter is shown to exist and none is written down: no formula is known for a set of representatives of 
R modulo 
Q, for an injection between two arbitrary sets, or for a total order containing \subseteq on \powerset{
R}. Where a formula exists, as for divisibility on 
N (@exm-divisibility-linear-extension), it is the better proof. Terms - chain: a subset in which any two elements are comparable (@def-chain). - linear extension: a total order containing a given partial order; “linear order” is a synonym of “total order” (@thm-order-extension). - maximality template: partial objects, unions of chains, Zorn’s lemma, completeness of a maximal object (@exm-method-maximality). - partial choice function: a set of pairs (i, x) with x \in A_i, at most one for each index (@thm-choice-from-zorn). - partial matching: a relation G \subseteq A 	imes B in which each element of A and of B occurs in at most one pair (@thm-cardinal-comparability). - set of representatives: a set meeting every equivalence class in exactly one element (@exm-zorn-representatives). - Zorn’s lemma: a non-empty partially ordered set in which every non-empty chain has an upper bound has a maximal element (@thm-zorn).

title: 6.1 Chains and Zorn's Lemma
content:
Chains and Zorn’s Lemma Section 3.4 proved that injections both ways give a bijection, and left open whether, for any two sets, at least one injection exists. Section 4.3 ended with a question about partially ordered sets: if every chain has an upper bound, must there be a maximal element? One principle answers both questions. This section states it, Zorn’s lemma, which answers the second question; explains why this volume does not prove it; and turns it into a method of proof, the maximality template, with two first uses. Section 6.2 uses the template to answer the first question. Matching two sets, one pair at a time Let A and B be sets, and suppose we want an injection from one of them into the other, in either direction. A natural plan is to match elements in pairs. Pick a_0 \in A and b_0 \in B and pair them. Then pick a_1 \in A \setminus \{a_0\} and b_1 \in B \setminus \{b_0\} and pair those. Continue until one side is used up. If A runs out first, every element of A has a partner, different elements have different partners, and the pairs form the graph of an injection A 	o B. If B runs out first, the same pairs read backwards form an injection B 	o A. For finite sets the plan works, because each step uses one more element of each side, and a finite set is used up after as many steps as it has elements (Section 2.5). Take A = \{1, 2, 3\} and B = \{x, y\}. Pair 1 with x, then 2 with y. Now B is used up, and reading the pairs backwards gives x \mapsto 1, y \mapsto 2, an injection B 	o A. For A = B = 
R the plan breaks down. Suppose we have made one step for each natural number. The elements of A used so far are a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots, the image of the function n \mapsto a_n on 
N, so they form a countable set (@prp-countable-image). But 
R is uncountable (@thm-reals-uncountable-decimal), so A is not used up; neither is B. The instruction “continue until one side is used up” has no last step, and the words “and so on” stand in for a step that is never stated: (N13) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, “an ‘and so on’ needs its step”. (The infinitely many unnamed choices of a_n and b_n are a second problem, the one Section 3.2 met.) Still, the attempt gets two things right, and they are the thesis of this section: Every unfinished matching can be enlarged by one more pair, and a growing family of matchings, put together, is again a matching. The first half is plain: if neither side is used up, an unused a and an unused b make one more pair. The rest of the section makes “growing family” exact and supplies a principle that turns these two facts into a finished matching. We return to the matching in Section 6.2. Chains Look at the matchings the plan produces, each a set of pairs. Of any two of them, one was built from the other by adding pairs, so one is a subset of the other: under \subseteq, any two are comparable. That is what “growing family” means, and it makes sense in any partially ordered set. [Chain] Let (X, \preceq) be a partially ordered set. A subset C \subseteq X is a chain if any two elements of C are comparable: for all x, y \in C, x \preceq y or y \preceq x. So a chain is a subset on which \preceq is total (@def-partial-order); in a totally ordered set, every subset is a chain. Examples. - In (
N, \mid), the set \{1, 2, 4, 8, \dots\} = \{ 2^n : n \in 
N \} is a chain: for m \le n, 2^n = 2^{n-m} \cdot 2^m, so 2^m \mid 2^n. The set \{2, 3\} is not, since 2 
mid 3 and 3 
mid 2. - In (\powerset{\{1, 2, 3\}}, \subseteq), the set \{ \emptyset, \{2\}, \{2, 3\} \} is a chain. - Degenerate cases: \emptyset is a chain, vacuously, and so is every one-element set \{x\}, by (PO1). Decide: (a) Is \{ \{1\}, \{1, 2\}, \{3\} \} a chain in (\powerset{\{1, 2, 3\}}, \subseteq)? (b) Is \{0, 1, 5, 25\} a chain in (
N, \mid)? (c) Is \{3, 6, 0\}? (d) In (
R, \le), which subsets are chains? (a) No: \{1, 2\} 
ot\subseteq \{3\} and \{3\} 
ot\subseteq \{1, 2\}. (b) Yes. 1 divides every natural number, 25 = 5 \cdot 5, and every natural number a divides 0 = 0 \cdot a; so any two of the four are comparable. (c) Yes: 6 = 2 \cdot 3, and 3 \mid 0, 6 \mid 0. (d) All of them, since \le is total on 
R. Why do chains matter for the matching? Take two pairs from the union of a growing family of matchings. Each pair comes from some matching of the family, and the two matchings are comparable, so both pairs lie in the larger of the two. Any condition that speaks about two pairs at a time can then be checked inside one matching. The same works for any finite number of elements, and that is the content of the next lemma. The lemma speaks about a set of sets ordered by \subseteq. That is always a partially ordered set: each member of a set of sets \sS is a subset of  igcup \sS, and \subseteq is a partial order on \powerset{ igcup \sS} (@exm-subset-order-not-total), which stays one when restricted to the subset \sS, since (PO1)–(PO3) are statements about all elements. [Finitely Many Members of a Chain] 1. Let C be a chain in a partially ordered set (X, \preceq), let n \ge 1 and x_1, \dots, x_n \in C. Then some x_k satisfies x_j \preceq x_k for j = 1, \dots, n. 2. Let \sS be a set of sets, partially ordered by \subseteq, and \sC \subseteq \sS a chain. Then C \subseteq  igcup \sC for every C \in \sC; and if n \ge 1 and z_1, \dots, z_n \in  igcup \sC, then some single C \in \sC contains all of z_1, \dots, z_n. (a) By induction on n (@thm-induction with n_0 = 1). For n = 1, take k = 1: x_1 \preceq x_1 by (PO1). For the step, let x_1, \dots, x_{n+1} \in C, and by the induction hypothesis let x_k with k \le n be above x_1, \dots, x_n. Since C is a chain, x_{n+1} \preceq x_k or x_k \preceq x_{n+1}. In the first case x_k is above all n + 1 elements. In the second, x_{n+1} is: x_j \preceq x_k \preceq x_{n+1} gives x_j \preceq x_{n+1} by (PO3) for j \le n, and x_{n+1} \preceq x_{n+1} by (PO1). (b) The first claim is the definition of the union. For the second, induct on n (@thm-induction with n_0 = 1). For n = 1: z_1 \in  igcup \sC means that z_1 \in C for some C \in \sC, and one use of ulename{\exists E} (@fd1:def-rules-existential) names such a C. For the step, by the induction hypothesis some C' \in \sC contains z_1, \dots, z_n, and one use of ulename{\exists E} gives C'' \in \sC with z_{n+1} \in C''. Since \sC is a chain, C' \subseteq C'' or C'' \subseteq C', and the larger of the two contains all of z_1, \dots, z_{n+1}. Each step of the induction in (b) makes one use of ulename{\exists E}, so no choice is involved. Writing “use ulename{\exists E} n times” instead would be the “and so on” that (N13) flags; the induction is what supplies its step. (a) Is there a chain of subsets of 
N, none of whose members contains both 0 and 1, whose union contains both? (b) Is there such a family of subsets that is not a chain? (a) No. If 0 and 1 lie in the union of a chain, then by @lem-chain-union (b) with n = 2 some member contains both. (b) Yes: \{ \{0\}, \{1\} \} has union \{0, 1\}, and neither member contains both. This is exactly what “chain” rules out. Zorn’s lemma Return to the question of Section 4.3: in a partially ordered set in which every chain has an upper bound, is there a maximal element? A naive attempt: start at any p_0. If p_0 is not maximal, there is p_1 \succ p_0; if p_1 is not maximal, there is p_2 \succ p_1; and so on. The p_n form a chain, which has an upper bound u; if u is not maximal, continue above u, and so on. Each single step is legitimate. But the chain p_0 \prec p_1 \prec \cdots may have an upper bound that is again not maximal, the next chain may too, and “continue past every such bound” is neither a finite process nor one indexed by 
N. It is (N13) once more: the “and so on” has no step. Instead of a proof, there is a principle, stated as its own result. Zorn’s Lemma Let (P, \preceq) be a non-empty partially ordered set in which every non-empty chain has an upper bound in P. Then P has a maximal element. We do not prove @thm-zorn. It cannot be proved from the rules of logic and the working rules for sets of Chapter 1 alone: it is equivalent to the axiom of choice (@ax-choice), which, as Section 3.2 records, can be neither proved nor refuted from the other axioms. One half of the equivalence, that Zorn’s lemma implies the axiom of choice, is the first application below (@thm-choice-from-zorn). The other half, which builds a maximal element from a choice function, is proved in Axiomatic Set Theory, Chapter 4, together with the other equivalents. As with the axiom, we use the lemma openly and cite it at each use. Zorn (1935) put the principle in this form, which suits algebra, where the objects to be built are sets ordered by inclusion. Why each hypothesis is needed. Each of three small examples breaks one hypothesis and has no maximal element. - (
N, \le) is non-empty and total, and has no maximal element, since n < n + 1. The chain hypothesis fails: the chain 
N has no upper bound in 
N. - The empty partially ordered set satisfies the chain hypothesis vacuously, since it has no non-empty chain, and it has no maximal element. “Non-empty” is needed. - The set of finite subsets of 
N, ordered by \subseteq, is non-empty, as \emptyset belongs to it, and has no maximal element. For finite F, 
N is not a subset of F, since a subset of a finite set is finite (@prp-subset-finite) and 
N is infinite (@exm-hilbert-hotel); for m \in 
N \setminus F, the set F \cup \{m\} is finite (@prp-disjoint-union-count) and strictly larger. By the contrapositive of Zorn’s lemma, some non-empty chain has no upper bound in this set, and here one is visible: \{ \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\} : n \in 
N \}, that is, \emptyset, \{0\}, \{0, 1\}, \dots. An upper bound would be a finite set containing every natural number, hence containing 
N, which is impossible. Maximal, not greatest, and not unique. Zorn’s lemma produces a maximal element, by no formula, and says nothing about how many there are. By @prp-greatest-maximal a greatest element would be maximal, but the converse fails (@exm-maximal-not-greatest). In the applications below there are usually many maximal objects and no greatest one; a proof that treats “the” maximal element as unique, or as above everything, has gone wrong. Let P = \{ \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1, 3\} \}, ordered by \subseteq. List the chains with at least two elements; check that every non-empty chain has an upper bound in P; name the maximal elements. The only comparable pair of different elements is \{1\} \subseteq \{1, 3\}, so the only chain with at least two elements is \{ \{1\}, \{1, 3\} \}, with upper bound \{1, 3\}. A one-element chain \{p\} has the upper bound p. The maximal elements are \{2\} and \{1, 3\}: two of them, as the warning says, and no greatest element. [Every chain, or every non-empty chain] Some books ask for an upper bound of every chain, the empty one included. An upper bound of \emptyset is any element of P (@def-order-bounds), so that form contains “P 
e \emptyset” as a special case. The two forms say the same thing. The maximality template Zorn’s lemma is almost always used in one pattern. Its first use proves the half of the equivalence with the axiom of choice that this volume can prove. [Zorn’s Lemma Gives Choice] Assume @thm-zorn. Let I be a set and (A_i)_{i \in I} a family of non-empty sets. Then there is a function c \colon I 	o  igcup_{i \in I} A_i with c(i) \in A_i for every i \in I. This is the conclusion of @ax-choice, so the axiom follows from Zorn’s lemma. [Scratch work] A choice function can be built one index at a time, like the matching of the first subsection. Call a set of pairs (i, x) with x \in A_i, at most one pair for each i, a partial choice function: it is a graph (@def-function) defined on part of I. Order these by \subseteq: the larger of two comparable ones agrees with the smaller and is defined at more indices. Write U \coloneqq  igcup_{i \in I} A_i. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Givens Goal --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- A_i 
e \emptyset for each i \in I c \colon I 	o U with c(i) \in A_i for all i P: the G \subseteq I 	imes U with (C1) (i, x) \in G \Rightarrow x \in A_i and (C2) (i, x), (i, y) \in G \Rightarrow x = y; order \subseteq Zorn’s hypotheses: P 
e \emptyset, and each non-empty chain has an upper bound in P \emptyset \in P; for a chain \sC, try  igcup \sC: (C1) and (C2) mention at most two pairs (@lem-chain-union) a maximal M \in P is defined at every i \in I M maximal; suppose i_0 is missed M \cup \{(i_0, x_0)\} \in P, strictly larger: a contradiction ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ The last row is a proof by contradiction (@exm-method-choosing-the-form): a missed index gives a larger partial object. Choosing x_0 \in A_{i_0} is one use of ulename{\exists E}, which Section 3.2 showed is always allowed; Zorn’s lemma does the infinitely many. Let U and P be as in the table. Then P \subseteq \powerset{I 	imes U} is a set, partially ordered by \subseteq. P is non-empty: \emptyset satisfies (C1) and (C2) vacuously. Chains have upper bounds: let \sC \subseteq P be a non-empty chain and H \coloneqq  igcup \sC \subseteq I 	imes U. If (i, x) \in H, it lies in some G \in \sC, so x \in A_i by (C1) for G. If (i, x), (i, y) \in H, some G \in \sC contains both (@lem-chain-union (b) with n = 2), so x = y by (C2) for G. So H \in P, and G \subseteq H for every G \in \sC: H is an upper bound of \sC in P. Zorn: by @thm-zorn, P has a maximal element M. M is defined everywhere: suppose some i_0 \in I has no pair (i_0, x) \in M. Since A_{i_0} 
e \emptyset, take x_0 \in A_{i_0}, and let M' \coloneqq M \cup \{(i_0, x_0)\}. Then M' \subseteq I 	imes U, since i_0 \in I and x_0 \in A_{i_0} \subseteq U; M' satisfies (C1), and it satisfies (C2), because the only pair of M' with first coordinate i_0 is (i_0, x_0). So M' \in P, M \subseteq M', and M 
e M', as (i_0, x_0) 
otin M; this contradicts the maximality of M. Hence for every i \in I there is a pair (i, x) \in M, and by (C2) exactly one. By @def-function, M is the graph of a function c \colon I 	o U, and c(i) \in A_i by (C1). If I = \emptyset, then P = \{\emptyset\}, and the proof produces the empty function, which is correct. Of the proof’s four steps, only the last is about choice functions; the first three run the same way in every use of the lemma, and that is worth recording. [Method: the maximality template] Template. To show that a complete object exists: (1) partial objects: let P be the set of partial objects, of which the complete ones are the finished case, ordered by \subseteq (extension); check P 
e \emptyset, usually with the empty or the given starting object. (2) chains: for a non-empty chain \sC \subseteq P, show  igcup \sC \in P; each defining condition mentions finitely many elements, which lie in one member (@lem-chain-union). (3) Zorn: P has a maximal element M (@thm-zorn). (4) complete: suppose M is not complete; use the missing piece to build a strictly larger partial object, a contradiction. When to use it. The object can be built piece by piece, each condition on it checks finitely many pieces at a time, and the pieces cannot be listed. The usual failure. The union of a chain is not a partial object, because a condition mentions infinitely many pieces (“finite”, “countable”); step (4) builds an object that is not strictly larger, or not in P; and treating M as the greatest or the only complete object. The second use runs the template with a shorter plan. [A set of representatives] Let \sim be an equivalence relation on a set X. Show that there is a set S \subseteq X that meets every equivalence class in exactly one element. [Scratch work] By the method of @exm-method-maximality. A partial object should be a set that meets each class at most once, so that the complete ones meet each class exactly once. “At most once” reads: s \sim t implies s = t, a condition on two elements at a time, so step (2) works. For step (4), a class [x] that is missed gives the larger set S \cup \{x\}, and no choice is needed, since x is already in hand. Let P be the set of S \subseteq X such that for all s, t \in S, s \sim t implies s = t; order it by \subseteq. Then \emptyset \in P. For a non-empty chain \sC \subseteq P, any two elements s, t of  igcup \sC lie in one member (@lem-chain-union (b)), so s \sim t gives s = t:  igcup \sC \in P, an upper bound of \sC. By @thm-zorn, take a maximal M \in P. Suppose some class [x] (@def-equivalence-class) contains no element of M. Then x 
otin M, since x \in [x] by (Eq1). And M \cup \{x\} \in P: let s, t \in M \cup \{x\} with s \sim t. If both lie in M, then s = t. If s = x and t \in M, then t \sim x by (Eq2), so t \in [x] \cap M, which is impossible; the case t = x, s \in M is the same with the letters exchanged; and if s = t = x, there is nothing to show. So M \subsetneq M \cup \{x\} in P, contradicting maximality. Hence M meets every class, and by the condition defining P in at most one element: S \coloneqq M works. The axiom of choice gives the same set in one line, by choosing one element from each class; the template’s advantage shows when the pieces interact, as in Section 6.2. On 
R, the relation x \sim y \iff x - y \in 
Q is an equivalence relation (Section 4.2, after @exm-reals-mod-integers). A set of representatives for it inside [0, 1] is a set of real numbers that Measure and Integration, Chapter 1 shows has no length, and no formula for one is known. Let X = 
Z and m \sim n \iff m - n is even. Describe the partial objects of @exm-zorn-representatives that have two elements, and the maximal ones. They are the sets \{e, o\} with e even and o odd: two even or two odd integers are related, since their difference is even, so a partial object holds at most one of each parity. Conversely, \{e, o\} is a partial object: with e = 2a and o = 2b + 1, e - o = 2(a - b - 1) + 1 is odd, hence not even (no integer is both, @thm-even-or-odd), so e 
ot\sim o. These are exactly the maximal elements, since any third integer has the parity of e or of o (every integer is even or odd, @thm-even-or-odd), and \emptyset and the one-element sets are not maximal, since each lies strictly inside some \{e, o\}. There are many maximal elements, such as \{0, 1\} and \{4, -7\}, and no greatest one. Check that the union is a partial object. Here is an almost-correct proof that 
N has a maximal finite subset. “Let P be the set of finite subsets of 
N, ordered by \subseteq. A chain has its union as an upper bound. By Zorn’s lemma, P has a maximal element.” The conclusion is false, by the third example after @thm-zorn. The failing line is the second: the union is an upper bound in \powerset{
N}, but it need not be finite, so it need not lie in P. “Finite” is a condition on all the elements at once, and @lem-chain-union handles only finitely many. Section 6.2 applies the template twice more, first to the matching that opened this section. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-choice-from-zorn. 1. Where is “A_i 
e \emptyset” used, and which step fails without it? 2. Why does the chain step need @lem-chain-union only for n = 2? 3. Run the proof on I = \{1, 2\}, A_1 = \{0\}, A_2 = \{5, 6\}: list P, name its maximal elements, and decide whether P has a greatest element. 4. Which of the two hypotheses of @thm-zorn does the empty partially ordered set satisfy? (a) In the last step: x_0 \in A_{i_0} exists only because A_{i_0} 
e \emptyset. Without it, M could miss i_0 and still be maximal, and indeed no choice function exists if some A_i is empty. (b) Condition (C1) mentions one pair and (C2) mentions two; no condition defining P mentions more. (c) U = \{0, 5, 6\}, and P =  igl\{ \emptyset, \{(1, 0)\}, \{(2, 5)\}, \{(2, 6)\}, \{(1, 0), (2, 5)\}, \{(1, 0), (2, 6)\}  igr\}. The maximal elements are the last two, each the graph of a choice function. There is no greatest element: the two maximal elements are incomparable, and a greatest element would be maximal (@prp-greatest-maximal (a)), so it would be one of them and contain the other. (d) The chain hypothesis, vacuously; not non-emptiness. B. Practice [B1: Maximal chains] Let (X, \preceq) be a partially ordered set and C_0 \subseteq X a chain. Prove that there is a chain C \supseteq C_0 that is maximal: no chain contains C properly. [Hint] The partial objects are the chains containing C_0. Let P be the set of chains C \subseteq X with C_0 \subseteq C, ordered by \subseteq; then C_0 \in P. Let \sK \subseteq P be a non-empty chain and H \coloneqq  igcup \sK. Then H \supseteq C_0, since \sK has a member and each member contains C_0. Any x, y \in H lie in one member K \in \sK (@lem-chain-union (b)), which is a chain, so x and y are comparable. So H \in P, and it is an upper bound of \sK. By @thm-zorn, P has a maximal element C. If a chain D \supsetneq C existed, then D \supseteq C_0, so D \in P and C \subsetneq D, contradicting maximality. So C is a maximal chain containing C_0. [B2: Name the move, then complete it] Here is the frame of a proof that for every set \sF of non-empty sets there is a subfamily \sD \subseteq \sF of pairwise disjoint sets such that every member of \sF meets some member of \sD. Let P be the set of subfamilies \sE \subseteq \sF whose members are pairwise disjoint (E \cap E' = \emptyset for E 
e E' in \sE), ordered by \subseteq. Then \emptyset \in P. For a non-empty chain of such subfamilies, two members E 
e E' of its union lie in one subfamily of the chain, so E \cap E' = \emptyset; the union lies in P and is an upper bound. By Zorn’s lemma, P has a maximal element \sD. \vdots … Hence every member of \sF meets some member of \sD. Name the move, then complete it. The move is step (4) of @exm-method-maximality: a missing piece gives a strictly larger partial object. Suppose F \in \sF meets no member of \sD. Then F 
otin \sD: otherwise F would meet itself, as F \cap F = F 
e \emptyset. And \sD \cup \{F\} is pairwise disjoint, since F \cap D = \emptyset for every D \in \sD by assumption. So \sD \subsetneq \sD \cup \{F\} \in P, against the maximality of \sD. The check F 
otin \sD is what makes the new family strictly larger, the failure the method box warns about. Hence every member of \sF meets some member of \sD. [B3: A small poset of partial injections] Let A = \{1, 2\} and B = \{b\}. List the relations G \subseteq A 	imes B in which each element of A and each element of B occurs in at most one pair, ordered by \subseteq. Name the maximal elements. For each, is every element of A paired? Every element of B? They are \emptyset, \{(1, b)\} and \{(2, b)\}; the only other subset of A 	imes B, \{(1, b), (2, b)\}, fails because b occurs twice. The maximal elements are \{(1, b)\} and \{(2, b)\}. Neither pairs every element of A; each pairs every element of B, and read backwards it is an injection B 	o A. (Section 6.2 shows that this always happens: a maximal partial injection uses up one side.) [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement and refute each false one. 1. If every chain of a non-empty partially ordered set P has an upper bound in P, then P has a greatest element. 2. Every non-empty finite partially ordered set has a maximal element. 3. The set of subsets of 
N that contain no two consecutive numbers, ordered by \subseteq, has a greatest element. 4. If P is a non-empty partially ordered set in which every non-empty chain has an upper bound, then every p \in P lies below some maximal element of P. 5. The set of countable subsets of 
R, ordered by \subseteq, has a maximal element. Hint for (d): apply Zorn’s lemma to the elements above p. (a) False. Take P = \{ \{1\}, \{2\} \} under \subseteq. Its chains are \emptyset, \{\{1\}\} and \{\{2\}\}, each with an upper bound in P. But P has no greatest element, since \{1\} and \{2\} are incomparable. (b) True. Let P be non-empty and finite, and let C be a non-empty chain of P. Then C is finite (@prp-subset-finite); list it as x_1, \dots, x_n with n \ge 1. By @lem-chain-union (a), one x_k is above all of them, an upper bound of C in P. By @thm-zorn, P has a maximal element. (Section 4.3, Exercise R4 proves this without Zorn’s lemma, by induction.) (c) False. The set E of even numbers and the set O of odd numbers both contain no two consecutive numbers. A greatest element G would contain E and O, so 0, 1 \in G, which are consecutive. (In fact E and O are both maximal: adding any n 
otin E to E puts n and n + 1 in it (n is odd by @thm-even-or-odd, so n + 1 is even), and adding any n 
otin O to O does the same. So Zorn’s lemma, if applied here, gives a maximal element, never a greatest one, as the warning after @thm-zorn says.) (d) True. Let p \in P, and let Q \coloneqq \{ q \in P : p \preceq q \}, ordered by \preceq; then p \in Q. A non-empty chain \sK of Q is a chain of P, so it has an upper bound u \in P; for any c \in \sK, p \preceq c \preceq u, so u \in Q by (PO3). By @thm-zorn, Q has a maximal element m, and p \preceq m. If m \prec q for some q \in P, then p \preceq q by (PO3), so q \in Q, against the maximality of m in Q. So m is maximal in P. (e) False. Let C \subseteq 
R be countable. Then C 
e 
R, since 
R is uncountable (@thm-reals-uncountable-decimal); for x \in 
R \setminus C, the set C \cup \{x\} is countable (@prp-union-two-countable) and strictly larger. So no countable set is maximal. (By the contrapositive of Zorn’s lemma, some non-empty chain of countable sets has no countable upper bound; the answer does not need one.) C. Going deeper [C1: Find the error] Claim: every chain C_0 of a partially ordered set X lies in a maximal chain. “Proof”: Let P be the set of chains containing C_0, ordered by \subseteq; then C_0 \in P. Let \sK be a non-empty chain in P. Every K \in \sK is a subset of  igcup \sK, so  igcup \sK is an upper bound of \sK. By Zorn’s lemma, P has a maximal element C. A chain containing C contains C_0, so it lies in P; hence C is a maximal chain. Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? The conclusion is true: it is Exercise B1. The argument does not prove it. It never checks that  igcup \sK is a chain, that is, that it lies in P; the upper bound in @thm-zorn must belong to P. The step’s general form, “the union of a chain of partial objects lies in P”, is false: among the finite subsets of 
N, the chain \{ \{0, \dots, n - 1\} : n \in 
N \} has union 
N, which is not finite (the warning before these exercises). Here the conclusion of the step happens to be true, which is exactly why it must be proved, not assumed. The repair is the chain step of B1: two elements of  igcup \sK lie in one member K \in \sK (@lem-chain-union (b)), which is a chain, so they are comparable. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: the conclusion is true, with B1 cited. - 3: the missing check named:  igcup \sK \in P. - 3: a counterexample to the general inference “the union of a chain of partial objects lies in P” (in any partially ordered set), with the remark that here the step’s conclusion is true but unproved. - 2: the repair via @lem-chain-union. Fatal errors (0 for the step): calling the conclusion false; “repairing” the proof by assuming that a union of chains is always a chain. [C2: Exit check: when no choice is needed] 1. Let \sim be an equivalence relation on 
N. Without Zorn’s lemma or the axiom of choice, give a set S meeting every class exactly once, and prove that it does. 2. Do the same for an equivalence relation on a set X with an injection j \colon X 	o 
N. 3. Which ingredient of @exm-zorn-representatives does your answer to (a) make unnecessary, and why? [Hint 1] Each class is a non-empty set of natural numbers. Which element of it can be named without choosing? (a) Let S \coloneqq \{ m_x : x \in 
N \}, where m_x is the least element of [x]. It exists by @thm-well-ordering, since [x] \subseteq 
N contains x and so is non-empty, and it is unique (@prp-greatest-unique), so the rule names one value. Every class is met: m_x \in [x] \cap S. At most once: let m_x, m_y \in S lie in the same class [z]. Then m_x \in [x] \cap [z], so [x] = [z], and likewise [y] = [z], since different classes are disjoint (@thm-classes-partition). So [x] = [y], these classes have the same least element, and m_x = m_y. Hence S meets each class [x] in m_x and nowhere else. (b) For x \in X, the set j([x]) \subseteq 
N is non-empty, so it has a least element k_x (@thm-well-ordering), and since j is injective exactly one s_x \in [x] has j(s_x) = k_x. Let S \coloneqq \{ s_x : x \in X \}. The argument of (a) applies word for word, with s_x for m_x: equal classes give equal k_x, hence equal s_x. (c) Zorn’s lemma, that is, the whole argument with P, chains and a maximal M: a rule names each representative, so nothing needs to be chosen (@exm-method-name-the-choice). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) each class has a well-defined representative (well-ordering, and the rule names one value). - 3: (a) every class met, and met at most once (justified). - 2: (b) the least value of j, and injectivity naming one element. - 2: (c) Zorn’s lemma named as the unnecessary ingredient, because a rule names each representative. Fatal errors (0 for the step): “choose an element of each class” in (a) or (b), which is the axiom of choice.

title: 6.2 Using Zorn's Lemma
content:
Using Zorn’s Lemma Section 6.1 turned Zorn’s lemma into a four-step template. This section uses it twice. The first use finishes the matching that opened Section 6.1 and answers the question Section 3.4 left open: any two sets are comparable in size. The second extends any partial order to a total one, the infinite form of putting tasks in an order that respects their prerequisites. An optional last subsection shows the same template in linear algebra. Back to comparing sizes Section 3.4 defined \card{A} \le \card{B} as the existence of an injection A 	o B (@def-card-le) and proved that injections both ways give a bijection (@thm-schroder-bernstein). It left open whether at least one of the two injections always exists. Section 6.1 tried to build one by matching elements pair by pair, and the attempt got two things right: an unfinished matching can be enlarged by one pair, and a growing family of matchings, put together, is again a matching. Those are steps (4) and (2) of the maximality template (@exm-method-maximality), and Zorn’s lemma supplies the rest. [Any Two Sets Are Comparable] For all sets A and B, \card{A} \le \card{B} or \card{B} \le \card{A}. By the method of @exm-method-maximality. The partial objects are the partial matchings: relations G \subseteq A 	imes B in which each element of A and each element of B occurs in at most one pair. The union of a chain of them is one, since each condition mentions two pairs at a time. A maximal matching uses up A or B, since otherwise one more pair fits; read in the right direction, it is an injection. Let P be the set of relations G \subseteq A 	imes B such that - (M1) if (a, b), (a, b') \in G, then b = b'; - (M2) if (a, b), (a', b) \in G, then a = a'; ordered by \subseteq. It is a set of subsets of A 	imes B, so \subseteq is a partial order on it. Partial objects. \emptyset \in P, since (M1) and (M2) hold vacuously; so P 
e \emptyset. Chains. Let \sC \subseteq P be a non-empty chain and H \coloneqq  igcup \sC \subseteq A 	imes B. Any two pairs of H lie in a single member G \in \sC (@lem-chain-union (b), with n = 2). So if (a, b), (a, b') \in H, then b = b' by (M1) for G; and (M2) for H follows in the same way. Hence H \in P, and G \subseteq H for every G \in \sC: H is an upper bound of \sC in P. Zorn. By @thm-zorn, P has a maximal element M. M uses up a side. Suppose some a_0 \in A occurs in no pair of M, and some b_0 \in B occurs in no pair of M. Then M' \coloneqq M \cup \{ (a_0, b_0) \} satisfies (M1) and (M2), because the new pair shares no coordinate with a pair of M. So M' \in P, M \subseteq M', and M 
e M', since (a_0, b_0) 
otin M. This contradicts the maximality of M. Hence every a \in A occurs in a pair of M, or every b \in B does. Case 1: every a \in A occurs. By (M1) it occurs in exactly one pair, so M is the graph of a function f \colon A 	o B (@def-function). If f(a) = f(a') = b, then (a, b), (a', b) \in M, so a = a' by (M2): f is injective, and \card{A} \le \card{B}. Case 2: every b \in B occurs. Consider the inverse relation M^{-1} = \{ (b, a) : (a, b) \in M \} \subseteq B 	imes A (@def-relation). Every b \in B occurs as a first coordinate of M^{-1}, and by (M2) in exactly one pair; so M^{-1} is the graph of a function g \colon B 	o A. By (M1), g(b) = g(b') = a gives b = b': g is injective, and \card{B} \le \card{A}. Section 6.1’s “continue until one side is used up” has become step (4): a maximal matching cannot be continued, and so a side is used up. The words “and so on” never appear. [Trichotomy for Sizes] For all sets A and B, exactly one of \card{A} < \card{B}, \card{A} = \card{B}, \card{B} < \card{A} holds. At least one. By @thm-cardinal-comparability, \card{A} \le \card{B} or \card{B} \le \card{A}. In the first case, either \card{A} = \card{B}, or not, and then \card{A} < \card{B} by @def-card-le. The second case gives \card{B} = \card{A}, hence \card{A} = \card{B} (@prp-equinumerous-properties (b)), or \card{B} < \card{A}. At most one. \card{A} < \card{B} excludes \card{A} = \card{B} by @def-card-le. \card{B} < \card{A} excludes \card{B} = \card{A}, and therefore \card{A} = \card{B}, by symmetry (@prp-equinumerous-properties (b)). Finally, \card{A} < \card{B} and \card{B} < \card{A} together give injections A 	o B and B 	o A, so \card{A} = \card{B} by @thm-schroder-bernstein, contradicting \card{A} < \card{B}. Comparability is itself equivalent to the axiom of choice, a fact proved in Axiomatic Set Theory, Chapter 4: this book needed choice for it, and no proof can avoid it. Run the proof of @thm-cardinal-comparability on A = \{1, 2, 3\} and B = \{x, y\}: describe the maximal elements of P, and say which case of the proof occurs. A partial matching has at most two pairs, since each of x, y occurs at most once. The maximal elements are the six two-pair matchings \{ (a, x), (a', y) \} with a 
e a' in A (three choices of a, then two of a'). A matching with fewer pairs is not maximal: it leaves some element of A and some element of B unpaired, and one more pair fits. No maximal M pairs every element of A: that would be an injection A 	o B, impossible by @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a). So Case 2 occurs every time: M^{-1} is an injection B 	o A. This is the finite example of Section 6.1, where the matching (1, x), (2, y) ran out of B. A maximal matching tells us which side is used up, not that the sizes differ. For A = B = 
N, the identity \{ (n, n) : n \in 
N \} is a maximal matching that uses up both sides. So is \{ (n, n + 1) : n \in 
N \}: it pairs every element of A, and although 0 \in B is unpaired, no element of A is left to pair it with. That matching is an injection and not a bijection, although \card{
N} = \card{
N}. The proof only promises an injection, and that is all it delivers. Extending a partial order Suppose a project consists of tasks, and some tasks must be done before others. Write u \preceq v when task u must come no later than task v: either u = v, or u must be finished before v can start, directly or through a sequence of prerequisites. Counting each task as coming no later than itself makes \preceq reflexive; passing prerequisites along makes it transitive; and no two different tasks can each be required before the other, or nothing could ever start. So \preceq is a partial order. A schedule puts the tasks in one line, and it respects the prerequisites when its order, a total order, contains \preceq. For finitely many tasks there is a procedure: pick a task with no unfinished prerequisite, do it, and repeat. Here is a small case. Five tasks, survey S, financing F, design D, permit P and building B, with four prerequisites: S 	ext{ before } D, \qquad F 	ext{ before } D, \qquad D 	ext{ before } B, \qquad F 	ext{ before } P . The order they generate consists of the five pairs (t, t), the four given pairs, and the two pairs (S, B) and (F, B) that the prerequisites pass along through D: eleven pairs in all. At the start, S and F have no prerequisites. Picking S, then F, leaves D and P free; picking D, then P, frees B. That gives the schedule S, \ F, \ D, \ P, \ B . Picking F first instead, then P, then S, then D, then B, gives a second schedule F, \ P, \ S, \ D, \ B . Each contains all eleven pairs: in both lists S and F come before D, D before B, F before P, and hence S and F before B. So schedules are not unique (there are seven in all), and the procedure needs the tasks in hand, one free task at a time, until none is left. For an infinite set with no list there is no last step, and the maximality template does the work instead. Its engine is a single move: two incomparable elements can be made comparable without breaking anything. A partial order on X is a relation on X, a subset of X 	imes X (@def-relation), so it makes sense to say that one partial order is contained in another. [Adding One Comparison] Let \preceq be a partial order on a set X, and let a, b \in X be incomparable. Let R \coloneqq {\preceq} \cup \{ (x, y) \in X 	imes X : x \preceq a 	ext{ and } b \preceq y \} . Then R is a partial order on X, {\preceq} \subseteq R, and (a, b) \in R \setminus {\preceq}. R puts everything below a below everything above b. A new pair can break antisymmetry or transitivity only by producing b \preceq a, and incomparability forbids that. Call a pair (x, y) new if x \preceq a and b \preceq y, and old if x \preceq y. Every pair of R is old or new. The pair (a, b) is new, since a \preceq a and b \preceq b by (PO1), and it is not old, since a and b are incomparable. By the definition of R, {\preceq} \subseteq R. (PO1): x \preceq x for every x \in X, and {\preceq} \subseteq R. (PO2): let x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x. If both pairs are old, x = y by (PO2) for \preceq. If (x, y) is new and (y, x) old, then b \preceq y \preceq x \preceq a, so b \preceq a by (PO3), which incomparability excludes. If (x, y) is old and (y, x) new, then b \preceq x \preceq y \preceq a, excluded in the same way. If both are new, then b \preceq x (from (y, x)) and x \preceq a (from (x, y)), so again b \preceq a. Only the first case can occur, and it gives x = y. (PO3): let x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} z. If both pairs are old, x \preceq z by (PO3). If (x, y) is old and (y, z) new, then x \preceq y \preceq a and b \preceq z, so (x, z) is new. If (x, y) is new and (y, z) old, then x \preceq a and b \preceq y \preceq z, so (x, z) is new. If both are new, x \preceq a and b \preceq z directly. In every case x \mathrel{R} z. Apply @lem-one-step-order-extension to \subseteq on \powerset{\{1, 2\}} with a = \{1\} and b = \{2\}. Which pairs does R add to \subseteq? A new pair (x, y) needs x \subseteq \{1\} and \{2\} \subseteq y: x \in \{ \emptyset, \{1\} \} and y \in \{ \{2\}, \{1, 2\} \}. Of these four pairs, all but (\{1\}, \{2\}) already belong to \subseteq. So R adds exactly one pair, and it is the total order \emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1, 2\}. The lemma adds one comparison. The template adds them all at once. [Every Partial Order Extends to a Total Order] Let \preceq be a partial order on a set X. Then there is a total order T on X with {\preceq} \subseteq T. This book’s word is “total” (@def-partial-order); “linear order” is a common synonym, and T is then called a linear extension of \preceq. By the method of @exm-method-maximality. The partial objects are the partial orders on X containing \preceq. The union of a chain of them is one, since (PO2) and (PO3) each mention two pairs. A maximal one is total, because @lem-one-step-order-extension enlarges any partial order that has an incomparable pair. Let P be the set of partial orders R on X with {\preceq} \subseteq R, a set of subsets of X 	imes X, ordered by \subseteq. Then {\preceq} \in P, so P 
e \emptyset. Let \sC \subseteq P be a non-empty chain and H \coloneqq  igcup \sC \subseteq X 	imes X. Since \sC has a member, and that member contains \preceq, so does H; in particular (PO1) holds for H. If (x, y), (y, x) \in H, some single R_0 \in \sC contains both (@lem-chain-union (b)), so x = y by (PO2) for R_0. If (x, y), (y, z) \in H, some R_0 \in \sC contains both, so (x, z) \in R_0 \subseteq H by (PO3) for R_0. Hence H \in P, and it is an upper bound of \sC. By @thm-zorn, P has a maximal element T. Suppose T is not total, and let a, b \in X be incomparable for T. By @lem-one-step-order-extension, applied to T, there is a partial order R on X with T \subseteq R and T 
e R. Since {\preceq} \subseteq T \subseteq R, R \in P, contradicting the maximality of T. So T is total. One comparison at a time. It is tempting to skip Zorn’s lemma and settle every incomparable pair at once, each in some direction. That can fail. Take equality on X = \{1, 2, 3\}, where no two different elements are comparable, and decide the three pairs as 1 before 2, 2 before 3, 3 before 1. Each decision alone is harmless, but together they break transitivity, and adding the pairs that transitivity demands puts 1 before 3 and 3 before 1, against (PO2). @lem-one-step-order-extension adds one comparison and then passes the consequences along; the next comparison is made in the new order, where the earlier ones are already visible. The template is what turns this one-step move into a total order when the pairs cannot be listed. Sometimes no Zorn is needed, because a formula gives the extension. [A total order containing divisibility] On 
N, let x \sqsubseteq y mean: y = 0, or x 
e 0 and x \le y. Show that \sqsubseteq is a total order on 
N containing \mid, and that \le does not contain \mid. In words, \sqsubseteq is the usual order on the positive integers with 0 moved to the top. (PO1): if x = 0, then x \sqsubseteq x by the first alternative; otherwise x \le x. Total: let x, y \in 
N. If y = 0, then x \sqsubseteq y; if x = 0, then y \sqsubseteq x; if both are non-zero, x \le y or y \le x, by totality of \le. (PO2): let x \sqsubseteq y and y \sqsubseteq x. If y = 0, then y \sqsubseteq x cannot hold by the second alternative, which needs y 
e 0; so x = 0 = y. The case x = 0 is the same with the roles exchanged. If both are non-zero, x \le y \le x, so x = y. (PO3): let x \sqsubseteq y and y \sqsubseteq z. If z = 0, then x \sqsubseteq z. Otherwise the second alternative holds for (y, z): y 
e 0 and y \le z. Then x \sqsubseteq y with y 
e 0 also holds by the second alternative: x 
e 0 and x \le y. So x \le z, and x \sqsubseteq z. Contains \mid: let a, b \in 
N with a \mid b, say b = ka with k \in 
Z (@def-divides). If b = 0, then a \sqsubseteq b. If b 
e 0, then a 
e 0, since 0 \mid b would mean b = k \cdot 0 = 0. With a, b > 0, k > 0, so k \ge 1 and b = ka \ge a: a \sqsubseteq b. \le does not contain \mid: 2 \mid 0, since 0 = 0 \cdot 2, but 2 \le 0 fails. Where a formula exists, it is the better proof. @thm-order-extension matters for orders such as \subseteq on \powerset{
R}, for which no formula for a total extension is known. Put 0, 1, 4, 6, 12 in \sqsubseteq-order. Which two of them are comparable under \sqsubseteq but not under \mid? 1 \sqsubseteq 4 \sqsubseteq 6 \sqsubseteq 12 \sqsubseteq 0. Every pair is comparable under \sqsubseteq, which is total. Under \mid: 1 divides all of them, all of them divide 0, 4 \mid 12 and 6 \mid 12. The remaining pair is 4, 6: 4 \sqsubseteq 6, but neither divides the other. So 4 and 6 are the only such pair.
