For a reader who has met vector spaces, it sketches, without proving here, how Linear Algebra, Section 1.8 uses the same template. A basis of a vector space V is a linearly independent set of vectors that spans V. The theorem there is that every linearly independent set S \subseteq V lies in a basis. In the language of @exm-method-maximality, the partial objects are the linearly independent sets containing S, ordered by \subseteq; S itself is one. Independence is a condition on finitely many vectors at a time: a set is independent when no finite non-trivial combination of its vectors is 0. So a dependence among vectors of the union of a chain involves finitely many vectors, which lie in one member of the chain (@lem-chain-union (b)), and that member is independent: the union is a partial object. Zorn’s lemma gives a maximal independent set M. It spans V, since a vector outside its span could be added to M without creating a dependence, giving a strictly larger partial object. With S = \emptyset, every vector space has a basis, including 
R as a vector space over 
Q, where no basis can be written down. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-cardinal-comparability. 1. Where does the proof use (M1), and where (M2)? 2. Why can “some a \in A is unpaired” and “some b \in B is unpaired” not both hold for a maximal M? 3. If A = \emptyset, what is M, and which case occurs? 4. In two sentences, give the proof’s idea. (a) The chain step uses both, to show that the union of a chain lies in P. The step “M uses up a side” uses both for M, to see that M \cup \{ (a_0, b_0) \} still satisfies them. Case 1 uses (M1) to get a function A 	o B and (M2) for its injectivity; Case 2 uses (M2) to get a function B 	o A and (M1) for its injectivity. (b) Then the pair (a, b) can be added: M \cup \{ (a, b) \} satisfies (M1) and (M2) and is strictly larger, so M is not maximal. (c) A 	imes B = \emptyset, so P = \{ \emptyset \} and M = \emptyset. Case 1 occurs: every element of \emptyset occurs in M, vacuously, and M is the graph of the empty function \emptyset 	o B, which is injective. If also B = \emptyset, Case 2 holds as well. (d) A maximal partial matching between A and B cannot be extended, so it uses up A or B. Read in the right direction, it is an injection. B. Practice [B1: Name the move, then complete it] Let R be a relation from A to B whose domain is A (@def-relation). Prove that there is a function f \colon A 	o B whose graph is contained in R. Below, the proof is started; the second half is blank. Name the move, then complete it. Let P be the set of G \subseteq R such that each a \in A occurs in at most one pair of G, ordered by \subseteq. Then \emptyset \in P. \underline{\hspace{8em}} Hence the graph of f is contained in R. The move is the maximality template, @exm-method-maximality; steps (2) to (4) remain. Completion. Let \sC \subseteq P be a non-empty chain. Its union lies in R, and two pairs of the union lie in one member of \sC (@lem-chain-union (b)), so an element of A occurs in at most one pair of the union. The union is in P and is an upper bound of \sC. By @thm-zorn, P has a maximal element M. Suppose some a_0 \in A occurs in no pair of M. Since a_0 is in the domain of R, there is b_0 with (a_0, b_0) \in R (one use of ulename{\exists E}). Then M \cup \{ (a_0, b_0) \} \subseteq R, a_0 occurs in it once, and it is strictly larger than M: a contradiction with maximality. So each a \in A occurs in exactly one pair of M, and M is the graph of a function f \colon A 	o B (@def-function), with M \subseteq R. [B2: A total order on the subsets of a three-element set] 1. Write the eight subsets of \{1, 2, 3\} in a list such that A \subsetneq B always puts A before B, and prove that it does. 2. How many total orders on \powerset{\{1, 2\}} contain \subseteq? (a) \emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}, \{1, 2\}, \{1, 3\}, \{2, 3\}, \{1, 2, 3\}. The list is arranged by the number of elements. If A \subsetneq B, then A has fewer elements than B (@prp-subset-finite), so A comes in an earlier block of the list. (b) Two. The empty set must come first, since \emptyset \subseteq Y for every Y, and \{1, 2\} last, since every Y \subseteq \{1, 2\}. The sets \{1\} and \{2\} are incomparable under \subseteq, so they may come in either order, and both orders work. [B3: A total order on the plane] On 
R^2, let (x_1, x_2) \le_p (y_1, y_2) mean x_1 \le y_1 and x_2 \le y_2; and let (x_1, x_2) \le_l (y_1, y_2) mean x_1 < y_1, or x_1 = y_1 and x_2 \le y_2. 1. Show that \le_p is a partial order and not total. 2. Show that \le_l is a total order containing \le_p. (a) (PO1), (PO2) and (PO3) for \le_p hold coordinate by coordinate, from the same properties of \le on 
R; for (PO2), x_1 = y_1 and x_2 = y_2 give equal pairs. The points (0, 1) and (1, 0) are incomparable: 0 \le 1 but 1 
ot\le 0 in the second coordinate, and the reverse in the first. (b) That \le_l is a total order is the argument of Section 4.3, Exercises A1 (d) and C1 (a), with 
R in place of 
N: it uses only trichotomy and transitivity of \le. Containment: if x_1 \le y_1 and x_2 \le y_2, then either x_1 < y_1, or x_1 = y_1 and x_2 \le y_2; in both cases (x_1, x_2) \le_l (y_1, y_2). C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: an order is the intersection of its total extensions] Let \preceq be a partial order on a set X, and let \sT be the set of total orders on X that contain \preceq. Prove that {\preceq} =  igcap \sT. [Hint 1] For a pair (a, b) not in \preceq, you need one T \in \sT without it. If a and b are incomparable, find a partial order containing \preceq and the pair (b, a). By @thm-order-extension, \sT 
e \emptyset, so the intersection is defined, and {\preceq} \subseteq  igcap \sT since every T \in \sT contains \preceq. Let (a, b) \in X 	imes X with (a, b) 
otin {\preceq}. Then a 
e b by (PO1). Since a \preceq b fails, either b \preceq a or a and b are incomparable. Case b \preceq a. Every T \in \sT contains (b, a). If it also contained (a, b), then a = b by (PO2) for T. So no T \in \sT contains (a, b), and since \sT 
e \emptyset, (a, b) 
otin  igcap \sT. Case a, b incomparable. @lem-one-step-order-extension, with b, a in place of a, b, gives a partial order R \supseteq {\preceq} with (b, a) \in R. @thm-order-extension applied to R gives a total order T \supseteq R. Then T \in \sT and (b, a) \in T, so (a, b) 
otin T by (PO2), as a 
e b. Hence (a, b) 
otin  igcap \sT. In both cases (a, b) 
otin  igcap \sT, so  igcap \sT \subseteq {\preceq}. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: \sT 
e \emptyset, cited from @thm-order-extension. - 1: {\preceq} \subseteq  igcap \sT. - 2: the two cases are exhaustive, because a \preceq b fails. - 2: the case b \preceq a, with (PO2) and a 
e b. - 2: a partial order containing \preceq and (b, a) (for example, the lemma with a and b exchanged). - 2: the extension of R to a total order and the conclusion. Fatal error (0 for the case concerned): applying the lemma to (a, b) unexchanged, which puts (a, b) into the extension instead of keeping it out. [C2: Find the error] Claim: any two sets are comparable. “Proof”: If A or B is empty, the empty function is an injection. Otherwise choose a_0 \in A and b_0 \in B and pair them. Choose a_1 \in A \setminus \{a_0\} and b_1 \in B \setminus \{b_0\}, and so on. When one set runs out, the pairs so far are an injection from it into the other. Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? The conclusion is true: it is @thm-cardinal-comparability. The argument does not prove it. It fails at “and so on … when one set runs out”, the gap that (N13) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue flags: an “and so on” needs its step, and here the process has no last step in general. Indexed by 
N, it uses a countable set of elements of each side (@prp-countable-image), and for A = B = 
R neither side runs out, since 
R is uncountable (@thm-reals-uncountable-decimal). That is a counterexample to the step “the process ends”. The argument also makes infinitely many choices with no rule (Section 3.2). The repair is the proof by the template, in which “cannot be continued” replaces “runs out”. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: the conclusion is true, with a citation. - 3: the failing line (“and so on \dots runs out”) identified, with the reason that it has no step. - 3: a counterexample to the step “the process ends” (for example A = B = 
R), with the countability reason. - 2: the repair by the maximality template. R. Review [R1: Surjections one way or the other] Let A and B be non-empty sets. Prove that there is a surjection A 	o B or a surjection B 	o A. By @thm-cardinal-comparability, \card{A} \le \card{B} or \card{B} \le \card{A}. In the first case, since A 
e \emptyset, @prp-card-le-surjection gives a surjection B 	o A. In the second, since B 
e \emptyset, the same proposition with the roles exchanged gives a surjection A 	o B. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: comparability cited, with the two cases. - 4: in the first case, a surjection B 	o A from @prp-card-le-surjection, with A 
e \emptyset used and the direction correct. - 3: the second case, with the roles exchanged and B 
e \emptyset used. [R2: Maximal chains give Zorn’s lemma] 1. Let C be a maximal chain of a partially ordered set (X, \preceq): a chain contained properly in no chain. Let u be an upper bound of C in X. Show that u \in C, that u is the greatest element of C, and that u is a maximal element of X. 2. Deduce @thm-zorn from the statement that every chain lies in a maximal chain. (a) Every element of C is below u, so C \cup \{u\} is a chain containing C; by maximality it is not larger, so u \in C. Then u \in C is above every element of C: it is the greatest element of C. Suppose u \prec x for some x \in X. For every c \in C, c \preceq u \preceq x, so C \cup \{x\} is a chain, and maximality gives x \in C. Then x \preceq u, and with u \preceq x, (PO2) gives x = u, contradicting u \prec x. So u is maximal in X. (b) Let P be a non-empty partially ordered set in which every non-empty chain has an upper bound. The empty set is a chain, so by Section 6.1, Exercise B1 (@exr-chains-and-zorn-b1) with C_0 = \emptyset, P has a maximal chain C. It is not empty: for p \in P, \{p\} is a chain properly containing \emptyset. So C has an upper bound u, and u is a maximal element of P by (a). Since Exercise B1 was proved from Zorn’s lemma, the two statements are equivalent. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: u \in C in (a). - 1: u is the greatest element of C. - 3: u is maximal in X, using (PO2). - 2: a maximal chain C from Exercise B1 with C_0 = \emptyset. - 1: C 
e \emptyset. - 2: an upper bound of C, and the conclusion. [R3: The basis theorem, read as a template] This item is optional and goes with the optional subsection. A set of vectors is linearly independent when no finite non-trivial combination of its vectors is 0. 1. Which of the template’s four steps uses that independence is tested on finitely many vectors at a time? 2. Why would the template fail for the property “S is a finite independent set”? 3. A maximal element of a partial order need not be greatest. What does this say about bases? (a) Step (2), the chains: a dependence among vectors of the union of a chain involves finitely many vectors, all in one member (@lem-chain-union (b)), and that member is independent. (b) The union of a chain of finite sets need not be finite (the second warning of Section 6.1), so step (2) fails: the union need not be a partial object. (c) This is the point of @exm-maximal-not-greatest. Maximal independent sets need not contain one another, so a vector space can have many bases, none of them greatest. In 
R^2, \{ (1, 0), (1, 1) \} and \{ (2, 0), (0, 3) \} are both bases, and neither contains the other.

title: Definition 1.1.2 (Divisibility)
content: Let \(a, b \in \nZ\) . We say that \(a\) divides \(b\) , written \(a \mid b\) , if there exists \(k \in \nZ\) with \(b = ka\) . Then \(a\) is a divisor of \(b\) , and \(b\) is a multiple of \(a\) .

title: Definition 1.1.1 (Even and Odd)
content: An integer \(n\) is even if \(n = 2k\) for some \(k \in \nZ\) , and odd if \(n = 2k + 1\) for some \(k \in \nZ\) .

title: Definition 1.1.3 (Prime Number)
content: An integer \(p\) is prime if \(p \ge 2\) and the only positive divisors of \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\) . A prime factor of an integer \(n\) is a prime \(p\) with \(p \mid n\) .

title: Example (A proof by cases)
content: Show that \(n^3 + 5n\) is even for every integer \(n\) .

title: Example (Divisors of a combination)
content: Let \(a, b, c \in \nZ\) with \(a \mid b\) and \(a \mid c\) . Show that \(a \mid bx + cy\) for all \(x, y \in \nZ\) .

title: Example (Same pattern, lattice midpoint)
content: Show that if two lattice points have the same parity pattern, then their midpoint is a lattice point.

title: Example (Method: proof by cases)
content: Template. Find a disjunction you already have, such as “ \(n\) is even or \(n\) is odd” ( @thm-even-or-odd ), “ \(x \ge 0\) or \(x < 0\) ”, or excluded middle ( @fd1:prp-excluded-middle ). Write one paragraph per case, labeled Case 1. , Case 2. . In each, add the case to the givens, unwind it, and reach the same goal. When to use it. The definitions or the algebra behave differently on different kinds of input, so the givens give no grip until you know which kind you have. The usual failure. Cases that do not cover every possibility (N8), or a case forgotten (N7). Before splitting, say why the cases are exhaustive.

title: Example (Method: disproof by counterexample, proof by example)
content: Template. To refute “for every \(x\) , if \(P(x)\) then \(Q(x)\) ”: name one \(x\) , check \(P(x)\) , and check that \(Q(x)\) fails. To prove “there is an \(x\) with \(P(x)\) ”: name one \(x\) and check \(P(x)\) . When to use it. The claim survives a few tries, yet you doubt it; or the statement is existential. Search small and extreme cases first: \(0\) , \(1\) , negative numbers, the smallest sets. The usual failure. A “counterexample” that does not satisfy the hypothesis; refuting a different claim from the one stated; and the mirror error, concluding “for every” from examples (N1). One example refutes a universal claim, and no number of examples proves one.

title: Example (Method: direct proof from a definition)
content: Template. To prove “if \(P\) , then \(Q\) ”: (1) assume \(P\) and write it out by its definition, giving each witness a new name; (2) write out what \(Q\) demands, for example which object must be produced; (3) close the gap by computation, on scrap paper if need be; (4) write the proof forwards: assume, unwind, compute, and rewind into the definition of \(Q\) , naming the witness and checking that it is of the required kind. When to use it. The hypotheses and the conclusion are defined notions, and the gap between them is computation. The usual failure. Stopping at the computation, as in “ \(c = (lk)a\) , done”, without checking that \(lk \in \nZ\) , which is the clause the definition demands. Also one name for two witnesses (N4), and using what is to be proved (N9).

title: Example (The parity of a sum)
content: Let \(m, n \in \nZ\) . If \(m\) and \(n\) have the same parity (both even or both odd), then \(m + n\) is even. If they have opposite parity (one even and the other odd), then \(m + n\) is odd.

title: Example (A pattern that breaks)
content: Is \(2p + 1\) prime for every prime \(p\) ?

title: Example (Two divisors, one product)
content: Prove or disprove: for all integers \(a, b, c\) , if \(a \mid c\) and \(b \mid c\) , then \(ab \mid c\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Write out “ \(6 \mid n\) ” and “ \(n\) is odd” by their definitions, each as a “there exists”. True or false, with reasons: \(-1\) is odd; \(7 \mid 0\) ; \(0 \mid 7\) ; \(1\) is prime. What must a counterexample to “every multiple of \(4\) is a multiple of \(8\) ” satisfy? Give one. In the proof of @thm-even-or-odd , name the four case splits and say why each is exhaustive.

title: Exercise (B1: Direct proofs)
content: Prove, for all integers \(a, b, c, d\) : if \(a \mid b\) , then \(a^2 \mid b^2\) ; if \(a \mid b\) and \(c \mid d\) , then \(ac \mid bd\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Two cases)
content: Prove that for every integer \(n\) , either \(4 \mid n^2\) or \(4 \mid n^2 - 1\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Name the move, then complete it)
content: Here is the frame of a proof that if \(m, n \in \nZ\) have opposite parity, then \(m^2 + n^2\) is odd. The statement is unchanged when \(m\) and \(n\) are exchanged, so we may assume … \(\vdots\) … Hence \(m^2 + n^2\) is odd. Name the move, then complete it.

title: Exercise (B4: Prove or disprove)
content: Prove each true statement and refute each false one with a counterexample. For all integers \(a, b, c\) : if \(a \mid b + c\) and \(a \mid b\) , then \(a \mid c\) . For all integers \(a, b, c\) : if \(a \mid b + c\) , then \(a \mid b\) or \(a \mid c\) . For every integer \(n\) , \(n^4 + n^2 + 1\) is odd. The sum of any three odd integers is even. There is an integer \(n > 5\) with \(n \mid n + 6\) . For all integers \(m, n\) : if \(mn\) is even, then \(m\) and \(n\) are both even.

title: Exercise (C1: Three cases)
content: By the method of @thm-even-or-odd , show that every integer has the form \(3k\) , \(3k + 1\) or \(3k + 2\) for some \(k \in \nZ\) , and that no integer has two of these forms. Deduce that for every integer \(n\) , \(n^2\) has the form \(3k\) (exactly when \(3 \mid n\) ) or the form \(3k + 1\) . Prove that for all integers \(a, b\) : if \(3 \mid a^2 + b^2\) , then \(3 \mid a\) and \(3 \mid b\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: Claim: if \(n \in \nZ\) and \(n^2\) is odd, then \(n\) is odd. “Proof”: Let \(n\) be odd, \(n = 2k + 1\) . Then \(n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1\) is odd. Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? Name the failing line. Give a counterexample to the illegal step itself. Write a correct proof.

title: Exercise (C3: Lattice points in space)
content: A lattice point of space is a point \((a, b, c)\) with \(a, b, c \in \nZ\) . Give eight lattice points of space no two of which have a lattice point as midpoint. Show that two lattice points of space with the same three parities have a lattice point as midpoint. Which principle, stated in this section and not yet proved, would show that among any nine lattice points of space two have a lattice point as midpoint?

title: Proposition 1.1.1 (Divisibility Is Transitive)
content: For all integers \(a, b, c\) , if \(a \mid b\) and \(b \mid c\) , then \(a \mid c\) .

title: Theorem 1.1.2 (Every Integer Is Even or Odd)
content: Every integer is even or odd, and no integer is both.

title: Definition 1.2.4 (Empty Set)
content: An empty set is a set with no elements: a set \(E\) such that \(\forall x\, (x \notin E)\) .

title: Definition 1.2.3 (Specification)
content: Let \(A\) be a set and \(P(x)\) a property of objects \(x\) . Then there is a set, written \[ \{ x \in A : P(x) \}, \] whose elements are exactly the elements of \(A\) that have the property \(P\) : for every \(y\) , \[ y \in \{ x \in A : P(x) \} \iff y \in A \text{ and } P(y). \]

title: Definition 1.2.1 (Equality of Sets)
content: Sets \(A\) and \(B\) are equal, \(A = B\) , if and only if they have the same elements: \[ \forall x\, (x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B). \]

title: Definition 1.2.2 (Subset)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. \(A\) is a subset of \(B\) , written \(A \subseteq B\) , if every element of \(A\) is an element of \(B\) : \[ \forall x\, (x \in A \to x \in B). \] We also say that \(A\) is contained in \(B\) , or that \(B\) contains \(A\) . If \(A \subseteq B\) and \(A \ne B\) , then \(A\) is a proper subset of \(B\) , written \(A \subsetneq B\) .

title: Example (Method: two inclusions)
content: Template. To prove \(A = B\) , write two paragraphs, labeled \((\subseteq)\) and \((\supseteq)\) , each an element-chase ( @exm-method-element-chasing ). The two paragraphs are separate boxes: neither uses the other’s assumption. To compute a set, first guess it from small cases, then prove the guess this way. When to use it. A set equality that no known law gives at once. For “ \(S = \emptyset\) ”, only \((\subseteq)\) needs work. The usual failure. Proving one inclusion only, or using the assumption of the \((\subseteq)\) paragraph inside the \((\supseteq)\) paragraph. Logic and Proof wrote such a proof in prose ( @fd1:exm-rhetoric-double-inclusion ).

title: Example (Method: element-chasing)
content: Template. Begin “Let \(x \in A\) .” Unwind the definition of \(A\) to see what is known about \(x\) . Rewind the definition of \(B\) to see what must be shown, and reach it. End “Hence \(x \in B\) ; since \(x\) was arbitrary, \(A \subseteq B\) .” When to use it. The goal is an inclusion \(A \subseteq B\) , or any statement of the shape \(\forall x\, (x \in A \to \dots)\) . The usual failure. Checking some elements of \(A\) and stopping, entry (N1) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue (the second warning below shows it). Starting from \(x \in B\) instead, which proves the converse inclusion, entry (N5). Choosing a particular \(x\) , such as \(x = 0\) , where an arbitrary one is needed.

title: Example (Computing sets given by a property)
content: Show that \(\{ x \in \nZ : x^2 < 5 \} = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}\) . Show that \(\{ x \in \nR : x^2 < 0 \} = \emptyset\) .

title: Example (Three inclusions)
content: Show that \([1, 2] \subseteq [0, 3]\) . Let \(S\) be the set of integer multiples of \(6\) and \(T\) the set of integer multiples of \(3\) , as above. Show that \(S \subseteq T\) . By @def-divides , \(S\) consists of the integers \(x\) with \(6 \mid x\) , and \(T\) of those with \(3 \mid x\) . Let \(A\) be any set. Show that \(A \subseteq A\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Negate “ \(A \subseteq B\) ” in symbols, and then in words, with the negation pushed through the quantifier and the implication. True or false: \(\{1\} \in \{\{1\}, 2\}\) ; \(\{1\} \subseteq \{\{1\}, 2\}\) ; \(\emptyset \subseteq \emptyset\) ; \(\{\emptyset\} \subseteq \{1\}\) . Give a reason for each. List the elements of \(\{ n \in \nZ : 0 < n^2 \le 9 \}\) . In an element-chasing proof of \(A \subseteq B\) , the first sentence is “let \(x \in A\) ”. Which rule of logic gives its first clause, and which its second?

title: Exercise (B1: A set given by an equation)
content: Prove that \(\{ x \in \nR : x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0 \} = \{1, 2\}\) , by two inclusions.

title: Exercise (B2: A subset of the empty set)
content: Let \(A\) be a set with \(A \subseteq \emptyset\) . Prove that \(A = \emptyset\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Every set has something outside it)
content: Let \(A\) be a set, and let \(R_A = \{ x \in A : x \notin x \}\) as in @thm-russell . Let \(A^{+}\) be the set whose elements are the elements of \(A\) together with the object \(R_A\) (it exists by (W2) and (W3)). Show that \(A \subsetneq A^{+}\) . Deduce from @thm-russell that no set \(A\) has the property “every subset of \(A\) is an element of \(A\) ”.

title: Exercise (C2: Antisymmetry for sets of sets)
content: Can there be sets \(A\) and \(B\) , whose elements are themselves sets, such that \(A \subseteq B\) , \(B \subseteq A\) , and \(A \ne B\) ? Explain why the answer does not depend on what the elements of \(A\) and \(B\) are.

title: Proposition 1.2.3 (The Empty Set Is Unique)
content: If \(E\) and \(E'\) are empty sets, then \(E = E'\) .

title: Proposition 1.2.1 (Equality Is Two Inclusions)
content: For all sets \(A\) and \(B\) , \(A = B\) if and only if \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq A\) .

title: Proposition 1.2.2 (Inclusion Is Transitive)
content: For all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , and \(C\) , if \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq C\) , then \(A \subseteq C\) .

title: Theorem 1.2.4 (Russell’s Theorem)
content: For every set \(A\) , the set \(R_A = \{ x \in A : x \notin x \}\) is not an element of \(A\) . Hence there is no set of which every set is an element.

title: Definition 1.3.4 (Union and Intersection of a Family)
content: Let \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of sets. The union \(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\) is the set whose elements are exactly the objects lying in \(A_i\) for some \(i \in I\) : \[ x \in \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i \iff \exists i \in I\ (x \in A_i). \] If \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) is a family of subsets of a set \(X\) , the intersection is \[ \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i \coloneqq \{ x \in X : \forall i \in I\ (x \in A_i) \} . \] For a set \(\sS\) whose elements are sets, \(\bigcup \sS \coloneqq \bigcup_{A \in \sS} A\) ; and for a non-empty set \(\sS \subseteq \powerset{X}\) , \(\bigcap \sS \coloneqq \bigcap_{A \in \sS} A\) . In both, the family is indexed by \(\sS\) itself, the member with index \(A\) being \(A\) .

title: Definition 1.3.3 (Indexed Family)
content: Let \(I\) be a set. A family of sets indexed by \(I\) , written \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) , assigns to each \(i \in I\) a set \(A_i\) . The set \(I\) is the index set , and \(A_i\) is the member of the family with index \(i\) . If \(X\) is a set with \(A_i \subseteq X\) for every \(i \in I\) , we speak of a family of subsets of \(X\) .

title: Definition 1.3.2 (Power Set)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. The power set of \(X\) is the set \(\powerset{X}\) whose elements are exactly the subsets of \(X\) : \[ S \in \powerset{X} \iff S \subseteq X . \]

title: Definition 1.3.1 (Union, Intersection, Difference)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. The union \(A \cup B\) is the set whose elements are exactly the objects lying in \(A\) or in \(B\) : \(x \in A \cup B \iff (x \in A \vee x \in B)\) . The intersection \(A \cap B\) is the set \(\{ x \in A : x \in B \}\) : so \(x \in A \cap B \iff (x \in A \wedge x \in B)\) . The difference \(A \setminus B\) is the set \(\{ x \in A : x \notin B \}\) : so \(x \in A \setminus B \iff (x \in A \wedge x \notin B)\) . Sets \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint if \(A \cap B = \emptyset\) . If \(A \subseteq X\) , the difference \(X \setminus A\) is called the complement of \(A\) in \(X\) .

title: Example (A law by a chain)
content: Show that \((A \setminus B) \setminus C = A \setminus (B \cup C)\) for all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) .

title: Example (Unions and intersections of intervals)
content: Show that: \(\bigcup_{t \in (0, 1)} [t, 1] = (0, 1]\) ; \(\bigcap_{t \in (0, \infty)} (-t, t) = \{0\}\) , inside \(X = \nR\) ; \(\bigcap_{t \in (0, \infty)} (0, t) = \emptyset\) , inside \(X = \nR\) .

title: Example (Method: a chain of equivalences)
content: Template. For \(L = R\) : let \(x\) be arbitrary, and write \(x \in L \iff \dots \iff x \in R\) , one step per line. Each step either unwinds a definition ( @def-set-operations ) or applies a propositional equivalence to membership statements, with its name on the line; a step may act on a part of the line ( @fd1:prp-replacement ). Since \(\dashv\vdash\) is used like \(=\) ( @fd1:prp-provable-equivalence-basics (b)), the chain gives \(x \in L \dashv\vdash x \in R\) , so \(x \in L \leftrightarrow x \in R\) by (a), and @def-set-equality finishes. When to use it. Identities built from \(\cup\) , \(\cap\) , \(\setminus\) and families, where every step is reversible. The usual failure. A step that holds in one direction only, written as \(\iff\) : for example \(x \in A \implies x \in A \cup B\) . When a chain will not close, look for a small witness instead ( @exm-method-counterexample ); a truth table in the statements \(x \in A\) , \(x \in B\) , \(x \in C\) finds one, each row saying which of \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) a witness should lie in.

title: Example (Small power sets)
content: Compute \(\powerset{\emptyset}\) , \(\powerset{\{\emptyset\}}\) , and \(\powerset{\{1, 2\}}\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: These parts are about @thm-de-morgan-families and its proof. Which law of Logic and Proof , Chapter 6 is used in the \((\subseteq)\) half of the second law, and which of its directions is classical? Run the first law on \(X = \nZ\) , \(I = \{2, 3\}\) , and \(A_i\) the set of integer multiples of \(i\) . Describe both sides in words, and name two integers in each side and two outside it. What are the two sides of each law when \(I = \emptyset\) ? Let \(x \in X\) . Translate \(x \notin \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i\) into a statement with \(\exists\) . What is the correct translation if \(x \in X\) is not assumed?

title: Exercise (B1: Intersection and difference)
content: Prove that \(A \cap (B \setminus C) = (A \cap B) \setminus (A \cap C)\) for all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) , and name the propositional equivalence behind it.

title: Exercise (B2: Three families of intervals)
content: For each family, indexed by \(t \in (0, \infty)\) , compute the union and the intersection (inside \(X = \nR\) ), and prove each answer by two inclusions. \(A_t = [t, 1 + t]\) ; \(B_t = (-t, 1/t)\) ; \(C_t = (t, 2t)\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Canceling a union)
content: Give sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) with \(A \cup B = A \cup C\) and \(B \ne C\) . Then list the properties that any correct answer must have, so that a different answer can be checked against them.

title: Exercise (B4: Prove or disprove)
content: For all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) , decide which of these hold. Prove each true one by a chain of equivalences ( @exm-method-chain-of-iff ), and refute each false one with a concrete counterexample. \(A \setminus (A \setminus B) = A \cap B\) . \((A \cup B) \setminus B = A\) . \((A \cup B) \setminus B = A \setminus B\) . \(A \cup (B \setminus C) = (A \cup B) \setminus C\) . \(A \cap (B \setminus C) = (A \cap B) \setminus C\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Power sets and operations)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Decide whether \(\powerset{A \setminus B} = \powerset{A} \setminus \powerset{B}\) can hold. Then prove that every non-empty element of \(\powerset{A \setminus B}\) lies in \(\powerset{A} \setminus \powerset{B}\) . Show by an example that \(\powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B} = \powerset{A \cup B}\) can fail. Then prove that it holds if and only if \(A \subseteq B\) or \(B \subseteq A\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: Here is a “proof” that \((A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C) \subseteq A \cup (B \cap C)\) for all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) . Let \(x \in (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)\) . (2) Then \(x \in A \cup B\) and \(x \in A \cup C\) . (3) We consider two cases, according to \(x \in A \cup B\) . (4) Case \(x \in A\) . Then \(x \in A \cup (B \cap C)\) . (5) Case \(x \in B\) . Since \(x \in A \cup C\) , \(x \in C\) . (6) So \(x \in B \cap C\) , and hence \(x \in A \cup (B \cap C)\) . (7) In both cases \(x \in A \cup (B \cap C)\) , which proves the inclusion. Is the conclusion true? Which line fails, which rule does it break, and which entry of the catalogue of Logic and Proof , Chapter 8 does it commit? Give a counterexample to the illegal step itself: sets and an element for which the line’s premise holds and its conclusion fails. Repair the proof.

title: Proposition 1.3.2 (Smallest Closed Set)
content: Let \(X\) be a set with given starting elements and steps, and let \(\sS \subseteq \powerset{X}\) be the set of closed subsets of \(X\) . Then \(\sS\) is non-empty, and \(M \coloneqq \bigcap \sS\) is closed and lies inside every closed set: \(M\) is the smallest closed subset of \(X\) .

title: Theorem 1.3.3 (De Morgan’s Laws for Families)
content: Let \(X\) be a set and \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) a family of subsets of \(X\) , with any index set \(I\) , including \(I = \emptyset\) . Then \[ X \setminus \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcap_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) \quad\text{and}\quad X \setminus \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcup_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) . \]

title: Theorem 1.3.1 (Algebra of Sets)
content: For all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , and \(C\) : (commutativity) \(A \cup B = B \cup A\) and \(A \cap B = B \cap A\) ; (associativity) \((A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)\) and \((A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C)\) ; (distributivity) \(A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)\) and \(A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)\) ; (differences) \(A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C)\) and \(A \setminus (B \cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)\) .

title: Definition 1.4.2 (Cartesian product)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Their Cartesian product is the set \[ A \times B \coloneqq \{ (a, b) : a \in A, \ b \in B \} \] of all ordered pairs with first coordinate in \(A\) and second coordinate in \(B\) . Written out, an object \(p\) is an element of \(A \times B\) if and only if \[ \exists a \in A \ \exists b \in B \ \ p = (a, b) . \] For a set \(X\) we write \(X^2 \coloneqq X \times X\) , and, for \(n \in \nN\) with \(n \ge 2\) , \(X^n\) is the set of all \(n\) -tuples \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\) with every \(x_k \in X\) .

title: Definition 1.4.1 (Ordered pair)
content: For any objects \(a\) and \(b\) there is an object \((a, b)\) , the ordered pair of \(a\) and \(b\) ; we call \(a\) its first coordinate and \(b\) its second coordinate . Ordered pairs have the characteristic property : for all \(a, b, c, d\) , \[ (a, b) = (c, d) \iff a = c \text{ and } b = d . \]

title: Definition 1.4.3 (Relation)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. A relation from \(A\) to \(B\) is a subset \(R \subseteq A \times B\) . For \(a \in A\) and \(b \in B\) we write \(a \mathrel{R} b\) , read “ \(a\) is \(R\) -related to \(b\) ”, to mean \((a, b) \in R\) . A relation on \(A\) is a relation from \(A\) to \(A\) , that is, a subset of \(A^2\) . The domain of \(R\) is the set of first coordinates that occur, \(\{ a \in A : \exists b \in B \ \ a \mathrel{R} b \}\) , and its range is the set of second coordinates that occur, \(\{ b \in B : \exists a \in A \ \ a \mathrel{R} b \}\) . Turning every pair of \(R\) around gives a relation from \(B\) to \(A\) , the inverse relation \[ R^{-1} \coloneqq \{ (b, a) \in B \times A : (a, b) \in R \} . \]

title: Example (The coordinates of an element of a product)
content: Let \(p \in A \times B\) . Show that there is exactly one \(a\) and exactly one \(b\) such that \(a \in A\) , \(b \in B\) and \(p = (a, b)\) .

title: Example (Method: existence and uniqueness)
content: Template. “There is exactly one \(x\) with \(P(x)\) ” is two claims ( @fd1:def-unique-existence , @fd1:prp-unique-existence-use ). For existence , name a candidate \(x_0\) and check \(P(x_0)\) , or obtain one from a given “there exists”. For uniqueness , take \(x\) and \(x'\) with \(P(x)\) and \(P(x')\) , two names about which nothing else is assumed, and prove \(x = x'\) ; or show that every \(x\) with \(P(x)\) equals \(x_0\) . When to use it. Whenever a definition says “the”: the coordinates of a pair, the value \(f(x)\) , the empty set ( @prp-empty-set-unique ), an inverse. The usual failure. Proving only one half: a uniqueness proof with no candidate, or a candidate never shown to be the only one. Also checking \(P(x_0)\) twice and calling it uniqueness, and naming “the” object before either half is proved (entry (N14) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue ).

title: Example (Solving an equation between pairs)
content: Find all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\) with \((x + y, x - y) = (3, 1)\) . Then decide whether \((1, 2) = (2, 1)\) and whether \((1, 1) = (1, 1)\) .

title: Example (Relations as sets of pairs)
content: Write each relation as a set, and find its domain and range. The relation \(<\) on \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) . Divisibility on \(\{1, \dots, 6\}\) : \(a \mathrel{D} b\) when \(a \mid b\) . The unit circle, as a relation on \(\nR\) . The graph of squaring, as a relation on \(\nR\) . The two extreme relations from \(A\) to \(B\) : \(\emptyset\) and \(A \times B\) .

title: Example (Products, small and large)
content: Let \(a, b, c\) be three different objects, none of them a number. List \(\{1, 2\} \times \{a, b, c\}\) and \(\{a, b, c\} \times \{1, 2\}\) . Describe \(\nR^2\) and \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) as sets of points of the plane. What is \(\{1, 2\} \times \emptyset\) ?

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define \(A \times B\) in symbols, with its membership condition written out using quantifiers. Is \(((1, 2), 3) = (1, (2, 3))\) ? Justify your answer. Write the inverse of the relation \(<\) on \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) as a set of pairs. Is \(\emptyset\) a relation on every set \(A\) ? Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: An L-shaped region)
content: Let \(E \coloneqq ([0, 1] \times [0, 2]) \cup ([1, 2] \times [0, 1])\) . Describe \(E\) as a region of the plane. Then use @prp-product-set-laws to write \(E\) as \(([0, 2] \times [0, 1]) \cup (P \times Q)\) for intervals \(P\) and \(Q\) , and prove the equality.

title: Exercise (B2: The intersection law, written with two pairs)
content: Here is a proof of the inclusion \((\supseteq)\) of \(A \times (B \cap C) = (A \times B) \cap (A \times C)\) that works from the definition of the product and the characteristic property directly, without the shortcut \((\ast)\) . Its last sentence is blank. Name the move, then complete it. Let \(p \in (A \times B) \cap (A \times C)\) . Since \(p \in A \times B\) , there are \(a \in A\) and \(b \in B\) with \(p = (a, b)\) . Since \(p \in A \times C\) , there are \(a' \in A\) and \(c \in C\) with \(p = (a', c)\) ; the names \(a'\) and \(c\) are new, because nothing says that this second pair of coordinates is the first one again. Hence \((a, b) = (a', c)\) . \(\underline{\hspace{8em}}\)

title: Exercise (B3: Two products crossed)
content: Prove that \((A \times B) \cap (B \times A) = (A \cap B) \times (A \cap B)\) for all sets \(A\) and \(B\) .

title: Exercise (B4: Prove or disprove)
content: Prove each true statement by the method of @exm-method-uniqueness , or the section’s element arguments, and refute each false one with a concrete counterexample. For all real \(a\) and \(b\) there is exactly one pair \((x, y)\) of real numbers with \((3x - y, x + 2y) = (a, b)\) . For every real \(a\) there is exactly one pair \((x, y)\) of real numbers with \((x^2, y) = (a, 0)\) . For all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) : if \(A \times B = A \times C\) , then \(B = C\) . For all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) such that \(A\) has an element: if \(A \times B = A \times C\) , then \(B = C\) . There is exactly one set \(E\) with \(E \times E = \emptyset\) .

title: Exercise (C1: The square of a union)
content: Determine whether \((A \cup B) \times (A \cup B) = (A \times A) \cup (B \times B)\) for all sets \(A\) and \(B\) . Justify your answer. Prove the inclusion \((A \times A) \cup (B \times B) \subseteq (A \cup B) \times (A \cup B)\) . Prove, from @prp-product-set-laws , that \[ (A \cup B) \times (A \cup B) = (A \times A) \cup (A \times B) \cup (B \times A) \cup (B \times B) . \]

title: Exercise (C2: When one inclusion forces equality)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Prove that \(A \times B \subseteq B \times A\) if and only if \(A = B\) or \(A = \emptyset\) or \(B = \emptyset\) .

title: Proposition 1.4.1 (Products and Set Operations)
content: For all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) : \[ \begin{aligned} A \times (B \cup C) &= (A \times B) \cup (A \times C), \\ A \times (B \cap C) &= (A \times B) \cap (A \times C), \\ A \times (B \setminus C) &= (A \times B) \setminus (A \times C), \\ A \times \emptyset &= \emptyset, \end{aligned} \] and the mirror-image laws, with the varying factor on the left: \[ \begin{aligned} (B \cup C) \times A &= (B \times A) \cup (C \times A), \\ (B \cap C) \times A &= (B \times A) \cap (C \times A), \\ (B \setminus C) \times A &= (B \times A) \setminus (C \times A), \\ \emptyset \times A &= \emptyset . \end{aligned} \]

title: Definition 1.5.5 (Bijective)
content: A function is bijective (a bijection ) if it is both injective and surjective.

title: Definition 1.5.2 (Composition)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions, the codomain of \(f\) being the domain of \(g\) . Their composite is the function \[ g \circ f \colon X \to Z, \qquad (g \circ f)(x) \coloneqq g(f(x)) , \] read “ \(g\) after \(f\) ”.

title: Definition 1.5.1 (Function)
content: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets. A function from \(X\) to \(Y\) , written \(f \colon X \to Y\) , is given by a relation \(G \subseteq X \times Y\) , the graph of \(f\) , such that \[ \text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is exactly one } y \in Y \text{ with } (x, y) \in G , \] together with the set \(Y\) , the codomain of \(f\) . Formally, \(f\) is the pair \((G, Y)\) . The set \(X\) is the domain of \(f\) . For \(x \in X\) , the unique \(y\) with \((x, y) \in G\) is written \(f(x)\) , the value of \(f\) at \(x\) . We write \((x, y) \in f\) for \((x, y) \in G\) , and \(x \mapsto f(x)\) for the whole function when its domain and codomain are clear. In symbols, the condition on the graph is \[ \forall x \in X \ \ \exists! \, y \in Y \ \ (x, y) \in G , \] where, as with the bounded quantifiers of @fd1:def-bounded-quantifier , \(\exists! \, y \in Y \ \psi\) abbreviates \(\exists! \, y \, (y \in Y \wedge \psi)\) .

title: Definition 1.5.3 (Injective)
content: A function \(f \colon X \to Y\) is injective (an injection , or one-to-one ) if, for all \(x_1, x_2 \in X\) , \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\) implies \(x_1 = x_2\) . In symbols: \[ \forall x_1 \in X \ \ \forall x_2 \in X \ \ \bigl( f(x_1) = f(x_2) \to x_1 = x_2 \bigr) . \]

title: Definition 1.5.4 (Surjective)
content: A function \(f \colon X \to Y\) is surjective (a surjection , or onto ) if, for every \(y \in Y\) , there exists \(x \in X\) with \(f(x) = y\) . In symbols: \[ \forall y \in Y \ \ \exists x \in X \ \ f(x) = y . \]

title: Exercise (B2: Put the proof in order)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions. The following lines contain a proof that if \(g \circ f\) is surjective, then \(g\) is surjective , shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the six correct lines in an order that makes a proof, and say why each of the other two lines fails. Then \(g(y) = g(f(x)) = (g \circ f)(x) = z\) , by @def-composition . Let \(y \in Y\) . Since \(g \circ f\) is surjective, there is \(x \in X\) with \((g \circ f)(x) = z\) . Since \(z\) was arbitrary, \(g\) is surjective. Let \(y \coloneqq f(x)\) , an element of \(Y\) . Since \(f\) is surjective, \(y = f(x)\) for some \(x \in X\) . Let \(z \in Z\) . So \(z\) has a preimage under \(g\) , namely \(y\) .

title: Proposition 1.5.3 (Composition Is Associative)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) , \(g \colon Y \to Z\) , and \(h \colon Z \to W\) be functions. Then \[ h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f , \] and \(f \circ \id_X = f = \id_Y \circ f\) .

title: Proposition 1.5.2 (Functions and the Empty Set)
content: For every set \(Y\) there is exactly one function from \(\emptyset\) to \(Y\) : the pair \((\emptyset, Y)\) , called the empty function . If \(X\) is nonempty (it has an element), there is no function from \(X\) to \(\emptyset\) .

title: Proposition 1.5.1 (Equality of Functions)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon X' \to Y'\) be functions. Then \(f = g\) if and only if \(X = X'\) , \(Y = Y'\) , and \(f(x) = g(x)\) for every \(x \in X\) .

title: Theorem 1.5.4 (Composites of Injections and Surjections)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions. If \(f\) and \(g\) are injective, then \(g \circ f\) is injective. If \(f\) and \(g\) are surjective, then \(g \circ f\) is surjective. If \(f\) and \(g\) are bijective, then \(g \circ f\) is bijective.

title: Definition 1.6.2 (Inverse Function)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. A function \(g \colon Y \to X\) is a two-sided inverse , or an inverse , of \(f\) if it is both a left inverse and a right inverse of \(f\) : \[ g \circ f = \id_X \quad\text{and}\quad f \circ g = \id_Y . \] A function with an inverse is invertible . Its inverse is unique : if \(g\) and \(g'\) are both inverses of \(f\) , then \(g\) is a left inverse and \(g'\) a right inverse, so \(g = g'\) by @prp-inverse-unique . We call it the inverse of \(f\) and write it \(f^{-1} \colon Y \to X\) .

title: Definition 1.6.1 (Left and Right Inverses)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function, and let \(g \colon Y \to X\) be a function in the opposite direction. \(g\) is a left inverse of \(f\) if \(g \circ f = \id_X\) , that is, \(g(f(x)) = x\) for every \(x \in X\) . \(g\) is a right inverse of \(f\) if \(f \circ g = \id_Y\) , that is, \(f(g(y)) = y\) for every \(y \in Y\) .

title: Example (Running the construction)

title: Proposition 1.6.3 (Left and Right Inverses Agree)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. If \(g \colon Y \to X\) is a left inverse of \(f\) and \(h \colon Y \to X\) is a right inverse of \(f\) , then \(g = h\) .

title: Proposition 1.6.2 (Right Inverses Give Surjectivity)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. If \(f\) has a right inverse, then \(f\) is surjective.

title: Theorem 1.6.4 (Bijections Are the Invertible Functions)
content: A function \(f \colon X \to Y\) is bijective if and only if it has a two-sided inverse.

title: Theorem 1.6.1 (Left Inverses and Injectivity)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. If \(f\) has a left inverse, then \(f\) is injective. If \(X \ne \emptyset\) and \(f\) is injective, then \(f\) has a left inverse. Consequently, if \(X \ne \emptyset\) , then \(f\) has a left inverse if and only if \(f\) is injective.

title: Definition 1.7.1 (Image)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function and \(A \subseteq X\) . The image of \(A\) under \(f\) is the set \[ f(A) \coloneqq \{ y \in Y : \text{there exists } a \in A \text{ with } f(a) = y \}. \] We also write it \(\{ f(a) : a \in A \}\) . In symbols, for every \(y\) , \[ y \in f(A) \iff y \in Y \wedge \exists a \in A\ \, f(a) = y . \]

title: Definition 1.7.2 (Preimage)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function and \(B \subseteq Y\) . The preimage of \(B\) under \(f\) , also called its inverse image , is the set \[ f^{-1}(B) \coloneqq \{ x \in X : f(x) \in B \}. \] In symbols, for every \(x\) , \(x \in f^{-1}(B) \iff x \in X \wedge f(x) \in B\) . The preimage is defined for every function \(f\) , whether or not \(f\) has an inverse.

(2) Then \(y \in f(A)\) , so \(y = f(x)\) for some \(x \in A\) . (3) Also \(y \in f(B)\) , so \(y = f(x)\) for some \(x \in B\) . (4) Hence \(x \in A\) and \(x \in B\) , so \(x \in A \cap B\) . title: Exercise (B2: Two laws, element by element)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. title: Exercise (B3: The two readings of the inverse)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a bijection, with inverse function \(f^{-1} \colon Y \to X\) , and let \(B \subseteq Y\) . Prove that the image of \(B\) under the function \(f^{-1}\) equals the preimage of \(B\) under \(f\) . To keep the readings apart, write \(g \coloneqq f^{-1}\) for the inverse function, and prove \(g(B) = \{ x \in X : f(x) \in B \}\) . The remark in “Two readings of the inverse symbol” gives the argument in brief; write it out as two inclusions, tagging each step that names or exhibits a witness with \([\rulename{\exists E}]\) or \([\rulename{\exists I}]\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Images and differences)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function and \(A, B \subseteq X\) . Here are the first lines of a proof that \(f(A) \setminus f(B) \subseteq f(A \setminus B)\) . Name the move, then complete it. Let \(y \in f(A) \setminus f(B)\) . Then \(y \in f(A)\) , so there is \(a \in A\) with \(f(a) = y\) ; name it \(a\) \([\rulename{\exists E}]\) . Also \(y \notin f(B)\) . Show that the reverse inclusion can fail, with \(f(x) = x^2\) on \(\nR\) , \(A = \{-1, 1\}\) , and \(B = \{1\}\) . Prove that \(f(A \setminus B) = f(A) \setminus f(B)\) holds for all \(A, B \subseteq X\) if and only if \(f\) is injective.

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: A student proves the following claim: if \(f \colon X \to Y\) is injective and \(A \subseteq X\) , then \(f^{-1}(f(A)) \subseteq A\) . Let \(x \in f^{-1}(f(A))\) . (2) By the definition of preimage, \(x \in X\) and \(f(x) \in f(A)\) . (3) Since \(f(x) \in f(A)\) , we have \(x \in A\) . (4) Since \(x\) was arbitrary, \(f^{-1}(f(A)) \subseteq A\) . Is the claim true? Which line fails, and which rule does it skip? Give a counterexample to the failing step, and repair the proof.

title: Proposition 1.7.5 (Image and Preimage Round Trips)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. \(A \subseteq f^{-1}(f(A))\) for every \(A \subseteq X\) . Equality holds for all \(A \subseteq X\) if and only if \(f\) is injective. \(f(f^{-1}(B)) = B \cap f(X)\) for every \(B \subseteq Y\) ; in particular \(f(f^{-1}(B)) \subseteq B\) . Equality \(f(f^{-1}(B)) = B\) holds for all \(B \subseteq Y\) if and only if \(f\) is surjective.

title: Proposition 1.7.2 (Preimage under a Composite)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions, and \(C \subseteq Z\) . Then \[ (g \circ f)^{-1}(C) = f^{-1}\bigl(g^{-1}(C)\bigr). \]

title: Theorem 1.7.4 (Image of an Intersection)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. For all \(A, B \subseteq X\) , \(f(A \cap B) \subseteq f(A) \cap f(B)\) . The equality \(f(A \cap B) = f(A) \cap f(B)\) holds for all \(A, B \subseteq X\) if and only if \(f\) is injective.

title: Theorem 1.7.3 (Image of a Union)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function, and let \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of subsets of \(X\) . Then \[ f\Bigl(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\Bigr) = \bigcup_{i \in I} f(A_i). \]

title: Theorem 1.7.1 (Preimages of Set Operations)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. For every family \((B_i)_{i \in I}\) of subsets of \(Y\) , \(\displaystyle f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcup_{i \in I} B_i\Bigr) = \bigcup_{i \in I} f^{-1}(B_i)\) . For every family \((B_i)_{i \in I}\) of subsets of \(Y\) , \(\displaystyle f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcap_{i \in I} B_i\Bigr) = \bigcap_{i \in I} f^{-1}(B_i)\) , the intersection on the left taken in \(Y\) and on the right in \(X\) . For every \(B \subseteq Y\) , \(f^{-1}(Y \setminus B) = X \setminus f^{-1}(B)\) . For all \(B, C \subseteq Y\) , \(f^{-1}(B \setminus C) = f^{-1}(B) \setminus f^{-1}(C)\) .

title: Example (Method: the least element)
content: Template. (1) Name a set \(S\) whose least element would help: the failures, the values, the candidates. (2) Show that \(S\) is a non-empty subset of \(\nN\) , by giving an element; or a non-empty set of integers with an integer lower bound. (3) Take its least element \(m\) ( @thm-well-ordering ; for integers, @cor-well-ordering-integers below). (4) Use leastness: produce an element of \(S\) below \(m\) , a contradiction; or conclude what \(m\) must be. When to use it. A process that must stop; a quantity that can always be made smaller; the first time something happens; an object chosen to be extreme. The usual failure. Taking “the least element” of a set not shown to be non-empty, or of a set of rationals, or of a set of integers with no integer lower bound (the warning above); and forgetting to check that the smaller element lies in \(S\) again.

title: Theorem 2.1.4 (Induction Is Equivalent to Well-Ordering)
content: Let \(X \subseteq \nR\) contain \(0\) , be closed under \(n \mapsto n + 1\) , and have the predecessor property. Then \(X\) has the induction property if and only if \(X\) has the least-element property.

title: Theorem 2.1.3 (Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers)
content: Every non-empty subset of \(\nN\) has a least element.

title: Example (All Numbers Are Equal)
content: Here is a “theorem” and a “proof”. Find the line that fails. “Theorem.” For every integer \(n \ge 1\) and all real numbers \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) , we have \(x_1 = x_2 = \dots = x_n\) . “Proof.” For an integer \(n \ge 1\) , let \(P(n)\) be the statement “for all real numbers \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) , all the entries of the list \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) are equal”. We use @thm-induction with \(n_0 = 1\) . Base case. A list \(x_1\) of one number has only one entry, so all its entries are equal: \(P(1)\) holds. Step. Let \(n \ge 1\) be an integer, suppose \(P(n)\) , and let \(x_1, \dots, x_{n+1}\) be real numbers. The list \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) has \(n\) entries, so by \(P(n)\) its entries are all equal. The list \(x_2, \dots, x_{n+1}\) has \(n\) entries, so by \(P(n)\) its entries are all equal. The entry \(x_2\) lies in both lists, so every entry of either list equals \(x_2\) . Hence \(x_1 = x_2 = \dots = x_{n+1}\) , which is \(P(n + 1)\) . By @thm-induction , \(P(n)\) holds for every \(n \ge 1\) .

title: Example (Method: finding P(n) inside P(n + 1))
content: Template. (1) Write \(P(n + 1)\) out in full. (2) Find \(P(n)\) inside it: split off the last term, take out one factor, or separate the new piece from the old. (3) Apply the induction hypothesis to the old part. (4) Close the rest by computation. (5) Choose the base: the first \(n\) the claim covers from which steps (2)–(4) work, with any smaller \(n\) the claim covers checked directly. When to use it. \(P(n + 1)\) is built from \(P(n)\) by one operation: a term added, a factor multiplied, an element added to a set. The usual failure. Starting from \(P(n + 1)\) and deriving something true, which proves the converse, entry (N5) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue . A step that works only from some \(n\) on, with the base set lower (as in the gallery below). Using \(P(n + 1)\) inside its own step (N9).

title: Exercise (B1)
content: Prove that \(3 \mid n^3 + 2n\) for every \(n \in \nN\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Products of primes, used later)
content: An integer is a product of primes if it equals \(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k\) for some \(k \ge 1\) and primes \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) (a single prime counts, with \(k = 1\) ). Here \(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k\) has its school meaning, and multiplying two such products gives the product of the joined list; Section 2.3 defines finite products ( @def-sum-product ). Here is a proof that every integer \(n \ge 2\) is a product of primes, with its last step blank. Name the move, then complete it. Suppose not. Then the set \(F\) of integers \(n \ge 2\) that are not products of primes is non-empty and has the integer lower bound \(2\) , so it has a least element \(m\) by @cor-well-ordering-integers . Since a prime is a product of primes, \(m\) is not prime; as \(m \ge 2\) , it has a positive divisor \(a \notin \{1, m\}\) , and \(m = ab\) with \(b \in \nZ\) . As in the proof of @thm-prime-factor , \(b > 0\) and \(2 \le a < m\) . Since \(a < m = ab\) and \(a > 0\) , we get \(b > 1\) , so \(b \ge 2\) by the discreteness clause of @prp-integers-closed ; and since \(a \ge 2\) , \(b < 2b \le ab = m\) . So \(2 \le a < m\) and \(2 \le b < m\) , and as \(m\) is the least element of \(F\) , neither \(a\) nor \(b\) lies in \(F\) : both are products of primes. \(\dots\)

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: a flawed induction)
content: Here is a claim and a “proof”. Claim. Every integer \(n \ge 18\) is \(4a + 7b\) for some integers \(a, b \ge 0\) . For an integer \(n \ge 18\) , let \(P(n)\) be “ \(n = 4a + 7b\) for some integers \(a, b \ge 0\) ”. We use strong induction from base \(18\) ( @thm-strong-induction-from-base ). Base case. \(18 = 4 \cdot 1 + 7 \cdot 2\) , so \(P(18)\) holds. Step. Let \(n \ge 18\) be an integer, and suppose \(P(k)\) holds for every integer \(k\) with \(18 \le k \le n\) . Write \(n + 1 = (n - 3) + 4\) . Since \(n - 3 < n\) , the induction hypothesis gives \(n - 3 = 4a + 7b\) with integers \(a, b \ge 0\) . Then \(n + 1 = 4(a + 1) + 7b\) , with \(a + 1 \ge 0\) and \(b \ge 0\) , so \(P(n + 1)\) holds. By @thm-strong-induction-from-base , \(P(n)\) holds for every integer \(n \ge 18\) . Answer each question. (i) Is the claim true? (ii) Does the argument prove it? (iii) Which line fails, and for which \(n\) ? (iv) Which rule does that line break? (v) Give a counterexample to the failing step, not merely to some conclusion. (vi) Repair the proof.

title: Lemma 2.2.4 (Lowest Terms, Up to Factors of Two)
content: Every rational number can be written as \(p/q\) with \(p \in \nZ\) , \(q \in \nZ_{>0}\) , and \(p\) and \(q\) not both even.

title: Theorem 2.2.3 (Division Algorithm)
content: Let \(a \in \nZ\) and \(n \in \nZ_{>0}\) . Then there are unique integers \(q\) and \(r\) with \[ a = qn + r \quad \text{and} \quad 0 \le r < n . \]

title: Theorem 2.2.1 (Induction from a Base)
content: Let \(n_0\) be an integer, and for each integer \(n \ge n_0\) let \(P(n)\) be a statement. Suppose ( base case ) \(P(n_0)\) is true, and ( inductive step ) for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) , if \(P(n)\) is true then \(P(n + 1)\) is true. Then \(P(n)\) is true for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) .

title: Theorem 2.2.5 (Every Integer at Least Two Has a Prime Factor)
content: Every integer \(n \ge 2\) has a prime factor.

title: Theorem 2.2.2 (Strong Induction from a Base)
content: Let \(n_0\) be an integer, and for each integer \(n \ge n_0\) let \(P(n)\) be a statement. Suppose that, for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) : if \(P(k)\) is true for every integer \(k\) with \(n_0 \le k < n\) , then \(P(n)\) is true. Then \(P(n)\) is true for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) .

title: Corollary 2.3.2 (Recursion from a Base)
content: Let \(n_0\) be an integer, \(D \coloneqq \{ n \in \nZ : n \ge n_0 \}\) , \(X\) a set, \(a \in X\) , and \(g \colon D \times X \to X\) a function. Then there is exactly one function \(f \colon D \to X\) with \(f(n_0) = a\) and \(f(n + 1) = g(n, f(n))\) for every \(n \in D\) .

title: Definition 2.3.2 (Powers)
content: Let \(u \in \nR\) . The powers \(u^n\) , for \(n \in \nN\) , are defined by recursion: \[ u^0 \coloneqq 1, \qquad u^{n+1} \coloneqq u^n u . \]

title: Definition 2.3.1 (Finite Sums and Products)
content: Let \((a_k)_{k \ge 1}\) be a sequence of real numbers. The sums \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k\) and products \(\prod_{k=1}^{n} a_k\) , for \(n \in \nN\) , are defined by recursion: \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{k=1}^{0} a_k &\coloneqq 0, & \sum_{k=1}^{n+1} a_k &\coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k + a_{n+1}, \\ \prod_{k=1}^{0} a_k &\coloneqq 1, & \prod_{k=1}^{n+1} a_k &\coloneqq \Bigl(\prod_{k=1}^{n} a_k\Bigr) a_{n+1}. \end{aligned} \] The factorial of \(n \in \nN\) is \(n! \coloneqq \prod_{k=1}^{n} k\) . For integers \(m \le n + 1\) and reals \(a_k\) given for every integer \(k \ge m\) , \[ \sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^{n-m+1} a_{m-1+i}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^{n-m+1} a_{m-1+i} . \]

title: Exercise (C1: Two proofs by contradiction)
content: For each proof below: is the conclusion true? Is the argument valid? Name each flaw, and write a proof in the form that @exm-method-choosing-the-form recommends. Proof A. Claim: if \(n \in \nZ\) is odd, then \(n^2 + n\) is even. “Suppose \(n\) is odd and \(n^2 + n\) is odd. Write \(n = 2k + 1\) . Then \(n^2 + n = (2k + 1)(2k + 2) = 2(2k + 1)(k + 1)\) is even, which contradicts \(n^2 + n\) odd.” Proof B. Claim: for every \(n \in \nZ\) , if \(n^2 \ge 10\) , then \(n \ge 4\) or \(n \le -4\) . Suppose \(n^2 \ge 10\) . Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(n < 4\) or \(n > -4\) . Say \(n < 4\) , so \(n \le 3\) . If also \(n \ge -3\) , then \(n^2 \le 9 < 10\) ; so \(n \le -4\) . So \(n \le -4\) , which proves the claim.

Here that argument becomes a bound. Let \(p_1 \coloneqq 2\) , and let \(p_{n+1}\) be the least prime greater than \(p_n\) ; it exists by @thm-primes-infinite and @thm-well-ordering , and @cor-recursion-from-base makes \((p_n)_{n \ge 1}\) a sequence. title: Proposition 2.4.2 (The Cube Root of 2 Is Irrational)
content: \(\sqrt[3]{2}\) is irrational.

title: Theorem 2.4.1 (There Are Infinitely Many Primes)
content: For every \(n \in \nN\) there is a prime \(p\) with \(p > n\) .

title: Corollary 2.5.4 (The Number of Elements Is Unique)
content: Let \(A\) be a set and \(m, n \in \nN\) . If \(A\) has \(m\) elements and \(A\) has \(n\) elements, then \(m = n\) .

title: Corollary 2.5.3 (Pigeonhole for Finite Sets)
content: Let \(m, n \in \nN\) , let \(A\) have \(m\) elements, and let \(B\) have \(n\) elements. If \(m > n\) , there is no injection \(A \to B\) . If \(m < n\) , there is no surjection \(A \to B\) .

title: Corollary 2.5.7 (Removing a Point)
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) , let \(A\) have \(n + 1\) elements, and let \(a \in A\) . Then \(A \setminus \{a\}\) has \(n\) elements.

title: Definition 2.5.1 (Equinumerous Sets)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. We say that \(A\) and \(B\) are equinumerous , and write \(\card{A} = \card{B}\) , if there exists a bijection \(f \colon A \to B\) . In symbols, \[ \card{A} = \card{B} \iff \exists f \in B^A \ \ (f \text{ is injective} \wedge f \text{ is surjective}) . \]

title: Definition 2.5.2 (Finite Set, Number of Elements)
content: Let \(A\) be a set and \(n \in \nN\) . We say that \(A\) has \(n\) elements if \(\card{\{1, \dots, n\}} = \card{A}\) , that is, if there exists a bijection \(\varphi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} \to A\) . The set \(A\) is finite if it has \(n\) elements for some \(n \in \nN\) . In that case we write \(\card{A} = n\) .

title: Definition 2.5.3 (Infinite Set)
content: A set \(A\) is infinite if it is not finite: for every \(n \in \nN\) there is no bijection \(\{1, \dots, n\} \to A\) .

title: Example (Method: the pigeonhole principle)
content: Template. (1) Choose the pigeons, a set \(A\) whose number of elements you know, and the holes, a set \(B\) with fewer. (2) Define \(p \colon A \to B\) , “the hole of a pigeon”, and check that its values lie in \(B\) . (3) By @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a), \(p\) is not injective: two different pigeons \(a \ne a'\) share a hole. (4) Translate “same hole” back into the property you want. When to use it. The claim says “among any \(N\) objects, two have …”, or “some value is taken twice”, and \(N\) exceeds the number of possible values. The usual failure. Holes for which sharing a hole does not give the property: choose the holes by what two pigeons should share. Pigeons that need not be different: a list with repeats is not a set with \(N\) elements. Claiming to know which two pigeons share a hole.

title: Proposition 2.5.5 (Disjoint Unions)
content: Let \(m, n \in \nN\) , let \(A\) have \(m\) elements, let \(B\) have \(n\) elements, and suppose \(A \cap B = \emptyset\) . Then \(A \cup B\) has \(m + n\) elements.

title: Proposition 2.5.1 (Equinumerosity Is Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive)
content: For all sets \(A\) , \(B\) and \(C\) : \(\card{A} = \card{A}\) ; if \(\card{A} = \card{B}\) , then \(\card{B} = \card{A}\) ; if \(\card{A} = \card{B}\) and \(\card{B} = \card{C}\) , then \(\card{A} = \card{C}\) .

title: Proposition 2.5.8 (Counting Subsets)
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) . A set with \(n\) elements has \(2^n\) subsets: if \(\card{A} = n\) , then \(\card{\powerset{A}} = 2^n\) .

title: Proposition 2.5.6 (Subsets of Finite Sets)
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) , let \(A\) have \(n\) elements, and let \(S \subseteq A\) . Then \(S\) is finite and has \(k\) elements for some \(k \le n\) . If \(S \ne A\) , then \(k < n\) .

title: Theorem 2.5.9 (A Finite Set Has No Proper Copy)
content: Let \(A\) be a finite set and \(B \subsetneq A\) . Then \(A\) and \(B\) are not equinumerous: there is no bijection \(A \to B\) .

title: Theorem 2.5.2 (Pigeonhole Principle)
content: Let \(m, n \in \nN\) with \(m > n\) . Then there is no injection \(\{1, \dots, m\} \to \{1, \dots, n\}\) .

title: Corollary 3.1.7 (Products of Countable Sets)

title: Exercise (B2: Putting a proof in order)
content:
The lines (i)–(ix) below include the seven lines of a proof that \(2^m 3^n = 2^{m'} 3^{n'}\) implies \(m = m'\) and \(n = n'\) , for \(m, n, m', n' \in 
N\) , shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the seven lines in an order that makes a correct proof, and say why each of the other two lines fails. The left side is even, because \(m - m' \ge 1\) by the supposition; the right side is odd; no natural number is both ( @thm-division-algorithm , uniqueness of the remainder for divisor \(2\) ). This is a contradiction. Suppose \(2^m 3^n = 2^{m'} 3^{n'}\) . The left side is odd and the right side is even, a contradiction. Canceling \(2^m\) gives \(3^n = 3^{n'}\) . Suppose \(m 
e m'\) ; by symmetry, say \(m > m'\) . Since \(k \mapsto 3^k\) is strictly increasing on \(
N\) , \(n = n'\) . Since \(2\) and \(3\) are prime, unique factorization gives \(m = m'\) and \(n = n'\) . Canceling \(2^{m'}\) gives \(2^{m - m'} 3^n = 3^{n'}\) . So \(m = m'\) .

title: Axiom 3.2.1 (Axiom of Choice)
page: 3.2 Countable Unions and the Axiom of Choice
content: Let \(I\) be a set, and let \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of sets such that \(A_i\) is non-empty for every \(i \in I\) . title: Definition 3.3.1 (Decimal Expansion)
page: 3.3 Diagonal Arguments: Uncountable Sets and Cantor's Theorem
content: A digit sequence is a function \(k \mapsto d_k\) from \(\nZ_{>0}\) to \(\{0, 1, \dots, 9\}\) . For \(n \ge 1\) let \[ t_n \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{n} d_k 10^{-k} \] ( @def-sum-product ), where \(10^{-k} \coloneqq (1/10)^k\) ( @def-power ). The digit sequence is a decimal expansion of \(x \in [0, 1]\) if for every \(n \ge 1\) , \[ t_n \le x \le t_n + 10^{-n} . \]

title: Definition 3.4.1 (Comparing Sizes)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. We write \(\card{A} \le \card{B}\) , and say that \(A\) is at most as big as \(B\) , if there exists an injection \(A \to B\) . We write \(\card{A} < \card{B}\) , and say that \(A\) is strictly smaller than \(B\) , if \(\card{A} \le \card{B}\) and not \(\card{A} = \card{B}\) : there is an injection \(A \to B\) , and there is no bijection \(A \to B\) .

Often one map is an inclusion and the other squeezes \(B\) into a part of \(A\) . Do not hunt for the bijection: the theorem builds it. When to use it. \(A\) and \(B\) differ by “a little” (endpoints, a countable piece, a factor), so that a bijection would need cases; or \(A\) sits inside \(B\) , and \(B\) fits back into \(A\) . The usual failure. Two injections in the same direction. One injection that is not onto, read as strictness or as a bijection (the warnings after @def-card-le and after @exm-reals-open-interval ). A squeeze whose values leave the target: \(x \mapsto x/2\) sends \([0, 1]\) into \([0, \frac12]\) and hits \(0 \notin (0, 1)\) .

For \(0 \le x \le 1\) we have \(1/4 \le u(x) \le 3/4\) , so \(u\) does map into \((0, 1)\) . (2) If \(u(x) = u(y)\) , then \(x/2 = y/2\) , so \(x = y\) ; hence \(u\) is injective. (3) The inclusion \(\iota \colon (0, 1) \to [0, 1]\) is injective. (4) So there are injections in both directions between \([0, 1]\) and \((0, 1)\) . title: Theorem 3.4.3 (Schröder–Bernstein Theorem)

title: Example (Method: build a bijection by encoding and decoding)
content: Template. (1) Say what an element of the source must record for nothing to be lost. (2) Choose a code: a rule sending each element to an element of the target, and check that it lands there. (3) Write the decoder: a rule reading an element of the source back from each element of the target, and check that it is a function, with exactly one answer for each input. (4) Check both round trips and cite @thm-bijection-iff-inverse . When to use it. The two sets carry the same information arranged differently: two numbers in one, a pair of sequences in one sequence, a function of two variables as a function with function values. The usual failure. Checking one round trip only: \(\delta \circ \pi = \id\) alone shows only that \(\pi\) is injective ( @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective ). A decoder that is not a function, with two readings of one code or none (the interleaving of decimals, later in this section). If the decoder works on part of the target only, keep the injection and use @exm-method-injections-both-ways .

title: Example (Method: prove a law of sizes by a bijection of sets)
content: Template. (1) Write out what an element of each side is: a tagged element, a pair, a function, a function with function values. (2) Find the map that only regroups: compose with the inclusions, pair the coordinates, or curry. (3) Write the reverse regrouping. (4) Check both round trips with @prp-function-equality and @def-ordered-pair , and cite @thm-bijection-iff-inverse . When to use it. A law familiar from numbers, such as \(m^{n+k} = m^n m^k\) , is claimed for sets of any size; or a size is to be computed by rewriting a set step by step. The usual failure. Computing with symbols, as in “ \(\card{X}^{\card{Y} + \card{Z}} = \card{X}^{\card{Y}} \card{X}^{\card{Z}}\) ”, when no number \(\card{X}\) exists and the step is the law itself: (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue . Dropping the tags: with \(\cup\) in place of \(\sqcup\) the law fails: for \(X = \{0, 1\}\) and \(Y = Z = \{0\}\) , \(X^{Y \cup Z}\) has \(2\) elements and \(X^Y \times X^Z\) has \(4\) (Exercise B4 (b)).

title: Proposition 3.6.2 (Monotonicity)
content: Let \(A, A', B, B'\) be sets with \(\card{A} \le \card{A'}\) and \(\card{B} \le \card{B'}\) . Then \(\card{A \sqcup B} \le \card{A' \sqcup B'}\) ; \(\card{A \times B} \le \card{A' \times B'}\) ; if \(A' \ne \emptyset\) , then \(\card{A^B} \le \card{A'^{B'}}\) .

Definition 4.1.1 (Properties of a Relation)
content: Let \(X\) be a set and \(R\) a relation on \(X\) . Then \(R\) is reflexive on \(X\) if \(x \mathrel{R} x\) for every \(x \in X\) : \[ \forall x \in X \ \ x \mathrel{R} x ; \] symmetric if \(x \mathrel{R} y\) implies \(y \mathrel{R} x\) , for all \(x, y \in X\) : \[ \forall x \in X \ \forall y \in X \ \ \bigl( x \mathrel{R} y \to y \mathrel{R} x \bigr) ; \] antisymmetric if \(x \mathrel{R} y\) and \(y \mathrel{R} x\) together imply \(x = y\) , for all \(x, y \in X\) : \[ \forall x \in X \ \forall y \in X \ \ \bigl( (x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} x) \to x = y \bigr) ; \] transitive if \(x \mathrel{R} y\) and \(y \mathrel{R} z\) together imply \(x \mathrel{R} z\) , for all \(x, y, z \in X\) : \[ \forall x \in X \ \forall y \in X \ \forall z \in X \ \ \bigl( (x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} z) \to x \mathrel{R} z \bigr) . \]

title: Example (Method: proving or disproving a property of a relation)
content: Template. To prove a property, write it as the “for all” it is ( @def-relation-properties ), take arbitrary elements satisfying its hypothesis, unwind the relation’s definition and rewind the conclusion ( @exm-method-direct-proof ). To disprove it, exhibit one witness of the negated form and check each clause ( @exm-method-counterexample ). Record the verdicts in a table, each “no” with its witness. When to use it. A relation is given by a formula, a list or a picture, and the question is which properties it has: whether it is an equivalence relation, or a partial order. The usual failure. “Proving” a property from one example; refuting antisymmetry with a pair related one way only, which refutes symmetry instead; a witness for “not reflexive” that is not in \(X\) .

title: Proposition 4.1.1 (Divisibility on the Natural Numbers)
content: The relation \(\mid\) is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive on \(\nN\) . On \(\nZ\) it is reflexive and transitive, and not antisymmetric.

title: Definition 4.2.5 (Congruence Modulo n)
content: Let \(n \in \nZ_{>0}\) . Integers \(a\) and \(b\) are congruent modulo \(n\) , written \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\) , if \(n \mid a - b\) , that is, if \(a - b = kn\) for some \(k \in \nZ\) .

title: Definition 4.2.2 (Equivalence Class)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(X\) , and let \(a \in X\) . The equivalence class of \(a\) is \[ [a] \coloneqq \{ x \in X : x \sim a \} . \] When the relation must be named, we write \([a]_\sim\) . Any element of a class is called a representative of it.

title: Definition 4.2.1 (Equivalence Relation)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. An equivalence relation on \(X\) is a relation \(\sim\) on \(X\) ( @def-relation ) that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive on \(X\) ( @def-relation-properties ): for every \(x \in X\) , \(x \sim x\) ; for all \(x, y \in X\) , if \(x \sim y\) , then \(y \sim x\) ; for all \(x, y, z \in X\) , if \(x \sim y\) and \(y \sim z\) , then \(x \sim z\) . When \(x \sim y\) , we say that \(x\) is equivalent to \(y\) (under \(\sim\) ).

title: Definition 4.2.3 (Partition)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. A partition of \(X\) is a set \(\sP\) of subsets of \(X\) , called blocks , such that every block is non-empty : \(P \ne \emptyset\) for every \(P \in \sP\) ; the blocks are pairwise disjoint : for all \(P, Q \in \sP\) , if \(P \ne Q\) , then \(P \cap Q = \emptyset\) ; the blocks cover \(X\) : \(\bigcup \sP = X\) .

title: Definition 4.2.4 (Quotient Set)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(X\) . The quotient set of \(X\) by \(\sim\) is the set of all equivalence classes, \[ X/{\sim} \coloneqq \{ C \in \powerset{X} : C = [a] \text{ for some } a \in X \} . \] The quotient map is \(q \colon X \to X/{\sim}\) , \(q(a) \coloneqq [a]\) .

title: Proposition 4.2.5 (Congruence Respects Sums and Products)
content:
Let \(n \in 
Z_{>0}\) and \(a, a', b, b' \in 
Z\) . If \(a \equiv a' \pmod{n}\) and \(b \equiv b' \pmod{n}\) , then \[ a + b \equiv a' + b' \pmod{n} \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad ab \equiv a'b' \pmod{n} . \] Hence the operations \([a] + [b] \coloneqq [a + b]\) and \([a][b] \coloneqq [ab]\) on \(
Z/n\) are well defined .

title: Proposition 4.2.3 (Congruence Is an Equivalence Relation)
content: For every \(n \in \nZ_{>0}\) , congruence modulo \(n\) is an equivalence relation on \(\nZ\) .

title: Proposition 4.2.4 (The Integers Modulo n)
content:
Let \(n \in 
Z_{>0}\) . For every \(a \in 
Z\) there is exactly one \(r \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}\) with \([a] = [r]\) in \(
Z/n\) , namely the remainder of \(a\) on division by \(n\) . Hence \[ 
Z/n = \{ [0], [1], \dots, [n - 1] \} , \] and the \(n\) classes listed are pairwise different.

title: Theorem 4.2.1 (Equivalence Classes Partition the Set)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(X\) . For every \(a \in X\) , \(a \in [a]\) ; in particular every class is non-empty. For all \(a, b \in X\) , \([a] = [b]\) if and only if \(a \sim b\) . For all \(a, b \in X\) , if \([a] \cap [b] \ne \emptyset\) , then \([a] = [b]\) . The quotient set \(X/{\sim}\) is a partition of \(X\) .

title: Theorem 4.2.2 (Partitions and Equivalence Relations Correspond)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. Let \(\sP\) be a partition of \(X\) . For \(x, y \in X\) , let \(x \sim_{\sP} y\) mean that there is a block \(P \in \sP\) with \(x \in P\) and \(y \in P\) . Then \(\sim_{\sP}\) is an equivalence relation on \(X\) , and its classes are the blocks: \(X/{\sim_{\sP}} = \sP\) . Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on \(X\) . Then \(\sim_{X/{\sim}}\) , the relation of (a) for the partition \(X/{\sim}\) , is \(\sim\) itself. Hence every partition of \(X\) is the quotient set of exactly one equivalence relation on \(X\) , namely \(\sim_{\sP}\) .

title: Definition 4.3.3 (Greatest and Least Elements)
page: 4.3 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: An element \(g\) is a greatest element of \(A\) if \(g \in A\) and \(a \preceq g\) for every \(a \in A\) . An element \(l\) is a least element of \(A\) if \(l \in A\) and \(l \preceq a\) for every \(a \in A\) .

title: Definition 4.3.4 (Maximal and Minimal Elements)
page: 4.3 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: An element \(m\) is a maximal element of \(A\) if \(m \in A\) and there is no \(a \in A\) with \(m \prec a\) . An element \(m\) is a minimal element of \(A\) if \(m \in A\) and there is no \(a \in A\) with \(a \prec m\) .

title: Definition 4.3.2 (Upper and Lower Bounds)
page: 4.3 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: An element \(u \in X\) is an upper bound of \(A\) if \(a \preceq u\) for every \(a \in A\) , and a lower bound of \(A\) if \(u \preceq a\) for every \(a \in A\) . The set \(A\) is bounded above if it has an upper bound in \(X\) , bounded below if it has a lower bound in \(X\) , and bounded if both.

title: Definition 4.3.5 (Supremum and Infimum)
page: 4.3 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: Let \((X, \preceq)\) be a partially ordered set and \(A \subseteq X\) . An element \(s \in X\) is a least upper bound , or supremum , of \(A\) in \(X\) if \(s\) is an upper bound of \(A\) , and \(s \preceq u\) for every upper bound \(u\) of \(A\) . An element \(i \in X\) is a greatest lower bound , or infimum , of \(A\) in \(X\) if \(i\) is a lower bound of \(A\) and \(u \preceq i\) for every lower bound \(u\) of \(A\) .

title: Definition 4.3.1 (Partial Order)
page: 4.3 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: Let \(X\) be a set. A partial order on \(X\) is a relation \(\preceq\) on \(X\) that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive on \(X\) ( @def-relation-properties ): for every \(x \in X\) , \(x \preceq x\) ; for all \(x, y \in X\) , if \(x \preceq y\) and \(y \preceq x\) , then \(x = y\) ; for all \(x, y, z \in X\) , if \(x \preceq y\) and \(y \preceq z\) , then \(x \preceq z\) . The pair \((X, \preceq)\) is a partially ordered set . Elements \(x, y \in X\) are comparable if \(x \preceq y\) or \(y \preceq x\) . The partial order is total if every two elements of \(X\) are comparable. The strict part of \(\preceq\) is the relation \(\prec\) on \(X\) given by \[ x \prec y \iff x \preceq y \ \text{ and } \ x \ne y . \] We also write \(y \succeq x\) for \(x \preceq y\) .

title: Definition 4.3.6 (Well-Ordered Set)
page: 4.3 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: A partially ordered set \((X, \preceq)\) is well-ordered , and \(\preceq\) is a well-order on \(X\) , if \(\preceq\) is total and every non-empty subset of \(X\) has a least element.

title: Proposition 4.3.2 (Greatest and Maximal Elements)
page: 4.3 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: Let \((X, \preceq)\) be a partially ordered set and \(A \subseteq X\) . A greatest element of \(A\) is a maximal element of \(A\) . If \(\preceq\) is total, then a maximal element of \(A\) is a greatest element of \(A\) . The same holds for least and minimal elements.

title: Proposition 4.3.1 (Greatest and Least Elements Are Unique)
page: 4.3 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: A subset \(A\) of a partially ordered set has at most one greatest element and at most one least element.

title: Definition 5.1.2 (Indicator Function)
content: Let \(X\) be a set and \(A \subseteq X\) . The indicator function of \(A\) is \(\ind_A \colon X \to \{0, 1\}\) , \[ \ind_A(x) \coloneqq \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x \in A, \\ 0 & \text{if } x \in X \setminus A . \end{cases} \]

title: Definition 5.1.1 (Restriction, Extension, Inclusion)
content: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets and \(A \subseteq X\) . For \(f \colon X \to Y\) , the restriction of \(f\) to \(A\) is the function \(f|_A \colon A \to Y\) , \(f|_A(a) \coloneqq f(a)\) , as in Section 1.5. For \(g \colon A \to Y\) , an extension of \(g\) to \(X\) is a function \(f \colon X \to Y\) with \(f|_A = g\) . The inclusion map of \(A\) into \(X\) is \(\iota_A \colon A \to X\) , \(\iota_A(a) \coloneqq a\) .
