title: Proposition 5.1.3 (Set Operations as Arithmetic of Indicators)
content: Let \(A, B \subseteq X\) . For every \(x \in X\) , write \(u \coloneqq \ind_A(x)\) and \(v \coloneqq \ind_B(x)\) . Then: \(\ind_{A \cap B}(x) = uv\) ; \(\ind_{X \setminus A}(x) = 1 - u\) ; \(\ind_{A \cup B}(x) = u + v - uv\) ; \(\ind_{A \triangle B}(x) = u + v - 2uv\) ; \(A \subseteq B\) if and only if \(\ind_A(x) \le \ind_B(x)\) for every \(x \in X\) .

title: Proposition 5.1.1 (Restrictions)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function and \(B \subseteq A \subseteq X\) . \(f|_A = f \circ \iota_A\) . \((f|_A)|_B = f|_B\) . For every function \(g \colon Y \to Z\) , \((g \circ f)|_A = g \circ (f|_A)\) . If \(f\) is injective, then so is \(f|_A\) . \(f|_A(B) = f(B)\) .

title: Theorem 5.1.2 (Gluing Functions)
content: Let \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of subsets of a set \(X\) with \(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = X\) , and let \((f_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of functions \(f_i \colon A_i \to Y\) . Suppose the \(f_i\) agree on overlaps : \[ f_i(x) = f_j(x) \quad \text{for all } i, j \in I \text{ and every } x \in A_i \cap A_j . \] Then there is exactly one function \(f \colon X \to Y\) with \(f|_{A_i} = f_i\) for every \(i \in I\) .

title: Proposition 5.2.1 (The Fibers of a Function)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. The fibers \(f^{-1}(\{y\})\) over the points \(y \in f(X)\) are exactly the classes of \(\sim_f\) , and they form a partition of \(X\) . The rule \(y \mapsto f^{-1}(\{y\})\) is a bijection \(f(X) \to X/{\sim_f}\) . Hence \(\card{f(X)} = \card{X/{\sim_f}}\) .

title: Theorem 5.2.2 (Canonical Factorization)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function, let \(q \colon X \to X/{\sim_f}\) be the quotient map, and let \(\iota \colon f(X) \to Y\) be the inclusion map. There is exactly one function \(\bar f \colon X/{\sim_f} \to f(X)\) with \[ f = \iota \circ \bar f \circ q . \] It is given by \(\bar f([x]) = f(x)\) , and it is a bijection .

title: Theorem 5.2.3 (Functions out of a Quotient)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(X\) , let \(q \colon X \to X/{\sim}\) be its quotient map, and let \(g \colon X \to Z\) be a function. There is a function \(\bar g \colon X/{\sim} \to Z\) with \(\bar g \circ q = g\) if and only if \(g\) is constant on classes : for all \(x, x' \in X\) , if \(x \sim x'\) , then \(g(x) = g(x')\) . In that case \(\bar g\) is unique, and \(\bar g([x]) = g(x)\) . Suppose \(g\) is constant on classes. Then \(\bar g\) is injective if and only if , for all \(x, x' \in X\) , \(g(x) = g(x')\) implies \(x \sim x'\) . Suppose \(g\) is constant on classes. Then \(\bar g\) is surjective if and only if \(g\) is surjective.

title: Definition 5.3.1 (Binary Operation)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. A binary operation on \(X\) , or an operation on \(X\) , is a function \[ \ast \colon X \times X \to X . \] Its value at \((x, y)\) is written \(x \ast y\) rather than \(\ast(x, y)\) . A subset \(A \subseteq X\) is closed under \(\ast\) if \(a \ast b \in A\) for all \(a, b \in A\) .

title: Definition 5.3.2 (Associative, Commutative, Identity, Inverse)
content: Let \(\ast\) be an operation on a set \(X\) . \(\ast\) is associative if \((x \ast y) \ast z = x \ast (y \ast z)\) for all \(x, y, z \in X\) . \(\ast\) is commutative if \(x \ast y = y \ast x\) for all \(x, y \in X\) . An element \(e \in X\) is a left identity of \(\ast\) if \(e \ast x = x\) for every \(x \in X\) ; a right identity if \(x \ast e = x\) for every \(x \in X\) ; and an identity if it is both. Suppose \(\ast\) has an identity \(e\) , and let \(x \in X\) . An element \(y \in X\) is an inverse of \(x\) if \(x \ast y = e\) and \(y \ast x = e\) . The element \(x\) is invertible if it has an inverse.

title: Example (Method: compute one expression in two ways)
content: Template. To prove \(a = b\) when \(a\) and \(b\) are known only through equations: (1) find one expression \(m\) that the equations about \(a\) reduce to \(a\) , and the equations about \(b\) reduce to \(b\) ; (2) write the chain \(a = \dots = m = \dots = b\) , citing a hypothesis at each “ \(=\) ”. When to use it. Uniqueness of identities and of inverses, cancellation, and any goal equating two objects given by equations. The usual failure. Assuming \(a = b\) somewhere in the chain (entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue ); using associativity or commutativity that was not given; a bracket moved silently.

title: Example (A right identity that is not an identity)
content: Decide whether subtraction on \(\nZ\) is associative, and find its left and right identities.

title: Example (Without associativity, two inverses)
content: Let \(X = \{e, a, b\}\) with three different elements, and define \(\ast\) by the table below: the entry in row \(u\) and column \(v\) is \(u \ast v\) . \(\ast\) \(e\) \(a\) \(b\) \(e\) \(e\) \(a\) \(b\) \(a\) \(a\) \(e\) \(e\) \(b\) \(b\) \(e\) \(e\) Show that \(\ast\) is a commutative operation with identity \(e\) , that \(a\) has two different inverses, and that \(\ast\) is not associative.

title: Exercise (A1)
content:
Which of the following are operations: subtraction on \(
N\) ; subtraction on \(
Z\) ; \((x, y) \mapsto x/y\) on \(
R \setminus \{0\}\) ; \((x, y) \mapsto x/y\) on \(

Find all left identities and all right identities of \(\ast\) . State the template of the method of computing one expression in two ways, and say which expression it computes in the proof of @prp-operation-inverse-unique .

title: Exercise (B1: Deciding properties)
content: On \(\nR\) , let \(x \ast y \coloneqq x + y - xy\) . Determine whether \(\ast\) is associative and whether it is commutative, find its identity, and find which elements are invertible, with their inverses. Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B2: Every square is the identity)
content: Let \(\ast\) be an associative operation on a set \(X\) with identity \(e\) , such that \(x \ast x = e\) for every \(x \in X\) . Prove that \(\ast\) is commutative. Check the hypothesis for \(\triangle\) on \(\powerset{X}\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Two kinds of inverse)
content: In \(\nR^{\nR}\) , find, if they exist, the inverses of \(f(x) = x^3 + 1\) under composition and under pointwise \(+\) , and the inverses of \(g(x) = x^2\) under composition and under pointwise \(\cdot\) . Justify each answer.

title: Exercise (B4: Prove or disprove)
content: Prove or disprove each statement. Throughout, \(\ast\) is an operation on a set \(X\) . Every left identity of \(\ast\) equals every right identity of \(\ast\) . \(\ast\) has at most one left identity. If \(\ast\) is associative with identity, \(x\) is invertible and \(x \ast y = x \ast z\) , then \(y = z\) . If \(\ast\) is associative with identity \(e\) and \(x \ast y = e\) , then \(y \ast x = e\) . A commutative operation with an identity is associative.

title: Exercise (C1: Four factors)
content: Let \(\ast\) be an associative operation on a set \(X\) , and let \(a, b, c, d \in X\) . Writing \(uv\) for \(u \ast v\) , show that the five bracketings \[ ((ab)c)d, \quad (a(bc))d, \quad (ab)(cd), \quad a((bc)d), \quad a(b(cd)) \] are all equal.

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: Let \(\ast\) be an operation on a set \(X\) with identity \(e\) . A student argues: Let \(y\) and \(z\) be inverses of \(x\) . (2) Then \(x \ast y = e\) and \(x \ast z = e\) , so \(x \ast y = x \ast z\) . (3) Cancelling \(x\) on the left, \(y = z\) . (4) Hence an element has at most one inverse. Which line fails, and which hypothesis does it hide? Show that without that hypothesis the step of the failing line is false.

title: Exercise (C3: Transport by a bijection)
content: Let \(\varphi \colon X \to Y\) be a bijection, and let \(\ast\) be an operation on \(Y\) . For \(x, x' \in X\) , define \[ x \star x' \coloneqq \varphi^{-1}\bigl(\varphi(x) \ast \varphi(x')\bigr) . \] Show that \(\star\) is an operation on \(X\) with \(\varphi(x \star x') = \varphi(x) \ast \varphi(x')\) for all \(x, x' \in X\) . Show that \(\star\) is associative if and only if \(\ast\) is. Compute \(\star\) for \(X = Y = \nR\) , \(\varphi(x) = 1 - x\) and \(\ast = \cdot\) .

title: Proposition 5.3.5 (Composition on X^X)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. Composition \((g, f) \mapsto g \circ f\) is an associative operation on \(X^X\) with identity \(\id_X\) . An element \(f \in X^X\) is invertible under \(\circ\) if and only if \(f\) is bijective, and then its inverse under \(\circ\) is the inverse function \(f^{-1}\) . If \(X\) has two different elements, then \(\circ\) is not commutative on \(X^X\) .

title: Proposition 5.3.1 (An Identity Is Unique)
content: Let \(\ast\) be an operation on a set \(X\) . If \(e\) is a left identity and \(e'\) is a right identity of \(\ast\) , then \(e = e'\) . In particular, \(\ast\) has at most one identity.

title: Proposition 5.3.3 (Inverses of Products)
content: Let \(\ast\) be an associative operation on a set \(X\) with identity \(e\) . \(e\) is invertible, and \(e^{-1} = e\) . If \(x\) is invertible, then so is \(x^{-1}\) , and \((x^{-1})^{-1} = x\) . If \(x\) and \(y\) are invertible, then so is \(x \ast y\) , and \((x \ast y)^{-1} = y^{-1} \ast x^{-1}\) .

title: Proposition 5.3.2 (Inverses Are Unique for an Associative Operation)
content: Let \(\ast\) be an associative operation on a set \(X\) with identity \(e\) , and let \(x \in X\) . If \(y \ast x = e\) and \(x \ast z = e\) , then \(y = z\) . In particular, \(x\) has at most one inverse.

title: Proposition 5.3.6 (Operations on a Quotient)
content: Let \(\ast\) be an operation on a set \(X\) , and let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on \(X\) such that, for all \(x, x', y, y' \in X\) , \[ x \sim x' \text{ and } y \sim y' \quad \Longrightarrow \quad x \ast y \sim x' \ast y' . \] Then \([x] \ast [y] \coloneqq [x \ast y]\) is a well-defined operation on \(X/{\sim}\) , and the quotient map satisfies \(q(x \ast y) = q(x) \ast q(y)\) . Moreover: if \(\ast\) is associative, or commutative, then so is the operation on \(X/{\sim}\) ; if \(e\) is an identity of \(\ast\) , then \([e]\) is an identity of the operation on \(X/{\sim}\) ; if \(y\) is an inverse of \(x\) , then \([y]\) is an inverse of \([x]\) .

title: Proposition 5.3.4 (Pointwise Operations)
content: Let \(\ast\) be an operation on a set \(Y\) , and let \(X\) be a set. For \(f, g \in Y^X\) , define \(f \ast g \colon X \to Y\) by \[ (f \ast g)(x) \coloneqq f(x) \ast g(x) \qquad (x \in X) . \] This is an operation on \(Y^X\) , the pointwise operation, and: if \(\ast\) is associative, or commutative, on \(Y\) , then so is the pointwise operation on \(Y^X\) ; if \(e\) is an identity of \(\ast\) , then the constant function \(c_e \colon X \to Y\) , \(x \mapsto e\) , is an identity of the pointwise operation; if \(\ast\) is associative with identity \(e\) , then \(f \in Y^X\) is invertible if and only if every value \(f(x)\) is invertible in \(Y\) , and then the inverse of \(f\) is \(x \mapsto f(x)^{-1}\) .

title: Corollary 5.4.6 (Some Power Is the Identity)
content: Let \(X\) be a finite set and \(\sigma \in S_X\) . For an integer \(N \ge 1\) , \(\sigma^N = \id_X\) if and only if the length of every orbit of \(\sigma\) divides \(N\) . There is such an \(N\) .

title: Definition 5.4.2 (Iterates)
content: Let \(X\) be a set and \(f \colon X \to X\) . The iterates \(f^n \colon X \to X\) , for \(n \in \nN\) , are defined by \[ f^0 \coloneqq \id_X , \qquad f^{n+1} \coloneqq f \circ f^n . \] For \(\sigma \in S_X\) and \(n \in \nN\) , we also set \(\sigma^{-n} \coloneqq (\sigma^{-1})^n\) .

title: Definition 5.4.3 (Orbit, Forward Orbit, Fixed Point)
content:
Let \(X\) be a set and \(\sigma \in S_X\) . For \(x, y \in X\) , let \(x \sim_\sigma y\) mean that \(y = \sigma^k(x)\) for some \(k \in 
Z\) . The orbit of \(x\) under \(\sigma\) is \[ O_\sigma(x) \coloneqq \{ \sigma^k(x) : k \in 
Z \} . \] For an arbitrary function \(f \colon X 	o X\) , the forward orbit of \(x\) is \(\{ f^n(x) : n \in 
N \}\) . A fixed point of \(f\) is an \(x \in X\) with \(f(x) = x\) .

title: Definition 5.4.1 (Permutation)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. A permutation of \(X\) is a bijection \(\sigma \colon X \to X\) . The set of all permutations of \(X\) is written \(S_X\) ; it is a subset of \(X^X\) , the set of all functions \(X \to X\) .

title: Definition 5.4.4 (Cycle)
content: Let \(X\) be a set, \(k \ge 2\) , and \(x_1, \dots, x_k \in X\) distinct . The cycle \((x_1\ x_2\ \cdots\ x_k)\) is the function \(X \to X\) that sends \(x_j \mapsto x_{j+1}\) for \(1 \le j < k\) , sends \(x_k \mapsto x_1\) , and sends every other point of \(X\) to itself. Two cycles are disjoint if their sets of entries are disjoint.

title: Example (Method: follow an orbit)
content: Template. (1) List the forward orbit \(x, f(x), f^2(x), \dots\) . (2) On a finite set of \(n\) elements, two of the first \(n + 1\) terms are equal ( @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets ). (3) Take the first repeat, or the least return time ( @thm-well-ordering ). (4) Carry the repeat with the map’s structure: cancel if the map is injective; push forward with \(f^{l+1} = f \circ f^l\) always. When to use it. Repeated application of one map on a finite set: shuffles, the tick of a clock, maps on \(\nZ/n\) . The usual failure. Speaking of “the first repeat” without proving that a repeat exists; canceling a map that is not injective, which forgets the tail before the cycle.

title: Example (Squaring on an eleven-hour clock)
content: Let \(s \colon \nZ/11 \to \nZ/11\) , \(s([a]) \coloneqq [a^2]\) . Show that \(s\) is well defined, follow the forward orbit of \([2]\) , and find \(m\) and \(p\) . Does \([2]\) ever come back?

title: Example (The three-pile shuffle)
content: Let \(\sigma\) be the shuffle of twelve cards in three piles of four. Show that \(\sigma\) is a permutation of \(\{0, \dots, 11\}\) , find its orbits and their lengths, and find the least \(N \ge 1\) with \(\sigma^N = \id\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: For \(\sigma = (1\ 4)(2\ 3\ 5)\) on \(\{1, \dots, 5\}\) , write the two-line tables of \(\sigma\) , \(\sigma^{-1}\) and \(\sigma^2\) . Let \(f \colon \{1, \dots, 5\} \to \{1, \dots, 5\}\) send \(1 \mapsto 2\) , \(2 \mapsto 3\) , \(3 \mapsto 4\) , \(4 \mapsto 2\) , \(5 \mapsto 5\) . Find \(m\) and \(p\) as in @prp-eventually-periodic for \(x = 1\) , with \(m\) as small as possible. How many fixed points has the three-pile shuffle of twelve cards?

title: Exercise (B1: Doubling on nine hours)
content: Let \(d \colon \nZ/9 \to \nZ/9\) , \(d([a]) \coloneqq [2a]\) . Show that \(d\) is a permutation, decompose it into disjoint cycles, and find the least \(N \ge 1\) with \(d^N = \id\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Iterates commute)
content: Let \(f, g \colon X \to X\) . Prove that \(f^{n+1} = f^n \circ f\) for every \(n \in \nN\) , and that if \(f \circ g = g \circ f\) , then \(f^n \circ g = g \circ f^n\) for every \(n \in \nN\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Orbits are invariant)
content: Let \(\sigma \in S_X\) and \(x \in X\) . Prove that \(\sigma(O_\sigma(x)) = O_\sigma(x)\) .

title: Exercise (B4: Prove or disprove)
content: Prove or disprove each statement. If \(X\) is finite and \(f \colon X \to X\) is injective, then every \(x \in X\) has \(f^k(x) = x\) for some \(k \ge 1\) . If \(f \colon X \to X\) and \(f^N = \id_X\) for some \(N \ge 1\) , then \(f\) is a permutation. Every function from a finite non-empty set to itself has a fixed point. Every orbit of a permutation is finite. If \(X\) is finite and every orbit of \(\sigma \in S_X\) has length \(1\) or \(2\) , then \(\sigma \circ \sigma = \id_X\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: fifteen cards)
content: Fifteen cards lie at positions \(0, \dots, 14\) . Cut them into three piles of five and deal them back in turn, as in the hook, so that \[ \sigma(i) = \begin{cases} 3i & \text{if } 0 \le i \le 4, \\ 3i - 14 & \text{if } 5 \le i \le 9, \\ 3i - 28 & \text{if } 10 \le i \le 14 . \end{cases} \] Show that \(\sigma\) is a permutation, decompose it into disjoint cycles, and find the least \(N \ge 1\) with \(\sigma^N = \id\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: Here is a claim and a proof. Claim. For every function \(f\) from a finite set \(X\) to itself and every \(x \in X\) , there is \(k \ge 1\) with \(f^k(x) = x\) . Proof. By pigeonhole, \(f^i(x) = f^j(x)\) for some \(i < j\) . Apply \(f^{-i}\) to both sides: \(x = f^{j-i}(x)\) . Take \(k = j - i\) . Is the claim true? Find the line that fails, say why, and state what the argument does prove.

title: Exercise (C3: Each point, its own clock)
content: Let \(X\) be a finite set and \(\sigma \in S_X\) . Show that the length of \(O_\sigma(x)\) is the same for all points \(x\) of one orbit. Show also that if \(\sigma\) has exactly two orbits, then the number of elements of \(X\) is the sum of their lengths.

content: Let \(\varphi \colon X \to Y\) be a bijection. Show that \(\sigma \mapsto \varphi \circ \sigma \circ \varphi^{-1}\) is a bijection from \(S_X\) to \(S_Y\) , and that \(x\) is a fixed point of \(\sigma\) if and only if \(\varphi(x)\) is a fixed point of \(\varphi \circ \sigma \circ \varphi^{-1}\) .

Let \(f \colon

title: Exercise (R4)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) , \(A \subseteq X\) and \(B \subseteq Y\) . Show that \((f|_A)^{-1}(B) = A \cap f^{-1}(B)\) .

title: Proposition 5.4.7 (Forward Orbits of a Self-Map of a Finite Set)
content: Let \(X\) be a set with \(n\) elements, \(f \colon X \to X\) , and \(x \in X\) . There are integers \(m \ge 0\) and \(p \ge 1\) with \(m + p \le n\) such that \[ f^{l + p}(x) = f^l(x) \quad \text{for every integer } l \ge m . \]

title: Proposition 5.4.2 (Laws of Iterates)
content:
Let \(X\) be a set, \(f \colon X 	o X\) , and \(m, n \in 
N\) . \(f^{m+n} = f^m \circ f^n\) . \((f^m)^n = f^{mn}\) . If \(\sigma \in S_X\) , then \(\sigma^k \in S_X\) for every \(k \in 
Z\) ; \(\sigma^n \circ \sigma^{-n} = \id_X = \sigma^{-n} \circ \sigma^n\) ; and \(\sigma^{k + l} = \sigma^k \circ \sigma^l\) for all \(k, l \in 
Z\) .

title: Proposition 5.4.4 (Following an Orbit)
content: Let \(X\) be a finite set, \(\sigma \in S_X\) , and \(x \in X\) . Then there is a least integer \(k \ge 1\) with \(\sigma^k(x) = x\) . For this \(k\) : the points \(x, \sigma(x), \dots, \sigma^{k-1}(x)\) are distinct; \(O_\sigma(x) = \{ x, \sigma(x), \dots, \sigma^{k-1}(x) \}\) , so \(O_\sigma(x)\) has exactly \(k\) elements; for every \(m \in \nZ\) , \(\sigma^m(x) = x\) if and only if \(k \mid m\) . The number \(k\) is the length of the orbit \(O_\sigma(x)\) .

title: Proposition 5.4.1 (Permutations under Composition)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. If \(\sigma, \tau \in S_X\) , then \(\sigma \circ \tau \in S_X\) . \(\id_X \in S_X\) . If \(\sigma \in S_X\) , then \(\sigma^{-1} \in S_X\) , and \(\sigma \circ \sigma^{-1} = \id_X = \sigma^{-1} \circ \sigma\) . Hence \(S_X\) is closed under \(\circ\) , and \(\circ\) is an associative operation on \(S_X\) with identity \(\id_X\) , in which every element \(\sigma\) is invertible, with inverse \(\sigma^{-1}\) .

title: Theorem 5.4.3 (The Orbits of a Permutation Partition the Set)
content: Let \(X\) be a set and \(\sigma \in S_X\) . Then \(\sim_\sigma\) is an equivalence relation on \(X\) , and the class of each \(x \in X\) is \(O_\sigma(x)\) . Hence the orbits of \(\sigma\) form a partition of \(X\) . Moreover, \(x\) is a fixed point of \(\sigma\) if and only if \(O_\sigma(x) = \{x\}\) .

title: Theorem 5.4.5 (Cycle Decomposition)
content: Let \(X\) be a finite set and \(\sigma \in S_X\) . Let \(O_1, \dots, O_r\) be the distinct orbits of \(\sigma\) with at least two elements, choose \(x_i \in O_i\) , let \(k_i\) be the number of elements of \(O_i\) (so \(\card{O_i} = k_i\) ), and let \[ \gamma_i \coloneqq \bigl( x_i\ \ \sigma(x_i)\ \ \cdots\ \ \sigma^{k_i - 1}(x_i) \bigr) . \] Then \(\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_r\) are pairwise disjoint cycles, \(\gamma_i \circ \gamma_j = \gamma_j \circ \gamma_i\) for all \(i, j\) , and \[ \sigma = \gamma_1 \circ \gamma_2 \circ \cdots \circ \gamma_r , \] bracketed from the left; if \(r = 0\) , this says \(\sigma = \id_X\) .

title: Definition 6.1.1 (Chain)
content: Let \((X, \preceq)\) be a partially ordered set. A subset \(C \subseteq X\) is a chain if any two elements of \(C\) are comparable: for all \(x, y \in C\) , \(x \preceq y\) or \(y \preceq x\) .

title: Example (Method: the maximality template)
content: Template. To show that a complete object exists: (1) partial objects: let \(P\) be the set of partial objects, of which the complete ones are the finished case, ordered by \(\subseteq\) (extension); check \(P \ne \emptyset\) , usually with the empty or the given starting object. (2) chains: for a non-empty chain \(\sC \subseteq P\) , show \(\bigcup \sC \in P\) ; each defining condition mentions finitely many elements, which lie in one member ( @lem-chain-union ). (3) Zorn: \(P\) has a maximal element \(M\) ( @thm-zorn ). (4) complete: suppose \(M\) is not complete; use the missing piece to build a strictly larger partial object, a contradiction. When to use it. The object can be built piece by piece, each condition on it checks finitely many pieces at a time, and the pieces cannot be listed. The usual failure. The union of a chain is not a partial object, because a condition mentions infinitely many pieces (“finite”, “countable”); step (4) builds an object that is not strictly larger, or not in \(P\) ; and treating \(M\) as the greatest or the only complete object.

title: Example (A set of representatives)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(X\) . Show that there is a set \(S \subseteq X\) that meets every equivalence class in exactly one element.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: These questions are about the proof of @thm-choice-from-zorn . Where is “ \(A_i \ne \emptyset\) ” used, and which step fails without it? Why does the chain step need @lem-chain-union only for \(n = 2\) ? Run the proof on \(I = \{1, 2\}\) , \(A_1 = \{0\}\) , \(A_2 = \{5, 6\}\) : list \(P\) , name its maximal elements, and decide whether \(P\) has a greatest element. Which of the two hypotheses of @thm-zorn does the empty partially ordered set satisfy?

title: Exercise (B1: Maximal chains)
content: Let \((X, \preceq)\) be a partially ordered set and \(C_0 \subseteq X\) a chain. Prove that there is a chain \(C \supseteq C_0\) that is maximal : no chain contains \(C\) properly.

title: Exercise (B2: Name the move, then complete it)
content: Here is the frame of a proof that for every set \(\sF\) of non-empty sets there is a subfamily \(\sD \subseteq \sF\) of pairwise disjoint sets such that every member of \(\sF\) meets some member of \(\sD\) . Let \(P\) be the set of subfamilies \(\sE \subseteq \sF\) whose members are pairwise disjoint ( \(E \cap E' = \emptyset\) for \(E \ne E'\) in \(\sE\) ), ordered by \(\subseteq\) . Then \(\emptyset \in P\) . For a non-empty chain of such subfamilies, two members \(E \ne E'\) of its union lie in one subfamily of the chain, so \(E \cap E' = \emptyset\) ; the union lies in \(P\) and is an upper bound. By Zorn’s lemma, \(P\) has a maximal element \(\sD\) . \(\vdots\) … Hence every member of \(\sF\) meets some member of \(\sD\) . Name the move, then complete it.

title: Exercise (B3: A small poset of partial injections)
content: Let \(A = \{1, 2\}\) and \(B = \{b\}\) . List the relations \(G \subseteq A \times B\) in which each element of \(A\) and each element of \(B\) occurs in at most one pair, ordered by \(\subseteq\) . Name the maximal elements. For each, is every element of \(A\) paired? Every element of \(B\) ?

title: Exercise (B4: Prove or disprove)
content: Prove each true statement and refute each false one. If every chain of a non-empty partially ordered set \(P\) has an upper bound in \(P\) , then \(P\) has a greatest element. Every non-empty finite partially ordered set has a maximal element. The set of subsets of \(\nN\) that contain no two consecutive numbers, ordered by \(\subseteq\) , has a greatest element. If \(P\) is a non-empty partially ordered set in which every non-empty chain has an upper bound, then every \(p \in P\) lies below some maximal element of \(P\) . The set of countable subsets of \(\nR\) , ordered by \(\subseteq\) , has a maximal element. Hint for (d): apply Zorn’s lemma to the elements above \(p\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Find the error)
content: Claim: every chain \(C_0\) of a partially ordered set \(X\) lies in a maximal chain. “Proof”: Let \(P\) be the set of chains containing \(C_0\) , ordered by \(\subseteq\) ; then \(C_0 \in P\) . Let \(\sK\) be a non-empty chain in \(P\) . Every \(K \in \sK\) is a subset of \(\bigcup \sK\) , so \(\bigcup \sK\) is an upper bound of \(\sK\) . By Zorn’s lemma, \(P\) has a maximal element \(C\) . A chain containing \(C\) contains \(C_0\) , so it lies in \(P\) ; hence \(C\) is a maximal chain. Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it?

title: Exercise (C2: Exit check: when no choice is needed)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on \(\nN\) . Without Zorn’s lemma or the axiom of choice, give a set \(S\) meeting every class exactly once, and prove that it does. Do the same for an equivalence relation on a set \(X\) with an injection \(j \colon X \to \nN\) . Which ingredient of @exm-zorn-representatives does your answer to (a) make unnecessary, and why?

title: Lemma 6.1.1 (Finitely Many Members of a Chain)
content: Let \(C\) be a chain in a partially ordered set \((X, \preceq)\) , let \(n \ge 1\) and \(x_1, \dots, x_n \in C\) . Then some \(x_k\) satisfies \(x_j \preceq x_k\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n\) . Let \(\sS\) be a set of sets, partially ordered by \(\subseteq\) , and \(\sC \subseteq \sS\) a chain. Then \(C \subseteq \bigcup \sC\) for every \(C \in \sC\) ; and if \(n \ge 1\) and \(z_1, \dots, z_n \in \bigcup \sC\) , then some single \(C \in \sC\) contains all of \(z_1, \dots, z_n\) .

title: Theorem 6.1.3 (Zorn’s Lemma Gives Choice)
content: Assume @thm-zorn . Let \(I\) be a set and \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) a family of non-empty sets. Then there is a function \(c \colon I \to \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\) with \(c(i) \in A_i\) for every \(i \in I\) .

title: Theorem 6.1.2 (Zorn’s Lemma)
content: Let \((P, \preceq)\) be a non-empty partially ordered set in which every non-empty chain has an upper bound in \(P\) . Then \(P\) has a maximal element.

title: Corollary 6.2.2 (Trichotomy for Sizes)
content: For all sets \(A\) and \(B\) , exactly one of \(\card{A} < \card{B}\) , \(\card{A} = \card{B}\) , \(\card{B} < \card{A}\) holds.

content:
On \(

e 0\) and \(x \le y\) . Show that \(\sqsubseteq\) is a total order on \(

title: Exercise (A1)
content: These questions are about the proof of @thm-cardinal-comparability . Where does the proof use (M1), and where (M2)? Why can “some \(a \in A\) is unpaired” and “some \(b \in B\) is unpaired” not both hold for a maximal \(M\) ? If \(A = \emptyset\) , what is \(M\) , and which case occurs? In two sentences, give the proof’s idea.

title: Exercise (B1: Name the move, then complete it)
content: Let \(R\) be a relation from \(A\) to \(B\) whose domain is \(A\) ( @def-relation ). Prove that there is a function \(f \colon A \to B\) whose graph is contained in \(R\) . Below, the proof is started; the second half is blank. Name the move, then complete it. Let \(P\) be the set of \(G \subseteq R\) such that each \(a \in A\) occurs in at most one pair of \(G\) , ordered by \(\subseteq\) . Then \(\emptyset \in P\) . \(\underline{\hspace{8em}}\) Hence the graph of \(f\) is contained in \(R\) .

title: Exercise (B2: A total order on the subsets of a three-element set)
content: Write the eight subsets of \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) in a list such that \(A \subsetneq B\) always puts \(A\) before \(B\) , and prove that it does. How many total orders on \(\powerset{\{1, 2\}}\) contain \(\subseteq\) ?

title: Exercise (B3: A total order on the plane)
content: On \(\nR^2\) , let \((x_1, x_2) \le_p (y_1, y_2)\) mean \(x_1 \le y_1\) and \(x_2 \le y_2\) ; and let \((x_1, x_2) \le_l (y_1, y_2)\) mean \(x_1 < y_1\) , or \(x_1 = y_1\) and \(x_2 \le y_2\) . Show that \(\le_p\) is a partial order and not total. Show that \(\le_l\) is a total order containing \(\le_p\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: an order is the intersection of its total extensions)
content: Let \(\preceq\) be a partial order on a set \(X\) , and let \(\sT\) be the set of total orders on \(X\) that contain \(\preceq\) . Prove that \({\preceq} = \bigcap \sT\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: Claim: any two sets are comparable. “Proof”: If \(A\) or \(B\) is empty, the empty function is an injection. Otherwise choose \(a_0 \in A\) and \(b_0 \in B\) and pair them. Choose \(a_1 \in A \setminus \{a_0\}\) and \(b_1 \in B \setminus \{b_0\}\) , and so on. When one set runs out, the pairs so far are an injection from it into the other. Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it?

title: Exercise (R1: Surjections one way or the other)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be non-empty sets. Prove that there is a surjection \(A \to B\) or a surjection \(B \to A\) .

title: Exercise (R2: Maximal chains give Zorn’s lemma)
content: Let \(C\) be a maximal chain of a partially ordered set \((X, \preceq)\) : a chain contained properly in no chain. Let \(u\) be an upper bound of \(C\) in \(X\) . Show that \(u \in C\) , that \(u\) is the greatest element of \(C\) , and that \(u\) is a maximal element of \(X\) . Deduce @thm-zorn from the statement that every chain lies in a maximal chain.

title: Exercise (R3: The basis theorem, read as a template)
content: This item is optional and goes with the optional subsection. A set of vectors is linearly independent when no finite non-trivial combination of its vectors is \(0\) . Which of the template’s four steps uses that independence is tested on finitely many vectors at a time? Why would the template fail for the property “ \(S\) is a finite independent set”? A maximal element of a partial order need not be greatest. What does this say about bases?

title: Lemma 6.2.3 (Adding One Comparison)
content: Let \(\preceq\) be a partial order on a set \(X\) , and let \(a, b \in X\) be incomparable. Let \[ R \coloneqq {\preceq} \cup \{ (x, y) \in X \times X : x \preceq a \text{ and } b \preceq y \} . \] Then \(R\) is a partial order on \(X\) , \({\preceq} \subseteq R\) , and \((a, b) \in R \setminus {\preceq}\) .

title: Theorem 6.2.1 (Any Two Sets Are Comparable)
content: For all sets \(A\) and \(B\) , \(\card{A} \le \card{B}\) or \(\card{B} \le \card{A}\) .

title: Theorem 6.2.4 (Every Partial Order Extends to a Total Order)
content: Let \(\preceq\) be a partial order on a set \(X\) . Then there is a total order \(T\) on \(X\) with \({\preceq} \subseteq T\) .
